AGENCY:
National Institutes of Health, HHS.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
The National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) of the National Institutes of Health has modified its organizational structure.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Part N, National Institutes of Health (NIH), of the Statement of Organization, Functions, and Delegations of Authority for the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) is amended as set forth below to reflect the reorganization of the National Institute of Health, National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID), by retitling and updating the functional statement (1) the Office of the Chief of Staff for the Immediate Office of the Director to the Office of the Clinical Director within NIAID, (2) establishing the Intramural Clinical Management and Operations Branch, and the Office of Clinical Research Policy and Regulatory Operations within the Office of the Clinical Director, (3) establishing the Office of Biostatistics Research within NIAID, the Biostatistics Research Branch, and the Clinical Trials Research and Statistics Branch within the Office of Biostatistics Research, establishing the Laboratory of Viral Zoonoses and IRF-Frederick Comparative Medicine
(
printed page 73763)
Branch within the Division of Intramural Research of NIAID, (4) Abolishing all of the Division of Clinical Research within NIAID.
Section N,
Organization and Functions,
is amended as follows:
(1) In the
National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NM, formerly HNM)
retitle the following:
Office of the Chief of Staff for the Immediate Office of the Director (NM1J, formerly HNM1J)
to
Office of the Clinical Director (NM1J, formerly HNM1J).
(1) Develops, implements, and evaluates policies and practices related to the conduct of human subjects research within NIAID; (2) Advises the Director, NIAID, on the portfolio of clinical research conducted and sponsored by NIAID and reviews research protocols for relevance to the mission of the Institute, priority to meet the needs of the public health of the nation, ethics in human use, and appropriateness of scientific design; (3) Oversees the OCD branches; (4) Provides oversight of clinical research and all related clinical operations of intramural laboratories conducting clinical research programs; (5) Manages several clinical research projects involving national programs of clinical research in areas of the highest public health priorities; (6) Oversees Clinical Research Oversight Management (CROM) for intramural clinical research operations in NIAID including logistical and technical support for the NIAID Data and Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB); (7) Maintains regulatory surveillance over intramural clinical trials and protocols to ensure compliance with FDA regulations to establish and monitor regulatory policies for clinical trials and to monitor quality assurance standards and standard operating procedures regarding regulatory matters; (8) Provides expert policy analysis with regard to the management, coordination, and integration of all OCD programs and predicts and responds to the changing needs of a program for on-site and off-site domestic and international clinical research in developing countries and collaborative efforts with industry and international foundations; (9) Oversees design and conduct of studies in collaboration and consultation with NIAID intramural and extramural programs including data management and study coordination, analyses, and reporting of clinical, population and laboratory investigations; and (10) Supervises medical staff appointments, fellowship programs, and other clinical training programs.
(2) In the
Office of the Clinical Director (NM1J, formerly HNM1J)
establish the following:
Intramural Clinical Management and Operations Branch (NM1J2, formerly HNM1J2).
(1) Provides oversight of clinical research and all related clinical operations for intramural laboratories conducting clinical research; (2) Provides oversight of: (a) inpatient units and outpatient clinics in concert with the Clinical Center; (b) clinical protocol review and approval including assurance of scientific quality; (c) the quality of care delivered to NIAID patients and the quality of professional performance of NIAID health care providers for the intramural patient population; (d) continuing medical education; and (e) graduate physician training in allergy, immunology, and infectious diseases.
Office of Clinical Research Policy and Regulatory Operations (NM1J3, formerly HNM1J3).
(1) Provides support and logistical services for intramural clinical research operations in NIAID to include the provision of a protocol navigator/protocol development program; (2) Coordinates the support and logistical services for NIAID clinical research projects; (3) Maintains regulatory surveillance over DIR supported clinical trials and protocols to ensure compliance with FDA regulations; (4) Establishes and coordinates trans-NIAID clinical research policies on behalf of the NIAID Clinical Research Subcommittee and harmonizes best practices across NIAID Divisions; (5) Coordinates the development of the OCD response to inquiries from HHS, other Agencies, and NIH regarding a wide-array of legislative and policy issues pertaining to clinical research; (6) Establishes and monitors regulatory policies for DIR-conducted clinical trials and supports the NIAID Clinical Director in the harmonization of a coherent NIAID response based on input from other NIAID Divisions; (7) Establishes and monitors quality assurance standards and standard operating procedures regarding regulatory matters; (8) Coordinates with investigators on the appropriate utilization of available clinical data management systems; (9) Develops, assembles, maintains, and submits investigational new drug (IND) applications to the FDA, authorizes sites for clinical trials, reviews adverse experience reports for DIR sponsored trials, and prepares safety reports and IND interim and annual reports for the FDA; (10) Ensures that sponsor responsibilities for IND/IDE applications held by the Office are either fulfilled or that appropriate documentation transferring responsibilities of those regulatory obligations to include responsibility for maintenance and evaluation of clinical safety data; (11) Provides logistical and technical support for the NIAID intramural Data and Safety Monitoring Board; (12) Provides logistical and technical support for safety monitoring committees and independent medical monitors required for NIAID intramural clinical research; (13) Serves as liaison to the FDA, the pharmaceutical industry, the Office of Human Subjects Research Protections for regulatory issues during the initiation and conduct of clinical trials; (14) In conjunction with pharmaceutical collaborators, reviews the regulatory components of DIR Clinical Trial Agreements and Cooperative Research and Development Agreements; (15) Implements and maintains management information systems required to support regulatory and policy responsibilities; (16) Provides information and training relative to regulatory issues and logistical coordination of trials; (17) Provides consultation to NIAID officials and programs developing clinical trial protocols concerning scientific merit and protection of human subjects; and (18) Coordinates and communicates with other domestic and international government agencies and with other NIH and NIAID components to ensure accurate and timely exchange of information on regulatory issues.
(3) In the
National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NM, formerly HNM)
establish the following:
Office of Biostatistics Research (NM1K, formerly HNM1K)
(1) Provides institute-wide leadership, expertise, and strategic support in biostatistics to advance NIAID's scientific mission; (2) Advises NIAID leadership on policies and programmatic priorities to ensure statistical rigor, reproducibility, data integrity, and analytic accuracy; (3) Supports NIAID's rapid, adaptive, and data-driven response to emerging scientific and public health needs; (4) Facilitates the coordination, oversight, and administration of Data and Safety Monitoring Boards (DSMBs); and (5) Ensures the timely, accurate, and transparent communication and dissemination of research data and results.
Biostatistics Research Branch (NM1K2, formerly HNM1K2)
(1) Collaborates with intramural and extramural investigators to design, analyze, and report scientifically rigorous clinical, population-based, and laboratory studies; (2) Provides statistical leadership for safety monitoring activities and research
(
printed page 73764)
protocol development and review; (3) Directs and conducts an independent research program focused on advancing innovative biostatistical methods; (4) Provides subject matter expertise and leadership for NIAID and cross-institutional Data and Safety Monitoring Boards; (5) Establishes program priorities and recommends funding levels within the biostatistics research portfolio; and (6) Identifies and mentors high-potential biostatisticians developing novel statistical methodologies, and supports early-career investigators in grant submissions to foster the next generation of NIAID researchers.
Clinical Trials Research and Statistics Branch (NM1K3, formerly HNM1K3)
(1) Serves as the central resource for the design, coordination, and conduct of high-priority infectious disease clinical trials through innovative trial designs, advanced statistical methodologies, and robust data management and operations; (2) Functions as an operational hub that integrates and augments existing NIAID clinical research resources to enhance adaptability and responsiveness for special initiatives and rapid-response missions; and (3) Provides a turnkey clinical trials capability during outbreaks or urgent research responses, ensuring coordinated trial implementation, high-quality data management and analysis, and a flexible, nimble, and cost-effective operational model.
Laboratory of Viral Zoonoses (NM2Z13, formerly HNM2Z13)
(1) Work in the Laboratory of Viral Zoonoses at the Integrated Research Facility-Frederick may include: (1) In vitro work using standard and innovative cell culture and organoid models; (2) In vivo work using conventional laboratory and unconventional exotic animal species to develop surrogate models for emerging/re-emerging zoonotic infectious diseases; (3) Use cutting edge methods and state-of-the-art technologies in high/maximum biocontainment, at field sites, and for clinical trials; (4) Evaluate medical countermeasures to prevent or treat (re)emerging infectious diseases; and (5) Establish a world-renowned training site for researchers in high/maximum biocontainment.
IRF-Frederick Comparative Medicine Branch (NM2Z14), formerly HNM2Z14)
(1) Provides support to the IRF-Frederick through centralized animal care, including animal husbandry, clinical care, breeding, shipping and receiving, disease surveillance, and technical scientific support that includes performance of surgeries, experiments, administration of experimental materials, collection of tissue samples and necropsies; (2) Ensures compliance with the Animal Welfare Act, PHS and NIH Animal Care and Use Policies, DHHS Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals, and accreditation standards for the Association for Assessment and Accreditation of Laboratory Animal Care; (3) Provides training for animal care technicians, laboratory technicians, and investigators; (4) Supports high and maximum containment animal experimental protocols for DIR Principal Investigators, including special animal models of emerging and re-emerging biodefense related infectious disease agents requiring Animal Biosafety Level-3 and Animal Biosafety Level-4 containment; (5) Provides detailed summary reports of experiments; and (6) Optimizes facility resources, monitors facilities, and establishes standard operating procedures.
(4) In the
National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NM, formerly HNM)
remove the following:
Division of Clinical Research (NM9, formerly HNM9)
Office of Biostatistics Research (NM93, formerly HNM93)
Mathematical Biology Section (NM932, formerly HNM932)
Clinical Trials Research and Statistics Branch (NM933, formerly HNM933)
Biostatistics Research Branch (NM934, formerly HNM934)
Collaborative Clinical Research Branch (NM94, formerly HNM94)
Science Section (NM942, formerly HNM942)
Operations and Strategy Management Section (NM943, formerly HNM943)
Intramural Clinical Management and Operations Branch (NM95, formerly HNM95)
Program Planning and Analysis Branch (NM96, formerly HNM96)
Office of Clinical Research Policy and Regulatory Operations (NM97, formerly HNM97)
Office of the Chief Scientist for the Integrated Research Facility at Ft. Detrick (NM99, formerly HNM99)

abstract: Based on affirmative final determinations by the U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) and the U.S. International Trade Commission (ITC), Commerce is issuing countervailing duty (CVD) orders on hardwood and decorative plywood from the People's Republic of China (China), Indonesia, and the Socialist Republic of Vietnam (Vietnam).

[C-570-212, C-560-845, C-552-852]
(
printed page 73735)
AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
Based on affirmative final determinations by the U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) and the U.S. International Trade Commission (ITC), Commerce is issuing countervailing duty (CVD) orders on hardwood and decorative plywood from the People's Republic of China (China), Indonesia, and the Socialist Republic of Vietnam (Vietnam).
DATES:
Applicable November 17, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Rebecca Janz (China), Samuel Evans (Indonesia), and Katherine Smith (Vietnam), AD/CVD Operations, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-2972, (202) 482-2420, or (202) 482-0557, respectively.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On July 21, 2026, Commerce published in the
Federal Register
its affirmative final determinations in the CVD investigations of hardwood and decorative plywood from China, Indonesia, and Vietnam in accordance with sections 705(d) and 777(i) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act).
[
1
]
The scope of the investigations in Commerce's final determinations covered hardwood and decorative plywood and certain veneered panels.
[
2
]
As discussed below, the ITC found three domestic like products: hardwood and decorative plywood, stamped and certified softwood structural plywood, and softwood structural plywood downfall. On September 4, 2026, the ITC notified Commerce of its final determinations, pursuant to section 705(d) of the Act, that an industry in the United States is materially injured within the meaning of section 705(b)(1)(A)(i) of the Act by reason of subsidized imports of subject merchandise from China, Indonesia, and Vietnam.
[
3
]
Additionally, the ITC found that imports of stamped and certified softwood structural plywood and of softwood structural plywood downfall are negligible and, therefore, terminated the CVD investigations for these products.
[
4
]
On September 17, 2026, Commerce released draft revised scope language for comment by parties.
[
5
]
On September 23, 2026, we received comments from the Coalition for Fair Trade in Hardwood Plywood (the petitioner) and certain importers and exporters of the merchandise under investigation.
[
6
]
Based on these comments, we released a second version of the draft revised scope language, which included a certification program, for comment on October 8, 2026.
[
7
]
On October 14, 2026, we received comments on the second draft scope language from the petitioner and certain importers and exporters of the merchandise under investigation.
[
8
]
Scope of the Orders
The products covered by these orders are hardwood and decorative plywood from China, Indonesia, and Vietnam. For a complete description of the scope of the orders,
see
the appendix to this notice.
Scope Comments
As stated above, subsequent to the
ITC Final Determination,
we released draft revised scope language and received comments on these drafts from the petitioner and certain importers and exporters of the merchandise under investigation.
[
9
]
For a summary of the scope comments submitted by interested parties, and accompanying discussion and analysis of all comments timely received,
see
the Order Scope Memorandum, issued concurrently with these orders.
[
10
]
We note that several parties commented on whether to implement a certification program for certain modifications made to the scope based on the
ITC Final Determination.
Commerce intends address those comments in a changed circumstances review under section 751(b) of the Act and 19 CFR 351.216 at a later date.
CVD Orders
On September 4, 2026, in accordance with sections 705(b)(1)(A)(i) and 705(d) of the Act, the ITC notified Commerce of its final determinations that an industry in the United States is materially injured by reason of subsidized imports of hardwood and decorative plywood from China, Indonesia, and Vietnam.
[
11
]
As a result, and in accordance with sections 705(c)(2) and 706 of the Act, Commerce is issuing these CVD orders. As noted above, in its determinations, the ITC found three domestic like products: hardwood and decorative plywood, stamped and certified softwood structural plywood, and softwood structural plywood downfall. The ITC found that imports of stamped and certified softwood structural plywood and of softwood structural plywood downfall are negligible. The ITC made an affirmative determination with respect to hardwood and decorative plywood from China, Indonesia, and Vietnam. Because the ITC made distinct and different injury determinations for separate domestic like products, Commerce will instruct U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to assess
(
printed page 73736)
countervailing duties on entries of hardwood and decorative plywood (subject merchandise) from China, Indonesia, and Vietnam, and not on entries of stamped and certified softwood structural plywood or softwood structural plywood downfall from China, Indonesia, and Vietnam.
Hardwood and Decorative Plywood
The ITC describes hardwood and decorative plywood as a plywood product in which at least either the face or back veneer is composed of one or more species of hardwood and/or softwood. Because the ITC determined that imports of hardwood and decorative plywood from China, Indonesia, and Vietnam are materially injuring a U.S. industry,
[
12
]
Commerce will direct CBP that all unliquidated entries of hardwood and decorative plywood from China, Indonesia, and Vietnam entered, or withdrawn from warehouse, are subject to the assessment of countervailing duties pursuant to section 706 of the Act. Specifically, as a result of the
ITC Final Determinations,
in accordance with section 706(a) of the Act, Commerce will direct CBP to assess, upon further instruction by Commerce, countervailing duties for all relevant entries of hardwood and decorative plywood from China, Indonesia, and Vietnam. Countervailing duties will be assessed on unliquidated entries of hardwood and decorative plywood from China, Indonesia, and Vietnam entered, or withdrawn from warehouse, for consumption on or after January 22, 2026, the date of publication of the
Preliminary Determinations,
but will not include entries occurring after the expiration of the provisional measures period and before the publication of the
ITC Final Determinations,
under section 705(b) of the Act, as further described in the “Provisional Measures” section of this notice.
[
13
]
Stamped and Certified Softwood Structural Plywood
The ITC describes stamped and certified softwood structural plywood as all stamped and certified softwood structural plywood regardless of core composition.
[
14
]
Because the ITC determined that all imports of stamped and certified softwood structural plywood from China, Indonesia, and Vietnam are negligible, Commerce will direct CBP to terminate the suspension of liquidation for entries of stamped and certified softwood structural plywood from China, Indonesia, and Vietnam that were not previously excluded from the scope of the investigations. Specifically, Commerce will instruct CBP to terminate the suspension of liquidation of entries of stamped and certified softwood structural plywood that is certified, manufactured, and stamped to meet U.S. Products Standard PS-1-22 or PS 2-18 for Structural Plywood (including any revisions to those standards, or to a foreign structural plywood standard that Commerce has determined, in a scope ruling or other proceeding, to be substantially equivalent to PS-1-22 or PS 2-18) from China, Indonesia, and Vietnam entered, or withdrawn from warehouse, on or after January 22, 2026 (the date of the
Preliminary Determination
), and refund all cash deposits with respect to those entries pursuant to section 705(c)(2) of the Act.
Softwood Structural Plywood Downfall
The ITC describes softwood structural plywood downfall as plywood that was intended to be stamped and certified softwood structural plywood but did not obtain certification due to manufacturing defects.
[
15
]
Because the ITC determined that imports of softwood structural plywood downfall from China, Indonesia, and Vietnam are negligible, Commerce will direct CBP to terminate the suspension of liquidation for entries of softwood structural plywood downfall from China, Indonesia, and Vietnam. Specifically, Commerce will instruct CBP to terminate the suspension of liquidation of entries of plywood panels manufactured at a facility certified to produce structural plywood to PS 1-22 or PS 2-18 standards (or a Commerce-determined equivalent foreign standard), where the specific panels at issue were produced as part of a production run intended to meet such standards but did not receive the certifying agency's stamp or mark because they failed to meet the applicable bond performance, veneer grade, or other qualifying criteria of that standard from China, Indonesia, and Vietnam entered, or withdrawn from warehouse, on or after January 22, 2026 (the date of the
Preliminary Determination
), and to refund all cash deposits with respect to these entries pursuant to section 705(c)(2) of the Act.
Critical Circumstances
In addition, the ITC found that critical circumstances do not exist with respect to imports of merchandise subject to this investigation from China and Vietnam. As a result, we have instructed CBP to lift the suspension of liquidation and to refund all cash deposits for estimated countervailing duties with respect to entries of merchandise suspended by reason of our affirmative critical circumstances determinations that were entered, or withdrawn from warehouse, for consumption on or after October 24, 2025, (
i.e.,
90 days prior to the date of publication of the affirmative
China Preliminary Determination
and
Vietnam Preliminary Determination
), but before January 22, 2026 (
i.e.,
the date of publication of the
China Preliminary Determination
and
Vietnam Preliminary Determination
).

in the

The all-others rate applies to all producers or exporters not specifically listed, as appropriate. Appendix
Scope of the Orders
The merchandise covered by these orders is hardwood and decorative plywood, and certain veneered panels as described below. For purposes of these orders, hardwood and decorative plywood is defined as a generally flat, multilayered plywood or other veneered panel, consisting of two or more layers or plies of wood veneers in combination with a core or without a core. The veneers and, if present, the core are glued or otherwise bonded together. A hardwood and decorative plywood panel must have at least either the face or back veneer composed of one or more species of hardwood, softwood, or bamboo, regardless of any surface coverings. Hardwood and decorative plywood may include products that meet the American National Standard for Hardwood and Decorative Plywood, ANSI/HPVA HP-1-2024 (including any revisions to that standard).
For purposes of the orders a “veneer” is a slice of wood regardless of thickness which is cut, sliced or sawed from a log, bolt, or flitch. The face and back veneers are the outermost veneer of wood irrespective of additional surface coatings or covers as described below. The core of hardwood and decorative plywood (for those products that include a core) consists of the layer or layers of one or more material(s) that are situated between the face and back veneers. The core may be composed of a range of materials, including but not limited to hardwood, softwood, particleboard, or medium density fiberboard (MDF).
All hardwood and decorative plywood is included within the scope of the orders regardless of whether or not the face and/or back veneers are surface coated or covered and whether or not such surface coating(s) or covers obscures the grain, textures, or markings of the wood. Examples of surface coatings and covers include, but are not limited to: ultra violet light cured polyurethanes; oil or oil-modified or water-based polyurethanes; wax; epoxy-ester finishes; moisture-cured urethanes; paints; stains; paper; aluminum; high pressure laminate; MDF; medium density overlay (MDO); and phenolic film. Additionally, the face veneer of hardwood and decorative plywood may be sanded; smoothed or given a “distressed” appearance through such methods as hand-scraping or wire brushing.
All hardwood and decorative plywood is included within the scope even if it is trimmed; cut-to-size; notched; punched; drilled; or has undergone other forms of minor processing. All hardwood and decorative plywood is included within the scope of the orders, without regard to dimension (overall thickness, thickness of face veneer, thickness of back veneer, thickness of core, thickness of inner veneers, width, or length). However, the most common panel sizes of hardwood and decorative plywood are 1219 x 1829 mm (48 x 72 inches), 1219 x 2438 mm (48 x 96 inches), and 1219 x 3048 mm (48 x 120 inches). Subject merchandise also includes hardwood and decorative plywood that has been further processed in a third country, including but not limited to trimming, cutting, notching, punching, drilling, or any other processing that would not otherwise remove the merchandise from the scope of the orders if performed in the country of manufacture of the in-scope product.
The scope of the orders excludes the following items: (1) structural plywood (also known as “industrial plywood” or “industrial panels”) that is certified, manufactured, and stamped to meet U.S. Products Standard PS-1-22 or PS 2-18 for Structural Plywood (including any revisions to those standards, or to a foreign structural plywood standard that Commerce has determined, in a scope ruling or other proceeding, to be substantially equivalent to PS-1-22 or PS 2-18); (2) products which have a face and back veneer of cork; (3) hardwood plywood subject to the antidumping and countervailing duty orders on hardwood plywood from China. See Certain Hardwood Plywood Products from the People's Republic of China: Amended Final Determination of Sales at Less Than Fair Value, and Antidumping Duty Order,
83 FR 504
(January 4, 2018); and Certain Hardwood Plywood Products from the People's Republic of China: Countervailing Duty Order,
83 FR 513
(January 4, 2018); (4) multilayered wood flooring, as described in the antidumping duty and countervailing duty orders on multilayered wood flooring from China. See Multilayered Wood Flooring from the People's Republic of China: Amended Final Determination of Sales at Less Than Fair Value and Antidumping Duty Order,
76 FR 76690
(December 8, 2011); and Multilayered Wood Flooring from the People's Republic of China: Countervailing Duty Order,
76 FR 76693
(December 8, 2011), as amended by Multilayered Wood Flooring from the People's Republic of China: Amended Antidumping and Countervailing Orders,
77 FR 5484
(February 3, 2012); (5) multilayered wood flooring with a face veneer of bamboo or composed entirely of bamboo; (6) plywood which has a shape or design other than a flat panel, with the exception of any minor processing described above; (7) products made entirely from bamboo and adhesives (also known as “solid bamboo”); and (8) Phenolic Film Faced Plyform (PFF), also known as Phenolic Surface Film Plywood (PSF), defined as a panel with an “Exterior” or “Exposure 1” bond classification as is defined by The Engineered Wood Association, having an opaque phenolic film layer with a weight equal to or greater than 90g/m3 permanently bonded on both the face and back veneers and an opaque, moisture resistant coating applied to the edges. Structural plywood qualifying for part (1) of the above exclusion must bear the certifying agency's stamp or mark, applied in accordance with the requirements of the applicable standard, identifying the certification agency, applicable standard or grade designation, and the mill number or other facility-identifying code assigned by the certifying agency to the producing facility.
Also excluded from the scope of the orders are softwood structural plywood “downfall” panels, defined as plywood panels manufactured at a facility certified to produce structural plywood to PS 1-22 or PS 2-18 standards (or a Commerce-determined equivalent foreign standard), where the specific panels at issue were produced as part of a production run intended to meet such standards but did not receive the certifying agency's stamp or mark because they failed to meet the applicable bond performance, veneer grade, or other qualifying criteria of that standard.
Also excluded from the scope of the orders are wooden furniture goods that, at the time of importation, are fully assembled and are ready for their intended uses. Also excluded from the scope of the orders is “ready to assemble” (RTA) furniture. RTA furniture is defined as (A) furniture packaged for sale for ultimate purchase by an end-user that, at the time of importation, includes (1) all wooden components (in finished form) required to assemble a finished unit of furniture, (2) all accessory parts (
e.g.,
screws, washers, dowels, nails, handles, knobs, adhesive glues) required to assemble a finished unit of furniture, and (3) instructions providing guidance on the assembly of a finished unit of furniture; (B) unassembled bathroom vanity cabinets, having a space for one or more sinks, that are imported with all unassembled hardwood and hardwood plywood components that have been cut-to-final dimensional component shape/size, painted or stained prior to importation, and stacked within a singled shipping package, except for furniture feet which may be packed and shipped separately; or (C) unassembled bathroom vanity linen closets that are imported with all unassembled hardwood and hardwood plywood
(
printed page 73739)
components that have been cut-to-final dimensional shape/size, painted or stained prior to importation, and stacked within a single shipping package, except for furniture feet which may be packed and shipped separately.
Also excluded from the scope of the orders are kitchen cabinets that, at the time of importation, are fully assembled and are ready for their intended uses. Also excluded from the scope of the orders are RTA kitchen cabinets. RTA kitchen cabinets are defined as kitchen cabinets packaged for sale for ultimate purchase by an end-user that, at the time of importation, includes: (1) all wooden components (in finished form) required to assemble a finished unit of cabinetry; (2) all accessory parts (
e.g.,
screws, washers, dowels, nails, handles, knobs, hooks, adhesive glues) required to assemble a finished unit of cabinetry; and (3) instructions providing guidance on the assembly of a finished unit of cabinetry. Excluded from the scope of these orders are finished table tops, which are table tops imported in finished form with pre-cut or drilled openings to attach the underframe or legs. The table tops are ready for use at the time of import and require no further finishing or processing. Excluded from the scope of these orders are finished countertops that are imported in finished form and require no further finishing or manufacturing.
Also excluded from the scope of the orders are laminated veneer lumber (LVL) door and window components with (1) a maximum width of 44 millimeters, a thickness from 30 millimeters to 72 millimeters, and a length of less than 2413 millimeters, (2) water boiling point exterior adhesive, (3) a modulus of elasticity of 1,500,000 pounds per square inch or higher, (4) finger-jointed or lap-jointed core veneer with all layers oriented so that the grain is running parallel or with no more than 3 dispersed layers of veneer oriented with the grain running perpendicular to the other layers; and (5) top layer machined with a curved edge and one or more profile channels throughout.
Also excluded from the scope of these orders are certain door stiles and rails made of LVL that have a width not to exceed 50 millimeters, a thickness not to exceed 50 millimeters, and a length of less than 2,450 millimeters.
Also excluded from the scope of these orders are finished two-ply products that are made of one ply of wood veneer and one ply of a non-wood veneer material and the two-ply product cannot be glued or otherwise adhered to additional plies or that are made of two plies of wood veneer and have undergone staining, cutting, notching, punching, drilling, or other processing on the surface of the veneer such that the two-ply product cannot be glued or otherwise adhered to additional plies.

National Credit Union Administration
12 CFR Part 701
RIN 3133-AF93
AGENCY:
National Credit Union Administration (NCUA).
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The NCUA Board (Board) is issuing a final rule to amend its criteria for determining associational common bonds. The amendments clarify that requiring members to buy a good, product, or service from a group as a condition of membership will no longer automatically bar eligibility as a recognized association. After considering public comments, the Board finalizes the proposed rule with certain modifications. The Board's revisions detail how NCUA assesses client-customer relationships (including relevant examples). These changes also simplify NCUA's process for reviewing pre-approved groups.
DATES:
This final rule is effective on January 4, 2027.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
John Tamashiro, Director, Division of Consumer Access, Office of Credit Union Resources and Expansion at (703) 548-2577 or 1775 Duke Street, Alexandria, VA 22314, or Keisha Brooks, Attorney-Advisor, Office of General Counsel, at (703) 518-6540 or at the above address.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Introduction
A. Background
The Federal Credit Union Act (FCU Act) recognizes three types of federal charters—single common bond (occupational and associational), multiple common bond (more than one group each having a common bond of occupation or association), and community. NCUA's Chartering and Field of Membership Manual, incorporated as Appendix B to part 701 of NCUA's regulations (Chartering Manual) implements the FCU Act.
[
1
]
For chartering purposes, a common bond is a fundamental requirement for a recognized association.
[
2
]
In the Credit Union Membership Access Act (CUMAA), Congress found that “[a] meaningful affinity and bond among members, manifested by a commonality of routine interaction, shared and related work experiences, interests, or activities, or the maintenance of an otherwise well understood sense of cohesion or identity is essential to the fulfillment of the public mission of credit unions.”
[
3
]
While the FCU Act does not explicitly define “common bond,” the Board clarified its meaning in the Chartering Manual. A common bond is the characteristic or combination of characteristics which distinguishes a particular group of persons from the general public.
[
4
]
Furthermore, the Chartering Manual defines an associational common bond to include individuals and groups whose members participate in activities developing common loyalties, mutual benefits, and mutual interests.
[
5
]
Within this framework, the Chartering Manual reflects a long-standing policy that associations based primarily on a client-customer relationship do not meet associational common bond requirements.
[
6
]
Based on agency experience with particular requests, the members of an association based primarily on a client-customer relationship had only an interest in purchasing a good, product, or service from the group.
[
7
]
The group operated in a manner indistinguishable from a vendor providing a good, product, or service to the general public. Its charter and bylaws lacked provisions for membership governance or qualifications beyond paying for a good, product, or service. Membership fees (in terms of amount, timing, and structure) functioned merely as payments for a good, product, or service.
Still, the Chartering Manual does not preclude an association with an incidental client-customer relationship if other associational common bond requirements are met.
[
8
]
In such circumstances, NCUA staff generally considered a client-customer relationship as incidental when it served a secondary role in relation to the group's associational common bond and activities. For this purpose, NCUA often considered multiple factors.
For example, past chartering policies mentioned electric cooperatives as groups that could meet associational standards, even though purchasing
(
printed page 73657)
power was required.
[
9
]
These chartering policies noted that an electric cooperative must make a strong showing of common activities. Another important factor was electric cooperatives' distinctive relationship with their members. Unlike other client-customer groups, these members are both the owners and users of the cooperative.
The Chartering Manual also included one example of an incidental client-customer relationship—a fraternal association that offers insurance, which is not a condition of membership. This example led to the conclusion that, if a fraternal benefit association required its members to buy insurance from the group as a condition of membership, the association was automatically disqualified.
[
10
]
On April 8, 2026, the Board announced its proposal to amend the Chartering Manual to clarify that a multifaceted approach remains NCUA's position, even if purchasing a good, product, or service from a group is a condition of membership.
[
11
]
In the proposed rule, the Board preserved the long-standing policy that an association based primarily on a client-customer relationship does not qualify as a recognized association. The Board proposed eliminating the fraternal association example of an incidental client-customer relationship that had been interpreted as automatically barring some groups with a mandatory purchase condition from associational eligibility. As proposed, NCUA would evaluate the circumstances as a whole. The comment period ended on June 8, 2026.
The final rule adopts the April 8, 2026, proposed rule with certain modifications discussed more fully in the section summarizing the comments. After carefully considering the public comments, the Board is amending the April 8, 2026, proposal to increase transparency into NCUA's process for reviewing client-customer relationships. These changes explain key considerations and provide examples. The Board's other changes aim to make NCUA's pre-approved group reviews more efficient. The final rule amends the associational common bond criteria applicable to single associational charters and multiple common bond federal credit unions (FCUs). Accordingly, the final rule does not apply to occupational common bond charters, community charters, or federally insured state-chartered credit unions.
B. Legal Authority
The Board is issuing this final rule pursuant to its authority under the FCU Act. Under the FCU Act, NCUA is the chartering and supervisory authority for FCUs and the federal supervisory authority for federally insured credit unions (FICUs).
[
12
]
The FCU Act grants NCUA a broad mandate to issue regulations governing both FCUs and all FICUs. Section 120 of the FCU Act is a general grant of regulatory authority and authorizes the Board to prescribe rules and regulations for the administration of the FCU Act.
[
13
]
Section 207 of the FCU Act is a specific grant of authority over share insurance coverage, conservatorships, and liquidations.
[
14
]
Section 209 of the FCU Act is a plenary grant of regulatory authority to issue rules and regulations necessary or appropriate to carry out its role as share insurer for all FICUs.
[
15
]
Accordingly, the FCU Act grants the Board broad rulemaking authority to ensure that the federally insured credit union industry and the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund remain safe and sound.
The Board is also issuing this final rule pursuant to its rulemaking authority under Section 109 of the FCU Act.
[
16
]
Section 109 of the FCU Act establishes the field of membership framework for FCUs.
[
17
]
Section 109 also describes the membership criteria for federal charters and grants the Board rulemaking authority with respect to such charters.
[
18
]
Section 109(d)(3) further directs the Board to issue guidelines or regulations, after notice and opportunity for comment, setting forth the criteria that the Board will apply in determining whether a group may be added to an FCU's field of membership.
[
19
]
Sections 109(a) and 109(f)(2)(E) reference more general rulemaking authority with respect to associational groups and fields of membership.
[
20
]
Pursuant to its authority under the FCU Act, the Board implements these statutory requirements through the Chartering Manual.
II. Final Rule
A. Overview
This final rule follows publication of the April 8, 2026, proposed rule, and takes into consideration the comments received on the proposal. By the close of the public comment period on June 8, 2026, the Board received 18 public comments. Comments were submitted by credit union trade associations, credit union leagues, FCUs, one associational group, an individual, and a bankers association. All commenters except one supported the proposal. Most commenters supported considering a group's structure, purpose, and activities rather than automatically excluding the group based on a mandatory purchase condition. Several commenters urged NCUA to clarify certain aspects of the proposal, including definitions, examples, and documentation guidelines. One bankers association opposed the proposal.
After carefully considering the issues raised by the commenters, the Board has made the following changes to the proposal: (1) detailing NCUA's criteria in reviewing client-customer relationships, (2) adding relevant examples, and (3) simplifying NCUA's review process for pre-approved groups.
B. Discussion of Public Comments
This section of the preamble discusses the significant issues raised by the commenters, and the Board's responses to the comments.
Comments on NCUA's Statutory Authority
Several commenters observed that the proposal was consistent with NCUA's statutory authority, noting that neither the FCU Act nor CUMAA requires disqualifying associations due to a client-customer relationship. Most commenters agreed that a mandatory purchase condition should not automatically bar eligibility as a recognized association if the client-customer relationship is incidental to the association's mission and activities. Many commenters observed that the proposal provides measured regulatory relief for single associational and
(
printed page 73658)
multiple common bond FCUs. Two commenters described the categorical exclusion based on a mandatory purchase condition as an unnecessarily restrictive barrier to groups with legitimate common bonds. Another commenter highlighted that eliminating the exclusion would provide additional flexibility for small FCUs when adding associations to their fields of membership. Another commenter noted that imposing eligibility restrictions beyond statutory requirements could reduce consumer access to affordable financial services from FCUs. According to this commenter, such barriers diminish competition in local financial services markets and leave consumers with fewer options, particularly those of modest means.
One bankers association opposed the rule, contending that, contrary to congressional intent, the proposal contributed to the erosion of field of membership restrictions under the FCU Act. Citing concerns regarding competitive equity and statutory fidelity, the commenter observed that the distinctive legal and tax status of FCUs is justified by their restricted mission and membership. This commenter noted that the proposed amendment, while narrow in isolation, is part of a series of incremental changes that collectively could greatly expand credit union membership beyond congressional intent.
NCUA Response.
The Board welcomes the comments submitted on its April 8, 2026, proposed rule. After careful consideration, the Board believes that the regulatory changes are within the broad authority conferred in the FCU Act and consistent with congressional intent.
Section 109 of the FCU Act authorizes the Board to establish regulations for determining which groups meet field of membership requirements for FCUs.
[
21
]
Exercising this authority, the Board has periodically amended the Chartering Manual consistent with congressional objectives.
[
22
]
When appropriate, the Board has also adopted regulations designed to guard against excessive expansions.
[
23
]
The April 8, 2026, proposed rule was designed to address an unintended consequence stemming from the fraternal association example of an incidental client-customer relationship. As discussed in the preambles to the proposed rule and this final rule, the fraternal association example had led to the conclusion that, if a group required its members to buy a good, product, or service from the organization as a condition of membership, the group was automatically disqualified. This final rule clarifies that this example no longer automatically disqualifies such groups as associations that are based primarily on a client-customer relationship. The Board expects this change to enhance access to reliable financial services, especially for those of modest means, while reducing confusion. As discussed in this preamble, the Board notes that this change is distinct from the long-standing policy that associations that are based primarily on a client-customer relationship do not meet associational common bond requirements.
Excluding associations based primarily on a client-customer relationship will continue to serve as an effective gatekeeper to prevent unqualified groups from chartering or joining FCUs. The Board further notes that other provisions, like the threshold purpose requirement and the totality of the circumstances test, are designed to identify unqualified groups.
[
24
]
Lastly, NCUA has additional safeguards to protect the integrity of field of membership requirements, such as conducting quality assurance reviews and investigating field of membership complaints.
[
25
]
Accordingly, the Board disagrees with the comment that the proposal could result in eroding statutory field of membership restrictions contrary to congressional intent. Thus, the Board has made no changes in response to this comment.
Comments on Defining a Client-Customer Relationship
Several commenters requested clearer guidance on defining a client-customer relationship, particularly the meaning of “primarily” and “incidental.” One commenter recommended defining a client-customer relationship as one in which the organization's sole purpose is selling a good, product, or service to its clients or customers. This commenter suggested a definition focusing on whether a qualifying association would still exist without the client-customer relationship, or whether the common bond is contingent upon the transaction.
NCUA Response.
The Board acknowledges the concerns raised by the commenters. In the final rule, the Board intends for the terms “primarily,” “client,” “customer,” and “relationship” to be understood according to their common, ordinary meanings. For example, “primarily” means for the most part; chiefly.
[
26
]
The plain meaning of “client” includes a person who engages the professional advice or services of another; customer.
[
27
]
Additionally, “customer” ordinarily means one that purchases a commodity or service.
[
28
]
“Relationship” refers to the way in which two or more things or people are connected.
[
29
]
Further, given the definitions for common bond and associational common bond, the Board believes that introducing new regulatory definitions would be overly prescriptive.
[
30
]
After carefully considering the comments, the Board views a plain meaning approach as more suitable. Accordingly, the Board has made no changes to the final rule based on these comments.
Comments for Additional Guidance on Client-Customer Relationship Criteria
The Board proposed that NCUA would review the particular details of a group's structure, the scope and degree of its activities, and other factors surrounding its operation to determine whether the association is based primarily on a client-customer relationship. The Board also specifically sought comment on other relevant factors to determine whether an association's relationship with its members is primarily or incidentally a client-customer relationship.
Several commenters requested clarification on how NCUA would
(
printed page 73659)
weigh these factors, especially mandatory purchase conditions. These commenters also asked how NCUA would review groups exhibiting both qualifying and disqualifying features. One opposing commenter cautioned that a discretionary inquiry, if not accompanied by objective guardrails, could stretch the common bond requirement over time and invite pressure to reinterpret statutory limits.
NCUA Response.
After carefully considering the comments, the Board agrees that the final rule could provide additional transparency. Accordingly, the Board is amending the final rule to reflect the criteria used to evaluate client-customer relationships. These criteria include reviewing the group's mission, purpose, structure, and activities. Member qualifications and engagement beyond paying for services are also considered. Another consideration is how membership dues are structured.
In the final rule, a mandatory purchase condition remains a reasonable factor when evaluating a client-customer relationship. The final rule merely clarifies that such a requirement alone is not conclusive. A group with a mandatory purchase condition may be able to balance this indicator with strong evidence of an associational common bond through its organizational documents and common activities.
The frequency of member meetings, as well as opportunities to participate in furthering the association's goals, are other important indicators. Groups that sponsor a variety of opportunities for members to interact and assist in furthering defined associational goals are more likely to indicate an incidental client-customer relationship. Examples of such opportunities that develop common loyalties, mutual benefits, and mutual interests may include, but are not limited to, newsletters, community service activities, fraternal activities, or access to members-only events. In contrast, if a group's common activities are so insubstantial that it is indistinguishable from a vendor serving the general public (like a health club or an insurance company), this would suggest a strong client-customer relationship.
The Board reiterates that this change is simply a clarification reflecting how NCUA has historically evaluated client-customer relationships. The Board observes that these considerations align with NCUA's current approach. In response to the comments requesting further guidance, the Board is also including more examples of associations based primarily on a client-customer relationship and those with incidental client-customer relationships.
Comments on Pre-Approved Groups
In 2015, the Board automatically approved specific kinds of associations whose structures, practices, and functions routinely met associational common bond requirements.
[
31
]
Some associations within these pre-approved groups exhibited features of a client-customer relationship. To provide clarity, the preamble to the April 2026 proposed rule confirmed that pre-approved groups do not require additional NCUA review to demonstrate a valid associational common bond.
[
32
]
Two commenters acknowledged that the proposed rule would reduce review resources by preserving the option for automatically pre-approved groups. Another commenter noted continued confusion regarding the automatic pre-approval of certain fraternal associations and the prohibition against associations based primarily on a client-customer relationship. Additionally, another commenter suggested the Board establish clear, consistent, and expedited pathways for well-qualified expansion requests.
NCUA Response.
The Board recognizes that, in this area, the client-customer relationship provisions and other associational common-bond provisions could cause confusion for FCUs. After carefully considering the public comments, the Board has amended Chapter 2, Section III.A.1.b (Pre-Approved Groups) of the Chartering Manual. Drawing from the proposed rule's preamble, the changes reaffirm that, for chartering and expansion purposes, NCUA staff will not reassess a pre-approved group's client-customer relationship or the purpose of its formation.
By regulation, a pre-approved group has a defined purpose other than increasing credit union membership—for example, religious organizations, electric cooperatives, and alumni associations. Since 2015, NCUA has approved 95.62 percent of applications for pre-approved groups. None were denied for failing to meet the threshold purpose requirement. Moreover, the Board observes that electric cooperatives and qualifying fraternal benefit associations have long coexisted with the restriction on associations based primarily on a client-customer relationship. The Board believes the revisions clarify its expectations and will improve NCUA's efficiency in processing applications for pre-approved groups.
[
33
]
Comments on Sample Associations With Incidental Client-Customer Relationships
Several commenters proposed incorporating examples that differentiate an association with an incidental client-customer relationship from an association based primarily on a client-customer relationship. These comments recommended the following as examples of associations with an incidental client-customer relationship: (1) fraternal associations that offer insurance benefits, (2) educational associations, (3) consumer cooperatives, (4) associations offering financial, legal, insurance, and real estate services within a broader membership framework, and (5) associations with required membership benefits. One commenter suggested removing the Knights of Columbus as an example of a recognized association to avoid confusion.
NCUA Response.
The Board acknowledges the concerns raised by the commenters and appreciates their suggestions. After considering the recommendations, the Board is amending Chapter 2, Section III.A.3 (Sample Single Associational Common Bonds) to include more examples. For the reasons discussed in the preamble, the Board has added relevant examples for an electric cooperative and an organization that promotes educational initiatives among persons with a shared profession. The Board continues to believe that the Knights of Columbus provides a helpful illustration of a qualifying fraternal association. Accordingly, the Board has decided to retain the Chartering Manual's references to the Knights of Columbus. For consistency, the final rule also includes a reference among the sample single associational common bonds.
The Chartering Manual states that certain consumer cooperatives may qualify as an association.
[
34
]
Based on agency experience, these groups can differ significantly in their missions, structures, activities, and product offerings. This variation presents challenges for designating other consumer cooperatives as a
(
printed page 73660)
representative sample for prospective applicants. Due to similar concerns, the Board has also determined not to include the other suggested examples for incidental client-customer relationships.
Comments on Sample Associations Based Primarily on a Client-Customer Relationship
Commenters also suggested adding examples for the following associations based primarily on a client-customer relationship: (1) retail loyalty clubs and affinity programs, (2) health clubs, (3) groups with insurance benefits, (4) subscription relationships, programs, and commercial user bases that exist mainly for purchasing goods, products, or services, and (5) similar customer-facing arrangements in which the client-customer relationship is the core reason for the organization's existence.
NCUA Response.
The Board notes that the Chartering Manual lists health clubs (like YMCAs) and an insurance company as examples of associations based primarily on a client-customer relationship.
[
35
]
The Board identified buyer's clubs in past chartering policies.
[
36
]
In the preamble to the proposed rule, the Board also referenced a retail loyalty club as illustrating an association based primarily on a client-customer relationship.
[
37
]
After considering the comments, the Board has determined that these and other examples would be useful to potential applicants. The additional examples include paid subscription-based plans for media streaming, ride sharing, and local delivery services. The final rule consolidates these examples in one section.
[
38
]
Comments on Documentation Guidelines
One commenter recommended that the final rule specify the necessary supporting documentation, such as bylaws, membership criteria, evidence of member activity, governance rights, membership dues, purchase requirements, and a concise explanation outlining why the client-customer relationship is incidental rather than primary.
NCUA Response.
The Board expects the current requirements to be sufficient to demonstrate how a group meets the associational common bond requirements, including when a client-customer relationship exists. At NCUA's request, applicants must provide a copy of the association's charter, bylaws, or other equivalent documentation.
[
39
]
These applications generally include a definition of the group that may be served based on such documentation.
[
40
]
When applying for new federal charters, organizers must demonstrate that the group meets the appropriate common bond criteria. For single common bond expansions, applicants must show how the group shares the FCU's common bond.
[
41
]
Accordingly, the Board has made no changes based on this comment.
Comments on Charitable Organizations
One FCU requested clarification on charitable or cause-based organizations where donations may fulfill membership requirements. The commenter questioned how the proposed amendments would relate to individuals or honorary members who only make donations to the charitable organizations and foundations.
NCUA Response.
The Board proposed no changes to the existing provision that individuals or honorary members who only make donations to an association are not eligible to join the credit union.
[
42
]
The final rule has no effect on this restriction. Accordingly, the Board has made no changes to the final rule based on this comment.
Other Comments
Two commenters encouraged broader regulatory relief. One commenter recommended further streamlining the Chartering Manual and field of membership process. This commenter suggested modernizing the definition of association and membership to recognize digital communities, affinity groups, and modern economic relationships. Another commenter suggested redefining common loyalty and a common bond. While the Board appreciates the comments, these further amendments to the Chartering Manual are beyond the scope of this rulemaking. The Board will keep the suggestions for future consideration, as appropriate.
III. Regulatory Procedures
A. Executive Orders 12866, 13563, and 14192
Pursuant to
Executive Order 12866
(“Regulatory Planning and Review”), a determination must be made whether a regulatory action is significant and therefore subject to review by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA), within the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) in accordance with the requirements of the Executive Order.
[
43
]
Executive Order 13563
(“Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review”) supplements and reaffirms the principles, structures, and definitions governing contemporary regulatory review established in
Executive Order 12866
.
[
44
]
This final rule was drafted and reviewed in accordance with
Executive Order 12866
and
Executive Order 13563
. OIRA has determined that this final rule is not a “significant regulatory action” as defined by section 3(f) of
Executive Order 12866
.
Executive Order 14192
(“Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation”) requires that any new incremental costs associated with new regulations shall, to the extent permitted by law, be offset by the elimination of existing costs associated with at least 10 prior regulations.
[
45
]
This final rule is not an
Executive Order 14192
regulatory action because this rule is not significant under
Executive Order 12866
. This final rule is considered an
Executive Order 14192
deregulatory action.
B. Regulatory Flexibility Act
The Regulatory Flexibility Act generally requires an agency to conduct a regulatory flexibility analysis of any rule subject to notice and comment rulemaking requirements, unless the agency certifies that the rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.
[
46
]
If the agency makes such a certification, it shall publish the certification at the time of publication of either the proposed rule or the final rule, along with a statement providing the factual basis for such certification.
[
47
]
For purposes of this analysis, NCUA considers small credit unions to be those having under $100 million in assets.
[
48
]
The Board fully considered the potential economic impacts of the
(
printed page 73661)
regulatory amendments on small credit unions.
The final rule is designed to ease a regulatory burden for single associational common bond and multiple common bond FCUs of all sizes. This rule focuses on associational groups for a de novo FCU or who wish to join an existing FCU's field of membership. The Board believes that clarifying the associational common bond standards could provide more flexibility for groups with client-customer relationships. Under the final rule, such groups may no longer be deterred from applying for an FCU charter. Additionally, the amendments will enable such groups to avoid expending unnecessary time and resources to demonstrate eligibility. Only 21 de novo FCUs were chartered by NCUA from 2019 through 2025, of which 11 were either single associational de novo charters or multiple common bond de novo charters that included single associational groups. Given this context, based on its best assessment at this time, the Board expects that the final rule may result in a slight increase in federal charter applications, possibly leading to one or two de novo FCUs each year. To the extent there is any cost to small entities to voluntarily participate in the determination of whether the association is based primarily on a client-customer relationship, those costs are minimal and they are incurred infrequently.
The Board expects the amendment will offer multiple common bond federal charters greater flexibility in adding associations to their fields of membership. However, the regulatory relief is hard to quantify, as cases involving associations with purchase mandates are rare according to NCUA analyses. Based on its best assessment at this time, the Board does not expect that the amendments will likely cause a surge in associations with purchase mandates seeking FCU affiliation. Accordingly, NCUA certifies the final rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small credit unions.
C. Paperwork Reduction Act
The Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA) generally provides that an agency may not conduct or sponsor, and notwithstanding any other provision of law, a person is not required to respond to a collection of information, unless it displays a currently valid OMB control number. The PRA applies to rulemaking in which an agency creates a new or amends existing information collection requirements. For purposes of the PRA, an information collection requirement may take the form of a reporting, recordkeeping, or a third-party disclosure requirement. NCUA has reviewed this rule and determined that it does not create any new or revise any existing collections of information. Accordingly, no PRA submissions to OMB will be made with respect to this rule.
D.
Executive Order 13132
on Federalism
Executive Order 13132
encourages independent regulatory agencies to consider the impact of their actions on state and local interests.
[
49
]
NCUA, an agency as defined in
44 U.S.C. 3502(5)
, voluntarily complies with the executive order to adhere to fundamental federalism principles. NCUA expects that any effect on states or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government will be minor. This rule applies only to FCUs. It does not apply to state-chartered credit unions, which are subject to the field of membership requirements of their respective states. The rulemaking therefore does not have direct effect on the states, the relationship between the national government and the states, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government.
E. Assessment of Federal Regulations and Policies on Families
NCUA has determined that this final rule will not affect family well-being within the meaning of Section 654 of the Treasury and General Government Appropriations Act, 1999.
[
50
]
The final rule relates to field of membership requirements for FCUs, and any effect on family well-being is expected to be indirect.
F. Congressional Review Act
Subtitle E of the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996, also known as the Congressional Review Act (CRA), generally provides for congressional review of agency rules.
[
51
]
NCUA must submit a report to Congress and the Comptroller General when it issues a final rule, as defined by the CRA.
[
52
]
An agency rule, in addition to being subject to congressional oversight, may also be subject to a delayed effective date if the rule is a “major rule.” OIRA has determined that this rule is not a “major rule” within the meaning of the relevant sections of the CRA. NCUA will also file appropriate reports with Congress and the Comptroller General so this rule may be reviewed.

Chapter 2—Field of Membership Requirements for Federal Credit Unions
*
*

III—Associational Common Bond
III. A.1—General
A single associational federal credit union may include in its field of membership, regardless of location, all members and employees of a recognized association. A single associational common bond consists of individuals (natural persons) and/or groups (non-natural persons) whose members participate in activities developing common loyalties, mutual benefits, and mutual interests. Separately chartered associational groups can establish a single common bond relationship if they are integrally related and share common goals and purposes. For example, two or more churches of the same denomination, Knights of Columbus Councils, or locals of the same union can qualify as a single associational common bond. Individuals and groups eligible for membership in a single associational credit union can include the following:
Natural person members of the association (for example, members of a union or church members);
(
printed page 73662)
Non-natural person members of the association;
Employees of the association (for example, employees of the labor union or employees of the church); and
The association.
Generally, a single associational common bond does not include a geographic definition and can operate nationally. However, a proposed or existing federal credit union may limit its field of membership to a single association or geographic area. NCUA may impose a geographic limitation if it is determined that the applicant credit union does not have the ability to serve a larger group or there are other operational concerns. All single associational common bonds should include a definition of the group that may be served based on the association's charter, bylaws, and any other equivalent documentation. Applicants for a single associational common bond federal credit union charter or a field of membership amendment to include an association must provide, at the request of NCUA, a copy of the association's charter, bylaws, or other equivalent documentation, including any legal documents required by the state or other governing authority. The associational sponsor itself may also be included in the field of membership—
e.g.,
“Sprocket Association”—and will be shown in the last clause of the field of membership.
III.A.1.a—Threshold Requirement Regarding the Purpose for Which an Associational Group Is Formed and the Totality of the Circumstances Criteria
As a threshold matter, when reviewing an application to include an association in a federal credit union's field of membership, NCUA will determine if the association has been formed primarily for the purpose of expanding credit union membership. If NCUA makes such a determination, then the analysis ends and the association is denied inclusion in the federal credit union's field of membership. If NCUA determines that the association was formed to serve some other separate function as an organization, then NCUA will apply the following totality of the circumstances test to determine if the association satisfies the associational common bond requirements. The totality of the circumstances test consists of the following factors:
1. Whether the association provides opportunities for members to participate in the furtherance of the goals of the association;
2. Whether the association maintains a membership list;
3. Whether the association sponsors other activities;
4. Whether the association's membership eligibility requirements are authoritative;
5. Whether members pay dues;
6. Whether the members have voting rights; to meet this requirement, members need not vote directly for an officer, but may vote for a delegate who in turn represents the members' interests;
7. The frequency of meetings; and
8. Separateness—NCUA reviews if there is corporate separateness between the group and the federal credit union. The group and the federal credit union must operate in a way that demonstrates the separate corporate existence of each entity. Specifically, this means the federal credit union's and the group's respective business transactions, accounts, and corporate records are not intermingled.
No one factor alone is determinative of membership eligibility as an association. The totality of the circumstances controls over any individual factor in the test. However, NCUA's primary focus will be on factors 1-4.
III.A.1.b—Pre-Approved Groups
NCUA automatically approves the below groups as satisfying the associational common bond provisions. For this purpose, NCUA staff will not reassess the associational common bond of a pre-approved group regarding the purpose of the group's formation, the totality of the circumstances test, or a client-customer relationship. All other applicable requirements must be met. NCUA only approves regular members of an approved group. Honorary, affiliate, or non-regular members do not qualify. These groups are:
1. Alumni associations;
2. Religious organizations, including churches or groups of related churches;
3. Electric cooperatives;
4. Homeowner associations;
5. Labor unions;
6. Scouting groups;
7. Parent teacher associations (PTAs) organized at the local level to serve a single school district;
8. Chamber of commerce groups (members only and not employees of members);
9. Athletic booster clubs whose members have voting rights;
10. Fraternal organizations or civic groups with a mission of community service whose members have voting rights;
11. Organizations having a mission based on preserving or furthering the culture of a particular national or ethnic origin; and
12. Organizations promoting social interaction or educational initiatives among persons sharing a common occupational profession.
III.A.1.c—Additional Information
A support group whose members are continually changing or whose duration is temporary may not meet the single associational common bond criteria. Each class of member will be evaluated based on the totality of the circumstances. Individuals or honorary members who only make donations to the association are not eligible to join the credit union.
Student groups (
e.g.,
students enrolled at a public, private, or parochial school) may constitute either an associational or occupational common bond. For example, students enrolled at a church sponsored school could share a single associational common bond with the members of that church and may qualify for a federal credit union charter. Similarly, students enrolled at a university, as a group by itself, or in conjunction with the faculty and employees of the school, could share a single occupational common bond and may qualify for a federal credit union charter.
Tenant groups, consumer groups, and other groups of persons having an “interest in” a particular cause and certain consumer cooperatives may also qualify as an association.
Associations based primarily on a client-customer relationship do not meet associational common bond requirements. Health clubs are an example of a group not meeting associational common bond requirements, including YMCAs. However, having an incidental client-customer relationship does not preclude an associational charter if the associational common bond requirements are met. For example, an association that requires members to buy a good, product, or service from the group may still demonstrate that the client-customer relationship is incidental to the association's common bond, activities, and overall operations.
If a client-customer relationship exists, NCUA will review the particular details of the group's structure, the scope and degree of its activities, and other factors surrounding its operations to determine whether the association is based primarily on a client-customer relationship. In making this determination, NCUA's primary focus will be on the following considerations:
Whether a client-customer relationship is merely supportive or supplementary to the group's primary mission and goals that further an associational common bond or whether the client-customer relationship is the central purpose for which the group exists,
Whether the group's membership eligibility requirements and membership dues are principally based on a client-customer relationship, including whether purchasing a good, product, or service from the group is a condition of membership,
Whether the group provides opportunities for members to participate in activities that further an associational common bond or whether those activities are so insubstantial that the group is indistinguishable from a vendor providing a good, product, or service to the general public, and
Whether members connect with one another in the group's governance, meetings, or other common activities, or whether the members' connection is only an interest in purchasing a good, product, or service from the group.
No one factor alone is determinative. Examples of associations based primarily on a client-customer relationship and associations where such relationships are incidental appear in Chapter 2, Section III.A.3 (Sample Single Associational Common Bonds).
III.A.2—Subsequent Changes to Association's Bylaws
If the association's membership or geographical definitions in its charter and bylaws are changed subsequent to the effective date stated in the field of membership, the credit union must submit the revised charter or bylaws for NCUA's consideration and approval prior to serving members of the association added as a result of the change.
