III. Discussion
A. Commission Actions Subject to Environmental Review
18. The Commission restructures its NEPA rules as proposed to align with recent statutory and judicial precedent. Historically, the Commission presumed, without any analysis, that certain activities constituted MFAs and then categorically excluded them unless an enumerated circumstance (as defined in its rules) required an EA. As the Commission noted in the
NEPA NPRM,
the Commission has never taken the position that every form of license or authorization demonstrates a sufficient federal nexus to qualify as a federal undertaking or MFA. Commenters contend that NEPA requires agencies to make a threshold determination about whether an action qualifies as an MFA before being subject to environmental processing. The Commission agrees. The Commission therefore revises its rules to first consider whether a proposed action constitutes an MFA. To that end, the Commission codifies the statutory definition of MFA and its exclusions. If the proposed action is an MFA, only then will the Commission's revised rules determine whether it is categorically excluded. The Commission retains its existing CE to the extent a proposed action constitutes an MFA.
19. The Commission also establishes bright-line rules that independently operate from each other and clarify when certain actions fall outside NEPA applicability altogether. First, the Commission finds that the issuance of a spectrum license does not in itself create “substantial federal control and responsibility” over facilities deployed in connection with that license. Next, the Commission concludes that private infrastructure builds are not MFAs to the extent Commission funding is not directed towards them. The Commission also finds that its spectrum-licensing functions for earth stations and space stations do not constitute MFAs or give rise to MFAs. The Commission independently confirms, for the reasons detailed below, that deployments in connection with geographic area spectrum licenses are not MFAs, to the extent they do not require antenna structure registration. Under the Commission's rules, only towers that require notification to the FAA due to physical obstruction, as set forth in section 17.7, must be registered with the Commission. For the reasons described herein, the rules adopted in this
Order
(
printed page 74027)
support the Commission's goal of streamlining its environmental review process, promoting efficiency, and encouraging deployment of infrastructure that results in more competition and technological innovation. Though complementary, each of the separate rules serves its own distinct and specific purpose to promote that goal. It is the Commission's intent that each of these rules adopted in this
Order
shall be severable. If any of the rules are declared invalid or unenforceable for any reason, the Commission finds that the remaining portions of the regulatory framework continue to fulfill the Commission's goal of streamlining environmental review, promoting efficiency, and encouraging deployment of infrastructure that results in more competition and technological innovation, and that any remaining rules not deemed invalid or unenforceable shall remain in effect and be enforced to the fullest extent permitted by law.
20. The Commission does not alter the substance of the Commission's existing radiofrequency (RF) human-safety requirements for equipment and operations deployed in connection with spectrum licenses. The Commission also maintains the Commission's registration and compliance rules for antenna structures that require antenna structure registration. The Commission finds that these rules remain independently authorized under the Communications Act.
1. Defining Commission MFAs
21. The Commission codifies in the Commission's rules the statutory definition and exceptions for MFAs set forth in NEPA, as initially proposed. The new definition limits MFAs to those actions that “the agency carrying out such action determines is subject to substantial federal control and responsibility.” A number of commenters supported the Commission's proposal. As the Commission previously noted, the Commission has traditionally borrowed from relevant definitions in CEQ's regulations implementing NEPA. Given CEQ's recission of those regulations, the Commission finds that codifying the contours of NEPA's definition into the Commission's rules will provide necessary clarity. The Commission adopts these provisions nearly wholesale, with slight modifications, to make clear that they pertain to the Commission's actions.
22. The Commission also supplements its MFA definition with bright-line rules that provide upfront clarity regarding the most common deployment scenarios that the Commission and regulated entities have encountered over the years. These rules are discussed in the sections that follow. Important principles of statutory and constitutional law guide the Commission's consideration of these scenarios, and the Commission finds them necessary to recount here.
23. First, NEPA does not enlarge an agency's powers or enable an agency to take decisions that are otherwise unauthorized or unlawful. NEPA only applies to actions or outcomes over which federal agencies have preexisting statutory authority. By its express terms, NEPA's “policies and goals” are “supplementary to those set forth in existing authorizations of Federal agencies.” Agencies like the Commission, in turn, “have only those powers given to them by Congress, and enabling legislation is generally not an open book to which the agency [may] add pages and change the plot line.” Agencies must interpret statutes through the lens of separation of powers and “a practical understanding of legislative intent,” for “Congress intends to make major policy decisions itself, not leave those decisions to agencies.” Congress does not “hide elephants in mouseholes” by “alter[ing] the fundamental details of a regulatory scheme in vague terms or ancillary provisions.” NEPA contains no grant of regulatory authority. Nor does NEPA operate to countermand, or impliedly repeal, requirements in an agency's primary statute. Rather, as the Supreme Court recently reaffirmed, NEPA is a “purely procedural” requirement that does not affect the operation of or authority granted by the agency's “governing statute and any relevant substantive environmental laws.” NEPA is a “procedural cross-check, not a substantive roadblock.” In practical terms, NEPA does not mandate that an agency achieve particular environmental results, satisfy defined compliance benchmarks, or take specific mitigation activities. NEPA's processes are merely intended to constrain “uninformed—rather than unwise—agency action.” So long as those processes are followed, the statute is agnostic as to outcomes. And in following those processes, agencies “are not required to analyze the effects of projects over which they do not exercise regulatory authority.” That regulatory authority, in turn, is evaluated by virtue of an agency's primary statutory powers.
24. Nothing in the Communications Act or any other statute gives the Commission plenary authority over the construction of infrastructure deployed by its licensees. The Commission notes it has the authority to act under the public-interest and ancillary-authority provisions of the Communications Act but such authorities are bound by the Commission's primary statutory authorities. Time and again, the courts have recognized that the Communications Act does not explicitly “grant the Commission jurisdiction over the real estate industry, an area that is normally outside the Commission's scope of authority.” After all, it would be quite odd if the Commission had authority to regulate the particulars of the Sears Tower's construction. So too with the terrestrial impacts from space launches, a responsibility expressly assigned to another agency but not the Commission. Nor does the Commission have express authority to address environmental issues relating to thermal, optical, and other emissions that use electromagnetic spectrum outside frequencies suitable, from a technical standpoint, for radiocommunications that the Commission otherwise regulates, for example, to prevent harmful interference. Rather, the Commission's relevant authorities requiring consideration of environmental effects principally extend to spectrum-based radiation that may pose a hazard to human health, along with a limited category of antenna structures deemed a “menace to air navigation.”
25. Second, NEPA's “purely procedural” requirements attach to actions undertaken by the federal government. Indeed, Congress intended NEPA as a “responsibility of the Federal Government.” And by its express terms, NEPA governs “Federal” action. Each “agency carrying out such action” is individually responsible for its own NEPA compliance and must “determine” if that action constitutes an MFA. In this regard, the relevant question before us is whether Commission action constitutes an MFA, as relevant to discharge the Commission's procedural obligations under NEPA. On the other hand, “non-Federal action” generally falls outside an agency's NEPA procedural responsibilities.
26. The Commission lacks express authority to construct and operate communications infrastructure facilities like towers and earth stations and does not direct where such infrastructure should be placed by others. It generally does not direct funding towards the construction of specific infrastructure facilities but instead directs it toward the provision of service and rules respecting the service offered. Consequently, these facilities tend to be
(
printed page 74028)
purely privately built, entirely with non-Commission funding, and the Commission regulate their radiofrequency emissions directly or indirectly by virtue of its authority to issue spectrum licenses.
27. Third, agency action is subject to NEPA only if the agency finds that it has “
substantial
Federal control and responsibility.” This new substantiality requirement heightens the MFA standard. Before the FRA's passage, NEPA did not define MFA and the definition of MFA in CEQ's now-rescinded regulations did not contain a substantiality requirement.
28. Here, the Commission's analysis will “presume that Congress is knowledgeable about existing law pertinent to interpreting the legislation it enacts” and “when Congress enacts statutes, it is aware of relevant judicial precedent.” With the substantiality qualifier now added to NEPA, the Commission infers congressional intent to limit NEPA's applicability to Federal actions. The Commission's review of its NEPA rules will therefore give the inclusion of “substantial” due weight.
29. Finally, NEPA vests in the agency considerable discretion to find that an action is not an MFA. NEPA “does not mandate particular results, but simply prescribes the necessary process.” If the Commission reasonably “determines,” as a factual matter, that its level of control and responsibility is not “substantial,” then that is the end of the matter. But this discretion does not flow equally in both directions. As noted above, the Commission may not treat its actions as MFAs if doing so would exceed the agency's statutory authorities.
2. Privately Funded Deployments
30. Because nearly all towers and communications infrastructure are privately built without targeted Commission funding, the Commission proposed to clarify the contours of the MFA exclusion for “non-Federal actions” with “no or minimal Federal funding” and incorporate them into its rules.
31. The Commission confirms, as proposed, that there is “no or minimal Federal funding” for deployments for its purposes unless Commission funding is expressly directed towards and conditioned on the construction of the particular communications facility in question. Commenters such as CTIA, UTC, and WISPA support this interpretation. The Commission likewise confirms, as proposed, that Commission funding for unspecified private deployments or operator expenses is insufficient to give rise to an MFA. The Commission rejects the contrary position, which implies that Commission funding for overall operator expenses would transform an inchoate set of infrastructure projects into Commission MFAs.
32. The Commission expects its findings as to private deployments to be outcome determinative for many infrastructure projects at issue. As the Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit recently held, under NEPA's “plain text, either the absence of federal funding
or
the absence of federal control is sufficient to take a project outside the definition of `major federal action.' ” The Commission's conclusion applies with equal force to the wireless, satellite, and space deployments discussed below.
33. The Commission also declines, as proposed, to specify at this time what level of funding is “minimal.” With little experience and few relevant examples before it, the Commission finds this issue unnecessary to resolve now and best handled on a case-by-case basis when it arises. In calling for a safe harbor based on “a dollar amount or percentage of project cost provided by federal funding,” CCA claims that the Commission's proposed approach would “neither simplify nor expedite permitting.” The Commission disagrees. The Commission provides clarity for a significant number of private deployments without targeted Commission funding. To the extent that providers may receive federal funding under existing programs related to deploying service in underserved areas across the country, that funding is not tied directly to specifically placing facilities and therefore the deployment of those facilities is excluded from the MFA definition based on the plain language of the statute.
3. Wireless Deployments
34. The Commission sought extensive comment on whether wireless infrastructure deployments in connection with Commission-issued spectrum licenses give rise to an MFA. The Commission also asked commenters to address Commission rules subjecting certain licensees to minimum buildout and coverage requirements, including whether such rules, and the Commission's ability to enforce them, give the Commission substantial control and responsibility over the deployment of the facilities needed. Many parties have argued that common private infrastructure deployments are not MFAs because they lack the requisite Federal nexus.
35. The Commission first considered its general spectrum licensing activities. The Commission then examines considerations specific to geographic and site-based licenses. In addressing these issues, the Commission notes some ambiguity in how its analysis should proceed. On one hand, the relevant “action” might be characterized as “Federal” in view of the Commission's spectrum licensing functions. Under this framing, the relevant question is whether the Commission exercises “substantial Federal control and responsibility.” On the other, the relevant “action” might be characterized as “non-Federal” given the primary role of private companies in building their wireless facilities. Here, the relevant question is whether there is “no or minimal [Commission] involvement where [the Commission] cannot control the outcome of the project.” No matter how posed, the existence of “control” spans both framings and the Commission examines that common issue below. The Commission notes that the Eleventh Circuit recently considered this very issue—namely, how to characterize the non-Federal construction of a non-Federal building for MFA purposes, when a Federal agency would control or direct some of the building's operations after construction. Looking to substance rather than form, the court characterized the action as “non-Federal” because, for practical purposes, the action being challenged on environmental grounds was the “
construction
of the facility” not the “federal supervision of and support for immigration enforcement at the facility.”
Friends of the Everglades, Inc.,
174 F.4th at 832-33. In the end, the court found that this “non-Federal action” was not an MFA because the challengers failed to demonstrate both federal funding and federal control with respect to that construction.
Id.
Many commenters agree that the proper object of the MFA analysis for present purposes is the construction of private communications infrastructure, not the Commission's spectrum licensing activities. While the Commission finds
Friends of the Everglades
persuasive and compelling given its reasoning and materially similar fact pattern, our MFA analysis in the instant decision considers both “federal” and “non-federal” scenarios.
36.
Spectrum Licensing Generally.
The Commission finds that spectrum authorizations issued by the Commission do not constitute MFAs or give rise to MFAs. They do not condition Commission authorization on subsequent non-Federal infrastructure deployments so as to require the Commission to consider the
(
printed page 74029)
environmental effects of such deployments (if any) in a NEPA review before issuing a spectrum authorization. The Commission determines that its spectrum-licensing activities are too legally, factually, and causally attenuated from wireless deployments or their effects to create the requisite level of “control” for an MFA.
37. First, as commenters correctly observe, a Commission spectrum license is legally unrelated to subsequent infrastructure deployment. As defined by statute, a “license” allows for “the use or operation of apparatus for transmission of energy, or communications, or signals by radio.” A spectrum license authorizes the use of frequencies and enables the provision of associated wireless services. The Commission issues spectrum licenses to prevent harmful interference among different users and to ensure the efficient use of scarce frequencies. A license does not constitute Commission approval to build wireless infrastructure. And the Communications Act does not require consideration of environmental factors in determining whether to issue a spectrum license.
38. The Commission's rules do not legally require licensees to build new communications infrastructure upon receiving a spectrum authorization. Under the Communications Act, licensees retain broad discretion regarding when and where to obtain a license, what infrastructure facilities they need to deploy service using their license, and where to locate those facilities. Buildout requirements, discussed below, do not affirmatively require the deployment of infrastructure. Indeed, they can be satisfied through preexisting towers, collocation, or deployment over other types of existing structures.
39. Nor does the Communications Act require other Commission authorizations to deploy wireless infrastructure. It specifically relieves the Commission from the requirement to issue a “permit for construction” for “mobile stations” or “privately owned fixed microwave stations.” Moreover, the Communications Act expressly confirms that “[s]tate or local government[s] or instrumentalit[ies] thereof,” not the Commission, retain “authority” over the “placement, construction, and modification” of wireless infrastructure. State and local governments are traditionally responsible for zoning and permitting decisions, which reveal a greater indicia of control than those taken by the Commission.
40. Likewise, the Commission's authority to revoke or modify licenses is too logically attenuated from infrastructure deployments to create the requisite level of control for an MFA, as some have claimed. Here too, license revocation or modification affects the ability to transmit signals over spectrum and the service being offered. It does not affect the licensee's control of infrastructure facilities. Indeed, revocation or suspension of a license does not require dismantlement of a tower. In any event, the Commission does not have unfettered discretion to revoke or modify licenses. Sections 312 and 316 of the Communications Act of 1934, as amended (the Act), provide that the Commission may take such actions only in certain circumstances and only after completing required procedural steps.
41. Because licensees retain discretion over how and where they deploy the facilities they need to provide service, the Commission does not maintain control over the outcome of such infrastructure projects and does not need to consider the effects of non-Federal infrastructure deployment before issuing a spectrum license.
42. Second, the issuance of spectrum licenses bears no necessary factual connection with subsequent infrastructure deployments. As an initial matter, the holders of spectrum licenses need not deploy their own infrastructure. And they often do not. With the growth of neutral-host tower operators, spectrum licensees typically opt against building their own facilities. Industry data, for example, shows that the majority of towers are owned or operated by independent tower companies rather than Commission licensees. According to one estimate, the three top tower companies own 100,000 of the estimated 185,000 cell towers in the country.” Based on information from the FCC's ASR database, which reflects a subset of towers, as of June 16, 2026, the Commission estimates that approximately 80,816 antenna structures registered in ASR are owned by infrastructure companies that own 100 or more antenna structures. This total represents a little over half of the antenna structures contained in the ASR database and also includes antenna structures owned by subsidiary and holding companies associated with these companies. Other entities (such as electric utilities, state and local governments, and transportation companies, for example) also own antenna structures. The data represents antenna structures requiring ASR registration and those voluntarily registered but would not include all antenna structures owned by these companies. In contrast, the Commission estimates that about 21,857 antenna structures are owned by service providers (including smaller wireless service providers) that own 100 or more antenna structures.
43. In most cases, tower owners and operators lease space on their towers to multiple wireless service providers. Neutral-host infrastructure operators do not necessarily build their facilities in response to the issuance of a spectrum license. In fact, infrastructure operators may build facilities without having secured any tenants.
44. Communications infrastructure often serves multiple purposes beyond spectrum-based services. For example, communications infrastructure facilities support a range of services including edge computing, AI and IoT applications. In fact, the underlying structure may have been built for purposes other than for hosting Commission-licensed services. Antennas and network equipment are often located on pre-existing building rooftops, water towers, or utility poles. These pre-existing structures were built primarily for other purposes but are used to support communications infrastructure equipment.
45. Finally, the Commission's licensing activity bears an insufficient causal connection with subsequent infrastructure deployments. The Commission rejects the argument that spectrum licensing turns non-Federal infrastructure deployment into MFAs—either because deployment is foreseeable or because it would not have occurred “but for” the Commission's issuance of a license.
46. Even if this argument were true—which it is not, for reasons explained immediately above—it would lack any meaningful limiting principle. Courts have recognized that “federal control and responsibility mean something more than the power to grant or withhold a permit, otherwise every project subject to federal permitting would be a major federal action” and that “the reach of the major federal action stops where the federal control stops and does not extend to those actions' second and third order effects.” Likewise, “[a] property owner who builds an office building must comply with the Americans with Disabilities Act, but his compliance with federal law does not make it a federal building” that is subject to NEPA. Indeed, the Commission exercises far less Federal control over facilities through spectrum licensing than other agencies whose actions were found by the courts to bear a closer relationship to the environmental effects but still fell
(
printed page 74030)
outside NEPA. Some of these judicial decisions are especially persuasive because they predate the 2023 amendments to limit NEPA's scope, during an era when courts were much more likely to find the existence of an MFA.
47. In addition to proving overbroad, an MFA analysis centered on but-for causation would also gloss over the intervening decisions by private companies to site their infrastructure. In reality, once spectrum authorizations are issued by the Commission, licensees retain control and responsibility over their facility deployments as they would with any other business decision. The existence of Commission-mandated buildout requirements does not change this conclusion. Buildout requirements require licensees to offer spectrum-based services to the public. They are intended to ensure that licensed spectrum is used robustly. But they are not a monolithic category of requirements. They vary by radio service, including establishing a single link operating on the licensed spectrum, or serving a percentage of the population in the license area, or serving a portion of the geography of the license area, within specified timeframes typically ranging from 1 year to 10 years depending on the license type.
48. Buildout requirements are performance-based standards. They specify the desired outcome through service-related metrics, but not the method of compliance or “the construction of particular facilities in any specific place.” Licensees may elect to deploy antennas on new facilities or to collocate on existing towers or other infrastructure such as utility poles. They may elect to deploy on guyed towers, monopoles, small cells, or other novel structures. Indeed, meeting a buildout requirement may not require construction at all, in the case where improved technology allows a licensee to cover a greater population by, for example, changing an antenna.
49. The Commission's buildout requirements, notably, do
not
restrict the extent of wireless deployments on environmental grounds or otherwise. Indeed, geographic area licensees can and typically do continue to deploy facilities beyond those needed to satisfy the buildout requirements associated with a license, including to densify their network operations, to modify or add sites to improve coverage, and to maximize their use of licensed spectrum. That buildout requirements serve laudable objectives does not imply substantial Federal control and responsibility, as some have argued. Nor is it dispositive that buildout requirements may “have a substantial impact on licensees' construction plans.” Again, these arguments would sweep too broadly by disregarding the intervening break in causation—namely, spectrum licensees' independent decisions to build infrastructure in the time, place, and manner of their choosing.
50. The Commission notes that the Supreme Court has strongly disfavored the kind of causally attenuated NEPA analysis that would tie Federal action to hypothetical downstream effects. The Court recently noted that “a mere `but for' causal relationship is insufficient to make an agency responsible for a particular effect.” The Court indicated that “[s]imply stated, a court may not invoke but-for causation or mere foreseeability to order agency analysis of the effects of every project that might somehow or someday follow from the current project” and that “NEPA calls for the agency to focus on the environmental effects of the project itself, not on the potential environmental effects of future or geographically separate projects.” Although the Court's decision involved a different procedural posture, the Commission finds the recency and clarity of its guidance on NEPA causality persuasive here. The fact that non-Federal facilities might foreseeably be built following the issuance of the spectrum licenses does not mean that the Commission has substantial control and responsibility over the separate placement, number, and construction of those facilities. Based on the Commission's experience with both licensing activities and environmental review, the Commission believes that the connection is too attenuated to trigger NEPA's requirements.
51. For the foregoing reasons, the Commission finds that the issuance of a spectrum license does not give rise to an MFA. In addition to, and independently of, this overarching conclusion, the Commission also confirms that the issuance of several specific categories of Commission licenses on which the Commission sought comment in the
NEPA NPRM,
including geographic area, site-based, and earth station licenses, does not constitute an MFA.
52.
Geographic area licensing.
Geographic area licensing allows deployment anywhere in the authorized area. In the
Wireless Broadband Deployment Second R&O,
the Commission determined that a geographic license “only authorizes transmissions” and bears “an insufficient connection to in itself cause the construction [of facilities] to constitute . . . major Federal action under NEPA.” Consistent with that previous determination, the Commission affirms that its issuance of a geographic area license does not create substantial Federal control and responsibility over facilities deployed in connection with that license and therefore is not an MFA.
53. Many commenters support the Commission's proposed treatment of geographic area licenses. CTIA, for instance, contends that the issuance of geographic area licenses is “remote in time and regulatory reach from deployment of individual wireless facilities.” T-Mobile agrees that there is an insufficient nexus, explaining that “[l]icensees may build anywhere within the geographic area the license covers; the Commission does not specify locations where [licensees] can or must build.” Other commenters disagree. Dynamic Environmental, for example, argues that “[t]he granting of a geographic area license not only inevitably results in the construction or modification of countless facilities, it is a required component of that license.” Wired Broadband argues that “it is reasonably foreseeable that licensees will build out facilities upon acquiring their spectrum licenses.”
54. Independent from the Commission's general conclusions regarding spectrum licensing and other categories of licenses as discussed below, the Commission specifically finds that geographic area licensing does not provide for Commission involvement in facilities deployment decisions. Rather, geographic area licensees make their own determinations about what facilities to deploy, when to deploy them, and where to locate facilities to serve their broad licensed service area. For example, the Commission does not require a licensee to deploy on an existing structure, a building, or new towers; what facility to use is the licensee's decision. As commenters note, these licensees provide no information to the Commission about planned facility deployments such as information about project timelines, facility locations, facility designs, or local approvals. They also do not routinely provide the Commission with this information after facilities are deployed. As discussed above, geographic area licensees also often deploy facilities well beyond those needed to satisfy the buildout requirements associated with their licenses to densify their networks and improve their coverage. Indeed, it would not be operationally or legally practicable for the Commission to
(
printed page 74031)
consider any effects of particular geographic-area deployments at the time of licensing. To attempt otherwise would require the Commission to speculate about the number and impact of hypothetical, future deployments before a multi-year license term has even begun. Decisions based on that speculative analysis would likely constrain providers' deployment plans in a way that would undermine the flexibility geographic-area licenses were intended to offer. Because individual, private deployment decisions cannot be foreseen with any degree of precision, their second- and third-order effects cannot be reasonably foreseeable. CTIA Reply at 7-8. As discussed herein, the Supreme Court recently confirmed that NEPA does not require agencies to consider such hypothetical downstream effects. As these factors demonstrate, geographic area licensee choices about individual deployments are informed by business objectives and operate outside the Commission's regulatory reach.
55.
Site-based licensing.
With site-based licenses, the Commission has more information about the location of facilities, but still does not control or even influence licensees' facility deployment decisions. A site-based license is a permit for operating specific radio systems, such as land mobile, point-to-point, or point-to-multipoint systems, that are fixed to a particular physical location chosen by the licensee. Whereas geographic area licenses typically confer exclusive spectrum rights, site-specific licenses tend to authorize shared rights to use spectrum within a defined area. Accordingly, for site-specific deployments, the FCC requires an individualized permit for the primary purpose of deconflicting the potential of harmful interference between different licensees.
56. In the
NEPA NPRM,
the Commission sought comment on whether this type of licensing creates substantial Federal control and responsibility over the associated facilities deployment because the Commission has discretion to authorize the construction of specific facilities at a specific location, or whether additional indicia of Federal control and responsibility were necessary to determine that site-based licensing is an MFA. Some commenters argue that the requisite Federal nexus does not exist because, similar to geographic area licensing, with site-based licenses, the Commission “authorizes the use of spectrum, but the licensee is ultimately responsible for the actual construction at the site in compliance with the parameters of its permit without exceeding the authorized power or antenna height limits specified in the license.” Others argue that issuance of site-based licenses should be viewed as an MFA because issuing an authorization for a specific site gives the Commission substantial control and responsibility for the project and its environmental effects. Dynamic Environmental also argues that deployment of facilities in connection with site-based licenses is an MFA because site-based licenses give the Commission discretion “to authorize construction of specific facilities at a specific location.”
57. The Commission finds that the issuance of a site-based license does not create substantial Federal control and responsibility over the deployment of facilities in connection with that license and therefore is not an MFA. The Commission considers broadcast towers built pursuant to a Commission construction permit to constitute “site-based licensing” as used herein. Site-based licenses are different from geographic area licenses in that they authorize the provision of service from a transmitting facility in a specific location. As with geographic area licensing, however, it is the provider, and not the Commission, that chooses to apply for a site-based license to provide service and chooses the location of its facilities, the equipment used, and the manner in which service is provided. And as with geographic area licensing, the provider may elect to deploy antennas on new facilities or to collocate on existing towers or other infrastructure such as utility poles. Accordingly, the Commission, in issuing a site-based license, does not exercise regulatory authority over the underlying infrastructure used to host licensed services, but rather over the use of spectrum by site-based licensees. As the Supreme Court has held, “agencies are not required to analyze the effects of projects over which they do not exercise regulatory authority.” While service rules that apply to site-based licenses serve primarily to prevent harmful interference and may require an applicant to give the Commission information about planned deployments, such as the geographic coordinates, height, and transmitter angles of planned facilities, the applicant retains control over the deployment of any facilities needed to operate under the license and is responsible for complying with Commission-specified spectrum coordination procedures to ensure its proposed operations will not impermissibly interfere with another licensee's operations. If the applicant cannot successfully coordinate its proposed operations, it may choose to place its facilities in a different location, adopt alternative technical parameters to address the potential interference, or deploy service using another spectrum band. Also, to the extent that the Commission requires site-based licensees to meet certain performance benchmarks, to increase the efficient and intensive use of spectrum, the licensee retains control over how to meet those performance benchmarks.
58.
Unlicensed and License-by-Rule Operations.
In the
NEPA NPRM,
the Commission asked about other actions the Commission should consider as it updates its rules to account for the new definition of MFA. In particular, the Commission asked commenters to discuss whether it would be beneficial for the Commission to clarify that certain actions do not satisfy the definition of MFA or that they meet any of its enumerated exclusions, particularly those relating to non-Federal actions. For example, the Commission noted that the Commission has always considered NEPA as inapplicable to deployment of unlicensed wireless facilities, and the Commission proposed to codify that practice into its rules.
59. In responding comments, CTIA and WISPA agreed that the Commission should clarify that NEPA does not apply to unlicensed wireless facilities while Wired Broadband argues that authorizing spectrum for unlicensed use should be viewed as an MFA. WISPA further requested that the Commission clarify that deployment of facilities authorized-by-rule pursuant to section 307(e) of the Communications Act are not MFAs. The Commission agrees that the deployment of facilities to provide unlicensed or licensed-by-rule wireless services is not an MFA under the amended NEPA. Consistent with its determinations above, the Commission finds that no MFA exists because the Commission's involvement with respect to the deployment of such facilities is too limited because the Commission lacks control over unlicensed and license-by-rule providers' facility deployment decisions and instead focuses on technical rules with respect to their use of the spectrum. The Commission amends section 1.1302 of the rules to codify this determination.
4. Satellite and Space Deployments
60.
Satellite earth stations.
The Commission also concludes, for the same reasons, that infrastructure deployments associated with earth station licenses are not subject to
(
printed page 74032)
Commission control and responsibility. With respect to earth stations, the
NEPA NPRM
sought comment on the same basic questions concerning the definition of MFA as for other types of spectrum licensing.
61. Several commenters support the Commission's proposed finding as to earth stations. Satellite Operators states, for example, that the Commission's involvement with respect to the earth station facilities deployment is limited because the Commission is involved only with “authorizing use of the relevant spectrum frequencies, prevention of harmful interference among various spectrum users, certification of the relevant radiofrequency equipment, and ensuring emissions are within radiation hazard limits.” Other commenters disagree, arguing that any ground-based facilities deployed in connection with earth station licenses should be viewed as MFAs.
62. For the same reasons the Commission describes above with respect to terrestrial geographic area and site-based licenses, the Commission finds that the construction of earth stations is not an MFA. First, the Commission's rules do not legally obligate private satellite service providers to build communications infrastructure facilities. The Commission agrees with comments that, in issuing earth station licenses, the Commission does not exercise substantial control and responsibility over the deployment of earth station facilities. Like geographic area and site-based licensees, earth station licensees retain broad discretion over their facilities deployment decisions. The earth station licensing rules serve the primary purpose of managing spectrum use and preventing harmful interference. The Commission notes that the Commission grants blanket earth station licenses when the possibility of interference is remote. They do not give the Commission control and responsibility over the facilities satellite providers choose to deploy and where they deploy them. While Commission rules that apply to earth station licenses may require an applicant to give the Commission information about planned deployments, such as the geographic coordinates, height, and transmitter angles of planned facilities, the applicant retains control over the subsequent deployment of facilities and is responsible for complying with Commission-specified coordination procedures to ensure its proposed operations will not impermissibly interfere with another licensee's operations. If the applicant cannot successfully coordinate its proposed operations, it may choose to place its facilities in a different location, adopt alternative technical parameters to address the potential interference, or deploy service using another spectrum band. Also, to the extent that the Commission requires earth station licensees to meet certain performance benchmarks, to increase the efficient and intensive use of spectrum, the licensee retains control over how to meet those performance benchmarks. Finally, because the non-Federal deployment of earth station facilities receives no Commission funding and, as outlined above, is not subject to Federal control and responsibility, it is independently disqualified as an MFA on that basis.
63.
Space-based Operations.
As proposed, the Commission finds that Commission licensed space-based operations do not constitute MFAs. As an initial matter, they are considered “extraterritorial activities” which are listed as excluded from NEPA's definition of MFA. The Commission also finds that spectrum authorizations for space-based operations do not create “Federal control and responsibility” over subsequent non-Federal space-based deployments so as to constitute MFAs or give rise to MFAs. Further, the Commission observes that certain space-based operations or activities (such as manufacturing of pharmaceutical products) will be excluded from the MFA definition to the extent they fall under NEPA's exclusion for non-Federal actions “with no or minimal Federal funding.” Activities and operations are broad terms meant to capture a wide range of space-based undertakings ranging from debris removal to on-orbit satellite repair to activities still to be imagined. As the current space age continues new business cases in space proliferate and are not necessarily confined to more traditional undertakings. The Commission speaks broadly of space undertakings with “activities” and “operations” here and, indeed, attempts to take into account new proliferations and innovations in policy considerations.
64. The Commission issues licenses under parts 5, 25, and 97 for satellite and space-based communications, and in the future the Commission will issue licenses under a new part 100. In the
NEPA NPRM,
the Commission sought comment on whether such licensing activities qualify as MFAs and noted that parties have alleged in certain cases that satellites in orbit can create impacts on the atmosphere from launches and reentries, impacts from satellites reflecting sunlight, and orbital debris caused by increased collisions in space.” Commenters offered differing views. Some, like the Commercial Space Federation, argue that satellite and orbital operations are inherently extraterrestrial and therefore fall outside the scope of NEPA, which applies only to MFAs with impacts within the United States. Commenters also note that international law establishes that outer space is beyond the borders of any sovereign state, and thus actions occurring there cannot be said to occur within U.S. jurisdiction. Other commenters, such as Dark Sky International, contend that the NEPA exclusion for extraterritorial activities should not apply because certain space-related activities, such as rocket launches and satellite de-orbiting, result in environmental effects within the United States, including atmospheric impacts and light pollution.
65. The Commission finds that Commission licensed space-based operations and activities are excluded from the definition of MFA. Excluded from that definition are “extraterritorial” activities, defined as activities with effects located “entirely outside the jurisdiction of the United States.” The Commission agrees with commenters that the potential effects of Commission licensed space-based operations do not take place within U.S. territory but instead occur in outer space. The jurisdiction of the United States extends only to territories where the United States is sovereign and the United States is not legally sovereign over outer space, as other nations are free to enter and operate there, including operations the United States disapproves of.
66. The Commission's conclusion also flows from the Outer Space Treaty, which confirms that outer space is not U.S. territory: “Outer space . . . is not subject to national appropriation by claim of sovereignty, by means of use or occupation, or by any other means.” While Outer Space Treaty signatory nations “retain jurisdiction and control” over objects and persons they send into space, this does not transform space into U.S. territory and is not dispositive of whether the effects of licensing space-based transmissions occur within the territorial jurisdiction of the United States. Specifically, the Commission declines to conclude, as some commenters urge, that because the United States writ large has certain treaty rights and obligations to exercise extraterritorial jurisdiction over outer space activities, such activities can be considered as within Commission jurisdiction for purposes of NEPA. The rule implementing this decision tracks
(
printed page 74033)
the NEPA statute and excludes from the definition of MFA extraterritorial activities or decisions, which means Commission activities or decisions with effects located entirely outside of the jurisdiction of the United States. In this context, the Commission understands that the term jurisdiction is limited to territorial jurisdiction.
67. Certain commenters argue that NEPA regulations should apply to Commission-licensed space-based operations due to the potential for light pollution over U.S. territory. However, the Commission agrees with other commenters that “[w]hen the Commission authorizes a space station to utilize certain radio frequency spectrum from orbit, the immediate effect of the agency's decision is on the operation of satellites in space, outside the territorial jurisdiction of the United States.” As the Commission discussed in the context of other licensing activities, courts have found that the scope of MFAs “stops where the federal control stops and does not extend to those actions' second and third order effects.”
68. A few commenters such as Dark Sky International contend that certain aspects of space operations, including orbital debris mitigation, result in environmental effects within the United States. These comments do not allege an actual effect within U.S. jurisdiction, but instead refer to a vague and attenuated specter of undefined, ambiguous potential effects to the atmosphere. As the D.C. Circuit recently held, a contention that a project may give rise to “indirect domestic effects,” in that case, through increased carbon emissions, “does not suffice to bring the Project within NEPA's ambit.” The Commission's orbital debris rules are primarily focused on mitigating the effects of orbital debris in space. For example, Commission rules require GSO satellites be relocated at end of mission to an orbital altitude so as practically to never re-enter the Earth's atmosphere. For NGSO space stations ending their mission in or passing through the low-Earth orbit region below 2000 km altitude, applicants must include a statement disclosing whether any portion of the spacecraft is reasonably anticipated to survive atmospheric re-entry in an uncontrolled manner. Further, if an applicant is unable to certify their NGSO spacecraft will completely demise in the atmosphere, Commission rules require the applicant to certify that the calculated casualty risk for an individual spacecraft using the NASA Debris Assessment Software or a higher fidelity assessment tool is less than 0.0001 for the total earth's surface (of which the United States comprises 1.867%). Accordingly, the Commission agrees with other commenters that there is a lack of causal connection between the Commission's orbital debris rules and activity in the jurisdiction of the United States.
69. In any event, the Commission's debris mitigation rules are based on a specific determination that orbital debris could affect the cost, reliability, continuity, and safety of satellite operations and therefore has bearing on Congress's mandate that the Commission encourage “the larger and more effective use of radio in the public interest.” NEPA analysis has never been required for the promulgation of the Commission's debris mitigation rules and, as with radio transmissions from space, the Commission finds no basis for requiring NEPA analysis of this exercise of the Commission's licensing function.
70. Additionally, as an independent and alternative basis for its decisions, the Commission finds that spectrum authorizations for space-based operations do not create “Federal control and responsibility” over subsequent non-Federal space-based deployments so as to convert them into MFAs. While the Commission, through its satellite licensing rules, assigns spectrum used in connection with space-based operations and as part of those assignments specifies some technical parameters, operational characteristics, and orbital location of the spacecraft, licensees retain broad discretion and control over other aspects related to the deployment and operations of their space systems, subject to other agencies' regulatory requirements. Many of the concerns commenters pose regarding the potential effects of space-based operations relate to the technical specifications and physical configuration of the satellite outside the control of the Commission. The private satellite operator, not the Commission, designs, controls, and executes its own plan for post mission disposal. For these reasons, similar to the Commission's geographic, site-based, and earth station licensing activities, the Commission finds that non-Federal space-based deployments and operations are not Commission MFAs.
5. Antenna Structure Registration
71. The Commission finds that regardless of whether Antenna Structure Registration (ASR) qualifies as an MFA, the Commission retains statutory authority to require review for the limited category of antenna structures that require notice of proposed construction to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) due to physical obstruction. Generally, and absent an exception, towers more than 200 feet above ground level or located near an airport require notice to the FAA and ASR registration with the FCC under FAA and FCC rules. Antenna structures that do not meet these requirements are not covered by the ASR rules and do not require registration.
72. In the
NEPA NPRM,
the Commission asked whether the ASR requirements give the Commission “substantial Federal control and responsibility” over antenna structure facilities. Alternatively, the Commission sought comment on whether ASR falls into the exclusion for non-Federal actions “with no or minimal Federal involvement” under which the Commission “cannot control the outcome of the project.” The Commission asked whether the Commission's reliance on the FAA determination of no hazard should affect a determination of whether the Commission has sufficient control over tower facilities that are registered through the ASR system. The Commission also sought comment on whether ASR may fall into the exclusion for “activities or decisions that are non-discretionary and made in accordance with the agency's statutory authority.”
73. A number of commenters urge the Commission to continue to treat ASR as an MFA. AT&T, for example, states that “ASR filings require authorizations in which the FCC has significant control and responsibility.” PEER argues, similarly, that “[b]ecause construction may not proceed without ASR registration, the FCC exercises sufficient control over tower construction to trigger NEPA.” Other commenters argue that the Commission's involvement in tower registration is too limited. The Electric Utilities Coalition, for example, argues that ASR should not be considered an MFA because ASR is “a mere registration,” and the “FCC relies on the FAA to determine whether construction of a tower poses a hazard to air navigation.” It also contends that ASR should fall within the exclusion for non-Federal actions “with no or minimal Federal involvement” under which the Commission “cannot control the outcome of the project,” because “ASR only provides FAA clearance that the tower does not present a hazard to air navigation and does not involve any Commission funding for the construction of the tower or any other control over the construction of the tower.”
74. The Commission first finds that the Commission has statutory authority
(
printed page 74034)
to require ASR and related compliance obligations for antenna structures that are deemed a menace to air navigation. Section 303(q) of the Communications Act gives the Commission the authority “to require the painting and/or illumination of radio towers if and when in its judgment such towers constitute, or there is a reasonable possibility that they may constitute, a menace to air navigation.” As part of a broader suite of aviation safety rules across different statutes, section 303(q) incorporates the judgment of the FAA Administrator and provides the Commission with discretion to exercise its judgment in determining whether the structure poses a threat to safety. The Commission has determined that registration and review of planned facility construction is necessary in order for it to fulfill its statutory responsibility to require not only painting and illumination but also to “require the owner to dismantle and remove the tower when the Administrator of the [FAA] determines that there is a reasonable possibility that it may constitute a menace to air navigation.” Section 303(r) of the Act provides that the Commission shall “make such rules and regulations and prescribe such restrictions and conditions, not inconsistent with law, as may be necessary to carry out the provisions of this chapter.”
75. Based on this authority, the Commission's ASR rules require the registration of antenna structures that require notice of proposed construction to the FAA due to physical obstruction. Following FAA criteria, the rules provide that generally, and absent an exception, towers more than 200 feet above ground level or located near an airport require notice to the FAA and ASR registration with the FCC to ensure that they do not present a hazard to air navigation and incorporate FAA requirements for agency notification. The ASR rules do not apply to antenna structures that do not meet these criteria. Antenna structure owners must submit FCC Form 854 and a valid FAA determination of “no hazard” before the Commission will issue the antenna registration. To serve the public interest and ensure that members of the public have the opportunity to raise concerns about potential tower registrations, the rules include an environmental review component, requiring tower owners to conduct environmental review using the Commission's NEPA procedures. Under this requirement, applicants must complete a notice process and determine whether an EA, as specified under the agency's NEPA rules, is necessary for the proposed tower. Interested persons may also submit a request for environmental processing of the proposed antenna structure registration.
76. In addition to its statutory authority to require ASR and associated compliance measures, the Commission also exercises more control over towers that must be registered in ASR due to physical obstruction. The Commission's ASR program is a direct implementation of exclusive federal sovereignty over airspace in the United States. The Commission's statutory mandate to require proper lighting and marking of communications towers furthers the nationwide regulatory framework for maintaining the safety of United States airspace.
6. Conclusion
77. The Commission amends § 1.1302 to codify in the Commission's rules the statutory definition and exceptions for MFA set forth in NEPA. The Commission also amends § 1.1302 of the rules to codify the Commission's independent determinations that deployments of facilities in connection with geographic area spectrum licenses, site-based spectrum licenses, unlicensed or licensed-by-rule wireless services, and satellite earth stations do not qualify as an MFAs to the extent the deployments do not require antenna structure registration and that actions associated with space-based operations, including the launch, deployment, and operation of space stations are not MFAs. The Commission adopts its proposal to rescind § 1.1312 from the rules to remove environmental review requirements for facilities deployed in connection with facilities for which no preconstruction authorization is required. The Commission finds that § 1.1312 is no longer necessary for compliance with NEPA requirements based on its determination that deployment of facilities in connection with geographic area licensing does not qualify as an MFA. The Commission notes, however, as described further below, that equipment and operations deployed in connection with spectrum licenses remain subject to the Commission's existing RF requirements. The Commission maintains its registration and compliance rules for antenna structures that require antenna structure registration. The Commission finds that these environmental rules remain authorized under the Communications Act.
78. The Commission finds that these updates reflect the “best reading” of the amended NEPA statute, the Commission's exercise of environmental responsibilities under the Communications Act and administrative law, and the Supreme Court's “course correction” to NEPA in
Seven County Infrastructure Coalition.
Together, these developments outline a set of principles, discussed extensively at the beginning of this section, that provide the legal basis for the actions the Commission takes in this
Order.
The Commission agrees with comments that revising the Commission's NEPA rules to bring them into compliance with the current statutory and legal framework serves the public interest, consistent with section 319(d) of the Communications Act. To the extent that section 319(d) gives the Commission policy discretion to act in the public interest, that discretion does not enable the Commission to act ultra vires.
79. The Commission disagrees with comments suggesting that its findings would be inconsistent with the Court's decision in
United Keetoowah.
In
United Keetoowah,
the Court adopted a narrow holding that focused on the Commission's application of the public interest standard under section 319(d) in the context of its decision in the
Wireless Broadband Deployment Second R&O
to remove its limited approval authority to require environmental review of small cells under § 1.1312. The Court found that the Commission failed to justify its public interest determination and remanded back to the Commission to conduct further fact finding to justify its decision. The Court did not address the Commission's separate determination that a geographic license “only authorizes transmissions” and bears “an insufficient connection to in itself cause the construction [of facilities] to constitute . . . major Federal action under NEPA” nor did it find that the costs of greater flexibility outweighed its benefits. Here, the basis for the
Order
's findings was not addressed in
United Keetoowah.
The Commission's
Order
responds to legislative, judicial, and executive branch developments that transpired after
United Keetoowah.
Moreover, whereas the court's decision considered NEPA and NHPA issues in a conjoined setting, the Commission's
Order
addresses NEPA only. Simply put, the questions before the court in
United Keewotah
arose from a different set of substantive rules and a unique procedural posture. Recent developments to narrow the scope of actions subject to NEPA review provide an independent, extrinsic legal basis for the Commission's rule changes and supersede any discretionary policy-
(
printed page 74035)
based considerations to the contrary under a public interest analysis.
80. Additionally, the
United Keetoowah
decision focused on the Commission's limited approval authority in § 1.1312. At the time § 1.1312 was adopted, all Commission actions were assumed to be MFAs and the Commission retained limited approval authority to ensure that it could fully comply with Federal environmental laws. In this
Order,
the Commission updates its NEPA framework to first consider whether a particular action meets the definition of an MFA under the amended NEPA's requirements. As a result of the Commission's determination that spectrum authorizations issued by the Commission, including geographic-area licenses, do not constitute MFAs or give rise to MFAs, the rationale for § 1.1312 no longer exists. In rescinding § 1.1312, the Commission now determines that the public interest cannot be served by categorically requiring preconstruction review over deployments that are not MFAs as a matter of law.
81. Even so, the Commission finds that its revised NEPA framework will serve the public interest by bringing consumer and public benefits. Congress amended NEPA in significant ways based on its public-interest determination that NEPA had generated outsized permitting burdens relative to its procedural benefits. The Commission finds that updating its NEPA rules will further the public-interest benefits that Congress intended when it adopted the FRA. Information in the record shows that NEPA compliance adds an estimated five months of delay to the deployment of new technologies and service upgrades and that, without permitting reforms, the Commission's legacy environmental rules would result in over $2.2 billion in direct regulatory compliance costs between 2025-2035, and a total of at least $7.5 billion in welfare and economic activity loss over that same period. Additionally, as described further in Appendix D, the Commission's regulatory impact analysis for this proceeding shows that the changes the Commission adopts will increase economic welfare by reducing costs for wireless licensees. The Commission estimates the present value of the increased economic welfare created by the streamlining of the NEPA review procedures for 2026-2030 is $169.5 million at a 3% discount rate or $157.4 million at a 7% discount rate. By contrast, the potential harms raised by some commenters are less significant and unsupported. The Commission finds that the benefits of reducing the costs and delays associated with environmental review outweigh the potential harms and the Commission expects the rule changes it adopts will encourage the deployment of infrastructure that will result in greater competition and innovation. The Commission also finds that
CTIA-Wireless Ass'n
v.
FCC,
466 F.3d 105 (D.C. Cir. 2006), does not preclude the actions the Commission takes in this
Order.
That decision was issued well prior to the amendments to NEPA in 2023 and the Supreme Court's
Seven County Infrastructure Coalition
decision in 2025. As a consequence, the CTIA case has no bearing on the post-2023 meaning of an MFA and the legal framework applicable to NEPA to which today's actions respond.
B. Streamlining the Commission's Review Procedures
1. Commission's Categorical Exclusion and Extraordinary Circumstances Rules
82. NEPA requires an agency to prepare an environmental document—either an EA or an EIS—for a proposed agency action unless the action is subject to a CE, is nondiscretionary, or when otherwise excluded by law. For over 40 years, the Commission has determined and repeatedly reaffirmed that telecommunications infrastructure deployment presents limited environmental impact. Accordingly, the Commission applies an overarching, broad CE rather than multiple CEs tailored to various agency actions. Under this broad CE, Commission MFAs are categorically excluded from further environmental processing unless one or more of the extraordinary circumstances listed in § 1.1307 are implicated. The Commission also categorically excludes certain actions that involve alterations to existing facilities, such as collocations of equipment on existing antenna structures, pole replacements, or towers constructed in an established “antenna farm.” In the existing rules, § 1.1307(a), (b)(1)(i)(C), and the Note to (d) provide enumerated factors, which the Commission commonly refers to as extraordinary circumstances, that the Commission has determined, when present, may have a significant environmental effect and thus require preparation of an EA. Sections 1.1307(c) and (d) provide processes for identifying extraordinary circumstances not identified by applicants or otherwise enumerated in the rules which, if present, may have a significant environmental impact and thus require preparation of an EA. The Commission sought comment on whether changes to the Commission's rules governing when an EA is required are necessary, including whether it should keep its single broad CE or adopt a set of individual CEs, whether the Commission should delete or revise the list of extraordinary circumstances in § 1.1307(a) and the note to § 1.1307(d), and whether it should delete or revise §§ 1.1307(c) and 1.1307(d).
83.
Retention of the Commission's Broad Categorical Exclusion.
Under NEPA, an EA is required when a proposed MFA “does not have a reasonably foreseeable significant effect on the quality of the human environment, or if the significance of such effect is unknown,” unless the agency finds that the action is categorically excluded or excluded by another provision of law. For Commission actions, applicants initially determine whether an enumerated factor—or extraordinary circumstance—requiring the preparation of an EA is present. The Commission has long found that, generally, Commission actions that do not involve the factors enumerated in the Commission's rules have no significant effect on the quality of the human environment and are thus categorically excluded.
84. Consistent with the Commission's historical finding that communications infrastructure has limited environmental effects, the Commission will continue its existing approach of applying a broad CE with enumerated extraordinary circumstances which, if present, require the preparation of an EA. Industry stakeholders support this approach and praise it for providing efficiency and regulatory certainty while ensuring communications infrastructure is deployed in a responsible and sustainable manner. While some commenters suggested changes to the Commission's approach, such as adopting new, action-specific CEs or expanding the scope of the existing CE, the Commission declines to adopt these proposals because they are unnecessary and unsupported by the record. Commenters arguing for the expansion of the CE provide examples of scenarios already addressed by the Commission's existing rules. Accordingly, the record does not contain sufficient, detailed, or technical evidence supporting the Commission changing course after 40 years to require a more particularized approach with greater compliance burdens. Further, such a change is not required by the amended statute, relevant case law, or Commission policy objectives.
85.
Adoption of Another Agency's Categorical Exclusion.
To accelerate permitting, the amended NEPA statute prescribes the process by which one agency may adopt another's CE, where
(
printed page 74036)
appropriate. Under the statute, an agency must follow four steps when adopting another agency's CE: (i) identify the CE listed in another agency's NEPA procedures that covers a category of proposed actions or related actions; (ii) consult with the agency that established the CE to ensure that the proposed adoption of the CE to a category of actions is appropriate; (iii) identify to the public the CE that the agency plans to use for its proposed actions; and (iv) document adoption of the CE. The Commission now adopts a rule implementing this process.
86. In the
NEPA NPRM,
the Commission noted the potential for the Commission to adopt CEs from other agencies that have analyzed the potential environmental effects of communications facilities under NEPA, such as the NTIA or the Rural Utilities Service, and sought comment on whether the Commission, when applying an adopted CE, should consider the extraordinary circumstances of the agency originating an adopted CE, the Commission's own extraordinary circumstances, or both. The Commission also sought comment on whether and how to address third party petitions when applying a CE adopted from another agency.
87. While no commenters argue against the Commission's adoption of a rule allowing for the adoption of another agency's CE, some argue against the necessity or value of Commission's application of an adopted CE to a Commission MFA in some circumstances. The Commission agrees with comments that adopting another agency's CE may not make sense in many instances, for example, because of the broad nature of the Commission's own CE or because another agency's CE incorporates a requirement to determine whether an EA is required under the Commission's rules anyway. However, the Commission rejects the premise that there could never be circumstances under which it would be beneficial and appropriate for the Commission to adopt a CE from another agency. For example, it may be appropriate and beneficial to Commission licensees for the Commission to adopt another agency's CE applicable to new authorities or actions with which the Commission does not have adequate experience to make the determination required by
42 U.S.C. 4336e(1)
and that are not otherwise categorically excluded under the Commission's rules. CEs across the federal government vary greatly and are subject to changes and additions over time. Accordingly, the Commission adopts this rule to account for circumstances in which it may be appropriate for the Commission, and beneficial to Commission applicants, for the Commission to adopt another agency's CE, whether now or in the future.

Further Revisions to § 1.1306.
The Commission sought comment on whether, in the event the Commission chose to retain a broad CE, as it is doing today, it should revise what is now section 1.1306(a) to more closely track NEPA's definition of “categorical exclusion” as “a category of actions that a Federal agency has determined normally does not significantly affect the quality of the human environment.” Accordingly, the Commission modifies § 1.1306(a) to read: “Except as provided in § 1.1307(c) of this chapter, the Commission has determined that a Commission major Federal action not covered by paragraphs (b) and (c) of this section normally does not significantly affect the quality of the human environment and is categorically excluded from further environmental processing.” Among other changes to more closely adhere to the statutory definition, the Commission strikes the word “cumulatively” from the rules. These changes are supported by CTIA and WISPA.
93. The Commission rejects the contrary position of some commenters, including a coalition of state attorneys general, which argue that the Commission should evaluate cumulative effects because cumulative effects “occur as a result of the agency's decision” and are reasonably foreseeable, and because NEPA does not permit the wholesale discounting of a particular type of reasonably foreseeable effects just because they are cumulative. As an initial matter, this argument appears to presuppose a broad and now-outdated definition of MFA that would encompass private activities that are not directly funded or controlled by the Commission. In any event, the argument is premised on CEQ guidance from 1997 that significantly predates the 2023 amendments to NEPA. Since the 2023 amendments, the Supreme Court clarified that NEPA requires consideration of the “project at hand,” not the “environmental effects of [a] separate project” that “breaks the chain of proximate causation between the project at hand and the environmental effects of the separate project.” Even if the separate project is “factually foreseeable,” the Court explained, an agency is not reasonably held responsible for those effects. Therefore, NEPA only requires the Commission to evaluate the impact of individual projects, not the cumulative effects of multiple projects lacking a proximate cause to the individual project, even if those effects may be foreseeable. In evaluating the impact of an individual project, applicants, and the FCC, will take into account the existing condition of the environment.

The Commission revises to clarify this point and moves the text of the Note to a new § 1.1306(d) because the language of the Note is regulatory and not explanatory in nature, and therefore is more appropriately treated as rule text.

Under former Note 3 to § 1.1306, towers constructed in areas where similar antenna towers are clustered, called antenna farms, are categorically excluded unless the addition of a tower would cause human exposure to RF emissions in excess of the Commission's health and safety guidelines cited in § 1.1307(b). As with former Note 1, the Commission revises and moves the text of former Note 3 to new § 1.1306(e). The Commission also clarifies in new § 1.1306(e) that towers over 450 feet tall continue to require the preparation of an EA, even if they are located in an antenna farm because of the potential for such a tower to affect protected migratory or other bird species.

Decoupling NEPA and the NHPA.
Historically, the Commission's rules implementing section 106 of the NHPA have been incorporated in its NEPA rules and processes for purposes of efficiency and streamlining. Given the recent changes to the amended NEPA statute that require us to amend the Commission's NEPA rules and processes, the Commission sought comment on whether to decouple NEPA and NHPA review in its rules and, if so, whether to do so by deleting § 1.1307(a)(4), and whether there are any enumerated extraordinary circumstances which, if present, require the preparation of an EA, that should be omitted. For the reasons explained below, the Commission finds that that decoupling is appropriate and some streamlining of the categories of the Commission's extraordinary circumstances is warranted.

Sections 1.1307(c) and (d).

PEER's suggestion would undermine the intended purpose of these provisions to capture circumstances in which a proposed action may have a significant environmental effect not identified by applicants or enumerated in the rules. Instead, the Commission continues to apply the clear standards enumerated in the Commission's list of extraordinary circumstances, coupled with § 1.1307(c), under which the Commission can independently evaluate the merit to a claim that a proposed MFA will have a significant environmental effect.
