V. EPA Responses to Major Comments on the Proposed Determination
EPA announced its proposal to approve, in part, the Louisiana CCR permit program, and initiated a 60-day public comment period, on June 5, 2026 (
91 FR 34189
). EPA also held a public hearing on July 21, 2026. The public hearing provided interested persons with the opportunity to present information, views, or arguments concerning EPA's proposal. Oral comments received during the public hearing are documented in the transcript of the hearing, which, along with the written comments received during the public comment period, are included in the docket for this Action.
During the comment period, EPA received 43 written comments from members of the public, plus an additional comment from the public hearing. EPA received several comments that support approval of Louisiana's CCR permit program and LDEQ's ability to administer the program. Other commenters allege that LDEQ has demonstrated that it cannot be relied upon to adequately implement the program. These comments rely on language from the 2024 Alabama Program Denial (
89 FR 48774
, June 7, 2024) and judicial opinions on certain CCR court cases to support their position. The commenters provided detailed concerns about CCR facilities in Louisiana. Commenters also raised questions regarding certain definitions that are different from the Federal regulations and the adequacy of public participation. EPA also received several comments expressing concerns over CCR contamination of the environment, pertaining to concerns that LDEQ would not properly implement the program. EPA's responses to individual comments are provided in the Response to Comments document included in the docket for this Action.

Alternative Closure Demonstration Jurisdiction
Comment summary:
A commenter requested clarity regarding the
40 CFR 257.103(f)(2)
alternative closure demonstration requirements, which set forth the Part A demonstration and approval process finalized by EPA in 2020. The commenter asserted that, under
40 CFR 257.103(f)(2)
, and accordingly as incorporated by Louisiana, an unlined or clay-lined CCR surface impoundment could continue to receive CCR and non-CCR wastestreams after April 2021 if the facility submitted an application indicating its intent to cease operation of its coal-fired boiler(s) and complete closure of the impoundment within prescribed
(
printed page 73683)
timeframes—October 2023 for units 40 acres or smaller, and October 2028 for units larger than 40 acres.
In November 2020, three CCR facilities in Louisiana (Big Cajun II Power Plant, Brame Energy Center, Dolet Hills Power Station) submitted a timely Part A demonstration under
40 CFR 257.103(f)(2)
, and on January 11, 2022, EPA determined that the three CCR facilities' demonstrations were complete and confirmed that the cease waste receipt deadline is tolled until EPA issues its final decision. To date, EPA has not issued a final determination on these Part A demonstrations. The commenter urges the Agency to clarify whether EPA or LDEQ will have jurisdiction over pending Part A demonstrations upon EPA's final approval of LDEQ's State CCR permit program.
LDEQ's regulations incorporate the Part A provisions at
40 CFR 257.103
. Additionally, the commenter notes that LDEQ's permit program application stated that, upon EPA's approval, LDEQ would assume jurisdiction over any Part A demonstrations pending before EPA at that time, but EPA did not address this statement in its Proposed Decision.
On November 28, 2025, EPA proposed to extend the
40 CFR 257.103(f)(2)
alternative closure deadlines to cease coal combustion and complete closure of the underlying impoundment by three years—from October 17, 2028 to October 17, 2031. EPA's 2026 Unified Agenda anticipated a final rule by July 2026, but the revision has not yet been finalized. Because Louisiana incorporated the Federal CCR regulations as amended through July 1, 2022, the extended 2031 deadline, once finalized, would not be automatically incorporated into LDEQ's approved CCR permit program. This creates a potential regulatory gap for facilities with pending Part A demonstrations and/or those that in the future may operate under Part A demonstrations in Louisiana.
In the event LDEQ assumes jurisdiction of the pending Part A demonstrations in the State, the commenter urges EPA and LDEQ to coordinate on providing a prompt mechanism to allow Louisiana facilities with those pending or granted demonstrations to operate under the revised 2031 deadline, if finalized. 40 CFR 257.103(f)(2)

40 CFR 257.103(f)(2)
deadline into its State regulations and EPA can expeditiously approve this minor State program modification.

VI. Approval of the Louisiana CCR Permit Program
The partial Louisiana CCR permit program, as described in its Application and Units II and III of this preamble, is approved. Because this is a partial program approval, only the State requirements that have been approved will operate in lieu of the analogous Federal requirements in RCRA section 4005(d)(3). Accordingly, owners and operators of CCR units in Louisiana will remain responsible for compliance with all applicable requirements in
40 CFR part 257
for which Louisiana did not seek approval that are listed in Unit III.B. EPA will implement these provisions under the Federal CCR program, until and unless Louisiana submits a revised CCR permit program application and receives approval for these provisions. A permit issued by a State is not a shield for noncompliance with these
40 CFR part 257
provisions. For all CCR units in the State, the Federal regulations at
40 CFR part 257
will remain in effect until such time that LDEQ permits those units under its approved CCR permit program after providing an opportunity to comment on the entire permit consistent with the process required for new permits.
RCRA section 4005(d)(1)(D) specifies that EPA will review a State CCR permit program:
From time to time, as the Administrator determines necessary, but not less frequently than once every 12 years;
Not later than three years after the date on which the Administrator revises the applicable criteria for CCR units under
part 257 of title 40, CFR
(or successor regulations promulgated pursuant to RCRA sections 1008(a)(3) and 4004(a));
Not later than one year after the date of a significant release (as defined by the Administrator), that was not authorized at the time the release occurred, from a CCR unit located in the State; and
At the request of any other State that asserts that the soil, groundwater, or surface water of the State is or is likely to be adversely affected by a release or potential release from a CCR unit located in the State for which the program was approved.
RCRA section 4005(d)(4)(B) also provides that in a State with an approved CCR permitting program, the Administrator may commence an administrative or judicial enforcement action under RCRA section 3008 if:
The State requests that the Administrator provide assistance in the performance of an enforcement action; or
After consideration of any other administrative or judicial enforcement action involving the CCR unit, the Administrator determines that an enforcement action is likely to be necessary to ensure that the CCR unit is operating in accordance with the criteria established under the State's permit program.
VII. Final Action
In accordance with
42 U.S.C. 6945(d)
, EPA is approving the Louisiana partial CCR permit program.

In accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, the IRS is inviting comments on the information collection request outlined in this notice.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The IRS, in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA) (
44 U.S.C. 3506(c)(2)(A)
), provides the general public and Federal agencies with an opportunity to comment on proposed, revised, and continuing collections of information. This helps the IRS assess the impact and minimize the burden of its information collection requirements. Comments submitted in response to this notice will be summarized and/or included in the request for OMB approval. All comments will become a matter of public record, and viewable on relevant websites. For this reason, please do not include in your comments information of a confidential nature, such as sensitive personal information. Comments are invited on: (a) Whether the collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the agency, including whether the information shall have practical utility; (b) the accuracy of the agency's estimate of the burden of the collection of information; (c) ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; (d) ways to minimize the burden of the collection of information on respondents, including through the use of automated collection techniques or other forms of information technology; and (e) estimates of capital or start-up costs and costs of operation, maintenance, and purchase of services to provide information.
Title:
Form 5307—Application for Determination for Adopters of Modified Nonstandardized Pre-Approved Plans.
OMB Control Number:
1545-0200.
Form Number:
5307.
Abstract:
An adopting employer of a nonstandardized pre-approved plan that has made modifications to the terms of the pre-approved plan that are not extensive, or an adopting employer of any pre-approved plan (either standardized or nonstandardized) that amends its pre-approved plan solely to add language to satisfy the requirements of Internal Revenue Code (IRC) sections 415 and 416 due to the required aggregation of plans, use Form 5307 to request a determination letter from the IRS. The IRS uses the information to determine if the adopted plan is qualified under IRC sections 401(a) and 501(a). The form may not be used to request a determination letter for a multiple employer plan.

Pursuant to section 1009 of the Federal Advisory Committee Act, as amended, notice is hereby given of a meeting of the National Advisory Council for Complementary and Integrative Health.
The meeting will be open to the public as indicated below, with attendance limited to space available. Individuals who plan to attend and need special assistance, such as sign language interpretation or other reasonable accommodations, should notify the Contact Person listed below in advance of the meeting. The open session will be videocast and can be accessed from the NIH Videocasting and Podcasting website:
https://nccih.nih.gov/​about/​naccih
and through the NIH Videocast web page
https://videocast.nih.gov/​
.
The meeting will be closed to the public in accordance with the provisions set forth in sections 552b(c)(4) and 552b(c)(6), Title 5 U.S.C., as amended. The grant applications and the discussions could disclose confidential trade secrets or commercial property such as patentable material, and personal information concerning individuals associated with the grant applications, the disclosure of which would constitute a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy.

AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.
ACTION:
Notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM).
SUMMARY:
The FAA proposes to supersede Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2015-17-10, which applies to certain SOCATA (type certificate currently held by Daher Aircraft, SAS) (Daher) Model TBM 700 airplanes. AD 2015-17-10 requires repetitively inspecting the forging body of the main landing gear (MLG) for cracks and, depending on findings, performing corrective actions. AD 2015-17-10 allows for replacement of affected MLG with a reinforced landing gear as a terminating action for repetitive inspections. Since the FAA issued AD 2015-17-10, additional MLG serviceable parts have been developed, and it has been determined that dye penetrant is no longer an authorized inspection method. This proposed AD would continue to require the actions of AD 2015-17-10, add the additional serviceable parts, and eliminate the option of using dye penetrant as an inspection method. The FAA is proposing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.
DATES:
The FAA must receive comments on this NPRM by January 4, 2027.
ADDRESSES:
You may send comments, using the procedures found in
14 CFR 11.43
and
11.45
, by any of the following methods:
Federal eRulemaking Portal:
Go to
regulations.gov
. Follow the instructions for submitting comments.
Fax:
(202) 493-2251.
Mail:
U.S. Department of Transportation, Docket Operations, M-91, West Building Fifth Floor, Room W58-213, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590.
Hand Delivery:
Deliver to Mail address above between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays.
AD Docket:
You may examine the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-13817; or in person at Docket Operations between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays. The AD docket contains this NPRM, the mandatory continuing airworthiness information (MCAI), any comments received, and other information. The street address for Docket Operations is listed above.

For Daher Aircraft, Daher Aerospace, Daher-Socata, or EADS-Socata TBM material identified in this proposed AD, contact Daher Aircraft, SAS, Daher Aerospace Customer Support, Airplane Business Unit, Tarbes—Cedex 9, France; phone: +1 833 826 2273; email:

zakaria.f.abdi@faa.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Comments Invited
The FAA invites you to send any written relevant data, views, or arguments about this proposal. Send your comments using a method listed under
ADDRESSES
. Include “Docket No. FAA-2026-13817; Project Identifier MCAI-2026-00492-A” at the beginning of your comments. The most helpful comments reference a specific portion of the proposal, explain the reason for any recommended change, and include supporting data. The FAA will consider all comments received by the closing date and may amend the proposal because of those comments.
Except for Confidential Business Information (CBI) as described in the following paragraph, and other information as described in
14 CFR 11.35
, the FAA will post all comments received, without change, to
regulations.gov,
including any personal information you provide. The agency will also post a report summarizing each substantive verbal contact received about this NPRM.
Confidential Business Information
CBI is commercial or financial information that is both customarily and actually treated as private by its owner. Under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) (
5 U.S.C. 552
), CBI is exempt from public disclosure. If your comments responsive to this NPRM contain commercial or financial information that is customarily treated as private, that you actually treat as private, and that is relevant or responsive to this NPRM, it is important that you clearly designate the submitted comments as CBI. Please mark each page of your submission containing CBI as “PROPIN.” The FAA will treat such marked submissions as confidential under the FOIA, and they will not be placed in the public docket of this NPRM. Submissions containing CBI should be sent to Zakaria Abdi, Aviation Safety Engineer, FAA, 1600 Stewart Avenue, Suite 410, Westbury, NY 11590. Any commentary that the FAA receives which is not specifically designated as CBI will be placed in the public docket for this rulemaking.
(
printed page 73715)
Background
The FAA issued AD 2015-17-10, Amendment 39-18243 (
80 FR 51456
, August 25, 2015) (AD 2015-17-10), for certain SOCATA (type certificate currently held by Daher) Model TBM 700 airplanes. AD 2015-17-10 was prompted by MCAI originated by the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA), which is the Technical Agent for the Member States of the European Union. EASA issued AD 2006-0085R2, dated January 16, 2015 (EASA AD 2006-0085R2), to correct an unsafe condition identified as cracks in the MLG cylinder, which could cause the MLG to fail.
AD 2015-17-10 requires repetitively inspecting the forging body of the MLG for cracks and, depending on findings, corrective actions. AD 2015-17-10 allows for replacement of affected MLG with a reinforced landing gear as a terminating action for repetitive inspections The FAA issued AD 2015-17-10 to detect and address cracks in the MLG cylinder, which could cause the MLG to fail. Failure of the MLG cylinder could result in a collapsed MLG during takeoff or landing runs and possible reduced structural integrity of the airplane.
Actions Since AD 2015-17-10 Was Issued
Since the FAA issued AD 2015-17-10, EASA revised EASA AD 2006-0085R2 and issued EASA AD 2006-0085R3, dated December 2, 2025 (EASA AD 2006-0085R3), to more fully define affected and serviceable parts and allow for installation of additional part numbers of reinforced MLGs developed by Daher as optional terminating action for the repetitive inspections. EASA then superseded EASA AD 2006-0085R3 and issued EASA AD 2026-0076, dated April 10, 2026 (EASA AD 2026-0076) (also referred to as the MCAI). The MCAI states that the dye penetrant inspection is not authorized for accomplishing the repetitive special detail inspection. EASA AD 2026-0076 partially retains the requirements of EASA AD 2006-0085R3 and removes the dye penetrant inspection.
You may examine the MCAI in the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-13817.
Material Incorporated by Reference Under
1 CFR Part 51
The FAA reviewed Daher Aircraft Mandatory Service Bulletin (SB) 70-130, Revision 5, dated January 2026; and Daher Aerospace Mandatory SB 70-130, Revision 4, dated October 2025. This material specifies procedures for inspecting the forging body of the MLG for cracks and replacing any cracked part.
This proposed AD would also require Daher-Socata TBM Aircraft Mandatory SB 70-130, Revision 3, dated December 2014, which the Director of the Federal Register approved for incorporation by reference as of September 29, 2015 (
80 FR 51456
, dated August 25, 2015).
This material is reasonably available because the interested parties have access to it through their normal course of business or by the means identified in the
ADDRESSES
section.
FAA's Determination
These products have been approved by the civil aviation authority of another country and are approved for operation in the United States. Pursuant to the FAA's bilateral agreement with this State of Design Authority, that authority has notified the FAA of the unsafe condition described in the MCAI and material referenced above. The FAA is issuing this NPRM after determining that the unsafe condition described previously is likely to exist or develop on other products of the same type design.
Proposed AD Requirements in This NPRM
This proposed AD would require accomplishing the actions specified in the material already described, except as discussed under “Differences Between this Proposed AD and the Referenced Material.”
Differences Between This Proposed AD and the Referenced Material
Where Daher Aircraft Mandatory Service Bulletin No. SB 70-130, Revision 5, dated January 2026, provides instructions to contact Daher to obtain approved repair instructions and accomplish that repair accordingly, this AD instead requires contacting either the Manager, International Validation Branch, FAA; EASA; or Daher's EASA Design Organization Approval (DOA) for approved repair instructions and, within the compliance time specified therein, accomplish those instructions accordingly, including post-repair follow-on action(s), as applicable. If approved by the DOA, the approval must include the DOA-authorized signature.

Authority for This Rulemaking
Title 49 of the United States Code specifies the FAA's authority to issue rules on aviation safety. Subtitle I, section 106, describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII, Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the Agency's authority.
The FAA is issuing this rulemaking under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart III, Section 44701: General requirements. Under that section, Congress charges the FAA with promoting safe flight of civil aircraft in air commerce by prescribing regulations for practices, methods, and procedures the Administrator finds necessary for safety in air commerce. This regulation is within the scope of that authority because it addresses an unsafe condition that is likely to exist or develop on products identified in this rulemaking action.
Regulatory Findings
The FAA determined that this proposed AD would not have federalism implications under
Executive Order 13132
. This proposed AD would not have a substantial direct effect on the States, on the relationship between the national Government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government.
For the reasons discussed above, I certify that the proposed regulation:
(1) Is not a “significant regulatory action” under
Executive Order 12866
,
(2) Would not affect intrastate aviation in Alaska, and
(3) Would not have a significant economic impact, positive or negative, on a substantial number of small entities under the criteria of the Regulatory Flexibility Act.

The Proposed Amendment
Accordingly, under the authority delegated to me by the Administrator, the FAA proposes to amend
14 CFR part 39
as follows:
PART 39—AIRWORTHINESS DIRECTIVES
1.
The authority citation for part 39 continues to read as follows:
Authority:
49 U.S.C. 106(g)
,
40113
,
44701
.
§ 39.13
[Amended]
2.
The FAA amends § 39.13 by:
a.
Removing Airworthiness Directive 2015-17-10, Amendment 39-18243 (
80 FR 51456
, August 25, 2015); and
b.
Adding the following new airworthiness directive:
Daher Aircraft, SAS:
Docket No. FAA-2026-13817; Project Identifier MCAI-2026-00492-A.
(a) Comments Due Date
The FAA must receive comments on this airworthiness directive (AD) by January 4, 2027.
(b) Affected ADs
This AD replaces AD 2015-17-10, Amendment 39-18243 (
80 FR 51456
, August 25, 2015) (AD 2015-17-10), which superseded AD 2007-04-13, Amendment 39-14945 (
72 FR 7576
, February 16, 2007) (AD 2007-04-13).
(c) Applicability
This AD applies to Daher Aircraft, SAS Model TBM 700 airplanes, certificated in any category, manufacturer serial numbers 1 through 638 and 687, that have an affected part installed as defined in paragraph (f)(1) of this AD.
Note 1 to paragraph (c):
Airplanes on which Daher MOD 70-0190-32 has been embodied in production are not affected by the requirements of this AD, provided that, since first flight, no “affected part” has been installed on that airplane.
(d) Subject
Joint Aircraft System Component (JASC) Code 3200, Landing Gear System.
(e) Unsafe Condition
This AD was prompted by cracks reported on main landing gear (MLG) cylinders in service. The FAA is issuing this AD to detect cracks on MLG cylinder. The unsafe condition, if not addressed, could result in a collapsed MLG during take-off or landing runs and reduced structural integrity of the airplane.
(f) Definitions
For the purpose of this AD:
(1) An “affected part” is a MLG with forging body having part number (P/N) 21236-000-00, 21236-000-01, 22609-000-00, 22609-001-00, 22611-000-00, 22611-001-00, D67685, or D67686.
(2) A “serviceable part” is any MLG forging body that is not an affected part.
(g) Compliance
Comply with this AD within the compliance times specified, unless already done.
(h) Required Actions
(1) Within the compliance time specified in paragraphs (h)(1)(i) through (iii) of this AD, as applicable, and thereafter at intervals not to exceed 240 landings (LDGs), accomplish a special detailed inspection (SDI) (eddy current or fluorescent penetrant) of the ”affected part” in accordance with the Accomplishment Instructions C. of Daher Aircraft Mandatory Service Bulletin (SB) 70-130, Revision 5, dated January 2026 (Daher Mandatory SB 70-130, Revision 5).
(i) For airplanes with an “affected part” that was at 3,500 landings or more since the first installation on an airplane as of March 23, 2007 (the effective date retained from AD 2007-04-13), within 25 landings after March 23, 2007 (the effective date retained from AD 2007-04-13).
(ii) For airplanes with an “affected part” that was at 1,751 landings or more since the first installation on an airplane as of March 23, 2007 (the effective date retained from AD 2007-04-13) but less than 3,500 landings, within 100 landings after March 23, 2007 (the effective date retained from AD 2007-04-13).
(iii) For airplanes with “an affected part” that was either at or under 1,750 landings as of March 23, 2007 (the effective date of AD 2007-04-13): Upon or before accumulating 1,750 landings on “affected part” since new or within the next 100 landings after September 29, 2015 (the effective date retained from AD 2015-17-10), whichever occurs later.
(2) If, during any SDI as required by paragraph (h)(1) of this AD, any crack is suspected or confirmed, before further flight, remove the MLG leg and confirm the presence of the crack with a fluorescent penetrant inspection in accordance with the Accomplishment Instructions C. of Daher Mandatory SB 70-130, Revision 5.
(3) If, during the fluorescent penetrant inspection as required by paragraph (h)(2) of this AD, any crack is confirmed, before further flight, replace the part as specified in paragraph (i) of this AD or contact the Manager, International Validation Branch, FAA; the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA); or Daher's EASA Design Organization Approval (DOA) for approved repair instructions and, within the compliance time specified therein, accomplish those instructions accordingly, including post-repair follow-on action(s), as applicable. If approved by the DOA, the approval must include the DOA-authorized signature.
(
printed page 73717)
(i) Terminating Action
Modification of an airplane in service, by installation of a “serviceable part” as defined in paragraph (f)(2) of this AD in both left-hand and right-hand MLGs in accordance with the instructions of paragraph E of Daher-Socata TBM Aircraft Mandatory SB 70-130, Revision 3, dated December 2014; Daher Aerospace Mandatory SB 70-130, Revision 4, dated October 2025 (Daher Aerospace Mandatory SB 70-130, Revision 4); or Daher Mandatory SB 70-130, Revision 5, constitutes terminating action for the inspections required by paragraph (h)(1) of this AD.
Note 2 to paragraph (i) of this AD:
Daher Component Maintenance Manuals (CMM) 32-11-01 and 32-11-02 also contain instructions on the installation of a “serviceable part.”
(j) Calculating Unknown Number of Landings for Compliance
The compliance times of this AD are presented in landings instead of hours time-in-service (TIS). If the number of landings is unknown, hours TIS may be used by dividing the number of hours TIS by 1.35.
(k) Credit for Previous Actions
This paragraph provides credit for the actions required by paragraph (h) of this AD if those actions were performed before the effective date of this AD using Daher Aerospace Mandatory SB 70-130, Revision 4; Daher-Socata TBM Aircraft Mandatory Service Bulletin No. SB 70-130, Revision 3, dated December 2014; Daher Aircraft Mandatory SB 70-130, Revision 2, dated June 2014; Daher Aircraft Mandatory SB 70-130, Revision 1, dated November 2013; or EADS-Socata TBM Aircraft Mandatory SB 70-130, dated January 2006.
(l) Alternative Methods of Compliance (AMOCs)
(1) The Manager, International Validation Branch, FAA, has the authority to approve AMOCs for this AD, if requested using the procedures found in
14 CFR 39.19
. In accordance with
14 CFR 39.19
, send your request to your principal inspector or local Flight Standards District Office, as appropriate. If sending information directly to the manager of the International Validation Branch, send it to the attention of the person identified in paragraph (m)(1) of this AD and email to:
AMOC@faa.gov
.
(2) Before using any approved AMOC, notify your appropriate principal inspector, or lacking a principal inspector, the manager of the local flight standards district office/certificate holding district office.
(m) Additional Information
(1) For more information about this AD, contact Zakaria Abdi, Aviation Safety Engineer, FAA, 1600 Stewart Avenue, Suite 410, Westbury, NY 11590; phone: (316) 946-4141; email:
zakaria.f.abdi@faa.gov
.
(2) Material identified in this AD that is not incorporated by reference is available at the address specified in paragraph (n)(4) of this AD.
(n) Material Incorporated by Reference
(1) The Director of the Federal Register approved the incorporation by reference (IBR) of the material listed in this paragraph under
5 U.S.C. 552(a)
and
1 CFR part 51
.

title: Modernizing the Labor Market Test and Improving Protections for U.S. Workers in the PERM Immigrant Visa Program
abstract: The Department of Labor (Department or DOL) proposes to amend its regulations regarding the certification of job opportunities offered by employers seeking to employ aliens on a permanent basis in the United States. This Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM or proposed rule) strengthens the standards by which the Department receives and reviews employers' applications for permanent labor certification and improves the integrity of the overall employment-based immigrant visa program to more effectively protect the wages and job opportunities of U.S. workers similarly employed in the United States. AGENCY:
Employment and Training Administration, Department of Labor.
ACTION:
Notice of proposed rulemaking.
SUMMARY:
The Department of Labor (Department or DOL) proposes to amend its regulations regarding the certification of job opportunities offered by employers seeking to employ aliens on a permanent basis in the United States. This Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM or proposed rule) strengthens the standards by which the Department receives and reviews employers' applications for permanent labor certification and improves the integrity of the overall employment-based immigrant visa program to more effectively protect the wages and job opportunities of U.S. workers similarly employed in the United States. Among the issues addressed in this proposed rule are eliminating further administration of Schedule A, which exempts certain job opportunities from the statutorily required labor market test; strengthening the minimum standards of recruitment to ensure all employers seeking labor certification access the broadest pool of high-quality U.S. workers using the latest technologies and methods; enhancing safeguards for U.S. workers impacted by layoffs, including those laid off by employers using third-party staffing companies and establishing standards for employers to report layoffs; expanding requirements for employers to provide U.S. workers with notice of filing (NOF) applications for permanent labor certification; improving employer compliance with program requirements and consideration of qualified U.S. workers that is comparable to job opportunities for which permanent labor certification is not required; and codifying the Department's practice of electronically receiving, processing, and issuing final determinations on employer requests for prevailing wages and permanent labor certifications. The changes in this proposed rule are consistent with the Secretary of Labor's (Secretary) statutory responsibilities to certify that there are not sufficient workers in the United States who are able, willing, qualified, and available to fill the petitioning employer's job opportunity at the time of application for a visa and admission to the United States, and that the employment of such alien will not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed workers in the United States.

II. Revisions to
20 CFR Part 656
A. Statutory Framework
The Immigration and Nationality Act (INA or the Act), as amended by the Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986, assigns responsibilities to the Secretary relating to the admission and employment of certain aliens who intend to work and live permanently in the United States. The Act prohibits the admission of certain employment-based immigrants to perform skilled or unskilled labor as permanent residents unless the Secretary has determined and certified to the Secretaries of Homeland Security and State that (1) there are not sufficient workers who are able, willing, qualified, and available at the time of application for a visa and admission to the United States and at the place where the alien is to perform such skilled or unskilled labor; and (2) the employment of such alien will not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of workers in the United States similarly employed.
[
1
]
See
section 212(a)(5)(A)(i),
8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(5)(A)(i)
. In addition, the Act specifies that for aliens who are members of the teaching profession, referring to college and university teachers, and those possessing exceptional ability in the sciences or the arts, the Secretary must consider only equally or more qualified United States (U.S.) workers as qualified for the job opportunity offered.
[
2
]
See
section 212(a)(5)(A)(ii),
8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(5)(A)(ii)
. For all other job opportunities requiring the Secretary's determination and certification, each prospective U.S. worker who possesses the minimum qualifications required for the job opportunity and who will be available at the time and place needed to perform the services or labor required is considered available.
The INA provides for five “preference” categories, or immigrant visa classes, only two of which—the second and third preference employment categories (commonly called the EB-2 and EB-3 immigrant visa classifications)—generally require a labor certification.
[
3
]
An employer seeking to sponsor an alien worker for an immigrant visa under the EB-2 or EB-3 preference categories generally must file a visa petition with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) on the alien's behalf, and the petition must include a labor certification from the Secretary.
[
4
]
Further, the Department of State (DOS) may not issue a visa unless the Secretary has issued a labor certification in conformity with the relevant provisions of the INA.
[
5
]
The INA provides one exception, which applies only to certain aliens eligible for the EB-2 visa classification. If the Secretary of Homeland Security determines it is in the national interest to waive the permanent job offer requirement—permitting the alien to self-petition under the EB-2 visa classification—the Secretary's certification is not required for admission to the United States.
[
6
]
See
section 203(b)(2)(B);
8 U.S.C. 1153(b)(2)(B)
. All other EB-2 and EB-3 aliens cannot be admitted to the United States without being sponsored for permanent employment with a U.S. employer that first obtains the Secretary's statutory certification for the job offered.
See
section 203(b)(2)(A), (b)(3)(C);
8 U.S.C. 1153(b)(2)(A)
, (b)(3)(C).
Within the Department, the Secretary has delegated authority to make the required determination and issue the related certification to the Assistant Secretary for the Employment and Training Administration (ETA).
[
7
]
The Assistant Secretary for ETA, in turn, has delegated that authority to the Office of Foreign Labor Certification (OFLC). As a result, OFLC reviews requests for permanent labor certification, issues certifications, and carries out other statutory responsibilities as required by
8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(5)(A)
.
B. Current Regulatory Framework
A U.S. employer sponsoring an alien for permanent admission based on the
(
printed page 73918)
EB-2 or EB-3 visa classifications must demonstrate that the job requirements qualify for the visa classification it seeks, that the alien qualifies for the job opportunity, and—as it relates to a labor certification for the permanent labor certification program or PERM labor certification program—that qualified U.S. workers are not available to fill the position and that employment of the alien will not adversely affect wages and working conditions of similarly employed U.S. workers.
The Department's regulations,
20 CFR part 656
, implement the statutory provisions that govern the permanent labor certification (“PERM labor certification”) process and set forth the responsibilities of U.S. employers who seek to permanently employ aliens covered by the statutory labor certification requirements.
On May 6, 2002, the Department published an NPRM that proposed to streamline the permanent labor certification program.
[
8
]
A final rule implementing significant revisions to the permanent labor certification program was published on December 27, 2004, and took effect on March 28, 2005.
[
9
]
In addition, on February 13, 2006, the Department published an NPRM designed to enhance program integrity and reduce the incentives and opportunities for fraud and abuse in the permanent labor certification program.
[
10
]
The Department subsequently published a final rule on May 17, 2007, which took effect on July 16, 2007, commonly referred to as “the PERM fraud rule.”
[
11
]
This rule prohibited, among other things, the substitution of beneficiaries on permanent labor certification applications and resulting certifications; established a 180-day validity period for the use of approved labor certifications filed in connection with an I-140 Immigrant Petition with USCIS; prohibited the sale, barter or purchase of permanent labor certifications and applications; required employers to pay the costs of preparing, filing and obtaining certification, and strictly prohibited transferring such cost to the alien beneficiary; and established procedures for debarment of employers from the permanent labor certification program.
[
12
]
To receive a PERM labor certification under current regulations, the employer must first obtain a prevailing wage determination (PWD), conduct a good faith test of the domestic labor market for qualified U.S. workers, and post a NOF to employees before submitting an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
(the current Form ETA-9089) to OFLC for review and processing. A request for a PWD, which is collected through the
Application for Prevailing Wage Determination
(the current Form ETA-9141), enables OFLC to review the duties, requirements, and worksite location(s) of the job opportunity and provide the employer with the applicable prevailing wage rate(s).
[
13
]
The employer must offer a wage that equals or exceeds the PWD determined by OFLC and guarantee that the wage the employer will pay to the alien will equal or exceed the prevailing wage that is applicable at the time the alien begins work or from the time of admission to take up the certified employment. The PWD ensures that the recruitment of U.S. workers based on the employer's job opportunity offers at least the average wage paid to similarly employed workers in the specific occupation in the area of intended employment (AIE) or the applicable collective bargaining agreement (CBA) rate, and if the employer permanently hires aliens at the wage rate offered, doing so will not adversely affect workers similarly employed in the United States.
[
14
]
The statutorily required NOF, which must be provided to bargaining representative(s) or posted in conspicuous locations at all worksite locations, as applicable, helps inform the employer's employees of the job offered to the alien in the PERM labor certification process and provides U.S. workers and others with an opportunity to contact OFLC with information concerning the application.
[
15
]
The existing test of the domestic labor market generally involves the employer following a prescribed list of recruitment requirements, such as placing a job order with the State Workforce Agency (SWA) for 30 days and print newspaper advertisements on two different Sundays, which are intended to apprise U.S. workers of the job opportunity and give them an opportunity to apply.
[
16
]
Together, these pre-filing requirements enable the employer to provide information essential to OFLC's ability to reach the statutorily required determinations when reviewing an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
Upon completion of pre-filing requirements, the employer typically submits the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
electronically to OFLC using the Foreign Labor Application Gateway (FLAG) system, which contains a series of attestations made by the employer, guaranteeing the employer has taken or will take steps to comply with the PERM labor certification process under
20 CFR part 656
. After performing an initial review of the application, OFLC may grant or deny a PERM labor certification, request further information, select one or more applications for audit examination, and/or require the employer to undergo additional recruitment of U.S. workers under OFLC's supervision.
Where a PERM labor certification is approved, OFLC issues a Form ETA-9089—
Final Determination: Permanent Employment Certification Approval
(Final Determination), to the employer and the authorized attorney or agent, as applicable, that can be used to file an Immigrant Petition with USCIS. If, however, OFLC denies a PERM labor certification, the employer may appeal the denial. An employer currently has the option of requesting the Department's reconsideration or requesting review before the Board of Alien Labor Certification Appeals (BALCA or the Board). Presently, the employer must request reconsideration or BALCA review no later than 30 days from the date of the denial.
[
17
]
Where OFLC upholds its denial decision on reconsideration, an employer may further seek BALCA review within 30 days of the decision on reconsideration. If the employer does not pursue an appeal or if the employer's appeal is unsuccessful in overturning the denial decision, the employer may file a new
Application for Permanent Employment
(
printed page 73919)
Certification
with OFLC that meets the requirements of
20 CFR part 656
.
The PERM labor certification program is largely an attestation-based program, requiring the employer to attest that it has completed the required steps for the PERM labor certification process, met the conditions of employment on the application, and retained all applications and supporting documentation demonstrating compliance with program requirements. For example, the employer attests that the position has been open to any U.S. worker; U.S. workers who did apply were rejected for lawful, job-related reasons; the pay offered is at least the prevailing wage rate; and the job opportunity's terms and conditions are not contrary to federal, state, or local law.
[
18
]
The Department has integrity measures in place to protect and strengthen the PERM labor certification program. OFLC conducts pre-certification audits to ensure employer compliance with the requirements of
20 CFR part 656
. During audit review, OFLC currently requests all applications and supporting documentation to verify, among other requirements, that the employer posted the required NOF to its employees and conducted all applicable pre-filing recruitment steps, as required and as attested to on its application, and that no qualified U.S. worker was available for the job opportunity for which the employer seeks PERM certification.
[
19
]
In addition to audits, OFLC has the discretion to require an employer to conduct supervised recruitment to ensure an adequate and more current test of the U.S. labor market is performed to determine whether qualified U.S. workers are available to fill the employer's job opportunity.
[
20
]
With respect to program integrity measures, if OFLC discovers after issuing a certification that certification was not justified, OFLC may take further action, such as revocation. Additionally, if the Department learns an employer, attorney, or agent is involved in possible fraud or willful misrepresentation in connection with the PERM program, OFLC will refer the matter to other government entities, as appropriate, for investigation, and send a copy of the referral to the DOL Office of Inspector General (DOL-OIG). In these cases, or if the Department is notified by other government entities that an employer, attorney, or agent is under investigation for possible fraud or willful misrepresentation in connection with the PERM program, OFLC may suspend processing of any
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
involving such employer, attorney, or agent for an initial period of up to 180 calendar days and may extend the suspension of processing until completion of any investigation and/or judicial proceedings. Where OFLC finds the employer, attorney, agent, or any combination thereof, has violated the regulatory requirement(s) under
20 CFR part 656
, OFLC may pursue debarment action(s) in accordance with the standard and procedures set forth in
20 CFR 656.31(f)
for a reasonable period of not more than 3 years.
[
21
]
C. Recent Administrative Action Related to the Permanent Labor Certification Process
Beginning in 1965 and for the purpose of reducing delays in processing an alien's requests for an employment-based immigrant visa, the Department established through rulemaking, schedules or listings of occupations where the Secretary could pre-certify whether sufficient qualified workers in the United States were available to fill the employer's need for permanent labor.
[
22
]
One such schedule, referred to as Schedule A, set forth a list of occupations that the Secretary designated as in short supply of qualified U.S. workers, which permitted employers to bypass the statutory labor certification requirement prior to filing an Immigrant Petition requesting admission of an alien to perform permanent skilled or unskilled labor.
[
23
]
During the ensuing thirty years, the occupational listings in Schedule A were periodically reviewed and only revised eight times, the last time in 2004.
[
24
]
On December 21, 2023, the Department published a request for information,
Labor Certification for Permanent Employment of Foreign Workers in the United States; Modernizing Schedule A To Include Consideration of Additional Occupations in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) and Non-STEM Occupations.
[
25
]
The Department published the request for information to allow the public to provide input, including data, statistical metrics or models, studies, and other relevant information, on how the Department may establish a reliable, objective, and transparent methodology for revising Schedule A to include STEM and other non-STEM occupations where there may exist shortages of qualified U.S. workers, consistent with requirements of the INA. Specifically, the Department sought public comment on evaluating the utility of expanding Schedule A to include STEM and non-STEM occupations for which there may be an insufficient number of ready, willing, able, and qualified U.S. workers. Through the request for information, the Department requested input on the appropriate data sources and methods for determining whether labor shortages exist and asked the public how the Department could establish a reliable, objective, and transparent methodology for identifying both STEM and non-STEM occupations that are experiencing labor shortages.
The Department received over 2,000 comments in response to the request for information. The comments received ranged from opposition to the continuation of Schedule A to support for its expansion. Those opposed to the continuation and/or expansion of Schedule A characterized Schedule A as unnecessary, undermining statutory intent, a mechanism to bypass immigration rules, and/or harmful to U.S. workers. Additionally, none of the commenters who expressed support for Schedule A provided the Department with a suitable rationale or administratively feasible methodology to expand or maintain the current occupations listed on Schedule A. Several commenters supported either limiting or reducing Schedule A occupations, and provided some examples and citations, but they also did not provide a suitable rationale or administratively feasible methodology to determine which occupations to retain or remove from Schedule A. Although a handful of commenters
(
printed page 73920)
made concerted efforts to respond to questions posed in the request for information, responses received from commenters overall did not provide sufficient substantive information that would allow the Department to proceed with proposing changes to the regulations governing Schedule A. While many commenters successfully identified potential specific sources of economic or labor data that could be used, the commenters almost uniformly failed to specify which precise data markers or thresholds should be established or used to determine whether there was a labor shortage covering a particular geographic area warranting inclusion on Schedule A.
In terms of identifying STEM occupations, one consistent recommendation was that the Department should mimic DHS's “STEM Designated Degree Program List for the Optional Practical Training (OPT) STEM extension” to define STEM for purposes of identifying occupations for expanding Schedule A. However, the commenters failed to explain how a program which determines eligibility for aliens to engage in a limited period of post-graduation employment in the United States is applicable to the PERM program. The DHS STEM Designated Degree Program List enumerates the fields of study that DHS designates as STEM for purposes of the 24-month STEM OPT extension described at
8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(C)
. It has nothing to do with labor shortages and the comments did not address how the process for updating OPT is applicable to defining labor shortages within those degree fields and related occupational classifications. There are considerable substantive differences between the OPT and PERM program requirements, so while many commenters suggested that DHS' program for updating OPT would be useful for PERM, these commenters did not explain how it could be shaped to meet the very different nature of the two programs, and the respective objectives of each program. Commenters also suggested adding numerous non-STEM industries to Schedule A, but the commenters likewise failed to provide information that would sustain a factual determination that there is a labor shortage of those occupations in any particular geographic area.
In the absence of a reliable, objective, and transparent methodology for updating Schedule A or the relevant substantive information needed to develop such a methodology, the Department decided it could not add new occupations to Schedule A nor demonstrate that the occupations currently listed in Schedule A are still shortage occupations. The Department is now proposing through this rulemaking to eliminate Schedule A, which is explained further below in section III.C.
D. Need for Rulemaking
It is the policy of the Department to vigorously enforce all laws within its jurisdiction governing administration of the PERM labor certification program, which informs USCIS' approval of EB-2 and EB-3 immigrant visa petitions. The Department has not updated its regulations associated with the PERM labor certification process in nearly 20 years and changes in labor market dynamics, including increases in remote work, advances in electronic methods of recruiting highly qualified talent, high rates of turnover or layoffs in certain sectors of the U.S. economy, necessitate a need to strengthen the program's standards and procedures. Further, with the Trump Administration's executive actions to strengthen the nation's southern border, enhance interior enforcement efforts, and promote economic growth, employers may increasingly turn to legal labor pathways—like permanent and temporary employment work visas, and the Department must ensure that employers first access and consider the broadest pool of qualified and available U.S. talent before seeking to sponsor and hire an alien for permanent employment in the United States.
[
26
]
This proposed rule is also part of a broader Government effort to more faithfully enforce the immigration laws of the United States as set out by Congress.
[
27
]
In coordination with other federal agencies, the Department has launched major investigations and intensified enforcement actions, particularly related to third-party staffing firms in the technology sector, to combat fraud and abuse involving the PERM labor certification process and the H-1B visa classification where the majority of nonimmigrant workers are often sponsored for permanent employment in the United States.
[
28
]
In collaboration with other federal law enforcement partners, the DOL-OIG has uncovered widespread schemes in which employers and labor brokers submitted fraudulent applications, exploited aliens through coercive wage-kickback arrangements, and undercut American workers by flooding the market with below-wage labor. Where these federal law enforcement partners are investigating fraud or willful misrepresentations involving the PERM program, the Secretary has initiated suspensions of current and future filed PERM applications by certain employers.
[
29
]
Meanwhile, U.S. workers continue to face a challenging and disadvantageous labor market.
[
30
]
U.S. workers in computer-related occupations—particularly recent U.S. college graduates—are facing high unemployment and underemployment
(
printed page 73921)
rates.
[
31
]
In FY 2025, job opportunities in computer and technology related occupational classifications constituted the vast majority of H-1B and PERM jobs certified by DOL.
[
32
]
Further, employers in the technology sector are laying off large numbers of their U.S. workers while simultaneously filing applications requesting DOL certification for temporary H-1B and/or permanent workers.
[
33
]
As noted in Presidential Proclamation 10973 of September 18, 2026,
Restriction on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant Workers,
certain employers, including information technology (IT) staffing and outsourcing firms, have abused the system to suppress wages and displace American workers, flooding the domestic labor market with an abundant supply of low-paid entry-level workers and making it more difficult for American workers and recent graduates, especially in science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) fields, to find employment.
[
34
]
Through its program experience, the Department observes that many employers seeking to employ H-1B workers in these skilled positions, including those who engage in layoffs or utilize third-party staffing firms, are often concurrently sponsoring foreign nationals for PERM labor certification where a good faith test of the domestic labor market is a prerequisite to obtaining a certification from the Secretary, as Congress intended. In light of these circumstances, the Department is concerned that current regulations governing the PERM labor certification process do not require employers to conduct a sufficiently robust labor market test—one that utilizes methods that align with modern recruitment practices—and creates incentives for some employers to use different, potentially discriminatory, procedures for considering qualified U.S. applicants that they would otherwise not employ for the same or comparably similar job opportunities not subject to PERM labor certification.
Accordingly, this proposed rule seeks to strengthen the integrity of the PERM labor certification process to improve the program's protections for the U.S. workforce while ensuring that, consistent with statutory obligations, employers with true workforce shortages can access legal immigrant labor possessing the highest quality talent, without undue cost or administrative burden. In particular, and as discussed in detail within this preamble, this rule proposes the following major changes to the Department's PERM labor certification regulations, followed by a section-by-section discussion of all proposed changes:
Modernizing Recruitment To Attract High-Quality American Talent
Establishes a single set of recruitment requirements for all occupations and, except as permitted by Congress, eliminates the Department's continued management of Schedule A that administratively exempts certain occupations from the statutory labor certification requirement. Additionally, this rule proposes replacing PERM's print-intensive and self-selective menu of recruitment options with a modern set of electronic recruitment requirements that leverages use of the employer website(s), job search website(s), social media platform(s), and other job fairs or on-campus recruiting methods. These provisions will better align PERM's labor market test with modern recruitment practices and ensure employers conduct a more robust labor market test to access the broadest pool of qualified and available U.S. workers.
[
35
]
Expands the length of time advertisements are available to prospective U.S. applicants, including the job order placed with the SWA, to a period of no less than 90 calendar days or the total number of days the employer has customarily advertised for job opportunities in the same occupational classification during the most recent 12 months that did not require PERM labor certification, whichever is longer. This proposed rule also requires that all recruitment be completed no more than 60 calendar days and no fewer than 30 calendar days before the expected filing of the application with the submission of a recruitment report to DOL. Finally, this rule clarifies the minimum advertising content for all recruitment efforts and extends long-standing optional competitive recruitment procedures for college and university teachers, with minor updates, to professional athletes and professional sports team coaches. These provisions will provide U.S. workers with a fair chance to apply for permanent job opportunities and ensure that employer advertising and consideration of qualified U.S. workers is performed in the same manner as other job opportunities for which PERM labor certification is not required.
Improving Safeguards for U.S. Workers Impacted by Layoffs
Prohibits employers who have laid off U.S. workers in the same or similar occupation and at the place(s) of employment within the most recent 2 years from the date on which the employer requests PERM labor certification.
Expands the current requirement that employers engaging in layoffs consider qualified U.S. workers to a post-filing requirement—from the date on which the employer requests PERM labor certification through the date on which the Form I-140 petition is approved by USCIS or the final determination date, if the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
or Form I-140 petition is denied or withdrawn, whichever is later. If such layoffs occur, requires employers to document and provide such documentation to DOL that it has offered the job opportunity to those laid-off U.S. workers and, where not rejected
(
printed page 73922)
for a lawful, job-related reason(s), the U.S. worker was offered the job opportunity. Additionally, this rule prohibits third-party staffing companies from placing the alien(s) with another employer engaging in layoffs where there are indicia of an employment relationship between the alien and that other employer during the same layoff timeframe. These provisions will safeguard the rights of U.S. workers impacted by layoffs when such employers are concurrently seeking PERM labor certification from DOL and admission under an EB-2 or EB-3 visa classification from DHS.
Establishes an affirmative obligation for employers engaging in layoffs, including the placement of the alien(s) with another employer engaging in layoffs, to affirmatively notify DOL and, where a Form I-140 petition is pending for the alien(s), DHS not later than 5 business days after such layoff(s) occurs, and continually update their recruitment reports throughout the expanded layoff timeframe. The notification will trigger the INA 204(b) consultation process between the departments whereby DOL will determine the adequacy of the employer's compliance with the post-certification obligation to consider laid off U.S. workers, and inform USCIS of the continued validity, or revocation of the underlying labor certification based on DOL's assessment of the employer's compliance. These provisions will provide greater transparency to DOL and DHS, as applicable, on employers engaging in layoffs who are concurrently seeking PERM labor certification and better align the consideration of U.S. workers impacted by layoffs with the Department's statutory mandate to certify an insufficient number of qualified U.S. workers available at the time of application for a visa and admission of the alien(s) into the United States to perform the skilled or unskilled services for permanent employment.
Strengthening Employer Compliance and Program Integrity
Revises the standards and procedures for employers to provide notice to U.S. workers and the bargaining representative(s), as applicable, of filing the application by clarifying the requirements for providing such notice electronically to U.S. workers, including the intended placement of the alien(s) at third-party worksite locations, and expanding the timeframe to begin within 10 business days before the application is filed and remain available to U.S. workers through the date on which the Form I-140 petition is approved or the date of determination, if the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
or Form I-140 petition is denied or withdrawn, whichever is later. These provisions will better align with the statutory requirement and strengthen program integrity by permitting any person or employee of the employer, particularly those impacted by layoffs during the post-filing adjudication process of the application or who may have information related to fraud or misrepresentations, to take action and report such information bearing on the application to OFLC for appropriate action.
Clarifies the definitions of “employer” and “attorney” and “agent,” the use of these terms in the filing of an application, and enhances the obligations employers seeking to employ aliens must declare, under penalty of perjury, to assure compliance with terms and conditions of employment and program requirements, including the recruitment and consideration of U.S. workers in “good faith” and in a manner that is comparable to job opportunities that do not require PERM labor certification. These provisions will strengthen protections for similarly employed U.S. workers by providing better clarity regarding the responsibilities of employers and their authorized attorneys or agents, as applicable, and promote greater program compliance.
Enhances the Department's debarment authority by holding agents and attorneys, and their successors in interest, accountable for their own misconduct independent of the employer's violation(s) and extending debarment from the PERM labor certification program to all of the Department's labor certification and labor condition application programs. Prohibiting debarred entities from filing any new applications with OFLC or receiving any approvals from OFLC during the debarment period strengthens the debarment penalty, when imposed. Any application requesting PERM labor certification filed by debarred entities during the period of debarment will be denied without review. These provisions will improve program integrity and prevent unscrupulous employers from circumventing the PERM labor market test requirements.
Modernizing the Prevailing Wage and PERM Application Process
Establishes a single point of entry by requiring that employers, except in limited circumstances, electronically file applications requesting PWDs and PERM labor certifications and all supporting documentation through a centralized electronic system maintained by DOL and permits the use of electronic signatures meeting valid signature standards. These provisions will minimize unnecessary costs and burdens on DOL and employers, improve the quality of applications, reduce the frequency of delays associated with deficient applications, and better facilitate information sharing with other federal agencies.
Requires electronic methods for the OFLC Certifying Officer (CO) to send notices and requests to employers and issue PWDs and PERM labor certification decisions directly to USCIS. These provisions will codify OFLC's standard operating procedures to minimize delays, reduce unnecessary administrative costs for the employer and DOL, and expedite the delivery of final decisions to employers and their authorized attorneys or agents, as applicable, and to other federal agencies, while maintaining program integrity.
The Department invites all interested parties to participate in this rulemaking by submitting comments on all aspects of this rule, as described above. Comments that include written data, sources, and specific feedback on all aspects of this proposed rule would be most helpful to the Department.

20 CFR Part 656
A. Discussion of Proposed Technical and Summary Changes to
20 CFR Part 656
The Department proposes to revise various terms and phrases used throughout the regulation. These revisions are intended to improve readability, accuracy, or clarity and increase consistency within part 656 and across OFLC regulations and program administration. These modifications are explained below.
The Department proposes to use the term “
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,”
the current Form ETA-9089 form title, when referring to Form ETA-9089 and the related Form ETA-9141,
Application for Prevailing Wage Determination,
which contains information about the job opportunity necessary to the CO's review of the employer's request for permanent labor certification. This term would replace the form number throughout part 656 for clarity, and create consistency with other OFLC programs, with one exception—where Form ETA-9089 is used in section 656.3
(
printed page 73923)
for the definition of
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
The Department proposes to replace the term “Form ETA 750” throughout part 656, with
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
“Form ETA 750” has been eliminated as the form's use is no longer needed and the information collection has been discontinued. Consistent with directions provided to the public when implementing the form changes, the persons and entities that used the Form ETA 750 now must use the Form ETA-9089, which is now true for all
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification
processed under part 656.
[
36
]
The use of the terms “Form ETA-9089” and “Form ETA 750” is being deemphasized to ensure the continuing accuracy of the regulation regardless of changes to the form, the form number, or its associated appendices and related information collections.
The Department proposes to change the term “labor certification” to “permanent labor certification” throughout part 656 for clarity. This change would more clearly distinguish the type of labor certification program addressed in part 656—permanent (
i.e.,
immigrant)—from the labor certifications addressed in OFLC's regulations in part 655—temporary (
i.e.,
nonimmigrant).
The Department proposes to change the terms “alien labor certification” and “alien employment certification” to “permanent labor certification” for internal consistency throughout part 656.
The Department proposes to use the term “permanent employment” throughout part 656 wherever the term “employment” alone could be unclear and to ensure consistency with the definition of “permanent employment” in section 656.3.
The Department proposes to use the term “U.S. worker,” rather than “United States worker,” throughout part 656 to ensure consistency throughout the regulation and with the definition in section 656.3.
The Department proposes additional changes throughout the text to correct typographical errors and improve clarity and readability, including the use of acronyms, such as using “DOL” for “Department of Labor” or “Department,” “BALCA” or “Board” in place of “Board of Alien Labor Certification Appeals,” or “CO” for “Certifying Officer,” where appropriate. Such changes are non-substantive and do not change the meaning of the current text. Substantive changes to the current regulatory text are discussed in the corresponding section of the preamble.
As warranted, the Department is proposing to retitle numerous sections to align with the subject matter as it has been reorganized, which includes retitling or removing the title for various paragraphs, subparagraphs, clauses, etc.
B. Discussion of Proposed Revisions to
20 CFR Part 656, Subpart A
Under this proposed rule, subpart A would be expanded and renumbered from
20 CFR 656.1
through
656.3
to now include

1. Proposed
20 CFR 656.1
, Purpose and Scope
The Department is proposing to revise part 656, subpart A, and rename subpart A, “
General Provisions.”
The Department proposes to reorganize and revise the content of current paragraphs (a) and (b) in proposed paragraph (a) in addition to revising the remaining language that will be placed under proposed paragraph (b). Specifically, paragraph (a) will be subtitled “Purpose” and paragraph (b) will be subtitled “Scope.” The Department is proposing to add new language on the scope of this subpart at proposed section 656.1(b). The Department believes that this reorganization and proposed revisions will make this subpart clearer and easier to follow.
For proposed section 656.1(a), which discusses the purpose of this subpart and the Department's responsibilities under the INA, the Department proposes to eliminate content from current section 656.1(a) that restates the INA and to relocate content from current section 656.1(b) that describes the purpose of part 656 to proposed section 656.1(a), with revisions. After relocating content from current paragraph (b) to proposed paragraph (a), the Department proposes revisions to update terminology and to better address the purpose of part 656, which is to establish the requirements and procedures by which the Department makes determinations in connection with requests for permanent labor certification and certifies its determination to DHS and DOS. For example, the Department is proposing to revise the language at current section 656.1(b), which states that the regulations “set forth procedures through which such immigrant labor certifications may be applied for, and granted or denied,” and replace it with language stating that part 656 establishes “the requirements and the procedures by which the Department of Labor makes a determination in connection with applications for permanent employment certification and certifies its determination to the Department of Homeland Security and Department of State.” In addition, the Department proposes to retain the current sections containing the two statutory requirements for the Secretary's determination and certification—at current and proposed sections 656.1(a)(1) and (2)—with revisions to update terminology and improve readability. The Department believes that this proposed language simplifies the explanation for the regulations by using plain English, to make them easier to understand by the general public, and addresses the necessary details more thoroughly than the previous regulatory text.
The Department is also proposing new language at section 656.1(b), which discusses the scope of this part. The proposed language in this paragraph reiterates that part 656 contains the procedures that govern the PERM process. In addition, the new language proposed in section 656.1(b) makes clear that this part establishes standards and obligations regarding the terms and conditions with which employers must comply for permanent labor certification and sets forth integrity measures for ensuring employers' good faith recruitment of U.S. workers.
The Department is also taking this opportunity to remind stakeholders that compliance with the requirements contained in this part is the minimum standard for granting permanent labor certification. Compliance with this part does not establish compliance with, and is not a defense to separate liability under, Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (
42 U.S.C. 2000e
et seq.
),
8 U.S.C. 1324b
, or any other Federal, State, or local law governing employment. As discussed in this proposed rule, information obtained by the Department under this part may be provided to other federal enforcement agencies, including the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) and the Department of Justice,
(
printed page 73924)
Civil Rights Division, Immigrant and Employee Rights Section (DOJ-IER).
The Department is also proposing to eliminate section 656.1(c), which currently describes how stakeholders may send written correspondence or queries regarding the Department's regulations under part 656. The address provided in this section is no longer accurate and, rather than continually having to update an office or physical location address through future regulatory changes, the Department prefers to provide current contact information to stakeholders through more efficient means that allow for faster updates to the public, such as on OFLC's website and on its form instructions. Further, given OFLC's proposal to transition to full electronic processing, providing a street address would be less relevant, and the Department prefers to offer stakeholders alternative means of communication using email and online portal platforms.
2. Proposed
20 CFR 656.2
, Statutory Authority and Burden of Proof
The Department proposes to revise the heading of section 656.2 of subpart A from “Description of the Immigration and Nationality Act and of the Department of Labor's role thereunder” to “Statutory Authority and Burden of Proof” and the content of this section by removing and replacing the content of current paragraph (a), revising the content of current paragraph (b), and eliminating current paragraph (c).
The proposed revisions to section 656.2 are consistent with the Department's efforts in this rulemaking to simplify part 656 by removing unnecessary statutory restatements and content that extends beyond the Department's authority. 8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(5)(A)

In proposed sections 656.2(a) and (b), the Department proposes new and revised content that more clearly and simply states the delegation of the Secretary's statutory authority to OFLC and the employer's burden of proof.
Currently, section 656.3 defines relevant components of DOL. However, part 656 does not clearly address the delegation of the Secretary's authority within DOL. The proposed new language at 656.2(a) states in plain English that the Secretary's authority to issue permanent labor certifications and carry out other responsibilities required by
8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(5)(A)

Applications for Permanent Employment Certification

e.g.,

]

and, where the employer establishes eligibility to receive certification of an
