The Department is proposing the creation of a new section at 656.13 to enumerate by topic the assurances and obligations under the PERM program to which an employer must attest compliance. Organizing all existing and newly proposed required attestations into one section will improve clarity and navigation within part 656 and part 656 with similar regulatory provisions the Department has in the H-1B, H-2A and H-2B programs.
[
80
]
By clearly stating the employer's legal obligations in one provision of the regulations, the Department has determined this approach will make it easier for employers to find, understand, and comply with the program requirements. Further, the proposed changes in section 656.13 would enhance protections for U.S. workers, including protection of U.S. worker wages, and promote consideration of U.S. workers for job opportunities, notably by expanding contact and consideration requirements in layoff situations and preventing employers from laying off U.S. workers to create the perception of available vacancies and filing an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
with the intention of
(
printed page 73943)
replacing laid off U.S. workers with aliens.
See
proposed 656.13(e) and (f).
For proposed section 656.13, employers will be required to read and agree to comply with essential program requirements and worker protections for both U.S. and aliens when submitting an application under part 656, which will improve program integrity. Under penalty of perjury, employers will attest that they have read and reviewed every page of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
including all applicable appendices and supporting documentation, and to the best of their knowledge the information contained therein is true and accurate. In addition, employers will assure they understand that knowingly and/or willfully furnishing materially false information in the preparation of this form and any supplement thereto or to aid, abet, or counsel another to do so is a federal offense punishable by fines, imprisonment, or both under
18 U.S.C. 2
,
1001
,
1546
,
1621
. The clearer requirements will also enhance the Department's program integrity efforts, as clearer requirements provide a more straightforward path for enforcement of program requirements.
Specifically, the Department is proposing to take existing required attestations, currently codified at section 656.10(c), and replace and relocate them to this new proposed section 656.13, while further replacing the language of the existing attestations to strengthen program integrity. The Department proposes to replace and relocate regulatory content explaining the nature and effect of attestations from current section 656.10(c) to the introductory language of proposed section 656.13. In addition, the Department is proposing to relocate other existing obligations from current sections 656.10, 656.12, 656.17, and 656.20 to proposed section 656.13, again further revising them to create clear employer attestations in efforts to clarify and/or update compliance requirements. Finally, the Department also proposes new attestations to reflect new requirements through this proposed rule. The proposals in this rule strengthen U.S. worker protections and bolster program integrity by holding employers who choose to participate in the PERM program accountable to the Department, and to their responsibilities to both U.S. workers and aliens, with regard to the employer's filing of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
and participation in the PERM program.
Proposed new section 656.13(a) continues to require an employer seeking to permanently employ an alien to attest that the job opportunity is a bona fide, full-time, permanent position and adds that the terms and conditions of employment must comply with all applicable laws and regulations, consistent with current sections 656.10(c)(7) and (1). This proposed revision continues current sections 656.10(c)(5), (8), and (9) attestations, requiring the employer to attest that the job opportunity has been and is open to any qualified U.S. worker, any U.S. worker who applied was rejected for lawful, job-related reasons, and the job opportunity does not involve unlawful discrimination. The Department proposes to expand this attestation so that the job opportunities that are the subject of
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification
remain open to the employer's laid off-employees in the place(s) of employment in the same or similar occupation throughout the period in which the employer is establishing its sponsorship of an alien for permanent employment in the United States—between filing the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
and the date the Form I-140 petition is approved by USCIS or the date of determination, if the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
or Form I-140 petition is denied or withdrawn, whichever is later, which would form the basis for the alien's application for a visa and admission to the United States as a permanent resident.

81
]
In addition, the provision adds language explicitly requiring employers to comply with Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits workplace discrimination in the terms, conditions, or privileges of employment because of race, color, religion, sex, or national origin. Nothing in Title VII, “makes it illegal to discriminate on the basis of citizenship or alienage.”
Espinoza
v.
Farah Mfg. Co.,
414 U.S. 86, 95 (1973). The provision also adds language requiring compliance with the Antidiscrimination Provision of the Immigration and Nationality Act,
8 U.S.C. 1324b
, which prohibits discrimination because of citizenship status against protected individuals and, for employers not covered by Title VII, because of national origin. That law states that it is an unfair immigration-related employment practice to discriminate against a citizen or national of the United States based on their citizenship status.
8 U.S.C. 1324b(a)(1)
, (3).
Separately, and under the Department's own authority in
8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(5)(A)(i)(II)
, proposed section 656.13(a)(5) requires employers to offer U.S. workers terms, conditions, and privileges of employment no less favorable than those offered to the alien. Compliance with the PERM requirements is a floor; it does not establish compliance with Title VII or
8 U.S.C. 1324b
, and a departure from the PERM requirements may be relevant evidence in an enforcement action or private suit under those laws. This provision will prohibit an employer from rejecting any qualified U.S. worker over a prospective alien based on any cost justifications or basis, including differences in any term, condition, or privilege of employment, and compensation and fringe benefits between any qualified U.S. worker and a prospective alien. This proposed provision is necessary to ensure the integrity of the PERM program by prohibiting situations where the job offer is designed to match the skills of a particular alien. Unduly restrictive job postings have a chilling effect on the number of qualified U.S. workers who respond to job vacancy postings, and the Department will prohibit this practice with this proposal. These proposals strengthen U.S. worker protections and bolster program integrity by holding U.S. employers who participate in the program accountable to the Department and U.S. workers beyond the processing of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
Under proposed section 656.13(b), the Department continues the attestation required under current section 656.10(c)(6) to require the employer to attest that the job opportunity is not vacant due to a strike or employees being locked out in the course of a labor dispute involving a work stoppage. The proposal, however, expands the strike provision of the current regulation to clarify that it covers “all places of employment” included on the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
including third-party employers' locations. Through this proposed revised provision, the Department will improve program integrity and strengthen protections for U.S. workers.
To protect the integrity of the PERM labor certification program, deter fraud, and comply with the Department's statutory obligation to protect the wages of U.S. workers, the Department is proposing in section 656.13(c) to revise and clarify the already-required attestations in current sections
(
printed page 73944)
656.10(c)(1) through (4). For example, current section 656.10(c)(1) requires the employer to attest that it has offered, and will continue to offer, a wage that equals or exceeds the PWD. Proposed section 656.13(c) would more clearly state the employer's attestation that it has offered, and will continue to offer, a wage that equals or exceeds the highest of the Federal, State or local minimum wage or the PWD issued to the employer. The proposed paragraph clarifies that the offered wage requirement includes consideration of Federal, State, and local minimum wage rates, which is an existing requirement—for compliance with local, State, and Federal laws—under current section 656.10(c)(7). In addition, added content about the potential for an updated PWD reflects the potential for OFLC to obtain a new PWD, for example, during supervised recruitment. Further, this proposed provision adds new language stating that the offered wage cannot result in less favorable treatment of current or prospective U.S. workers in any terms, conditions, and privileges of employment, including compensation and fringe benefits, as compared with the alien (
i.e.,
must not be lower than the wage the employer pays, and the wage the employer advertises, for similarly situated positions). A violation of this certification is a serious matter that will result in denial and may result in revocation, debarment, and referral under 656.31 and 656.32. The Department solicits comments on this proposed provision, including how this attestation could be worded more clearly to ensure that wage compensation and other benefits for U.S. workers similarly employed are not adversely affected by the prospective employment of the alien(s) in the job opportunity. The proposed attestation continues to specify that the offered wage cannot be based on commissions, bonuses or other incentives, unless the employer guarantees an offered wage earned on a weekly, bi-weekly, or monthly basis that equals or exceeds the prevailing wage. The Department proposes expanding the attestation to accommodate the possibility of the Department issuing a new or revised PWD (
e.g.,
post-filing supervised recruitment) and, if so, the employer would be required to update its wage offer, unless notified otherwise by the Department.
The Department also proposes to continue to require the employer to attest that it has enough funds available to pay the offered wage for work performed in the job opportunity at the time of
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
submission. The Department proposes to revise this attestation for clarity and to include the citation to DHS's requirements regarding the employer's ability to pay at
8 CFR 204.5(g)(2)
, as USCIS will assess the employer's compliance during I-140 Petition review. These revisions would better apprise employers of this requirement, while avoiding duplicative regulatory provisions. In addition, citing to DHS's regulations would reduce the potential for confusion about the assessment to be performed when the employer files the I-140 Petition.
Under proposed section 656.13(d), the employer must attest that it has conducted, and will continue to conduct, recruitment of U.S. workers in good faith and in the same manner it normally recruits and considers U.S. workers in the same job opportunities that it does not request PERM labor certification, while also ensuring that its recruitment meets the standards set forth in proposed section 656.17. Through this proposed provision, the Department would require that the employer recruit U.S. workers in good faith and follow the same methods they would typically use for similar job opportunities where they do not seek PERM labor certifications for aliens, including when those methods they typically use for similar job opportunities exceed the requirements in proposed section 656.17. Where, how, and for how long an employer advertises a job opportunity in connection with the PERM labor certification program must be at least equal to the employer's practices for similar job opportunities unrelated to a PERM labor certification. Similarly, the employer's application process for candidates who apply for the employer's job opportunity that is the subject of the PERM application, must not disadvantage U.S. workers or be less available to U.S. workers than the employer's standard for same job opportunities that are unrelated to a request for PERM labor certification. Additionally, if required, interviews must be conducted by phone or arranged through other means (
e.g.,
virtual meetings, cloud calls, or other platforms or applications that facilitate communication without involving physical presence) to minimize costs for U.S. workers and facilitate the process should the applicant, for example, be unable to travel or be physically present at the employer's location for an interview. Further, the employer's representative who interviews or considers U.S. workers for the job offered to the alien must be a U.S. worker and one who normally interviews or considers, on behalf of the employer, applicants for job opportunities such as that offered the alien which do not involve labor certifications. Lastly, employers are prohibited from giving preferential treatment to aliens over U.S. workers concerning any requirements for applications and interviews related to the PERM application process.
These attestations are necessary because there have been several reports of employers creating separate recruitment processes for PERM applications that deter U.S. workers from applying for job opportunities.

]
The employer also required all applicants for PERM-related positions to mail paper applications, even though the company permitted electronic applications for other positions.

These provisions

would clarify expectations for employer conduct during the PERM application recruitment process.
Currently, if the employer has a layoff in the AIE within six months of filing the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
the employer must document that it has notified and considered all of the employer's potentially qualified laid off U.S. workers for the job opportunity to be offered in an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification. See
current section 656.17(k). The proposed rule would convert the existing layoff obligation into an employer attestation and relocate the provision to the newly proposed section 656.13(e) with revisions. As proposed, section 656.13(e)(1) would address layoffs prior to the employer's filing of an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
while section 656.13(e)(2) would address post-filing layoffs.
The Department's proposals regarding layoffs and consideration of laid-off U.S. workers are intended to provide U.S. workers additional protections against improper hiring conduct by employers
[
85
]
and prevent employers from laying off U.S. worker(s) and creating vacancies which are then filled with aliens using the PERM process.
[
86
]
As proposed, an employer would be required to attest that it has not laid off any U.S. worker(s) in the same or similar occupation that is the subject of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
in the area of intended employment of the place(s) of employment within 2 years prior to filing the application. The Department proposes to change the current term to describe similar occupations from “occupation for which certification is sought or in a related occupation” in current section 656.17(k) to “same or similar occupation” in proposed section 656.13(e), for readability. The Department does not intend for this proposed revision to change the employers' consideration of their laid-off employees post-filing of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
and reminds employers that their obligation is to consider all potentially qualified laid-off U.S. workers for job opportunities that are the subject of a pending or certified
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
The Department invites comments on this proposed change and ways to improve clarity.
If the employer could not make this attestation (
i.e.,
if it had engaged in such a layoff), the employer would be prohibited from filing the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
under the proposed rule.
The proposed 2-year timeframe during which layoffs would be prohibited supports the Department's goals in this rulemaking. Specifically, this proposal would enhance safeguards for laid-off U.S. workers and increase protection against employment discrimination for an extended period of time, while preventing misuse of the PERM labor certification program.
The Department proposes a 2-year period because the current 180-day layoff timeframe prior to the employer filing an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
may not adequately capture the relationship between an employer's layoffs and its subsequent efforts to obtain permanent labor certification. Workforce planning, recruitment, the PERM process, and related business decisions can unfold over an extended period, allowing a shorter restriction to be avoided simply by delaying the filing of an application. A 2-year period would provide a more meaningful safeguard against such circumvention while also allowing sufficient time for employers to rehire or retrain recently laid-off U.S. workers if demand for the same or similar occupations returns. This proposal seeks to ensure employers do not circumvent program requirements nor abuse the system for seeking to hire alien workers by conducting layoffs that are timed with respect to application or petition timeframes to avoid scrutiny or further having to justify the hiring of alien workers despite the employer experiencing layoffs. The Department seeks comment on whether 2 years is the appropriate period and whether a shorter or longer period would better accomplish these objectives.
The Department also believes the proposed period could encourage employers to invest in retraining existing workers as workforce needs change and could increase opportunities to rehire laid-off U.S. workers when demand for an affected occupation returns. For example, without access to the PERM labor certification program for 2 years, employers would be more likely to invest in training their existing workforce in new technology or other changes, rather than replacing them with aliens who received that training elsewhere. For layoffs that occur due to changed market conditions, this proposal could result in increased re-hiring of laid-off U.S. workers, if an employer's need for the occupation that was affected by layoffs returns.
In addition, simultaneously laying off U.S. workers and recruiting in the same or similar occupation(s) of the PERM application (or doing so in close proximity) is inherently problematic for the statutorily required determinations the Department must make in order to issue a PERM labor certification. An employer's layoff of U.S. workers who are available and willing to work at the place(s) of employment and who, until the layoff, were performing work for the employer in the occupation, or a similar occupation, at the place(s) of employment would preclude the Department from making the statutorily required determinations necessary to issue a PERM labor certification. In addition to furthering U.S. worker protections and program integrity, the proposed 2-year pre-filing anti-layoff provision aligns with the Department's goal of streamlining processing by preventing the filing of an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
where the employer's own actions have increased U.S. worker availability for the job opportunity that is the subject of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
Proposed section 656.13(e)(2) addresses layoff situations after an employer files their
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
As proposed, this provision would apply to an employer's layoff of any U.S. workers in the same or similar occupation that is the subject of the
(
printed page 73946)
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
in the place(s) of employment—including the placement of the alien with another employer, subject to proposed section 656.13(f)—after the filing of the application through the date on which the Form I-140 petition is approved by USCIS or the date of determination, if the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
or Form I-140 petition is denied or withdrawn, whichever is later. If any such layoff occurs, the employer would be required to notify the NPC (and USCIS in the case of a pending Form I-140 petition) not later than 5 business days after such layoff(s) occurs. This new notification requirement after such layoff(s) occurs ensures program integrity by informing and allowing OFLC and USCIS, if applicable, to take appropriate action with the employer's
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
and/or the employer's pending Form I-140 petition, respectively. The Department notes that the notification required by this provision will trigger the INA 204(b) consultation process whereby DOL will determine the adequacy of the employer's compliance with the post-certification obligation to consider laid off U.S. workers, and inform USCIS of the continued validity, or revocation of the underlying labor certification based on DOL's assessment of the employer's compliance.
In addition, the proposal would require the employer to offer the job opportunity that is the subject of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
to the laid-off U.S. worker(s) and document in an updated recruitment report whether the U.S. worker(s) refused the job opportunity, the employer rejected the U.S. worker(s) for the job opportunity for lawful, job-related reasons, or the employer hired the U.S. worker(s).
Under this proposed rule, the employer must seek to re-hire laid off U.S. worker(s) by offering the job opportunity to any potentially qualified laid off U.S. worker(s) before continuing with a PERM application. Failure to fill the job opportunity that is the subject of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
by re-hiring a laid-off U.S. worker who is qualified and available could raise an evidentiary inference of citizenship status discrimination, national origin discrimination or discrimination in any other class listed in anti-discrimination provision at proposed section 656.13(a)(4). Through this proposed requirement, the Department would protect against U.S. worker displacement and ensure that an employer's laid off U.S. workers have access to the job opportunity while the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
and Form I-140 petition are pending, before the employer uses the PERM labor certification to permanently employ an alien.
The Department seeks stakeholder comments regarding layoffs and what constitutes reasonable time periods and requirements for employers filing
Applications for Permanent Employment Certifications
before, during, and after layoffs.
This proposed provision would also protect against U.S. worker displacement and ensure that an employer's laid off U.S. workers have access to the job opportunity while the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
and Form I-140 petition are pending, before the alien uses the PERM labor certification and I-140 petition to apply for permanent residence.
Further, the Department proposes to require an employer who has laid off any U.S. worker(s) in the same or similar occupation that is the subject of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
in the area of intended employment of the place(s) of employment during the period set forth in proposed section 656.13(e)—including the placement of the alien with another employer, subject to proposed section 656.13(f)—to notify OFLC (and USCIS in the case of a pending Form I-140 petition), in writing or by any other method the Department might specify in a FRN (or as specified by USCIS in the case of a pending Form I-140 petition), not later than five business days after such layoff(s) occurs. This new notification requirement after such layoff(s) occurred ensures program integrity by informing and allowing OFLC and USCIS, if applicable, to take appropriate action with the employer's
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
and/or pending Form I-140 petition, respectively.
The Department also proposes a new attestation in proposed section 656.13(f) that would require the employer filing the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
to attest that they have not and will not place the alien with another employer where there are indicia of an employment relationship between the alien and the other employer, and the other employer has laid off U.S. workers who are employed in the same or similar occupation within the 2 years prior to filing of the application through the date the Form I-140 petition is approved by USCIS or the date of determination, if the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
or Form I-140 petition is denied or withdrawn, whichever is later. Although the Department recognizes that the alien's assignments may change after filing, the Department proposes to require the employer to identify on the application any third-party entities and sites to which the alien is assigned at the time of filing. This collection will improve the information available to the Department regarding third-party assignments and compliance with proposed section 656.13(f). This proposed provision would improve the integrity of the PERM program by ensuring U.S. workers will not be displaced by aliens, whether the aliens work directly for the employer or are employed by a secondary employer, such as a contractor.
For consistency across programs, the Department is proposing to use the criteria set forth in the Department's H-1B program regulations at
20 CFR 655.738(d)(2)
to assess indicia of an employment relationship between the other employer and the alien. Under
20 CFR 655.738(d)(2)
, the relationship between the alien and the other employer need not constitute an “employment” relationship, but other relevant indicia of an employment relationship may be considered, including: which employer has the right to control when, where, and how the alien performs the job; who furnishes the tools, materials, and equipment; where the work is performed, who sets the hours of work and the duration of the job; and whether the work performed is part of the other employer's regular business. The Department is considering whether to propose the implementation of a contract requirement between employers, which could align with the contract requirements in the H-1B program. Although the Department is not proposing a contract requirement in this rule, the Department welcomes comments on this consideration.
This proposed rule also codifies current requirements that employers and their agents, attorneys, and/or employees have not offered, and will not offer, for sale, barter or purchase
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification,
including applications certified by the Department, and have not sought or received, and will not seek to receive, payment of any kind from the worker(s) for any activity related to obtaining a PERM labor certification. The Department is proposing to relocate the language contained in current section 656.12, while also seeking to make some clarifying changes.
See
proposed section
(
printed page 73947)
656.13(g). This provision includes payment of the employer's attorneys' fees, whether as an incentive or inducement to filing, or as a reimbursement for costs incurred in preparing or filing an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
except when the work benefits the person or entity making the payment, based on an established business relationship with the employer. This provision serves to prevent fraud and abuse by those who unlawfully take advantage of the PERM labor certification program. The proposed rule, however, would continue to allow aliens to pay their own costs in connection with a PERM labor certification, including attorneys' fees, except where the same attorney represents both the alien and the employer, such costs must be paid by the employer. Under the proposed rule, payment includes, but is not limited to, monetary payments; wage concessions, including deductions from wages, salary, or benefits; kickbacks, bribes, or tributes; in kind payments; and free labor. Adding this provision to section 656.13 would serve as an additional guard rail to deter program abuse and bolster the integrity of the program.
See
proposed section 656.13(g).
The Department proposes to require employers to attest they will comply with applicable Federal, State, and local employment-related laws and regulations, including, but not limited to, employment-related health and safety laws, and all applicable provisions of the Fair Labor Standards Act,
29 U.S.C. 201
,
et seq. See
proposed section 656.13(h). The Department proposes this attestation to put employers on notice that compliance with these laws is a condition of certification and to strengthen coordination of enforcement among Federal agencies with authority to ensure compliance with program requirements and combat fraud and abuse. 18 U.S.C. 1592(a)
. This proposal will provide protection for aliens' rights from unscrupulous employers, such as those who take away aliens' passports with the intent to trap and coerce the worker and undermine the integrity of the program by deterring those workers from coming forward to report labor and employment-related issues to the Department and the government at large.
Proposed section 656.13(i) would require employers to attest to compliance with record retention requirements. Employers would continue to be required to retain all documents and records demonstrating compliance with part 656 for a period of 5 years, which the Department proposes to count from the date on which the Immigrant Petition is approved or denied or withdrawn. If the employer does not proceed to file an Immigrant Petition, it would be required to retain all records associated with the Application for Permanent Employment Certification for a period of 5 years from the expiration of the certification or denial or withdrawal.
See
proposed section 656.10(h).
Proposed section 656.13(j) adds a new attestation, which would require employers to attest that they will fully cooperate with any audit, supervised recruitment, compliance review, evaluation, or inspection conducted by DOL related to compliance with part 656, or by other government agencies investigating PERM practices. This proposal will deter fraud and abuse and improve the integrity of the PERM program because employers are put on notice of the Department's expectations and understand their obligations and responsibilities in the event of an audit examination or investigation.
Consistent with current practice, failure to attest to compliance with any of the required assurances and obligations would result in a denial of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
and a false certification would subject the employer to audit, supervised recruitment, debarment, referral, and criminal penalties under
18 U.S.C. 1001

5. Proposed New
20 CFR 656.14
, Notice of Filing
The NOF, required by the Act, is intended to make U.S. workers employed by the sponsoring employer aware that their employer is pursuing an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
for a particular job opportunity, and enable them to provide information directly to the Department if any of the material terms or conditions of employment being offered to the alien are different from or adversely affect those offered or provided to U.S. workers in similar positions, or if they have any other evidence or information bearing on the prospective employment of an alien in the job opportunity at the place(s) of employment that the Department should consider. U.S. workers can also provide information to the Department of any qualified and available U.S. workers who have not been considered for the job opportunity, such as during a layoff that may occur at any time prior to the filing of the application through approval of the Form I-140 petition by USCIS.
[
87
]
First, the Department proposes relocating the current regulatory text in section 656.10(d) to a new section at 656.14, with additional modifications to reorganize the section for clarity. The Department also proposes revising the standard for providing the NOF requirements to enhance transparency, strengthen program integrity, and acknowledge the widespread use of electronic tools by employers to disseminate other notices of employment-related guarantees or conditions (
e.g.,
Fair Labor Standards Act minimum wage requirements, Equal Employment Opportunity protections), especially due to remote or other hybrid telework environments.
The Department is proposing that after the language currently contained in sections 656.10(d)(i) and (ii) is relocated to the newly added section 656.14's paragraphs (a)(1) and (2), conforming changes be made. Specifically, the Department is proposing revisions that would clarify employers' obligations for the NOF when the employer seeks to apply for a PERM labor certification to permanently employ an alien in the United States. Proposed new section 656.14(a) would still require, if requested by the CO, employers to submit documentation showing that the NOF was posted. The proposed revisions would eliminate regulatory text listing the sections to which the NOF requirement applies (
i.e.,
656.15, 656.16, 656.17, 656.18, and 656.21), in favor of regulatory text that indicates that the NOF requirement applies to all applications under part 656, consistent with statute and other proposed regulatory changes. The proposed move to section 656.14 would streamline the current regulatory text by making it clear that the NOF is a general requirement; accordingly, the new regulatory text would eliminate the need for updates in the future should there be additional changes to the organization of part 656.
The Department makes minor revisions in proposed section 656.14(a)(1) to specify that the NOF, when given to a bargaining representative(s), must be in writing, either electronically or by mail. The employer must also provide a copy of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
to the
(
printed page 73948)
bargaining representative. Proposed section 656.14(a)(1) clarifies that employers must maintain documentation of where and when the employer's NOF was sent to the bargaining representative(s). These proposed revisions strengthen the NOF requirements to bolster the integrity of the PERM labor certification program and better align with similar notice requirements in the temporary labor certification programs.
In proposed 656.14(a)(1), the Department proposes to change the circumstances in which notification of bargaining representative(s) is required. Under the current rule, an employer must notify a bargaining representative, if there is a bargaining representative for the employer's employees in the occupational classification for which certification of the job opportunity is sought “in the employer's location(s) in the area of intended employment.” As proposed an employer would be required to notify the bargaining representative(s) for the employer's employees located at the place(s) of employment” listed on the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
This change—to require notice to bargaining representative(s) at the place(s) of employment—would ensure the bargaining representative(s) of similarly employed U.S. workers at all place(s) of employment listed on the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
must receive notice and resolves potential misinterpretation of the singular term “the area of intended employment” in the current provision. This approach better ensures the employer's employees receive notice of the filing of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
even if those place(s) of employment are in more than one AIE. As discussed in relation to the definition of “place(s) of employment” in proposed section 656.3, workforce mobility has increased over the past two decades and the place(s) of employment listed on an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
may encompass more than one AIE. The proposed change would ensure that all bargaining representatives representing employees in the occupational classification at the place(s) of employment receive direct notice of the filing of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
and can assess impact to U.S. workers. In addition, the proposed change would increase consistency of notification to the employer's employees at the place(s) of employment, whether or not there is a bargaining representative, as both the current and proposed rules require physical or electronic posting of the NOF for employees at the location where work will be performed. The Department also makes revisions in proposed section 656.14(a)(2) for situations where there is no bargaining representative(s) for any of the employer's employees located at the place(s) of employment. Currently, the employer must post the NOF physically at the place of employment, but the regulation does not specify the required number of posting locations required. Proposed section 656.14(a)(2) specifies that employers must post the NOF “in at least 2 conspicuous locations to all employees located at the place(s) of employment in which the work will be performed by the alien.” Posting the NOF physically in at least two conspicuous locations at all places of employment involved, as defined in proposed section 656.3, would allow individuals who work or traverse through different locations more opportunity to see the posting and would enhance the visibility of the NOF to employees. all

For employers who maintain internal or external website(s) that are “known and readily accessible to all employees, and customarily used by the employer for notices to employees about terms and conditions of employment,” the Department proposes that prominently displaying the NOF on those websites, in lieu of physical postings, would satisfy the statutory notice requirement under proposed 656.14(a)(2). The Department asserts that posting the NOF electronically would be particularly effective for businesses with employees who frequently telework or travel, and who may not see the NOF if it is only posted physically in the workplace.

8. Proposed
20 CFR 656.17
, Pre-Filing Recruitment Requirements
The Department is proposing to revise current section 656.17 and its section title (from “Basic Labor Certification Process” to “Pre-filing Recruitment Procedures”), in part, due to the proposed reorganization of part 656. The Department proposes to relocate the content of current paragraphs (a) and (c) of section 656.17 (“Filing applications” and “Filing date”) to proposed section 656.10; the content of current paragraph (k) of section 656.17 (“Layoffs”) to proposed section 656.13; and the content of current paragraphs (b), (h), (i), (j), and (l) of section 656.17 (“Processing,” “Job duties and requirements,” “Actual minimum requirements,” “Conditions of employment,” and “Alien influence and control over the job opportunity”) to proposed section 656.19. The Department also proposes to revise section 656.17 to remove obsolete language (
e.g.,
current paragraph (d) “Refiling procedures”) and to conform with other proposals contained in this proposed rule, such as the elimination of alternative procedures for sheepherders and occupations currently covered by Schedule A. The resulting proposed section 656.17 is designed to focus on pre-filing recruitment requirements. Moreover, under the proposed rule and as previously discussed, the pre-filing recruitment requirements proposed in section 656.17 would apply to all
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification,
unless the job opportunity was eligible for—and the employer opted to comply with—the optional pre-
(
printed page 73951)
filing recruitment requirements of proposed section 656.18.
Consistent with the current regulation, proposed section 656.17 would continue to require employers seeking a PERM labor certification to engage in pre-filing recruitment activities, conduct a good faith test of the labor market for qualified U.S. workers, and retain documentation to demonstrate compliance with program requirements. However, the Department proposes to eliminate the current distinction between pre-filing recruitment requirements for professional and non-professional occupations in section 656.17; the requirements of proposed section 656.17 would apply equally to professional and non-professional occupations. As discussed below, the Department proposes significant revisions to modernize the pre-filing recruitment steps required under section 656.17 that better reflect the widespread use of online or digital recruitment practices, ensure that recruitment efforts reach the broadest pool of qualified and available U.S. workers, and ensure the employers' labor market tests are conducted in good faith and consistent with their current hiring practices to reach prospective applicants for similar job opportunities outside the PERM labor certification process. The proposed approach will support recruitment of both professional and non-professional occupations, enabling the Department to further its goal of simplifying part 656.
Employer Obligations
Consistent with current section 656.17(e), proposed section 656.17(a) requires employers to attest, under penalty of perjury, that they conducted the pre-filing recruitment outlined in section 656.17, including compliance with all advertising requirements contained in proposed sections 656.17(b) through (e). Under the proposed rule, only employers filing
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification
for college or university teachers, professional athletes, or professional sports team coaches may opt not to conduct pre-filing recruitment under section 656.17; however, if they do not comply with pre-filing recruitment requirements of proposed section 656.17, they must comply with the pre-filing recruitment requirements of proposed section 656.18.
Both currently and under the proposed rule, the employer must maintain documentation, including copies of all advertisements and resumes or applications from prospective U.S. applicants considered for the job opportunity, to support the attestations made in the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
and recruitment report. Under this proposed rule, the employer would be required to submit the recruitment report (including resumes and applications of all U.S. workers who applied for the job opportunity) and documentation to prove compliance with recruitment requirements at the time of filing the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification. See
proposed sections 656.10(a)(3) and (4).
Required Recruitment
Under the current rule, employers are generally required to recruit during the 30-day to 180-day period before filing the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
Recruitment for nonprofessional occupations consists of placing a job order with the SWA for a period of 30 days and print advertisements on two different Sundays in a newspaper of general circulation in the AIE most appropriate to the occupation and the workers likely to apply for the job opportunity. Recruitment for professional occupations similarly consists of placing a SWA job order and two print advertisements—one of which may be a professional journal that is normally used for job opportunities requiring an advanced degree and experience—but also requires three additional steps. Employers self-select the three additional steps to take from a menu of ten (10) recruitment options. The list of recruitment options for professional occupations are intended to provide employers flexibility to select methods appropriate to the job opportunity that is the subject of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
The menu of options includes: job fairs; the employer's website; job search websites other than the employer's; on-campus recruiting; trade or professional organization newsletters or journals; private employment firms; employee referral programs with incentives; campus placement offices; local and ethnic newspapers; and radio and television advertisements.
The Department recognizes that print advertisements are no longer a meaningful method for recruitment, which impacts the informational value of the two print advertisements currently required for the PERM labor market test for both nonprofessional and professional job opportunities.

Based on information, stakeholder feedback, and anecdotal data from previous rulemakings for the H-2A and H-2B programs, print ads in newspapers have yielded very few, if any, applications from able, willing, and qualified U.S. workers. Further, the Department's experience in conducting audit examinations, has shown that very few U.S. workers have applied to job opportunities in response to print advertisements that employers have placed.

The modern methods of recruitment proposed in this rule ensure that recruitment for job opportunities that are the subject of
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification
is conducted in the manner that is at least the same as the employer's recruitment practices for job opportunities in the same or substantially comparable occupations that it does not seek PERM labor certification and most likely to reach the broadest pool of qualified U.S. workers in the current labor market.
In addition, the Department proposes to replace the current menu of options for additional recruitment for professional occupations with a standardized list of modern methods of recruitment, which would be applicable to both professional and nonprofessional occupations. As discussed below, the flexibility of the menu approach has not had the intended effect of ensuring appropriate recruitment for professional occupations. In addition, nonprofessional recruitment currently uses similar approaches to professional recruitment, including online advertising on job search websites and social media and recruitment through trade schools.

In the proposed rule, the Department would eliminate mandatory print advertisements for both professional and nonprofessional job opportunities and the current menu of additional recruitment options for professional occupations. Instead, for both professional and nonprofessional job opportunities, the proposed rule would require employers to comply with a standardized, mandatory list of modernized recruitment activities, which leverage online recruitment and the employer's own approach to recruit for similar job opportunities that are not the subject of an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
The proposed rule seeks to improve and modernize the PERM labor certification labor market test by replacing outdated and ineffective means of recruitment with modern and more effective forms of recruitment, while also retaining some forms of recruitment that remain standard and productive, to advertise job opportunities as broadly as possible in order to attract as many U.S. workers as possible. In addition, the proposed rule aims at leveraging employers' current approaches to recruitment outside the PERM labor certification program. The proposed rule would require employers to recruit U.S. workers for PERM labor certification job opportunities using the same methods they use when seeking to fill a vacancy in a non-PERM labor certification recruitment setting. The recruitment steps proposed in this paragraph would ensure that U.S. workers are informed of the job opportunity and are provided the opportunity to apply and be considered for the job opportunity prior to an alien being offered permanent employment through a PERM labor certification, which would allow the Department to make the certification required by the INA. The mandatory pre-filing recruitment activities required of all employers under proposed section 656.17 are outlined below.
Placement of the Job Order—
Proposed section 656.17(b)(1) would require the employer to place a job order with the SWA serving the place(s) of employment, consistent with the current rule. The Department proposes a revision to clarify that if the job opportunity covers more than one place of employment and the SWAs serving the places of employment are distinct, the employer would be required to place a job order with more than one SWA. Further, the proposed rule uses the term “place of employment” rather than “area of intended employment” to add specificity for the location(s) that determine placement of the job order with the particular SWA(s).
Placement of Advertisement on Employer's Website(s)
—As proposed in section 656.17(b)(2), if an employer maintains one or more websites for its business operations, it must place an advertisement for the job opportunity that is the subject of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
on those websites. If the employer customarily uses its website(s) for its business operations to recruit for job opportunities that are not the subject of an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
the advertisement for the job opportunity that is the subject of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
must be placed in the same manner (
e.g.,
same web page) the employer customarily uses to recruit for job opportunities. If the employer does not customarily use its website(s) for its business operations to recruit for job opportunities, the employer must post the job opportunity that is the subject of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
on all such website(s) in a conspicuous location (
e.g.,
the employer's contact page). The objective of the advertisement is to apprise as many U.S. workers of the job opportunity as possible and, therefore, the advertisement must be placed in a conspicuous location on each website the employer maintains for its business operations. Under the proposed rule, the employer is required to use all websites it maintains for business purposes to ensure the broadest dissemination of the job opportunity.
This proposal is intended to better apprise U.S. workers of the job opportunity and also make it more difficult for employers who are not recruiting in good faith to conceal job opportunities from U.S. workers, including those who are employed by the employer but might be interested in applying for the offered position, or U.S. workers who have been laid off, for example.
Placement of Advertisement on Job Search Website(s)
—Proposed section 656.17(b)(3) would require the employer to place an advertisement for the job opportunity on at least one job search website. This proposal specifies that compliance with paragraph (b)(3) requires placement of the advertisement on a job search website that is not the employer's own website (
i.e.,
the employer's business website in proposed paragraph (b)(2)) or the SWA's website (
i.e.,
job order posting in proposed paragraph (b)(1)).
The proposed rule requires employers to post advertisements on one or more job search website(s) using the same methods and website locations as the employer customarily uses for recruitment of its other job opportunities that are unrelated to requests for PERM labor certification. The intent is to ensure that while recruiting for a PERM labor certification job opportunity, the employer, at a minimum, uses all of the job search website methods it typically uses, and in the same manner that it typically uses, when recruiting outside of the PERM labor certification context to make jobs known to U.S. workers. In the event an employer does not customarily post advertisements on job search websites for job opportunities that are the same as the job offered in the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
compliance with proposed 656.17(b)(3) would require the employer to post an advertisement on one job search website that is appropriate for recruitment of the job opportunity.
For an employer whose business is job postings, providing job searches, or job matching (
e.g.,
an employer whose business includes a job search engine, job website, job board, job portal, or job aggregator, etc.; and/or an employer whose businesses performs tasks such as headhunting, staffing, or connecting employers and job seekers through job platforms, etc.) or, otherwise, the employer specializes in advertisement of job opportunities, compliance with proposed section 656.17 would require the employer to advertise on its own job search website(s) for proposed paragraph (b)(2) and, in addition, to advertise using a third-party commercial job search website for the proposed paragraph (b)(3).
