—Proposed section 656.17(b)(4) would require an employer who customarily uses one or more social media platforms to advertise
(
printed page 73954)
job opportunities in the same occupational classification to similarly do so during pre-filing recruitment for PERM labor certification. Under the proposed rule, the employer must use the same method(s) and location(s) and post this advertisement in a similar manner as it would for job opportunities unrelated to requests for PERM labor certification. The intent of this requirement is to ensure that while recruiting for a PERM labor certification, the employer, at a minimum, uses all of the methods it commonly uses when recruiting outside of the PERM labor certification context to make jobs known to U.S. workers.
If an employer does not customarily use a social media platform to advertise job opportunities in the same occupational classification, proposed paragraph (b)(4) does not require an advertisement on a social media platform. In this way, proposed paragraph (b)(4) contrasts with proposed paragraphs (b)(3) and (b)(5), which would require an employer who does not normally advertise job opportunities in the same occupational classification using the method described to do so during PERM labor certification pre-filing recruitment.
Job Fairs or On-Campus Recruitment
—Proposed section 656.17(b)(5) would require employers to advertise the job opportunity through at least one job fair, on-campus recruitment event, or college, university, or trade school placement office while the job order placed with the SWA, under proposed paragraph (b)(1), is actively circulating. Even if the employer does not normally recruit for the same or similar job opportunities through any one of these methods, compliance with proposed paragraph (b)(5) would require the employer to do so at least once, through one of the listed methods.
For employers whose recruitment methods for the same or similar job opportunity outside the PERM labor certification context includes recruitment through job fairs, on-campus recruitment events, and/or college, university, or trade school placement office, the employer would be required to recruit for the PERM-related job opportunity in the same way it recruits for non-PERM job opportunities. The Department recognizes that employers may customarily recruit through job fairs, on-campus recruiting events, and/or college, university, or trade school placement offices that may not be geographically close to the place(s) of employment because those job fairs are expected to attract qualified candidates or those colleges, universities, or trade schools offer programs of study that align with the job opportunity offered and whose students or alumni are likely to be good candidates for the employer's job opportunities. The Department does not intend for employers to artificially limit their recruitment under proposed paragraph (b)(5) based on geography. Rather, employers who customarily recruit through job fairs, on-campus recruitment events, and/or campus placement offices would use the same location(s) and manner for job opportunities that are the subject of
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification.
The Department welcomes comments on the proposed pre-filing recruitment methods listed above, as well as additional ideas or methods of recruitment that could be used in the PERM program. Specifically, the Department requests comments on whether to include a requirement to contact all U.S. workers currently employed at the place(s) of employment, similar to the requirement in the H-2B program under temporary final rules (TFRs) for fiscal years 2023, 2024, and 2025.
[
111
]
For this requirement, employers would be required to contact U.S. workers currently employed at the place(s) of employment to inform them of the job opportunity and request their assistance in recruiting qualified U.S. workers who may be seeking employment. As explained in the H-2B TFR and relevant for recruiting U.S. workers for permanent employment under this NPRM, the Department believes this method of positive recruitment is a reasonable and cost-effective way of broadening dissemination of available job opportunities and increasing the likelihood that qualified U.S. workers will apply.
[
112
]
Moreover, encouraging existing employees to provide referrals is generally recognized as an effective means for an employer to identify prospective applicants who would be well matched to the available job opportunity.
[
113
]
The Department also invites comments on how innovations in technology will impact the relevant forms of recruitment and whether there are alternative or additional methods of broadly disseminating job opportunities that could more effectively test the U.S. labor market while reducing unnecessary employer burden, including approaches that would facilitate and consolidate the publication of job opportunities. Commenters are encouraged to identify mechanisms that could increase the visibility and accessibility of PERM job opportunities to U.S. workers, improve the Department's ability to ensure compliance and/or assess the effectiveness of recruitment, or reduce reliance on multiple employer-directed recruitment activities.
Length of Active Recruitment
Section 656.17(c) of the proposed rule requires active recruitment for each method in proposed paragraphs (b)(1) through (b)(4) of this section to be performed for at least 90 calendar days. However, if during the prior 12 months, the employer has routinely advertised for the same or similar job opportunities unrelated to requests for PERM labor certification for more than 90 calendar days, then the employer must advertise for the PERM labor certification job opportunity for the longer period of time it routinely used in the prior 12 months. To comply with this paragraph, the employer must use whichever period of time is longer—90 calendar days or the employer's customary length of recruitment for the same or similar job opportunities in the prior 12-month period.
For example, where the employer normally posts a job opportunity for 120 calendar days, the employer must similarly post the job opportunity that is the subject of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
for 120 calendar days. The intent is for the employer to allow as much active recruitment time in connection with PERM labor certification recruitment as the employer allows on active
(
printed page 73955)
recruitment for non-PERM labor certification recruitment. The proposed text requires that the job opportunity for which the employer seeks a PERM labor certification is as broadly and widely advertised as possible and in accordance with the employer's own customary business recruitment standards, in order to reach as many potentially qualified U.S. applicants as possible. The Department thinks that the proposed 90-day period for active recruitment of U.S. workers is both reasonable and appropriate because this proposed minimum timeframe is consistent with the amount of time unemployed American workers are actively searching for work and therefore a sufficient period of time to test the U.S. labor market. According to the October 2026 Employment Situation Summary Report, the BLS estimated that the average number of weeks unemployed persons were actively looking for work in September 2026 was 25.4 weeks (
i.e.,
approximately 6 months), while the median duration was 12.1 weeks (
i.e.,
approximately 3 months) and, when excluding the long-term unemployed (
i.e.,
persons actively seeking work 27 weeks or longer), nearly 1.1 million unemployed persons were actively looking for work for 15 to 26 weeks.
[
114
]
When examining the most recent estimates of unemployed American workers actively searching for work within the prime working-ages of 25 to 54 years, this proposed timeframe is likewise reasonable and appropriate. For October 2026, BLS also estimated that the median number of weeks unemployed persons were actively looking for work was 13.2 weeks for those 25 to 34 years old; 15.4 weeks for those 35 to 44 years old; and 14.6 weeks for those 45 to 54 years old.
[
115
]
Additionally, the proposed 90-day advertising standard would provide a minimum level of consistency in recruitment efforts and ensure qualified U.S. workers have ample opportunity to apply and be considered for employment in the job opportunity. Because current regulations do not require any minimum timeframe, the amount of time employers make online advertisements available through their own website and other job search websites varies significantly, and often times these announcements are available for less time than the current 30-day job order placed with the SWA. For example, among the 200,124 applications granted PERM labor certification for professional occupations during FY 2021-FY 2025 that chose to advertise job opportunities through a website maintained by the employer, approximately 25 percent (50,361 applications) advertised for less than 15 calendar days, 34 percent (67,825 applications) advertised for 15 to 30 calendar days, and 41 percent (81,938 applications) advertised for 30 calendar days or more. Among the 387,518 applications where the employer chose to use an online job search website, approximately 62 percent (241,880 applications) advertised for less than 15 calendar days, 29 percent (113,165 applications) advertised for 15 to 30 calendar days, and 8 percent (32,464 applications) advertised for 30 calendar days or more.
[
116
]
Thus, the Department's most recent program experience demonstrates a clear need to propose a minimum regulatory standard that can achieve greater consistency in the length of time prospective qualified U.S. workers have to apply and be considered for employment in these job opportunities.
As discussed in detail below under section 656.17(f), the employer must document the length of its recruitment efforts for the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
and, as directed by the CO, provide documentation of the length of the employer's recruitment efforts for
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
with proof of the length of the employer's normal or typical recruitment standard for the same or similar job opportunities.
Completion of Active Recruitment
Section 656.17(d) of the proposed rule would require the employer to complete the recruitment activities of proposed paragraphs (b)(1) through (b)(4), between 30 to 60 calendar days before the employer files the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
This provision protects U.S. workers by ensuring the recruitment for the job opportunity does not become stale prior to the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
filing, and ensures that U.S. workers who may have availability for the job opportunity are made aware of the job in proximity to the filing of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
rather than many months ahead of time, potentially prior to when currently available U.S. workers have begun their job search. In contrast, the current rule permits employers to complete recruitment as much as 5 months in advance of filing.
Advertising Content Requirements
Proposed section 656.17(e) largely continues current advertising content requirements, with revisions to ensure that U.S. workers are better apprised of the job opportunities offered. In addition, under this proposed rule, the Department would expand the scope of the advertising content requirements. The current rule has been interpreted as limiting advertising content requirements to the mandatory print advertisements.
[
117
]
In contrast, proposed 656.17(e) would apply the advertising content requirements to all recruitment conducted for compliance with 656.17.
Through the years after the implementation of the current rule, employers began to include technical jargon and shortened terms in PERM-related newspaper advertisements. More often than not, advertisements used in recruitment for PERM labor certification have confused potential job applicants, rather than sufficiently apprising U.S. workers about the actual job duties, qualifications, and skills required. In addition, over time, the advertisements placed for compliance with the current rule have been recognized by applicants as PERM-specific advertisements and in many cases, U.S. workers no longer apply because they believe such ads signify the lack of a bona fide job opportunity.
[
118
]
This perspective from U.S. workers suggests that some employers are not making PERM-related job opportunities truly open to qualified U.S. workers, a problem this proposed rule addresses. Further, the proposed rule would require consistency throughout the recruitment process by requiring employers to solicit and recruit for U.S. workers using specific content intended to apprise U.S. workers of the job requirements, wages, locations and other pertinent details of the available job opportunities.
While proposed section 656.17(e)(1) would continue to prohibit advertising from containing terms and conditions
(
printed page 73956)
that are less favorable to U.S. workers than those offered to the alien, it adds that the terms and conditions offered in the advertising also, at a minimum, must comply with assurances set forth in proposed section 656.13. The proposed rule would ensure that U.S. workers are not disfavored in the recruitment process or dissuaded from applying for job opportunities that are subject to
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification
due to misleading or inaccurate information or prohibited terms.
The list of required advertising content in proposed section 656.17(e)(2), again, largely continues current requirements. However, the proposed list includes intentional revisions to better ensure that U.S. workers are apprised of the pertinent details of the available job opportunities and available U.S. workers can apply for the position. For example, rather than continuing to require advertisements to “[n]ame the employer” and “[d]irect applicants to report or send resumes, as appropriate for the occupation, to the employer,” the proposed rule requires advertisements to contain “[t]he employer's name and contact information.” The revised advertising content requirements proposed in section 656.17(e) are intended to both provide the necessary information for U.S. workers to determine whether they are interested in and qualified for the job opportunity and better match non-PERM recruitment situations.
Finally, proposed section 656.17(e)(3) would permit employers to recruit for multiple positions simultaneously using the same advertisement as long as that single advertisement complies with all the pre-filing recruitment time, placement, and duration requirements for each job opportunity; and includes sufficient information to inform U.S. workers of each job opportunity.
As proposed, all of the employer's advertisements for recruitment under this proposed section must include the following: the employer's name and contact information; a description of the job opportunity sufficient to apprise U.S. workers of the services or labor to be performed and the actual minimum qualifications or requirements to perform the services or labor sought; the place(s) of employment or geographic area of employment, including a statement as to whether the position offers remote work, full-time telework, or a hybrid combination of telework and on-site work, with enough specificity to apprise applicants of any travel requirements and where applicants will likely have to reside to perform the services or labor; the wage offer, or if there are multiple wage offers, the range of applicable wage offers (each of which must equal or exceed the highest of the prevailing wage or the Federal, State, or local minimum wage); a statement that overtime is available to the worker and the wage offer(s) for working any overtime hours (as applicable); and a statement that the job is a full-time position and, if the employer has more than one job opening, the total number of job openings the employer intends to fill.
The Department also proposes a new provision at section 656.17(e)(3) to provide some flexibility for employers who may be able to combine multiple positions in a single advertisement, while complying with the content requirements in proposed section 656.17(e). Permitting this flexibility would be financially efficient for employers, while ensuring the employer's advertisements contain content necessary to appropriately apprise U.S. workers of the job opportunities offered.
Recruitment Report
Section 656.17(f) of the proposed rule discusses the recruitment report the employer must prepare and maintain to document its recruitment efforts under part 656 and the results. A notable change from the current regulation is that under the proposed rule, the employer would submit the recruitment report (including the resumes and applications of all U.S. workers who applied for the job opportunity) concurrently with the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
The employer's submission of the recruitment report with the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
will allow the Department's review of the recruitment report for each
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
rather than solely reviewing recruitment reports during audit examinations or when submitted in connection with supervised recruitment, as is the case under the current regulation. In other words, under the proposed regulation, employers will be required to submit a recruitment report for each application and the Department will be able to review the report for every single application to assess employers' pre-filing recruitment activities and consideration of U.S. workers. As discussed for proposed sections 656.10(a)(3) and (4), the Department would also require the employer to submit the supporting evidence for the recruitment report—copies of all advertising and U.S. worker applicants' resumes or applications for the job opportunity. While the CO may review only the recruitment report in all cases, the employer's full documentation of compliance with recruitment and consideration of U.S. workers would be available for the CO to review, without additional correspondence. Also, as noted in connection with proposed sections 656.10(a)(3) and (4), employers would not incur additional new burdens as a result of this requirement because they are already required to prepare and maintain recruitment reports for each
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
and to provide the recruitment report and supporting documentation to the CO, upon request (
e.g.,
audit examination).
The Department proposes to require more specific content in the recruitment report under the proposed rule than the current rule mandates. Current section 656.17(g)(1) includes general language that requires the recruitment report to “describe[e] the recruitment steps undertaken and the results achieved, the number of hires, and, if applicable, the number of U.S. workers rejected, categorized by the lawful job-related reasons for such rejections.” This approach provides recruitment results to the CO in the form of data, which does not adequately reflect the success—or failure—of specific recruitment activities and does not adequately reflect the employer's consideration of U.S. workers who apply for the job opportunity that is the subject of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
The Department has determined that the current recruitment report content does not provide sufficient information for the CO to form a clear picture of the labor market test (
e.g.,
which recruitment activities successfully reach U.S. workers, how the employer considered U.S. applicants, why the employer did not offer the job opportunity to each U.S. worker who applied, or that the employer did offer the job opportunity to U.S. workers who applied, but they declined) or to verify information in recruitment reports, as appropriate, for program integrity.
The recruitment report under proposed 656.17(f)(1) would include specific factual information to provide a fuller picture of the employer's recruitment activities and results. As proposed, the recruitment report submitted with the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
would identify the name of each recruitment activity and the date(s) of advertisement; identify the uniform resource locator (URL) or other location of each advertisement, and, for each advertisement placed with a website,
(
printed page 73957)
platform, publisher, or the SWA, the platform or publisher generated confirmation number, receipt, or order identifier and the posting and expiration dates it generated; state the name and contact information and date of application of each U.S. worker (including any the employer laid off) who applied for or was referred for the job opportunity up to the date the employer finalizes its recruitment report for submission with the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
categorized by the advertising method through which the U.S. worker applied, indicating whether the U.S. worker met the actual minimum requirements, with the disposition of each U.S. worker specified, including whether the U.S. worker received a job offer and, if so, whether they accepted or declined; and, if applicable, for each U.S. worker who applied but was not hired, explain the lawful job-related reason(s) for not hiring that U.S. worker. The recruitment report would also identify the name and title of each employee of the employer who reviewed, screened, or interviewed each of the applicants listed.
As provided by the INA in section 212(a)(5)(A)(i) and (ii) and both the current and proposed rule in section 656.24(b)(2), the Department will not issue a PERM labor certification to an employer if able, willing, and qualified U.S. worker(s) are available for the job opportunity that is—or would be—the subject of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
To demonstrate eligibility for a PERM labor certification, the employer must document its reasons for not hiring each U.S. applicant who applied for the job opportunity in a recruitment report. In the event U.S. workers apply for the job opportunity and satisfy the minimum qualifications, as described on the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
or for a college or university teacher position or positions offered to aliens who have exceptional ability in the sciences or the arts, who are at least as qualified as the alien, the employer must consider each of those U.S. worker applicants. Unless the employer identifies lawful, job-related reason(s) for not hiring each qualified U.S. worker, the Department considers the U.S. worker(s) available and will not issue a PERM certification. The employer may offer the job opportunity to such U.S. workers to determine whether the U.S. worker(s) are willing and available and if no qualified U.S. workers accept the job offer, the employer could continue to pursue issuance of a PERM labor certification. However, if a qualified U.S. worker accepts the job offer, the Department would not issue a PERM labor certification, as the job opportunity can be filled by a U.S. worker; permanent employment of an alien is not necessary. In addition, the proposed recruitment report content would provide the CO with information necessary to assess whether the employer has satisfied its burden of proof with respect to this statutory and regulatory requirement.
Adding the proposed specificity to recruitment report content requirements would improve clarity for employers and the consistency of recruitment information submitted to the NPC. It will also allow the Department to make a more informed determination about the availability of U.S. workers when carrying out its statutory obligation to determine that there are not sufficient able, willing, and qualified U.S. workers available for the job opportunity. In addition, the proposal to require recruitment reports to identify which U.S. workers applied for the job opportunity through which recruitment activities would better enable the Department to update recruitment requirements to balance burden against the effectiveness of advertising activities in the future.
Duty to Update Recruitment Report—
Proposed section 656.17(f)(2), consistent with the proposed layoff attestation in section 656.13(e), would require the employer to update its recruitment report after initially submitting it with the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
in the event of a layoff. A recruitment report update would be required whenever the employer experiences a layoff of any U.S. worker(s) in the same or similar occupation as the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
in the place(s) of intended employment, until the employer withdraws the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
or related Form I-140 petition, the CO denies PERM labor certification or USCIS denies the related Form I-140 petition, or USCIS approves the related Form I-140 petition. The employer would prepare an updated recruitment report each time it experiences a layoff. Each time, the employer would sign and date the updated recruitment report. The recruitment report updates would not be submitted to the CO, unless requested. This proposal supports program integrity and protects U.S. worker access to job opportunities before they are permanently filed with an alien by enabling the CO to confirm compliance with required consideration of laid off U.S. workers while the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
and Form I-140 petition are pending.
Similar to proposed section 656.17(f)(1), proposed section 656.17(f)(2) specifies the content to be required for recruitment report updates. The employer would be required to update their recruitment report with (i) a detailed explanation of the method(s) used and date(s) on which the employer notified all potentially qualified laid off U.S. workers for the job opportunity, who had been employed in the same or similar occupation that is the subject of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
in the place(s) of intended employment, and (ii) the name and contact information of each U.S. worker notified, identifying each one who applied to the job opportunity up to the date of the preparation of the recruitment report, categorized by the notification method through which they applied for the job opportunity, and specifying the disposition of each U.S. worker and whether the job opportunity was offered to the U.S. worker and whether the U.S. worker accepted or declined.
Duty to Maintain Recruitment Documentation
—The Department is proposing to relocate the requirement to retain documentation to prove compliance with section 656.17 recruitment requirements from current section 656.17(e)(1) to proposed revised section 656.17(g). The proposed rule would continue to require employers to retain documentation associated with their pre-filing recruitment for the
Application for Permanent Employment Certifications
and add the required retention of documentation associated with their ongoing, post-filing consideration of any laid off workers, if applicable.
As is current practice, the CO may request the employer's documentation to verify compliance with timing, content, and activity requirements, as well as recruitment results. To demonstrate compliance, the employer must document each advertisement's date(s), content (
e.g.,
proof of publication or screen shot of the ad placed on a website), and location(s) (
e.g.,
physical location and/or website address) and each notification to laid off U.S. workers.
Finally, the Department proposes a new section 656.17(h) that would provide some flexibility for the OFLC Administrator to provide further clarifying guidance regarding recruitment requirements, methods, and practices that do not rise to the level of requiring rulemaking. The Department considers this to be an important option for the OFLC Administrator to address
(
printed page 73958)
questions or resolve confusion that may arise as recruitment methods continue to evolve.
9.
20 CFR 656.18
, Optional Pre-Filing Recruitment Requirements for College and University Teachers and Professional Athletes and Professional Sports Team Coaches
The Department proposes to retain the optional competitive recruitment and selection procedures currently available to an employer seeking to permanently hire a college or university teacher at section 656.18, with revisions. Consistent with the current regulation, the employer would be permitted to conduct recruitment for a job opportunity involving a college or university teacher using the normal pre-filing recruitment procedures set forth in section 656.17. Alternatively, if the employer selected the alien using a competitive recruitment process, the employer would have the option of following the optional pre-filing recruitment procedures set forth in section 656.18.
The Department proposes expanding the optional pre-filing recruitment alternative available in proposed section 656.18 to include professional athlete or professional sports team coach job opportunities and rename proposed section 656.18 to reflect the changed content. The current regulations do not address pre-filing recruitment or documentation requirements for such job opportunities. As a result, while employers seeking to permanently employ professional athletes and professional sports team coaches must engage in pre-filing recruitment, they have not been required to comply with the standard pre-filing recruitment requirements of current section 656.17. Consistent with the Department's goals of clarifying program requirements and maintaining program integrity, the Department proposes to specify recruitment and documentation requirements for
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification
involving professional athletes and professional sports team coaches in this proposed rule, while maintaining the current flexibility for alternative recruitment practices appropriate to these job opportunities. The Department proposes to permit an employer seeking to permanently employ an alien as a professional athlete or professional sports team coach to either comply with the normal pre-filing recruitment procedures set forth in proposed section 656.17, or the alternative process in proposed section 656.18. The Department invites comments regarding the proposal to permit such employers to demonstrate a competitive recruitment and selection process under proposed section 656.18, rather than requiring compliance with proposed section 656.17. In addition, the Department invites comments that provide information about the means and methods of recruitment used for professional athletes and professional sports team coaches (
e.g.,
private executive recruiters, talent scouts, multi-session tryouts or interview panels), which may not be captured in the standard pre-filing recruitment requirements of 656.17. The Department invites the public to provide input that can better inform the pre-filing recruitment standards and documentation requirements to ensure potentially qualified and available U.S. workers are afforded a fair chance to apply for professional athlete and professional sports team coaching positions.
To use the optional recruitment and documentation procedures at section 656.18, both currently and under the proposed rule, the employer must be able to document that the alien was selected for the job opportunity using a competitive recruitment and selection process. Also consistent with the current regulation, this proposed rule would require the employer to prepare and retain documentation showing compliance with the requirements of the optional pre-filing recruitment procedures for submission to the CO, upon request. However, under the proposed rule, such employers also would submit the recruitment report and all evidence of compliance with the advertising requirements and consideration of U.S. workers (including resumes and applications of all U.S. workers who applied for the job opportunity) proposed in section 656.18 when filing their
Application for Permanent Employment Certification—
a change for all employers, as discussed in proposed section 656.10.
The documentation necessary to show compliance using a competitive recruitment and selection process for a college or university teacher job opportunity under proposed 656.18 would include the following list, which the Department retains from the current rule with minor conforming modifications: (1) a written statement, signed and dated by an official who has actual hiring authority from the employer, providing a detailed description of the recruitment procedures undertaken; (2) a final report or other documentation from the organizational or administrative body making the recommendation or selection of the alien at the completion of the competitive recruitment and selection process; (3) evidence of all other recruitment sources utilized; (4) a copy of at least one print or electronic advertisement for the job opportunity placed in a national professional journal, giving the name and the date(s) of publication; and which states the job title, duties, and requirements; and (5) a written statement attesting to the degree(s) of the alien's educational or professional qualifications and academic achievements. In paragraph (b), the Department proposes to require employers who use the competitive recruitment and selection option under proposed section 656.18 to both retain the documentation listed in paragraph (a) and submit it to the CO when filing the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
The Department notes that attestations regarding the competitive recruitment and selection process are collected in Appendix D of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.

Applications for Permanent Employment Certification.
The Department proposes to eliminate current section 656.18(c), which requires an employer to submit the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
for a college or university teacher within 18 months of the alien's selection through a competitive recruitment and selection process. Instead, these applications would be
(
printed page 73959)
subject to the same filing requirements as all other
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification,
including proposed section 656.10(b), which requires application submission within 30 calendar days after completion of pre-filing recruitment requirements. This proposed change is discussed in section 656.10.

10. Proposed
20 CFR 656.19
, Processing of an Application
As previously discussed in connection with proposed section 656.10, the Department proposes to move the current content of section 656.19 (“Live-in household domestic service workers”) to proposed section 656.10(e), so that all filing requirements are located in section 656.10 of this proposed rule. Then, the Department proposes to repurpose current section 656.19 to address the processing of
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification
submitted to OFLC and retitle section 656.19 as “Processing of an application.”
Consistent with the Department's proposed reorganization of part 656, the Department proposes to relocate provisions from other areas of the current regulation that address the review and processing of
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification
submitted to OFLC to proposed section 656.19. Specifically, the Department proposes to move content about the CO's assessment of the job opportunity described in the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
from current sections 656.17(h) (“Job duties and requirements”) and 656.17(j)(2) (“Conditions of employment”) to proposed section 656.19(d). Similarly, text currently found at section 656.17(i) (“Actual minimum requirements”) would be relocated to proposed section 656.19(e). These proposals would streamline the regulations, while improving clarity for employers regarding how applications are assigned for review and promoting more effective and fair processing by OFLC.
Proposed section 656.19 would address the CO's assignment of
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification
for review, rules for correspondence between the NPC and employers during processing, including requirements for responding, and the CO's assessment of the job opportunity offered in the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
The provisions proposed in this section would apply to all employers who must obtain a PERM labor certification before filing a Form I-140 petition with USCIS, including sheepherders, professional athletes and professional sports team coaches, and job opportunities currently designated as Schedule A (including aliens with exceptional ability).
In proposed paragraph (a), the Department considered codifying its application assignment process but decided against including these details in the proposed regulatory text. The NPC currently processes applications by assigning
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification
for staff review in the order received, using application filing dates. Specifically, the CO or other designated staff assigns for review all of the
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification
received in a certain month and year, before moving to assign applications filed in the next month and year. After being assigned, each designated staff organizes their monthly workload and initiates review of each application for compliance with PERM labor certification program requirements. After initial review, the CO or designated staff may initiate other processing steps, such as an audit examination under section 656.20 or supervised recruitment under section 656.21, or issue a final determination, approving or denying the application, pursuant to section 656.24. Processing times for any particular
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
received and assigned for review within that processing month may vary, depending on the unique circumstances of each application, contents of each application, and the applicable processing steps. While the Department intends to continue this practice for the foreseeable future, new technology or program enhancements may create necessary modifications. Any future changes, including minor tweaks to processing or order, would require the Department to propose another rule to codify its revised practices. Accordingly, the Department does not find it efficient or necessary to codify its internal review process.

11. Proposed
20 CFR 656.20
, Audit
The PERM labor certification audit process is a pre-decisional integrity measure that enables the CO to request and review documentation the employer is required to maintain, currently under section 656.10(f), to verify compliance with program requirements and form attestations before issuing a PERM labor certification. This proposed rule seeks to modify and clarify the audit examination process for employers under part 656.
Discretion
Consistent with the current regulation, the proposed rule allows the CO to select an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
for audit review prior to the issuance of a final determination. The current rule lists two reasons in section 656.20(a) why the CO might select an application for audit—random selection or for quality control purposes. These examples could be misunderstood as limiting the CO's discretion, which was not the Department's intent. The proposed rule revises this language to clarify that the CO has the discretion to choose an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
for audit for any reason(s) the CO might deem necessary to ensure compliance with the laws and regulations governing the PERM labor certification process. This discretion is necessary so that the CO can effectively use the audit tool to verify compliance and to bolster the integrity of the program. The CO may—or may not—select an application for audit based on any variety of internal and/or external factors, such as filing trends, specific industries or types of employers, complaints received from members of the public or referrals from other government agencies, program needs, etc., but ultimately the proposed rule clarifies that the CO has the necessary discretion to choose an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
at any time prior to the issuance of a final determination. Under the proposed rule, the Department seeks to ensure the CO's ability to select applications for audit is clear, as the CO's discretion with this integrity tool strengthens the overall integrity of the program.
(
printed page 73961)
Audit Notice
Proposed 656.20(b) continues current practice of requiring the CO to issue a written notice to the employer (
i.e.,
Notice of Audit Examination), after selecting an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
for audit examination. In addition, proposed paragraph (b) codifies the CO's current practice of sending a copy of the audit notice to the employer's agent or attorney, if applicable, to ensure proper notice. The proposed audit notice will contain similar content to current audit notices, such as informing the employer of the selection of its application for audit review, identifying the documentation the employer is required to provide in response to the audit, specifying a due date by which the employer must respond to the CO for the audit, and advising the employer of the consequences of noncompliance with the audit notice.
The Department proposes revising the audit response due date in section 656.20(b)(2) to support processing efficiency. Currently, section 656.20(a)(2) requires the CO to specify the same due date in all audit notices—30 calendar days from the audit notice issuance date. Proposed section 656.20(b)(2) would permit the CO to specify a date “no more than 30 calendar days” from the audit notice issuance date as the due date for the employer's response. The Department notes that employers attest at the time of filing the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
that they have prepared documentation demonstrating program compliance. Compliant employers will therefore be ready to submit a response to the audit notice quickly. This proposal permits the CO to require a faster audit response than 30 days without harm to the employer, particularly as the Department proposes to retain the option for an employer to request a one-time extension of up to 30 calendar days, if needed, in proposed section 656.20(c).
In addition, the Department proposes revising the audit notice's content to better advise employers of the potential consequences for failure to comply with the audit process. Current section 656.20(a)(3) has been relocated to proposed section 656.20(b)(3), and continues to require that the audit notice advise the employer that failure to respond by the due date will result in denial and ineligibility for review by BALCA under section 656.26. Separately—and not included in required audit notice content subparagraphs—current 656.20(b) addresses substantial failure to respond to the audit notice, stating that it may result in denial or supervised recruitment. The current provision fails to ensure that the employer is notified of all potential consequences of noncompliance with audit examination (
e.g.,
debarment) in the audit notice. The Department proposes to relocate the content of current section 656.20(b) to proposed section 656.20(b)(4), with revisions for readability and to include all potential consequences of failure to fully comply with the audit process. Proposed section 656.20(b)(4) improves notice to employers by ensuring the audit notice advises of all potential consequences of noncompliance with the CO's audit examination: denial of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
under section 656.24; imposition of supervised recruitment under section 656.21 for the current application or future application filings for up to two years; or debarment under section 656.31(f) from filing any labor certification applications or labor condition applications or receiving any approvals from OFLC for up to three years. These consequences are not new. The Department is proposing to both simplify the language in the audit notice and make it more complete.
One-Time Extension Request
In proposed section 656.20(c), the Department proposes to continue to permit an employer to request an extension of a response deadline once during audit examination. The Department proposes one change to the current one-time extension request provision. Currently, the one-time extension request provision in paragraph (c) refers only to the initial Notice of Audit Examination due date (current subparagraph 656.20(a)(2)). It does not reference requests for supplemental information and/or documentation the CO may make under current paragraph 656.20(d). The Department proposes to remove this limitation and permit an employer to request an extension of any one response deadline during audit examination. This proposed change is consistent with a similar provision in section 656.21 for supervised recruitment processing, which permits one extension request to any one response deadline during supervised recruitment. In addition, this proposed change acknowledges that a response to a supplemental audit information and/or documentation request may require more time to prepare and submit to the CO than the employer's initial response, which would largely encompass information and/or documents the employer attested to having prepared before filing the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
Continuing current procedure, the employer must request an extension in writing, before the due date of the response, and the CO at their discretion, may grant one extension of up to 30 additional calendar days for the employer to respond. Where granted, the CO issues a written notice to the employer that specifies the new date by which the employer must respond with the requested information and/or documentation. This proposal clarifies in section 656.20(c) that this is a “one-time extension,” and the extension will not automatically be granted but rather will be granted at the CO's discretion. Only one extension request during audit examination will be approved by the CO.
Actions During Processing
The Department proposes to revise current section 656.20(d) by adding a heading (“Actions during processing”), updating content in paragraph (d)(1) for clarity and to reflect the proposed response deadline of up to 30 days, and retaining paragraph (d)(2) without change. Existing section 656.20 paragraphs (d) and (d)(1) state that before making a final determination the CO may “request supplemental information and/or documentation,” while current paragraph (d)(2) states that the CO “may require the employer to conduct supervised recruitment under 656.21.” In proposed paragraph (d), the Department continues its current practice, where, if the CO determines further information is needed to verify program compliance, the CO may request supplemental information from the employer and/or impose supervised recruitment requirements. The CO may request supplemental information more than once during audit examination, each time providing up to 30 calendar days for response. This provision is intended to ensure that employers are aware the CO may request supplemental information to have full information before rendering a final determination on the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
The Department also clarifies that the CO will not consider any information the employer submits that is beyond the approved deadline(s) for the audit response(s), that is not in response to a CO's request, or that is not provided in the manner specified by the CO's request for supplemental information.
These proposed regulatory changes will add more clarity to the process by clearly specifying when and how supplemental information must be
(
printed page 73962)
provided to the CO to ensure employers submit the necessary information when requested by the CO and that requesting and submitting supplemental information is done as efficiently as possible to avoid unnecessary delays in the audit examination.
Correspondence in Audit
Furthering technological efficiency measures and updates, and modernization efforts developed and implemented over time for OFLC's programs, the Department is now proposing to codify in section 656.20(e) that the CO will issue all notices or requests electronically to the employer—and the employer's agent or attorney, if applicable—during audit using the electronic mail (email) address the employer designates in the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
There is an exception for employers permitted to file by mail, as set forth in § 656.10(c). For these employers, the CO will send any notice or request via traditional methods to assure next day delivery. This proposal increases transparency and supports the Department's modernization goals.
The Department proposes in paragraph (e) to also require employers to communicate electronically, except where the employer has been granted permission to file by mail in section 656.10(c), in which case the employer must send responses to the CO using a method that assures next-day delivery. As discussed above, the Department is proposing to adopt the current practice regarding response due dates in the H-2A program—employer responses must be sent by the due date specified by the CO, or by the next business day if the due date falls on a Sunday or Federal holiday. This proposal furthers the Department's goals to modernize and streamline processes to support processing efficiency.
Failure To Comply With Audit
In proposed section 656.20(f), the Department proposes to clarify the actions the CO may take as the result of an audit examination, and address the potential for debarment based on noncompliance with audit examination requirements. Under the current and proposed rules, the CO may: order the employer to conduct supervised recruitment under 656.21 before the CO issues a final determination on the current
Application for Permanent Employment Certification;
deny the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
under section 656.24; deny the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
under section 656.24 and order supervised recruitment under 656.21 for the employer's future filings for up to 2 years; and/or deny the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
under section 656.24 and pursue debarment against the employer, agent, and/or attorney for up to 3 years under 656.31(f). Although debarment is not a new possible consequence of noncompliance with audit examination, it is not mentioned in current section 656.20 of the current rule; rather, it appears in current section 656.31(f)(1)(iv). Moreover, proposed paragraph (f) better clarifies that failure to comply with audit requirements will lead to denial under section 656.24 and potential debarment under section 656.31, while an inadequate audit response will be denied under section 656.24. The CO may also determine it is appropriate to impose supervised recruitment for future applications for up to two years, in addition to denial. The Department proposes to change language referring to “a substantial failure” to provide required documents to “failed to comply with audit requirements ordered by the CO” in the audit examination. This proposed change simplifies the standard of review with a more objective test.
During audit examination, the employer must fully respond to the audit, including any supplemental RFI issued to the employer, and must return the response to the CO in the manner specified by the audit notice. Failure to provide the information requested will result in a denial because the CO will lack the information it requires to properly assess the application for compliance. The proposed changes ensure that employers are fully aware of the consequences of not complying with audit examinations.
Potential Referrals
The Department proposes a new section 656.20(g) to inform employers that the CO will refer information provided in response to an audit to other enforcement agencies where the findings indicate a possible violation of law within an agency's jurisdiction, and will provide such information upon an agency's request. Such referrals are in addition to internal referrals provided for elsewhere in part 656 and serve as an additional means of deterring fraud and suspicious activity. Under this proposed rule, the CO will refer audit findings and underlying documentation for an employer, or an attorney or agent, to any enforcement agency, including the DOL-OIG, DHS, DOS, EEOC, and DOJ. This includes referring any findings that an employer discouraged an eligible U.S. worker from applying, or failed to hire, discharged or otherwise discriminated against an eligible U.S. worker to DOJ, Civil Rights Division, Immigrant and Employee Rights Section and/or the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. Proposed section 656.20(g) serves as an additional means of deterring fraud and suspicious activity and notifies the public fully of the Department's intention to cooperate with fellow agencies to the maximum extent possible to protect the integrity of the permanent labor certification program.
12. Proposed
20 CFR 656.21
, Supervised Recruitment
The Department proposes clarifications to the supervised recruitment provisions in section 656.21. OFLC uses supervised recruitment as a means of enhancing program integrity by directing the employer through specific recruitment steps under part 656. Through this integrity measure, OFLC ensures the adequacy of the employer's test of the labor market for U.S. workers and ensures the employer's consideration of U.S. applicants for the available job opportunity.
When the CO places an employer into supervised recruitment, the CO guides the employer through an additional recruitment process. Consistent with the current rule, under the proposed rule, the CO may impose supervised recruitment on an employer for a single
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
or for all of the employer's future-filed
Application(s) for Permanent Employment Certification
for a period of up to 2 years if the CO determines the employer failed to fully comply with audit examination requirements. Once in supervised recruitment, the employer must demonstrate its compliance with the additional recruitment requirements specified by the CO, in addition to compliance with all other requirements of part 656, in order to receive a PERM labor certification.
Discretion
The proposed rule revises language in section 656.21(a) to more clearly state the CO's discretion to place an employer in supervised recruitment. Proposed section 656.21(a) replaces “[w]here the Certifying Officer determines it appropriate” with “[t]he CO may, at their discretion, require supervised recruitment.” Under both the current and proposed rule, the CO has discretion to place an employer in supervised recruitment; however, the proposed rule more clearly states this discretion. In addition, proposed section
(
printed page 73963)
656.21(a) replaces “for the pending application or future applications pursuant to § 656.20(b),” which could be interpreted as requiring the pending application to undergo audit before supervised recruitment, with “on any
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
pending a final determination or for all of an employer's future
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification
for up to two years pursuant to § 656.20(f).” By more clearly providing the CO maximum discretion to induct an employer into supervised recruitment at any phase of processing an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
the Department provides employers with clearer notice regarding the potential for supervised recruitment and supports the CO's efforts to quickly and efficiently address trends and concerns regarding program integrity. Furthermore, the proposed revision in paragraph (a) adds the specific period during which the CO may order supervised recruitment for an employer's future filings to add clarity to proposed section 656.21(a). The period stated in proposed 656.21(a) is not new. Current section 656.20(f) specifies the potential period for which the CO may order supervised recruitment for an employer's future
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification
as up to two years. This proposal would provide important information relating to supervised recruitment in one place.
By clarifying the CO's discretion regarding supervised recruitment, the Department seeks to both streamline processing and safeguard U.S. workers by ensuring a robust test of the labor market.
Supervised Recruitment Notice
The Department proposes to repurpose section 656.21(b) to formalize the “Notice of Supervised Recruitment” procedure, with revisions. To increase the consistency of the audit and supervised recruitment procedures and improve clarity for employers subject to supervised recruitment procedures, the Department proposes to repurpose section 656.21(b) so that it codifies current practice, through which the CO issues a written notice to the employer, currently called “Notice of Supervised Recruitment,” with a copy to the employer's attorney or agent, if the employer has such a representative.
In proposed section 656.21(b)(1), the Department proposes new content outlining the type of information and instructions to be provided to the employer in the Notice of Supervised Recruitment. As proposed, the notice will specify the procedures the employer must follow to conduct supervised recruitment, including “the required method(s) and content for advertising the job opportunity to prospective U.S. applicants (
e.g.,
whether to have applicants respond directly to the NPC), timeframes for compliance with the supervised recruitment process, and state that supervised recruitment will be incorporated as bona fide conditions and terms of the
Application(s) for Permanent Employment Certification.”
To simplify proposed section 656.21 and acknowledge that advertising methods and contents are assessed by the CO on case-by-case basis, the Department does not propose to retain the list of required advertisement content in current section 656.21(b)(2) that currently applies to newspaper advertisements. Further, this approach provides the CO with flexibility to customize instructions for each job opportunity to the employer in the Notice of Supervised Recruitment, including advertisement content, to ensure the supervised recruitment efforts are appropriately guided to solicit referrals from the broadest pool of potentially qualified and available U.S. workers. Among the greater flexibilities afforded the CO under the proposed rule to customize recruitment and advertising content, as appropriate, during supervised recruitment, proposed section 656.21(b) would permit—but not require—the CO to require the employer's advertisements to direct applicants to send resumes or applications for the job opportunity to the NPC, rather than the employer.

The current rule requires applicants to apply only to the CO and the CO to refer those applicants to the employer. With this proposed change, the Department intends to balance the competing goals of supervising labor market testing and using advertisements to test U.S. worker availability for PERM job opportunities that blend in with non-PERM advertisements.
In addition, the Department proposes to add new content in proposed section 656.21(b)(2) that would implement the same consequences for failure to provide required documents by the due date(s) as currently applies during audit examination. While in audit examination processing, if the employer fails to provide required documentation by the due date, the CO will deny the application, with the denial ineligible for review by BALCA under section 656.26.

Currently, supervised recruitment requires placement of print advertisements in all cases, as well as any other measures the CO may add.
See
current sections 656.21(b) and (d). In addition, the current rule specifies advertisement content, requires the employer to submit a draft advertisement for CO review within 30 calendar days of the supervised recruitment notice date, and requires communication between the CO and employer regarding the timing of advertisements in paragraphs (b) and (c).

Because supervised recruitment may require the employer to repeat a pre-filing recruitment activity under supervision—for example, reposting an advertisement on the employer's website for a longer period of time or changing the location of the posting on the website, or the CO can require an additional advertisement on a website other than the employer's or the SWA's during supervised recruitment—the Department proposes language in paragraph (c) to clarify that the supervised recruitment process is in addition to the pre-filing recruitment requirements in section 656.17 or 656.18.
Proposed paragraph (c) further discusses the various potential additional requirements that could constitute supervised recruitment; however, the CO would not be limited to the list in proposed paragraph (c). Supplemental Information Request
The Department proposes to relocate content from current section 656.21(f) to proposed section 656.21(d), with revisions, to address requests for documentation or information during supervised recruitment. Proposed section 656.21(d) has been revised for consistency with current practice in supervised recruitment and the similar provision for audit examination in proposed section 656.20(d). Consistent with proposals for correspondence during processing, the Department proposes in section 656.21(e) to require the CO to send notices and requests to the employer with a copy to the employer's attorney or agent, if the employer has such a representative, and the employer to respond electronically, unless the employer was permitted to file by mail as set forth in § 656.10(c). For employers permitted to file by mail, the CO would be required to send any notice or request and the employer to respond via traditional methods to assure next day delivery. Consistent with other proposals in this rule and current practice in the H-2A program, the proposed rule would require employer responses during supervised recruitment to be sent by the due date specified by the CO, or by the next business day if the due date falls on a Sunday or Federal holiday. This proposal improves transparency about the CO's correspondence during supervised recruitment, in addition to furthering the Department's goals to modernize and streamline processes to support processing efficiency.
Failure To Comply With Supervised Recruitment
The Department proposes revising section 656.21(f) to clarify the consequences of failure to comply with the supervised recruitment process or requirements. Current section 656.21(f) simply states that the CO will deny the application if the employer fails to “supply the CO with the required documentation or information within 30 days of the date of the request.” However, the CO also must deny certification if the employer submits the required documentation or information, but the substance of that documentation or information does not support certification. For example, the CO will deny the application if the employer submitted its recruitment report, but the recruitment report does not contain required content, such as lawful, job-related reasons for rejecting the U.S. workers who applied. The additional recruitment during supervised recruitment, when ordered, is part of the CO's assessment of U.S. worker availability and prevention of adverse impact to U.S. workers similarly employed. An employer's failure to perform the additional recruitment required, in compliance with the CO's instructions, precludes certification. In addition, the Department proposes revising section 656.21(f) to add that debarment of the employer and/or its attorney or agent is a possible consequence of noncompliance with supervised recruitment orders. Adding the proposed language in section 656.21(f) is consistent with changes proposed in section 656.20 (Audit) and improves notice of the consequences of noncompliance, which include taking appropriate measures to ensure the integrity of the PERM labor certification program under section 656.31(f).

Additionally, the CO will refer findings that an employer, attorney, or agent, “discouraged an eligible U.S. worker from applying, or failed to hire, discharged or otherwise discriminated against an eligible U.S. worker” to DOJ, Civil Rights Division, Immigrant and Employee Rights Section and/or the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. The text in proposed section 656.21(g) aligns with a similar provision in proposed section 656.20 (Audit). These proposed provisions serve as an additional means of deterring fraud and suspicious activity and notify the public of the
(

Department's intention to cooperate with fellow agencies to the maximum extent possible to protect the integrity of the PERM labor certification program.
One-Time Extension Request
The Department proposes to relocate current section 656.21(g) to proposed section 656.21(h), with revisions for clarity and consistency with a similar provision in proposed section 656.20(c) for audit examination. The proposed rule continues to permit an employer to request one extension to any one response deadline during the supervised recruitment process. Consistent with current practice, where an employer requests an extension, it must do so in writing, before the due date of the supervised recruitment response, and the CO at his or her discretion, may grant one extension of up to 30 additional calendar days for the employer to respond. 20 CFR 656.24
