Consistent with the Department's proposals throughout this rulemaking to reorganize part 656 and simplify language to clarify program requirements and procedures, the Department proposes revisions to the section addressing PERM labor certification determinations at section 656.24. The proposed changes in this section are largely organizational and for conformity with the overall proposed rule. For example, proposed section 656.24 contains paragraph headings to more clearly identify topics and simplifies procedural matters related to issuing final determinations to certify or deny an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
The Department also proposes relocating the content of current section 656.24(f), which discusses supervised recruitment, to proposed section 656.21(f) and the content of current section 656.24(g), which discusses reconsideration, to proposed section 656.24(d)(2). Below, the Department summarizes proposed section 656.24 and highlights proposed changes.
The Department retains its explanation of the OFLC Administrator's role and delegation of authority to COs to issue determinations for
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification
in proposed section 656.24(a) (Determinations), with conforming changes. The Department is proposing to revise the current language in section 656.24(a), to clarify that the OFLC Administrator's authority to review and issue determinations for
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification
is not limited to “special or unique problems.” The proposed language clarifies that authority resides with the OFLC Administrator, who may, in their discretion, delegate that authority to COs. The proposed provision states that, “the OFLC Administrator has sole discretion to certify, deny, or suspend processing of
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification
under 656.31(b) or for other appropriate reasons or to delegate authority to the CO to do so.”
See
proposed section 656.24(a). The Department emphasizes that the proposed language is not intended to change current practice. While the OFLC Administrator has the authority to review applications and issue final determinations, the COs at NPCs will continue to issue final determinations in most cases. The Department is revising this provision to add clarity, as well as align this language with several other provisions which discuss authority and delegation.
Proposed section 656.24(b) continues to address the three criteria for certification of an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
In addition to conforming modifications, the Department proposes revisions intended to increase clarity and consistency within part 656 and across the Department's regulations. With only minor clarifying changes, proposed subparagraph (b)(1) continues to require the employer to have met all the requirements of part 656 as a condition of certification. Proposed subparagraphs (b)(2) and (b)(3) continue to address the statutorily required determinations—that there are insufficient U.S. workers able, willing, qualified, and available to fill the employer's job opportunity and that the employment of the alien will not have an adverse effect upon the wages and working conditions of U.S. workers similarly employed—with revisions.
In proposed subparagraph (b)(2), the Department adds language regarding the CO's assessment of U.S. worker availability using information gathered from the U.S. labor market test, as provided in the employer's recruitment report. As modified, proposed subparagraph (b)(2) is consistent with similar provisions in the H-2A and H-2B programs at sections
20 CFR 655.51(b)
and
20 CFR 655.161(b)
, respectively. It is the employer's responsibility to ensure that it submits a recruitment report that clearly articulates lawful, job-related reason(s) for not hiring any U.S. worker who applies for the job opportunity that is the subject of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
Proposed section 656.24(b)(2) would better notify employers how the CO will assess U.S. worker availability in the event the employer's recruitment report fails to clearly state reason(s) that are lawful, job-related reasons for not hiring a U.S. worker. The CO will “count as able and qualified” any U.S. worker who was referred or applied for the job opportunity and for whom the employer does not identify a lawful, job-related reason for rejection in the recruitment report. This language supports efficient and faster processing, as the CO can reach a determination based on the information stated in the recruitment report, without additional requests and delays.
For most
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification,
current section 656.24(b)(2)(i) governs the CO's assessment of an employer's recruitment results. The Department proposes no substantive change to the standard of review for recruitment reports subject to assessment under section 656.24(b)(2)(i). Consistent with current practice, a U.S. worker is considered able and qualified for the job opportunity if the worker, by education, training, experience, or a combination thereof, is able to perform the duties involved in the normally accepted manner, as customarily performed by other U.S. workers similarly employed, or can acquire the skills necessary to perform the duties involved during a reasonable period of on-the-job training. This assessment may be referred to as a “minimally qualified” assessment. The Department proposes to retain this subparagraph with one minor revision to identify the CO as the decisionmaker.
For
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification
involving a college or university teacher job opportunity, the CO currently applies the alternative assessment of U.S. worker availability found at current section 656.24(b)(2)(ii), which is a limited exception to the “minimally qualified” assessment. This alternative assessment reflects Congress' October 20, 1976 amendments to the INA at section 212(a)(5)(A)(ii), which implemented an “equally qualified” assessment for these job
(
printed page 73966)
opportunities.
[
121
]
Under this proposed rule, the CO would continue to apply this alternative assessment to count as available, any U.S. worker who applies or is referred to a college or university teacher job opportunity and who is “at least as qualified” (
i.e.,
“equally qualified”) as the alien selected.
The Department proposes to expand current section 656.24(b)(2)(ii) to include job opportunities involving aliens who have exceptional ability in the sciences or the arts. This proposal further implements Congress' October 20, 1976 amendments to the INA at section 212(a)(5)(A)(ii), which also excepted aliens who have exceptional ability in the sciences and arts from the generally applicable “minimally qualified” assessment of U.S. worker availability and, instead, required application of the “equally qualified” assessment.
[
122
]
Although Congress extended the “equally qualified” assessment standard to PERM labor certifications for aliens who have exceptional ability in the sciences or the arts at the same time as college and university teachers, it was not necessary to address it in part 656 as long as job opportunities involving aliens who have exceptional ability in the sciences or the arts were included in Schedule A, Group II, and exempt from engaging in a labor market test.
[
123
]
With the proposed elimination of Schedule A, the Department expects to receive
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification
from employers seeking to permanently employ aliens who have exceptional ability in the sciences or the arts and will be required to assess U.S. worker availability using the statutory standard at INA section 212(a)(5)(A)(ii).
[
124
]
Such employers would be required to engage in the pre-filing recruitment activities proposed in section 656.17(a), and submit a recruitment report to OFLC when filing the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
as provided in proposed section 656.10(a)(1). Accordingly, proposed section 656.24(b)(2)(ii) clarifies that any U.S. worker who is “at least as qualified” (
i.e.,
“equally qualified”) as the alien who has exceptional ability in the sciences or the arts would be considered available.
The Department proposes minor conforming changes in proposed subparagraph (b)(3). In addition, the Department proposes a modification to state that, in reaching the determination regarding adverse effect, the CO will consider information about working conditions that are “normal to the occupation and industry,” rather than “prevailing . . . in the occupation.” The Department notes that current subparagraph (b)(3) contains the only instance in part 656 where the current rule suggests a “prevailing” standard for assessing a job opportunity or occupation. The proposal to use a “normal” standard for the occupation and industry, here, is consistent with the CO's assessment of the information the employer provides about the job opportunity and related occupation on the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
and during processing.
[
125
]
In addition, using a “normal” standard better aligns with publicly available resources and information, which facilitates efficient review of
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification.
Finally, the Department proposes to reorganize the content of current sections 656.24(c), (d), and (e) to focus final determination issuance procedures in proposed sections 656.24(c) (Approved certification) and 656.24(d) (Denied Certification). Proposed sections 656.24(c) and 656.24(d) reflect changes to conform with electronic filing and communication proposals throughout this rule and OFLC's current practice of electronically sending the certified
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
directly to USCIS upon approval. For employers permitted to file by mail under proposed section 656.10(c), the CO would continue to send certifications by mail and denials by means normally assuring next-day delivery, to ensure full access to reconsideration and administrative review options. In addition, paragraph (d) identifies “Notice of Denial” as the name of the notice issued when the CO denies certification, a proposal to add clarity, as discussed in section 656.26 below.
To add clarity for employers, the Department further proposes to revise the content relocated from current 656.24(e) to proposed section 656.24(d) for Notice of Denial content. Currently, section 656.24(g) provides the option for an employer to request reconsideration by the CO after receiving a denial, but this option is not listed in the denial notice content requirements. To ensure employers who receive a Notice of Denial are apprised of their full set of options after denial, proposed subparagraphs (d)(2) and (d)(4) ensure that the employer is informed that it has three options—it may request reconsideration by the CO under proposed 656.26(a), review by BALCA under proposed 656.26(b), or may not appeal and, instead, file a new
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
Proposed subparagraph (d)(3) continues to apprise employers that if they wish to request reconsideration or review of the denial, they must do so within 30 calendar days of the denial date; after 30 calendar days have passed, the window to appeal the denial closes and the denial becomes final. These are not new options, but in the proposed rule they are more clearly stated. Further, the proposed rule would require these options to be explained in the Notice of Denial.
14. Proposed
20 CFR 656.26
, Review of Denied Permanent Labor Certifications
Consistent with the Department's general proposal to reorganize part 656 to follow the ordinate flow of processing an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
the Department proposes to rename section 656.26's heading to read “Review of denied permanent labor certification” (currently “Board of Alien Labor Certification review of denials of labor certification”) and transfer the language currently contained in section 656.24(g), which addresses requests for reconsideration by the CO of an application's denial, under the proposed revised section 656.26(a). With this proposed change, section 656.26 would cover the options available to an employer who receives an application denial—requests for reconsideration by the CO and requests for review by BALCA. In addition, the Department proposes to redesignate current sections 656.26(a) through (c) as proposed sections 656.26(b) through (d) and to revise the existing regulatory language in section 656.26 to codify existing practices and provide clarity to employers, attorneys, agents, and BALCA regarding the reconsideration and appellate processes.
Requests for CO Reconsideration vs. Requests for BALCA Review
Currently, when the CO denies an
Application for Permanent Employment
(
printed page 73967)
Certification,
the CO must include certain language in the notice to the employer. Current section 656.24(e) requires the CO to “quote the request for review procedures at § 656.26(a) and (b).” The request for review procedures articulates how an employer may request review of the denial by BALCA. In the 2002 NPRM,
Labor Certification for the Permanent Employment of Aliens in the United States; Implementation of New System
(“2002 NPRM”),
[
126
]
the Department noted that the regulations at that time were silent on the possibility of motions for reconsideration by the CO after a final determination and that while, historically, COs “sometimes honored such motions” for reconsideration, they “generally treated them as requests for review and transmitted the matter to the” BALCA.
[
127
]
The 2002 NPRM proposed to preserve the ability for employers to submit motions for reconsideration, and the Department then amended the regulations to “specifically provide that while motions for reconsideration before the [CO] may be filed, [the CO] may, in his/her complete discretion, choose to treat the motion as a request for review.”
[
128
]
Thus, the Department adopted two avenues of review of a final determination in the current rule—either the employer requests review by BALCA, or it requests reconsideration by the CO.
[
129
]
In practice, most employers, after an initial denial, choose to submit a request for reconsideration by the CO rather than submitting a request for review by BALCA. It became the general practice of OFLC to deem requests that did not specifically ask for BALCA review to be requests for reconsideration. After the denial of the request for reconsideration, the CO would automatically transmit the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
to BALCA for review. This was done regardless of whether the employer requested review by BALCA after the request for reconsideration was denied. Those cases were then docketed at BALCA. This practice continued for many years. As a result, BALCA was inundated with cases—at one point reaching over 3,760 docketed cases in a fiscal year.
[
130
]
There were a number of issues with this process as it evolved. First, many employers did not want their cases to be sent to BALCA for review after their requests for reconsideration were denied. OFLC automatically sending the applications for review by BALCA meant that not only was the case docketing an extra administrative burden to BALCA and to the CO, who created the administrative file for review, but it was also a burden to the employer who then had to wait for the case to be docketed only to then file a motion for it to be dismissed. Second, this waiting period could jeopardize an employer's attempts to file future PERM labor certification applications because, pursuant to current section 656.24(e)(6), an employer may not file a “new application in the same occupation for the same [alien] . . . while a request for review is pending with the [BALCA].” If an employer intended to file a new PERM labor certification application, it would again have to wait for the matter to be docketed, then file a dismissal and wait for the order to be issued.
For example, in
Lindsborg Community Hospital Association,
on April 10, 2012, the CO denied a request for reconsideration and forwarded the case to BALCA.
[
131
]
The employer attempted to withdraw the case on May 7, 2012, and the CO—because the case had already been sent to BALCA—sent the letter to BALCA as well.
[
132
]
Due to a docketing error of some kind, BALCA had not received the employer's withdrawal request as of September 17, 2012.
[
133
]
The employer explained that the pending appeal meant that it could not file a new
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
“and that this may have implications for the timing of the new application and the supporting prevailing wage determination.”
[
134
]
Had the employer been required to specifically request an appeal in the first instance, this lengthy delay between the denial on reconsideration (Apr. 10, 2012) and eventual dismissal from BALCA (Sept. 19, 2012) would have been eliminated. Also, BALCA noted in a footnote that the employer's motion for reconsideration had “said nothing about requesting BALCA Review” and that the regulation “does not state that the CO must automatically forward an Appeal File to BALCA if the CO denies reconsideration. Thus, the fact that the matter was treated as an appeal may not have been procedurally correct.”
[
135
]
The high number of appeals was extremely burdensome to BALCA and the CO—an unnecessary burden, especially in light of the fact that employers were not actively requesting such appeals. In addition, the Department's approach resulted in delays that could cause harm to employers seeking to file for permanent labor certifications.
The delays and administrative burdens on COs and BALCA led to an internal processing change that has been in effect since October 27, 2014.
[
136
]
As before, an employer may submit either a request for review by BALCA or a request for reconsideration by the CO, and the CO may still deem the request for BALCA review as a request for reconsideration.
[
137
]
Now, after the CO has determined to deny the request for reconsideration, the CO no longer automatically transmits that
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
to BALCA for review. Instead, the CO includes language in the reconsideration decision notice affirming the earlier denial that explains to the employer that the employer has the ability to request review by BALCA and has 30 calendar days from the date of the reconsideration decision notice to do so. This process significantly cut down the administrative burdens for the CO, BALCA, and employers because now only those decisions that employers wish to pursue are sent to BALCA. The table below shows the difference between the years when the CO was automatically sending cases to BALCA for review without employer's request as compared to when employers had to specifically request BALCA review after the CO denied request for reconsideration. The decrease in the number of cases docketed was significantly lower when employers had to request for BALCA review.

It is likely that there are additional reasons for the declining docketed appeals; however, the data show a pattern of significant decrease of cases docketed when the CO no longer automatically sent cases to BALCA after denial on reconsideration. Currently, the CO only sends cases for BALCA review if an employer actively submits the request. The proposed section 656.26 would codify this current practice.
Although this processing change is not contradictory to the regulations in any way, it was not fully captured by the text of the current regulations. Notably, the older process by which the CO would transmit
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification
to BALCA immediately after denying the request for reconsideration was also not fully captured by the plain text of the current regulations. Regardless of which process would ultimately have been the chosen and lasting path by the Department, a change in regulatory text is needed to codify the current practice to provide clarity and transparency regarding this part of the permanent labor certification process.
Also, the fact that the processes are not actually encompassed in the regulations leads to procedural postures that are difficult to navigate. For example, if an employer requested reconsideration and the denial was affirmed, the employer was told that they could request review by BALCA within 30 calendar days; however as noted, there is no regulatory provision granting 30 calendar days to further appeal to BALCA—which itself is troublesome—but also, if the employer failed to appeal within that 30 calendar day timeframe, there was no regulatory provision to which either the CO or ALJs could cite that would allow for the dismissal or closure of an untimely filing.
With this NPRM, the Department proposes to amend sections 656.26 and 656.27 of the current regulations to codify the current practice that has been in place for over a decade and to articulate the full appellate process and provide transparency and clarity on program requirements and procedures of part 656.
Final Determinations
Currently, the term “Final Determination” is used for the initial denial of the PERM labor certification as well as for the notice sent after reconsideration is denied. This fact leads to, in many cases, having two “Final Determinations,” which is confusing to the regulated community. The Department proposes to call the notice after a PERM labor certification is denied the “Notice of Denial,” and call the notice issued after a request for reconsideration is denied a NORD. This proposed change in terminology clarifies the meaning of each of the CO's decisions and helps to distinguish which document the CO, an agent/attorney, employer, or even BALCA may be referring.
Section 656.26(a), Request for Reconsideration by the CO
In addition to proposing to relocate current section 656.24(g) to the proposed new section 656.26(a), the Department is seeking to change the reconsideration language in the provision at section 656.26(a). Most significantly, the Department proposes to include a subparagraph (5) in the proposed new section 656.26(a). Proposed subparagraph (a)(5) would explain that if reconsideration is requested, the CO will reconsider the application's denial, and then if the CO determines that the request for reconsideration should be denied, the CO will issue a NORD informing the employer of the determination. Proposed subparagraphs (a)(5)(i) through (vi) outline required NORD content. The proposed language states the notice will: state the reasons for the denial; quote the procedures for review by BALCA; advise that an employer has 30 calendar days from the date of the reconsideration determination to request review or the denial will become the final determination of the Secretary and the employer will have failed to exhaust administrative remedies; and advise that an employer may file a new application after the reconsideration is denied if a request for review is not filed with the Board, but otherwise a new application in the same occupation for the same alien cannot be pending while a request for review is pending with BALCA. The intent of this proposed subsection is to clarify, via both the regulatory text and the Notice of Reconsideration Denial, that an employer may, after the reconsideration is denied, make a formal appeal to BALCA within 30 calendar days, and to articulate the consequences for not doing so. As stated above, this proposed rule codifies this current practice and provides transparency and clarity in part 656.
The Department also proposes edits to the existing reconsideration regulatory language that would be relocated and contained in the new proposed section 656.26's paragraphs (a)(1) through (4). The new proposed paragraph (a)(1) states clearly that the employer may request reconsideration by the CO after the Notice of Denial is issued. The Department proposes to remove “For applications submitted after July 16, 2007” that would be included in proposed paragraph (a)(2), as the phrase is no longer necessary. Proposed paragraph (a)(4) asserts that an employer “must clearly state” with its request whether it is seeking review by BALCA or is making a request for reconsideration by the CO, and, if it does not do so, the CO will construe the request as a request for reconsideration by the CO.
In proposed paragraph (a)(4) the Department is proposing to remove the discretion for the CO to determine whether to treat the request as a reconsideration request or not and makes it very clear to employers that if they themselves are not clear as to their desired review process their request will be construed, by default, as requests for reconsideration. The Department believes its proposal to construe unclear requests as requests for reconsideration by the CO is largely more beneficial to the employer. Under this approach, the CO can review additional information submitted with the request for reconsideration (assuming it meets the documentary requirement of section
(
printed page 73969)
656.26's paragraphs (a)(2)(i) and (ii)). A case sent straight to BALCA—a procedure that does not allow for the introduction of new evidence on appeal—must be persuasive using a more limited pool of information. In fact, BALCA has objected to the CO's decision in previous cases to send to BALCA “requests” that were not entirely clear, or consistent internally, as to what was being requested—reconsideration and/or review—precisely because doing so precluded the introduction of new evidence.
[
138
]
Finally, an employer may also receive a faster answer if the CO is given the opportunity to review a denial on reconsideration rather than sending the denial to BALCA and waiting for a decision and, potentially, an order remanding the case. Should an employer wish to move straight to BALCA review, it must clearly state as such.
Section 656.26(b), Request for Review by BALCA
In light of the proposed explicit incorporation of the “request for reconsideration” into the regulations, corresponding edits would also be needed to section 656.26, including redesignating existing paragraph (a) to (b), (b) to (c), and (c) to (d) following the addition of the reconsideration provision at paragraph (a). In redesignated paragraph (b)(1), the Department proposes new regulatory text to explain that a request for review by BALCA may be filed if a request for reconsideration is denied. The Department proposes including cross citations to other parts of the regulations for clarity and symmetry. As such, this section now proposes that BALCA may review a PERM labor certification denial pursuant to proposed section 656.24(d), a request for reconsideration denial under proposed new section 656.26(a), as well as a PERM labor certification revocation, or debarment under section 656.32 or section 656.31(f).
The Department proposes edits to the language that would be contained in redesignated paragraph (b)(2) to incorporate the provision for “denial on reconsideration” and again provide a 30-calendar-day timeline to employers for filing appeals to BALCA for denials on reconsideration and the way they should do so. Paragraph (b)(2)(iv) still refers to a “final determination,” but this reference is not a defined term and instead refers to the last or final determination of the reviewing official before the appeal.
The Department is also proposing non-substantive edits to subparagraph (b)(4) to clarify that with respect to the review of a PERM labor certification denial or a denial of a reconsideration motion, only items that were before the CO when the CO made the decision may be considered, even if other documents are in the physical appeal file sent to BALCA. Because the CO will include the appeal request in the administrative file transmitted to BALCA, the file will contain paperwork submitted on appeal. However, pursuant to the regulations, BALCA is not permitted to consider this additional submitted evidence.
The Department also proposes amending the regulations at (c)(2) and (3) to remove the physical address of BALCA from the regulatory text primarily because that physical address is no longer accurate—but also because as the Department streamlines and modernizes its processes, it is best to leave out specific physical addresses from regulatory texts as those might change from time to time and the Department is able to provide easier and faster updates to the public about the physical addresses or locations, as well as general information regarding its offices, services and procedures, electronically, via its website or when requested by the methods it specifies for requesting information. Corresponding edits were also made to (d)(2) and (3) removing the physical address from the text. Finally, it should be noted that electronic submission to BALCA, as well as to the Associate Solicitor for Employment and Training Legal Services is highly encouraged.
15. Proposed
20 CFR 656.27
Consideration by and Decisions of BALCA
The Department proposes to revise existing section 656.27 by adding new provisions, repurposing and redesignating paragraphs, and changing regulatory language for clarity and conformity with other proposed revisions introduced through this proposed rule. The Department proposes to repurpose section 656.27(c) to add a new standard of review provision. This proposal would result in the redesignation of current paragraphs (c), (d), and (e) as proposed paragraphs (d), (e), and (f). Similarly, the Department proposes adding a new provision to provide BALCA with the authority to remand cases to the CO when the merits of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
have not yet been fully assessed, resulting in the redesignation of current paragraph (c)(3) as proposed paragraph (d)(4). Also, in proposed section 656.27(d) (current section 656.27(c)), the Department proposes to add review of denials on reconsideration to the list of adverse decisions BALCA may review and to clarify that such review will be limited to an on-the-record review. In proposed paragraphs (e) and (f) (current paragraphs (d) and (e)), the Department proposes to codify its existing practice of including the employer's attorney or agent, if applicable, in communication during appeal. Throughout proposed section 656.27, the Department also proposes minor conforming changes for consistency throughout the proposed rule. In addition, the Department is proposing to remove language from current section 656.27(e)(1) that requires “good cause” to be shown for hearing rescheduling requests. This proposed change is intended to provide BALCA with more control and flexibility in hearing scheduling and requests for rescheduling.
Standard of Review
In proposed paragraph (c), the Department seeks to incorporate the arbitrary and capricious standard of review into requests for review of denials of PERM labor certifications under proposed section 656.24(d), denials of requests for reconsideration under proposed section 656.26(a), or affirmations of PWDs under section 656.41. As the regulation is currently silent on the standard of review, this proposed change clarifies and ensures BALCA is conducting review under part 656 in a consistent manner. Other employment-based visa programs administered by OFLC require use of the arbitrary and capricious standard of review on appeal to BALCA.
[
139
]
This change further aligns the PERM program
(
printed page 73970)
with the other employment-based visa programs administered by OFLC.
Presently, BALCA explains that it uses a form of de novo review, “limited in scope by
20 CFR 656.27(c)
” or in other words, as limited by the record.
[
140
]
However, BALCA has also said that “[t]he Board will not decide an appeal on grounds for denial not raised while the case was before the CO.”
[
141
]
It also stated that “our review of the preliminary decisions entrusted by regulation to the discretion of the CO is typically more limited, and we examine those decisions with an eye toward whether they are arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law.”
[
142
]
The fact that BALCA seems to have combined different scopes of review—arbitrary and capricious for “preliminary decisions,” yet it conducts a modified “de novo” review that does not consider issues not already before the CO—demonstrates why clearly articulating one consistent standard of review in the regulations will help provide clarity to the regulated community, attorneys/agents and judges themselves. The Department proposes to adopt the standard of review “arbitrary and capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law” to make it consistent with the other employment-based visa programs. The Department does not believe that this will result in significant changes in adjudication because BALCA is limited in their review to the administrative record pursuant to current section 656.27(c) (proposed section 656.27(d)), and BALCA already does not decide an appeal based on new denial grounds or on new arguments not made before the CO.
[
143
]
The Department proposes minor edits to section 656.27 paragraph (d) to account for the addition of review of denials on reconsideration by the CO as well as to note that on-the-record review is conducted on the basis of the record upon which the “CO's final determination” was made. Here “final determination” refers to the last determination by the reviewing official before it moves to BALCA—for example, the denial of the PERM labor certification, the denial of the reconsideration request, or the affirmation on the PWD.
Section 656.27(d)(2)-(3) Directing Certification and Remands
In the 2004 PERM Final Rule, the Department eliminated the possibility of remands from BALCA to the CO in the PERM program.
[
144
]
At that time, the Department believed that the cases that would have made it to BALCA would have been sufficiently developed such that remand would be unnecessary.
[
145
]
Furthermore, the Department, at the time, explained that the processing model for applications requesting PERM labor certification did “not contemplate the type of interchange between the employer and the [CO]” and “it is not apparent what the [CO] would do if a case were `remanded'.”
[
146
]
Through years of actual administrative practice, however, the Department has discovered that there have been cases—though not frequent—with a record sufficient enough to determine that the CO was arbitrary and capricious in the denial, but still not enough to determine that certification is warranted. The purpose of the PERM labor certification program is to allow the Secretary to determine and certify that “there are not sufficient United States workers who are able, willing, qualified and available at the time of application for a visa and admission into the United States and at the place where the alien is to perform the work; . . . and the employment of the alien will not adversely affect the wage and working conditions of United States workers similarly employed.”
[
147
]
For certification to be issued in circumstances where the CO has not yet fully evaluated the merits of the case would violate the regulations and statute.
[
148
]
A remand, rather than an order directing certification, in a situation where the CO has not fully reviewed an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
and all supporting documentation would allow the CO to examine the merits of the application and to determine whether the application truly establishes that there are not sufficient U.S. workers able, willing, qualified and available for the position, and also that the alien's employment will not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of U.S. workers similarly employed.
[
149
]
BALCA has recognized this principle before and has actually remanded cases for further processing, even though remands are not currently provided for in the regulations. BALCA has stated, “[w]hile the Board generally eschews remands to allow further processing of an application, such remands are appropriate where an application was denied on preliminary grounds, and the merits of the application have not been addressed.”
[
150
]
The Department agrees with BALCA and believes that remand may be the most appropriate way forward in certain cases; and therefore, is proposing to add a new provision, subparagraph (d)(3), to codify remands from BALCA for clarity and transparency purposes. The intent is for remands to be used sparingly and only in situations where, based on the facts and posture of the case, as well as the underlying reasons for denial, the CO had been unable to evaluate the underlying merits of the decision. If a case is sufficiently developed, then affirmance of the denial or reversal of the denial and an order directing certification would be appropriate. However, for example, if an employer failed to respond to an audit and did not submit appropriate documentation, a remand to allow for resubmission and further analysis for the CO would be inappropriate. In contrast, if the CO has listed all the legal reasons for denial after a thorough evaluation, but BALCA determines that the CO was arbitrary and capricious in their denial, certification rather than remand may be more appropriate as the CO already evaluated the merits of the application.
In addition, remand is an essential component of the Department's proposal in this NPRM regarding section 656.6 to better hold program violators accountable for their misconduct by preventing successors in interest to debarred persons or entities from participating in the program during the debarment period, without unnecessarily disrupting processing for proper filings. As discussed in proposed section 656.6, once the CO discovers an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
has been filed by a successor in interest to a debarred person or entity, the CO would deny the application solely on that basis and without review. The Notice of Denial would offer the person or entity the option to appeal the CO's determination
(
printed page 73971)
of their successor in interest status under section 656.26. However, as the CO would not have reviewed the merits of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
or reached any determination apart from successor in interest status, if BALCA overturns the CO's determination regarding the successor in interest status, remand would be the appropriate procedural order to allow the application to move forward.
To that end, the Department is proposing to allow for remands in subparagraph (d)(3), and to correspondingly revise proposed subparagraph (d)(2) to make clear that a grant of certification may only be directed when the CO had the opportunity to review the merits of the application.

In turn, the proposed new paragraph (a) would continue to include the current 180-calendar day validity period for a PERM labor certification. Consistent with the current rule, this NPRM would require the employer to submit a PERM labor certification to USCIS with its Immigrant Petition (
i.e.,
Form I-140 petition) for the alien within 180 calendar days of the date the CO approves the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
If the employer does not submit an Immigrant Petition to USCIS using the approved
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
for the alien within 180 calendar days of approval, the PERM labor certification, as it is the case under the current rule, expires and cannot be used. However, the Department has become aware of the practice of PERM labor certifications being reused to subsequent Form I-140 petitions filed with USCIS for the same alien in violation of this prescribed validity period of 180 days, based on a mistaken interpretation of the provision. Therefore, the Department proposes a revision to the current regulatory language to explicitly prevent reuse of a PERM labor certification once it is used in support of the first or initial Form I-140 petition filing for the alien.
Specifically, some employers have been using their PERM labor certifications more than once, including filing after the 180-calendar day validity period has expired. For example, after receiving an Immigrant Petition denial from USCIS and unsuccessfully pursuing an appeal, some employers have filed, and USCIS has accepted, a subsequent Immigrant Petition using the same approved PERM labor certification. These employers assert to USCIS that current section 656.30(b) allows the approved PERM labor certification to remain valid indefinitely, so long as the employer first used it during the 180-calendar day validity period to file an Immigrant Petition with USCIS. Under this interpretation, a PERM labor certification could be several years out-of-date by the time an employer attempts to use it in support of a subsequent Immigrant Petition, which undermines the original PWD and labor market test.
The Department strongly disagrees with this interpretation of its PERM labor certification validity rule. The Department did not intend to permit use of the same PERM labor certification more than 180 calendar days after approval or in connection with subsequent Form I-140 petition filings for the alien. The Department asserts that the statutorily required determinations underlying a PERM labor certification are based on an assessment of the labor market for a certain job opportunity at a certain point in time and a new, updated assessment is necessary for each subsequent Immigrant Petition. The ability to use a PERM labor certification in perpetuity, so long as it was timely filed with a first Immigrant Petition is a fundamentally inconsistent interpretation of the Secretary's determinations, and contradicts statutory intent, and must be clarified to ensure the integrity of the PERM labor certification process. In addition, issuing this clarification and closing this perceived loophole will significantly reduce the continued costs of adjudicating and litigating subsequent filings with USCIS. Although the Department anticipates that this clarifying change would likely result in a marginal increase in filings in its PERM labor certification program, the Department has determined that this cost is necessary to serve its statutory
(
printed page 73972)
duty and preserve, above all, the integrity of the program.
Accordingly, the Department proposes to resolve this misinterpretation by revising the language that under the proposed reorganization of section 656.30 would be included in proposed new paragraph (a) to explicitly limit the validity of a PERM labor certification to the “initial Immigrant Petition.” With this proposed revision, the Department clarifies that a PERM labor certification may be used in connection with one Immigrant Petition, which must be submitted to USCIS within 180 days of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification'
s approval. If USCIS adjudicates the initial Immigrant Petition and denies it—and after any appeals with USCIS have been exhausted and other due process rights afforded—the PERM labor certification is no longer valid for use when filing a new Immigrant Petition.
As explained in the beginning of this section, the Department also proposes redesignating this section 656.30's current paragraph (c) as paragraph (b). In addition to redesignating paragraph (c) as new paragraph (b), the Department proposes revising the regulatory language to clarify the scope of a PERM labor certification's validity that already exists, in large part, on the Office of Management and Budget (OMB)-approved form—
Final Determination: Permanent Employment Certification Approval,
and to conform with other proposals in this proposed rule. First, the Department proposes to remove language that has become outdated and language discussing Schedule A and sheepherder
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification,
which this NPRM proposes to eliminate. Second, the Department is proposing revised language to clarify that a PERM labor certification is valid only for the employer to whom the CO issued the approval, or its successors in interest. Proposed section 656.30(b) further clarifies that a PERM labor certification is only valid for the job opportunity, the alien, the place(s) of intended employment, and the employer named on the approved
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
while recognizing that the employer may change its corporate form and should not lose access to the PERM labor certification due to a legitimate business transaction related to a change to its corporate structure.
Finally, the Department is proposing to eliminate current section 656.30(e), which outlines an outdated process for requesting duplicate PERM labor certifications from the OFLC CO. Through past information technology initiatives, the Department has eliminated the issuance of PERM labor certifications in paper form; now that PERM labor certifications are issued electronically through the OFLC FLAG system, employers, aliens, and their authorized attorneys or agents, as applicable, no longer need to request duplicate PERM labor certifications to submit to USCIS or DOS. Through a combination of existing data sharing agreements with USCIS and DOS and direct customer access to their authorized FLAG system accounts, OFLC makes all approved PERM labor certifications, as well as information related to any application, available real-time to USCIS and DOS. Once this change is implemented, the government agencies that collaborate with OFLC to administer the temporary and permanent labor certification programs will continue to have access to OFLC's FLAG system to obtain PERM labor certification records and verify data and information related to
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification.
Therefore, there is no longer a need to issue duplicate approved PERM labor certifications, when this process occurs electronically. Eliminating these paper government records serves to safeguard government resources, reduce burden on employers, and reduce costs to the public, the filing community, and the federal agencies processing these cases. This proposal also seeks to strengthen integrity measures by minimizing the number of original PERM labor certifications that are issued in paper-format. By eliminating this provision, the Department is not prohibiting the issuance of paper-based PERM labor certification records or duplicates to USCIS or other federal agencies, if and when necessary, but no longer needs to issue them directly to employers, aliens, or their authorized attorneys or agents, as applicable.

1. Need for Regulation
The Department has determined that this rulemaking is necessary to modernize the permanent labor certification (PERM) program so that it continues to fulfill the Secretary's statutory responsibilities under section 212(a)(5)(A) of the INA. The current regulatory framework has remained largely unchanged since 2005, despite significant changes in labor market conditions, recruitment practices, technology, and the manner in which employers recruit and hire workers.
Modernizing the PERM program is a regulatory action the Department must undertake to be able to adapt existing regulations governing the statutory permanent labor certification requirement to the current characteristics and demands of the labor market in the United States, address challenges encountered by the Department to more effectively administer the program while addressing employers' bona fide workforce needs who rely on the program to employ aliens in permanent positions that cannot be filled by qualified and available U.S. workers. For example, over the past two decades, employers have increasingly shifted away from print advertising toward electronic recruitment platforms, remote work has become commonplace across many industries, and workforce mobility and employer hiring practices have evolved considerably. At the same time, the Department has gained substantial operational experience administering the PERM program and identified areas where existing regulations no longer adequately reflect current labor market realities or provide sufficient clarity regarding employer obligations, as well as program administration, integrity and enforcement. These developments demonstrate the need to update the Department's regulations to ensure that the statutory PERM labor certification requirement remains an effective mechanism for determining whether qualified U.S. workers are available for permanent job opportunities and whether the employment of aliens would adversely affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed U.S. workers.
The Department has also determined that rulemaking is necessary to strengthen protections for U.S. workers and improve integrity of the labor market test required by the INA. Decades of experience administering the PERM program has revealed opportunities to better ensure that employers recruit U.S. workers in good faith using recruitment methods that better reflect contemporary hiring practices and provide the broadest exposure possible of available job opportunities to prospective U.S. applicants. Moreover, the Department has identified the need to strengthen safeguards related to layoffs, clarify employer obligations during the recruitment and adjudication process, improve notice requirements, enhance oversight of third-party employment arrangements, and increase accountability for employers, attorneys, and agents participating in the program. In addition, following its review of public comments received in response to the Department's 2023 RFI concerning Schedule A, the Department concluded that it lacks a reliable, objective, and transparent methodology for maintaining or expanding Schedule A in a manner consistent with its statutory responsibilities. Accordingly, the Department has determined that regulatory changes are necessary to ensure that labor market testing more accurately reflects current labor market conditions and that all employers seeking permanent labor certification are subject to standards that are consistent, transparent, and aligned with the INA.
This rulemaking is also intended to modernize and streamline administration of the PERM program by codifying electronic filing and communication practices, clarifying regulatory standards, simplifying procedures, and eliminating outdated requirements that no longer provide meaningful regulatory value. The Department proposes to consolidate and reorganize regulatory provisions, modernize and streamline prevailing wage and application processing procedures, clarify integrity actions, as well as the appeals and review processes, and remove obsolete
(
printed page 73980)
requirements associated with paper processing and duplicative regulatory provisions. These changes are expected to improve administrative efficiency, reduce unnecessary burdens on employers and the Department, facilitate coordination with DHS, and improve the consistency and predictability of program administration.
Accordingly, the Department is proposing comprehensive revisions to
20 CFR part 656
that modernize recruitment requirements, strengthen protections for U.S. workers, enhance program integrity, improve processing efficiency, and update the regulatory framework governing permanent labor certifications to better reflect current labor market conditions and the Department's statutory responsibilities. Collectively, the proposed revisions are intended to preserve employers' ability to access employment-based immigration pathways when qualified U.S. workers are unavailable, while ensuring that the PERM labor certification process continues to provide meaningful protections for the U.S. workforce and supports the fair and effective administration of the Nation's employment-based immigration system.

3. Subject-by-Subject Analysis
In this section, the Department describes all anticipated benefits, costs, and cost-savings of the proposed rule, including both quantified and unquantified impacts. Each impact is described, and quantifiable impacts are estimated while nonquantifiable impacts are discussed qualitatively.
i. Benefits Discussion
The Department expects the proposed rule to generate substantial benefits by modernizing the PERM labor certification process, strengthening protections for U.S. workers, improving the integrity and efficiency of the employment-based immigrant visa system, and reducing administrative inefficiencies for employers and the Federal Government. Collectively, the proposed changes would better align the PERM program with current labor market conditions, modern recruitment practices, and the Department's statutory obligations under INA section 212(a)(5)(A), and modernize the program so that it becomes more efficient and transparent.
A principal benefit of the proposed rule is the modernization of existing recruitment methods used to test the U.S. labor market for purposes of filing a PERM application. The current PERM framework relies heavily on print newspaper advertisements and recruitment methods established nearly two decades ago, which no longer reflect how employers recruit workers or how workers search for employment opportunities. The proposed rule replaces outdated print-focused recruitment requirements with modern electronic recruitment methods, including advertisements on employer websites, commercial job search websites, social media platforms, and SWA job orders, as well as job fairs or campus recruiting events. These proposed changes are expected to improve dissemination of job opportunities to U.S. workers and increase the likelihood of qualified and available U.S. workers becoming aware of and applying for PERM-related positions before employers seek to permanently employ aliens.
The proposal also would require employers to recruit U.S. workers using the same recruitment methods and timeframes they customarily use for comparable non-PERM positions. This approach is expected to improve the equality of employment opportunities by disincentivizing employers from departing from their ordinary PERM recruitment methods or efforts they normally employ, in ways that may discourage U.S. worker participation. By requiring recruitment practices that more closely resemble real-world hiring practices, the rule would strengthen the integrity of the labor market test and improve confidence that PERM recruitment is conducted in good faith.
The Department also expects significant benefits from the proposed extension of recruitment duration requirements. Under the proposed rule, most advertisements would remain active for at least 90 calendar days, or longer if the employer normally recruits for similar positions for a longer period. Longer recruitment periods are expected to improve labor market exposure for job opportunities and provide workers additional time to find out about the job offer, become familiar with the job requirements and apply for available positions. The Department believes this longer recruitment timeframe would better reflect actual labor market conditions and would align more closely with the amount of time unemployed workers spend searching for employment.
Another major benefit the Department believes would derive from the proposed rule is enhanced protection for U.S. workers impacted by layoffs not only throughout the PERM process but also while the employer pursues the visa petition before DHS. Specifically, the proposal would expand current layoff-related protections by prohibiting the filing of a PERM application within the 2 years after a relevant layoff and, in the event a relevant layoff occurs after filing a PERM application, requiring employers to consider laid-off U.S. workers during a significantly broader timeframe extending through adjudication of the associated Form I-140 petition or final case resolution. The Department expects these changes to reduce the risk of employers seeking permanent foreign labor while simultaneously displacing U.S. workers in the same or similar occupations. These provisions are also expected to improve employment opportunities for laid-off workers and better align labor certification determinations with actual labor market conditions at the time of adjudication of PERM applications and visa petitions.
The proposed rule also seeks to prohibit the placement of aliens at third-party worksites experiencing layoffs where indicia of an employment relationship exist between the alien and the third-party employer. This provision is expected to reduce the risk of indirect displacement of U.S. workers through staffing arrangements or contractor relationships and improve accountability and transparency in third-party employment arrangements.
The Department further expects benefits from increased transparency requirements related to layoffs and notice obligations. Employers would be required to notify DOL and, where applicable, USCIS, of layoffs occurring
(
printed page 73981)
during the relevant period and update recruitment reports accordingly. Expanded NOF requirements, including electronic notice procedures and notice obligations for third-party worksites, are expected to improve U.S. workers' awareness of pending labor certification applications and facilitate the reporting of fraud, misrepresentation, or the existence of qualified U.S. workers to the Department and USCIS.
The proposed elimination of Schedule A is also expected to produce important benefits. The Department determined that it currently lacks a reliable, objective, and transparent methodology to justify continuing categorical labor market test exemptions for occupations listed on Schedule A. Eliminating Schedule A would ensure that all occupations subject to PERM labor certification requirements undergo a labor market test unless exempted by statute. The Department expects this change to improve consistency with the INA's labor certification requirements and provide U.S. workers an opportunity to apply for all PERM-covered positions.
The proposed rule also contains substantial program integrity improvements. These changes include enhanced employer attestations, expanded audit and supervised recruitment authority, stronger debarment provisions, successor-in-interest liability standards, and independent accountability for attorneys and agents. The Department expects these changes to deter fraud and abuse, improve compliance with program requirements, and strengthen public confidence in the PERM labor certification process. Expanded authority to hold attorneys, agents, and successor entities accountable for misconduct is expected to reduce opportunities for program circumvention and abusive filing practices.
The proposal would also modernize and streamline the administration of the PERM program through mandatory electronic filing and expanded electronic communications. These changes are expected to reduce paperwork burdens, lower mailing and administrative costs, improve application completeness and data quality, reduce processing delays associated with deficient applications, and facilitate faster communication between OFLC and stakeholders. The vast majority of employers already use electronic filing systems, based on FY 2021-FY 2025 data, approximately 99.61 percent of PERM labor certification applications were filed electronically. Department expects the transition costs associated with mandatory electronic filing to be minimal for most employers.
In addition, the Department estimates that the proposed centralized electronic processing and electronic transmission of determinations to USCIS will improve interagency coordination, facilitate data sharing, reduce duplicative submissions, and improve fraud detection capabilities. The Department also expects operational efficiencies and better public experience with the program from codifying existing adjudicative practices, clarifying audit and appeal procedures, and reducing unnecessary BALCA docketing.
The proposed rule would further improve regulatory clarity and predictability by modernizing existing terminology, consolidating procedures, and clarifying definitions and standards throughout part 656. These changes are expected to improve the regulated community understanding of program requirements, reduce ambiguity and inadvertent noncompliance, improve adjudicative consistency, and reduce litigation risk.
Overall, the Department expects the proposed rule to generate substantial benefits by improving labor market testing, strengthening protections for U.S. workers, increasing transparency and accountability by all program participants, modernizing program administration, reducing inefficiencies, and enhancing the integrity of the PERM labor certification process. The proposals are expected to create a more effective, transparent, and administratively efficient system that better reflects contemporary labor market conditions while preserving access to employment-based immigration pathways for employers with legitimate workforce needs.
ii. Costs
In the following sections, the Department presents the costs estimated to be incurred by relevant stakeholders.
a. Quantifiable Costs
Rule Familiarization
To quantify rule familiarization costs, the Department employs a methodology that reflects the structure of the PERM filing market. PERM applications are primarily filed either by outside immigration law firms on behalf of employers or directly by employers themselves, although agents also may file PERM applications on behalf of employers. Accordingly, the Department estimates familiarization costs separately for two groups: (1) unique law firms that submitted PERM applications on behalf of employers, and (2) unique employers that filed PERM applications directly without outside legal counsel.
For law firms, the Department assumes that one attorney per firm is responsible for reviewing and understanding the regulatory changes associated with the rule. The Department values this time using the fully-loaded hourly compensation rate for Attorneys. For employers filing without outside counsel, the Department assumes that one Human Resources (HR) specialist per employer is responsible for rule familiarization and values this time using the fully loaded hourly compensation rate for HR Specialists.
The Department used the hourly compensation rates presented in Exhibit 1 to estimate rule familiarization costs. BLS's OEWS data show that the mean hourly wage of HR Specialists (SOC 13-1071) is $39.42 and the hourly rate of an Attorney is $89.35 (SOC 23-1011).

b. Nonquantifiable Costs
In this section, the Department describes various non-quantifiable costs of the proposed rule.
Record Retention Period Restarted 5 Years From Date of Certification Expiration or Denial/Withdrawal of the Application for Permanent Employment Certification, or 5 Years From the Date on Which the Immigrant Petition Is Approved or Denied (§ 656.10)
The principal cost associated with the extended record retention period is the incremental cost of storing documentation for a longer period than currently required for applications with extended processing timelines.
The Department was unable to quantify the incremental storage costs associated with the extended retention period with sufficient precision to report a point estimate, for several reasons, and accordingly treats the costs of this provision as a nonquantifiable cost.
First, the additional retention burden is not uniform across the population of employers filing Applications for Permanent Employment Certification, it varies significantly depending on the processing trajectory of each individual application. Employers whose applications proceed through standard adjudication and result in a timely filed and approved Form I-140 petition would experience little or no meaningful extension of their retention obligations relative to the current rule, as the practical difference between a retention period measured from the date of filing and one measured from the date of certification expiration would be modest in the absence of prolonged processing. By contrast, employers whose applications are subject to audit examination, supervised recruitment, BALCA review, or extended USCIS adjudication of the associated Form I-140 petition could face a substantially longer retention period under the proposed rule than under current regulations. Because the Department cannot predict with confidence which applications will follow each processing path at the time of filing, it cannot reliably estimate the average incremental retention duration across the full population of filers.
Additionally, the incremental cost per unit of additional retention time varies significantly across employers depending on whether they maintain physical or electronic records, the volume of documentation associated with each application, and the nature of each employer's existing document management infrastructure. For the substantial majority of employers who already use electronic filing and document management systems, as evidenced by the near-universal rate of electronic filing in the PERM program,
(
printed page 73984)
with approximately 99.61 percent of Applications for Permanent Employment Certification filed electronically during FY 2021-FY 2025, the marginal cost of retaining records for an extended period is expected to be negligible, consisting primarily of incremental electronic storage costs that are difficult to isolate and are likely to be minimal relative to overall compliance costs. For the small subset of employers who maintain physical records, the incremental cost would depend on local storage rates and individual document volumes that the Department does not have sufficient data to estimate reliably across the regulated community.
The Department notes that the proposed change does not require employers to collect or create any new documentation; it requires only that documentation already required to be prepared and retained under existing program regulations be preserved for a period that more reliably ensures its availability for program oversight purposes throughout the full adjudication lifecycle of the application and associated petition. For these reasons, the Department concludes qualitatively that the incremental retention costs associated with this provision are minimal relative to the significant program integrity benefits of ensuring that complete documentation remains accessible for the full period during which OFLC and partner agencies may have occasion to request and review it.
The Department requests comment and data that could inform its assessment of the incremental costs associated with the proposed record retention requirements. Specifically, the Department requests comment and data on, the proportion of applications that proceed to audit or BALCA review, the time elapsed between PERM approval or denial and I-140 adjudication, the number of employees potentially affected, the extent of any additional recruitment, hiring, delay, or administrative burdens, and costs associated with those impacts. The Department also requests data on how these costs might vary depending on employer size, industry, and other circumstances.
Permanent Labor Certification Validity Limited to One Use and One Employer (§ 656.30)
The primary costs associated with this clarification fall on employers who have previously relied on the interpretation that an approved permanent labor certification remains available for use in connection with subsequent Form I-140 petitions for the same alien, provided it was timely filed with an initial petition. For employers in this situation whose initial petitions are denied, and whose appeals before USCIS or the federal courts are ultimately unsuccessful, the proposed clarification would require them to obtain a new permanent labor certification, including full compliance with the pre-filing recruitment requirements of proposed section 656.17, before filing a subsequent petition with USCIS. This would involve conducting a new labor market test, obtaining a new PWD from OFLC, and preparing and submitting a new
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
all of which impose meaningful time and cost on affected employers and their authorized representatives.
The magnitude of this cost is difficult to estimate reliably for several reasons. First, the Department does not have comprehensive data on the number of employers who have reused approved permanent labor certifications in connection with subsequent Form I-140 petitions, as this practice occurs in the context of USCIS adjudication rather than OFLC processing and is therefore not fully captured in the Department's program data. Second, the costs imposed on any individual employer will depend on the circumstances of the underlying denial, the duration of any appellate proceedings before USCIS or the federal courts, and the extent to which labor market conditions and prevailing wage rates have changed in the intervening period, all of which will vary considerably across affected employers.
Because the proposed clarification forecloses a practice that the Department has determined is inconsistent with the intent of the current rule and with the Secretary's statutory obligations under INA section 212(a)(5)(A), the population of employers who would incur these costs going forward is expected to consist primarily of those who have been relying on an interpretation of the regulation that the Department considers erroneous, rather than those engaging in conduct the Department intended to permit.
The Department concludes qualitatively that the costs of this clarification are real, and in some cases may be significant for individual employers affected by it.
Those costs are a necessary consequence of the Department's obligation to administer the permanent labor certification program in a manner consistent with the Secretary's statutory mandate and are proportionate to the program integrity benefits the clarification is designed to achieve.
Recruitment Report Required at Time of Filing (§ 656.10, § 656.17)
The Department acknowledges that requiring submission of the recruitment report at the time of filing will impose an incremental upfront documentation burden on employers and their authorized attorneys or agents. Under the current rule, employers whose applications are not selected for audit are not required to submit the recruitment report at any point during processing. Under the proposed rule, all employers would be required to upload or otherwise submit the recruitment report at the time of filing. Because this change applies to the full universe of applications, rather than only to those selected for audit, it represents a broader expansion of the submission requirement than any prior change in program administration.
Nonetheless, the Department expects the incremental burden of this requirement to be modest for most employers and their representatives and accordingly treats the costs of this provision as a non-quantifiable cost.
Because employers are required to prepare and maintain the recruitment report before filing the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
the substantive work of compiling the report is already required under current regulations. The proposed change imposes only the additional step of transmitting the completed report to OFLC at the time of filing rather than retaining it solely in the employer's records. For approximately 99.61 percent of employers who already file electronically using the FLAG System, this additional step consists primarily of uploading the recruitment report into the electronic filing system as part of the standard submission process, a task the Department considers de minimis in isolation. The incremental time associated with this step will vary depending on the format and organization of the employer's existing recruitment documentation, the complexity of the employer's pre-filing recruitment activities, and the capabilities of the employer's document management systems, making it difficult to estimate reliably across the full population of filers.
Furthermore, the incremental burden of this requirement will also vary depending on the degree to which employers and their authorized attorneys or agents have already integrated recruitment report preparation into their standard pre-filing workflows. For immigration law
(
printed page 73985)
firms that handle large volumes of PERM filings and have established document management practices, the additional step of uploading the recruitment report concurrently with the application is expected to impose little marginal burden beyond what is already incurred in preparing and organizing the report for retention. For employers who file without outside legal counsel and who may have less standardized pre-filing documentation practices, the incremental burden of ensuring the recruitment report is in a form suitable for submission at the time of filing may be somewhat greater, though the Department expects this cost to decrease over time as employers adapt their pre-filing workflows to the new requirement.
The Department notes that this provision is expected to generate offsetting administrative efficiencies for both employers and OFLC. By enabling OFLC to review the recruitment report for every application as a standard part of adjudication, rather than only upon audit selection, the proposed rule is expected to reduce the frequency of post-filing requests for documentation, support faster adjudication of compliant applications, and reduce the uncertainty and administrative burden associated with responding to audit notices for employers whose applications might otherwise have been selected for that purpose. For these reasons, the Department concludes qualitatively that the incremental costs associated with the universal recruitment report submission requirement are modest and proportionate to the significant program integrity and adjudicative efficiency benefits expected from this change.
Mandatory Electronic Filing
The Department assumes there is a modest cost associated with mandatory electronic filing falls on the small subset of employers who currently file by mail and who may need to establish access to the FLAG System or otherwise adapt their filing practices to comply with the electronic filing requirement. These costs may include the time necessary to establish or access a FLAG System account, convert or upload supporting documentation in an appropriate electronic format, and modify existing administrative procedures used to prepare and submit applications.
The Department expects this transition cost to be minimal for most affected employers, given that the FLAG System is publicly accessible and that the Department proposes to retain a limited exception to mandatory electronic filing for employers who can demonstrate to the OFLC Administrator that they are unable or limited in their ability to use or access electronic filing. This exception ensures that mandatory electronic filing does not impose an unreasonable burden on employers with genuine technological constraints. The Department concludes qualitatively that the transition costs associated with mandatory electronic filing are minimal relative to the cost savings the requirement is expected to generate for the employer community and OFLC.

2-Year Pre-Filing Anti-Layoff Provision
The Department expects that the proposed expansion of the layoff period from 180 days to 2 years could generate costs that cannot be reliably quantified. The proposed provision could also impose costs on employers by reducing their flexibility to use the permanent labor certification program following a relevant layoff. Employers whose legitimate workforce needs change during the 2-year period may be unable to pursue permanent labor certification for workers in the same or occupations even when subsequent business conditions create a need for additional workers. These employers could incur costs associated with delaying hiring, conducting additional recruitment, retraining or redeploying existing workers, modifying business operations, or using alternative sources of labor. To the extent that relevant visas are thus freed for use by other employers—those with PERM certifications but facing a visa backlog due to statutory caps—there would be partially-offsetting cost savings associated with their accelerated hiring.
Because the Department lacks sufficient information regarding the extent of relevant layoffs, and subsequent employer hiring needs, the effects of this provision are discussed qualitatively. The Department requests public comments and data linking employers' layoff histories to their standing within relevant visa backlogs and invites interested individuals, organizations, and stakeholders to share their feedback and suggestions.
