b. Nonquantifiable Cost-Savings
Permanent Labor Certification Validity Limited to One Use and One Employer (§ 656.30)
The Department expects the clarification of permanent labor certification validity to generate meaningful cost savings for USCIS and, indirectly, for the broader employer community, by reducing the volume of Form I-140 petitions filed in reliance on stale or improperly reused permanent labor certifications.
Under the current rule, as interpreted by some employers, and current USCIS procedures, an approved permanent labor certification may be reused in connection with successive Form I-140 petitions for the same alien, potentially years after the underlying labor market test was conducted, so long as it was timely filed with an initial petition. Each such petition requires USCIS to expend adjudicative resources to review and process a filing that the Department has determined is inconsistent with the intent of the permanent labor certification program and with the Secretary's statutory obligations under INA section 212(a)(5)(A). Where USCIS denies such petitions, additional costs are incurred through the appellate process, including administrative appeals before the USCIS Administrative Appeals Office and, in some cases, litigation in the federal courts. By clarifying that a permanent labor certification is valid for use in connection with one initial Form I-140 petition only, the proposed rule is expected to reduce the frequency of such filings going forward, generating cost savings for USCIS in the form of reduced adjudicative and administrative costs associated with processing petitions based on stale certifications.
To the extent that the clarification also reduces the frequency of federal court litigation arising from USCIS denials of petitions based on reused certifications, the proposed rule is expected to generate additional cost savings for both USCIS and DOJ in the form of reduced litigation costs. The Department is unable to quantify these savings with precision, as it does not have comprehensive data on the volume of petitions currently filed in reliance on reused certifications or the rate at which such petitions are denied and subsequently litigated. However, the Department concludes qualitatively that these cost savings are real and contribute meaningfully to the overall net benefits of the proposed clarification.
Mandatory Electronic Filing (§ 656.10 & § 656.40)
The Department expects the requirement to file
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification
and
Applications for Prevailing Wage Determination
electronically through the FLAG System to generate meaningful cost savings for both employers and OFLC. Because approximately 99.61 percent of
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification
and more than 99 percent of
Applications for Prevailing Wage Determination
were already submitted electronically during FY 2021-FY 2025, mandatory electronic filing does not represent a change in practice for the substantial majority of employers and their authorized representatives. Rather, it codifies and extends to the full population of filers the efficiencies that the Department and most employers have already realized through voluntary adoption of electronic filing.
For employers who currently file electronically, the cost savings associated with mandatory electronic filing are already being realized and are not incremental to the proposed rule. For the small subset of employers who currently file by mail (approximately 0.39 percent of PERM filers based on recent program data) mandatory electronic filing is expected to eliminate the costs associated with paper-based submission, including printing, postage, and private courier or expedited mailing fees. The Department notes that nearly all employers who currently file by mail disclosed valid email addresses on their applications, suggesting that these filers have access to the internet and are likely capable of transitioning to electronic filing without significant investment in new technology or infrastructure.
For OFLC, mandatory electronic filing is expected to generate operational cost savings by reducing the administrative burden associated with receiving, sorting, scanning, and manually processing paper applications. Electronic filing also reduces the frequency of processing delays attributable to illegible, incomplete, or misdirected paper submissions, and supports more efficient interagency data sharing with USCIS and DOS by enabling direct electronic transmission of certified applications and PWDs. The Department considers these savings to be genuine reductions in Federal administrative costs that contribute to the overall net benefits of the proposed rule.
Elimination of Duplicate Labor Certifications (§ 656.30)
The Department expects the elimination of the process for requesting duplicate paper permanent labor certifications under current section 656.30(e) to generate cost savings for employers (potentially), their authorized representatives (potentially), and OFLC (more certainly) by removing an administrative procedure that is no longer necessary given the Department's transition to fully electronic processing and direct electronic transmission of approved certifications to USCIS and DOS.
Under the current rule, employers, aliens, and their authorized attorneys or agents may request duplicate paper copies of approved permanent labor certifications from the CO for submission to USCIS or DOS. This process requires employers or their representatives to identify the need for a duplicate, submit a request to OFLC, and await issuance of the duplicate certification before proceeding with downstream immigration filings. For OFLC, processing duplicate certification requests requires staff time to locate, verify, and issue the requested documentation. These costs, derived by
(
printed page 73987)
both employers and the Federal Government, are entirely avoidable given that OFLC now transmits approved permanent labor certifications directly to USCIS electronically through existing data sharing agreements, and that employers, aliens, and their authorized representatives have real-time access to approved certification records through their FLAG System accounts.
By eliminating the duplicate certification process, the proposed rule removes a procedural step that generates administrative costs without producing program benefits that are meaningful under current operating conditions as they might have been under other conditions. The Department expects that, for employers and authorized representatives who did not use the duplicate certification process, this elimination will have no effect on their burden. For those who voluntarily used the process, its elimination represents a loss of flexibility and a potential cost, as these entities will need to rely on FLAG System access or other means to provide certification documentation to USCIS or DOS, rather than a straightforward savings. For OFLC, cost savings would be in the form of reduced staff time spent processing requests that are no longer necessary for the downstream submission process. The Department also expects this change to strengthen program integrity by reducing the number of original paper permanent labor certifications in circulation, thereby reducing the risk of fraud associated with the possession and potential misuse of paper certification documents. The Department concludes qualitatively that eliminating the duplicate certification process would generate administrative cost savings for the Federal Government and potentially for employers and their representatives who did not rely on the duplicate process, there would be no change in burden. For those who did rely on it, they may incur costs from the loss of flexibility to request duplicate certifications. Such costs could include additional time and resources needed to obtain or verify certification records through alternative procedures. The Department is unable to reliably quantify these costs and seeks public comment on their potential magnitude, including the time and resources needed to obtain or verify certification records through alternative means. The Department requests comment and data that could inform its assessment of this provision.
Elimination of Post-PWD Supplemental Information Submission (§ 656.40)
The Department expects the elimination of the supplemental information submission step currently available under section 656.40(h), which requires employers to submit a request for redetermination before they may seek Center Director Review (CDR) of a PWD under section 656.41, to generate cost savings for employers and their authorized representatives by streamlining the prevailing wage review process and eliminating a procedural step that imposes compliance costs without commensurate program integrity benefits.
Under the current rule, employers who disagree with a PWD issued by OFLC must first submit supplemental information to the NPC under section 656.40(h) before they are eligible to request review by the Center Director under section 656.41. This two-stage review process requires employers and their authorized representatives to prepare and submit supplemental information at the redetermination stage, await a response from the NPC, and then, if the redetermination is unfavorable, prepare and submit a separate request for Center Director Review (CDR). Each stage of this process imposes incremental costs on employers in the form of attorney or agent time spent preparing submissions, coordinating with the NPC, and managing the administrative timeline associated with a multi-stage review process.
By eliminating the redetermination step and permitting employers to proceed directly to Center Director Review (CDR) under section 656.41 when they disagree with a PWD, the proposed rule reduces the number of procedural steps employers must navigate to obtain review of an unfavorable determination. The Department expects this change to generate cost savings for employers by reducing the total time and professional fees associated with challenging a PWD, and to generate operational efficiencies for OFLC by reducing the volume of supplemental submissions the NPC must review and adjudicate outside of the standard RFI process established in proposed section 656.40(c). The Department concludes qualitatively that the elimination of the post-PWD supplemental information submission step generates meaningful cost savings for the regulated community and contributes to the Department's broader goal of streamlining and modernizing the administration of the PWD process.

5. Regulatory Alternatives
OMB Circular A-4, which outlines best practices in regulatory analysis, directs agencies to analyze alternatives if such alternatives best satisfy the philosophy and principles of
E.O. 12866
. The Department considered two primary alternatives:
Alternative 1: Mandating Additional Recruitment Methods and Longer Recruitment Periods
As an alternative to the proposed rule, the Department considered mandating additional recruitment methods and longer recruitment periods. Under this alternative, the Department could have required employers to conduct a more extensive labor market test by mandating additional recruitment methods and longer recruitment periods beyond those proposed in this NPRM. For example, the Department could have required all employers to conduct recruitment through multiple commercial job search websites, mandatory social media advertising regardless of customary practice, and mandatory employee referral programs. Similarly, the Department could have required all recruitment advertisements to remain active for periods exceeding 90 calendar days, such as 120 or 180 calendar days, to maximize labor market exposure and increase opportunities for U.S. workers to apply. Although the Department recognizes that these more stringent requirements could potentially provide additional protections for U.S. workers and further strengthen program integrity, the Department determined that such approaches would likely impose substantially greater administrative and compliance burdens on employers, increase processing complexity, and reduce operational flexibility for employers with legitimate workforce needs. The Department also determined that these approaches could significantly increase application preparation costs and prolong recruitment timelines without proportionate additional benefits in many cases. Accordingly, the Department determined that the proposed rule appropriately balances the need to strengthen labor market protections and program integrity while avoiding unnecessary burdens on employers and the administration of the PERM program.
(
printed page 73989)
Alternative 2: Elimination of Print Newspaper Advertisement Requirements
As an alternative to the proposed rule, the Department considered a narrower regulatory approach that would have focused solely on eliminating the mandatory print newspaper advertisement requirements currently applicable to the PERM labor certification process, while otherwise retaining the existing recruitment framework and procedural requirements under
20 CFR part 656
. Under this alternative, employers would continue to comply with the existing PERM labor certification structure, including the distinction between professional and nonprofessional occupations, the current menu-based recruitment system for professional occupations, and existing recruitment timing and notice requirements. However, the Department would eliminate the requirement that employers place print advertisements in newspapers of general circulation on two different Sundays or in professional journals, as currently required under section 656.17.
In place of mandatory print advertisements, the Department considered allowing employers to satisfy the recruitment requirement through alternative electronic recruitment methods, such as commercial job search websites or employer websites, while preserving the remainder of the current regulatory framework. This alternative would have recognized significant changes in labor market recruitment practices and the declining utility of print newspapers as a meaningful recruitment tool for many occupations.
The Department considered this alternative because current labor market practices increasingly rely on electronic recruitment methods rather than traditional print media. Online job platforms, employer career websites, and social media platforms have become the primary means through which employers advertise vacancies and workers search for employment opportunities. In contrast, print newspaper circulation has significantly declined in recent years, including among local and ethnic newspapers traditionally relied upon for recruitment. As a result, the Department recognized that retaining mandatory print newspaper advertisements may impose costs on employers while producing diminishing recruitment value for U.S. workers.
However, after consideration, the Department determined that this limited alternative would not adequately address broader structural and integrity concerns within the PERM labor certification process. Although eliminating print newspaper advertisements would modernize one component of the labor market test, the Department concluded that retaining the remainder of the current recruitment framework would fail to sufficiently align PERM recruitment requirements with contemporary labor market conditions and employer hiring practices. In particular, the Department determined that simply removing print newspaper advertisements without adopting broader modernization measures would not adequately address inconsistencies in recruitment quality, insufficient labor market exposure, or concerns regarding employer recruitment practices that may deter participation by qualified U.S. workers. The Department also determined that this alternative would not sufficiently strengthen protections for U.S. workers impacted by layoffs, improve transparency during adjudication, or address integrity concerns involving third-party placements, inadequate notice procedures, or inconsistent employer recruitment practices.
The Department invites public comments on these or other possible alternatives with the goal of ensuring a thorough consideration and discussion at the final rule stage.

Executive Order 13272
(Proper Consideration of Small Entities in Agency Rulemaking)
The Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980 (RFA),
5 U.S.C. 601
et seq.,
as amended by the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996,
Public Law 104-121
(Mar. 29, 1996), hereafter jointly referred to as the RFA, requires agencies to prepare an initial regulatory flexibility analysis (IRFA) when proposing, and a final regulatory flexibility analysis (FRFA) when issuing, regulations that will have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. The Department conducted the IRFA below of the effect on small entities from the proposed rule.
1. Why the Department Is Considering Action
The Department is considering this rulemaking to modernize and streamline the permanent labor certification (PERM) program and ensure that its regulations continue to fulfill the Department's statutory responsibilities under section 212(a)(5)(A) of the INA. Under the INA, before certain employment-based immigrants may be admitted to the United States for permanent employment, the Secretary must determine and certify that there are not sufficient U.S. workers who are able, willing, qualified, and available to perform the work and that the employment of the alien will not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed U.S. workers.
The Department's current PERM regulations were largely established in 2004 and have not undergone comprehensive modernization in approximately two decades. During that time, substantial changes have occurred in labor market conditions, recruitment practices, workforce mobility, and the use of technology in hiring. Employers increasingly rely on electronic recruitment methods, including online job boards, employer websites, social media platforms, and virtual recruitment events, while the use and effectiveness of traditional print newspaper advertising have declined significantly. The Department has determined that the current regulatory framework does not fully reflect these developments and may not consistently ensure that available job opportunities are advertised to the broadest possible pool of qualified U.S. workers.
The Department is also considering this action to strengthen protections for U.S. workers and improve program integrity. Through its administration of the PERM program, the Department has identified areas where existing regulations could be clarified or updated to better address issues involving layoffs, third-party worksite arrangements, notice requirements, recruitment practices, employer accountability, and compliance oversight. The Department believes that updating these requirements would improve transparency, enhance the effectiveness of labor market testing, and provide greater assurance that employers seeking permanent labor certification are conducting recruitment in good faith and providing qualified U.S. workers a meaningful opportunity to compete for available positions.
In addition, the Department seeks to modernize and streamline program administration by codifying electronic filing and communication practices, clarifying regulatory standards, reducing reliance on outdated procedures, and improving operational efficiency. These changes are intended to support timely processing, reduce administrative burdens associated with obsolete requirements, and improve consistency and integrity across the Department's foreign labor certification programs
(
printed page 73990)
while continuing to provide employers with access to lawful employment-based immigration pathways when qualified U.S. workers are unavailable.
2. Objectives of and Legal Basis for the NPRM
The objective of this NPRM is to modernize the permanent labor certification (PERM) program, improve protections for U.S. workers, strengthen program integrity, and increase the efficiency and transparency of the Department's administration of employment-based permanent labor certifications. Through this rulemaking, the Department seeks to update regulatory standards and procedures that have remained largely unchanged since implementation of the current PERM framework in 2005, while continuing to provide employers with access to permanent employment-based immigration pathways when qualified and available U.S. workers cannot be found.
The proposed rule would update labor market test requirements to better reflect contemporary recruitment practices and labor market conditions. Among other changes, the Department proposes to replace outdated print-focused recruitment requirements with modern electronic recruitment methods, establish a more uniform recruitment framework applicable to most occupations, clarify recruitment content and timing requirements, and require employers to recruit U.S. workers in a manner that is comparable to recruitment conducted for similar positions outside the PERM process. The Department also proposes to strengthen worker protections by expanding requirements related to layoffs, NOF obligations, and consideration of qualified U.S. workers throughout the labor certification process.
In addition, the NPRM proposes measures intended to enhance program integrity and improve compliance with statutory and regulatory requirements. These measures include revised employer attestations, expanded audit and supervised recruitment authorities, strengthened debarment provisions, successor-in-interest accountability standards, and additional requirements governing attorneys and agents participating in the PERM process. The Department also proposes to modernize program administration through mandatory electronic filing and communications, clarification of PWD procedures, and codification of existing electronic processing practices.
The legal basis for this NPRM is found principally in section 212(a)(5)(A) of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(5)(A)
, which requires the Secretary to determine and certify, before certain employment-based immigrants may be admitted to the United States, that there are not sufficient U.S. workers who are able, willing, qualified, and available to perform the labor or services involved in the employment opportunity and that employment of the alien will not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed U.S. workers. Additional authority is provided by section 212(p) of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1182(p)
, governing PWDs, and other statutory authorities delegated to the Secretary for administration of the permanent labor certification program. The Department is issuing this NPRM pursuant to these statutory authorities and its responsibility to establish procedures necessary to carry out the labor certification requirements of the INA.

6. Relevant Federal Rules Duplicating, Overlapping, or Conflicting With the NPRM
The proposed rule concerns the administration of the permanent labor certification process under section 212(a)(5)(A) of the INA, an area of authority specifically delegated to DOL. The regulations in
20 CFR part 656
govern the standards and procedures by which the Department determines whether there are sufficient qualified and available U.S. workers for a job opportunity and whether the employment of an alien would adversely affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed U.S. workers.
Although other Federal agencies, including DHS and DOS, administer related aspects of the employment-based immigration system, their regulations address separate statutory responsibilities, such as immigrant visa petition adjudication, visa issuance, and admission of aliens. The proposed revisions in this NPRM are intended to complement, rather than duplicate or conflict with those requirements. However, as USCIS administers the immigrant petition process after DOL grants permanent labor certification, the proposed revisions may require DHS to make technical revisions to
8 CFR 204.5
in the event the Department eliminates Schedule A and other minor changes regarding USCIS requests to OFLC for duplicate Applications for Permanent Employment Certification and outdate references to discontinued DOL Form ETA-750.
7. Alternatives to the Proposed Rule
The RFA requires agencies to consider significant alternatives that accomplish the objectives of the proposed rule while minimizing impacts on small entities. The Department considered the following alternatives.
Alternative 1: Reduced Recruitment Duration for Small Employers
As an alternative to the proposed requirement that most recruitment activities remain active for at least 90 calendar days, the Department considered allowing small employers to satisfy the recruitment requirement through a shorter advertising period, such as 30 or 60 calendar days. This approach would reduce recruitment costs and administrative burdens for small businesses by shortening the duration of required job advertisements and reducing the time needed to complete the labor market test. However, the Department determined that a uniform recruitment period better promotes consistency across employers and provides U.S. workers with a meaningful opportunity to learn about and apply for available job opportunities. Accordingly, the Department is proposing a single recruitment standard applicable to all employers.
Alternative 2: Retention of Current Recruitment Framework With Limited Modernization
The Department considered retaining the existing PERM recruitment framework while eliminating only the
(
printed page 74001)
mandatory newspaper advertisement requirements and permitting electronic recruitment methods as substitutes. Under this alternative, employers would continue to follow the current distinction between professional and nonprofessional occupations and the existing recruitment timelines. This approach would reduce compliance costs for small businesses by avoiding many of the new recruitment, notice, and reporting requirements proposed in this NPRM. However, the Department concluded that this narrower approach would not sufficiently address concerns regarding the effectiveness of the labor market test, evolving recruitment practices, program integrity, and protections for U.S. workers. Therefore, the Department determined that the proposed rule more effectively advances its statutory objectives.
The Department welcomes commenter feedback on these regulatory alternatives and invites suggestions for any other regulatory alternatives that commenters believe would be feasible and appropriate.

§ 656.1
Purpose and scope.
(a)
Purpose.
This part establishes the requirements and the procedures by which the Department of Labor (Department or DOL) makes a determination in connection with
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification
and certifies its determination to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Department of State (DOS). A permanent labor certification issued under this part reflects a determination by the Secretary of Labor (Secretary), pursuant to
8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(5)(A)
, that:
(1) There are not sufficient workers who are able, willing, and qualified United States (U.S.) workers available at the time of application for a visa and admission to the United States and at the place where the alien is to perform the skilled or unskilled services; and
(2) The employment of the alien will not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of workers in the United States similarly employed.
(b)
Scope.
This part sets forth the procedures governing the labor certification process for the permanent employment of aliens in the United States. It also establishes standards and obligations with respect to the terms and conditions of the permanent labor certification with which employers must comply and sets forth integrity measures for ensuring employers' good faith recruitment of U.S. workers and continued compliance with the terms and conditions of the permanent labor certification.
§ 656.2
Statutory authority and burden of proof.
(a) The Secretary has delegated the authority to issue permanent labor certifications and execute other statutory responsibilities required by
8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(5)(A)
to the Office of Foreign Labor Certification (OFLC). Determinations on an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
are made by the OFLC Administrator who, in turn, may delegate this responsibility to designated staff (
e.g.,
a Certifying Officer (CO)).
(b) The employer has the burden of proof to establish eligibility to receive certification of an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.

The employer's actual minimum requirements must be normal for the occupation and must not exceed the Specific Vocational Preparation (SVP) required in the Standard Occupational Classification (SOC) code, as indicated by the Occupational Network (O*NET) Job Zones, or must not be materially different from the requirements stated in the employer's recruitment for job opportunities that were not subject to PERM labor certification in the same or substantially comparable occupational classifications during the 12 months preceding the date on which recruitment began for the job opportunity stated in the

The person who makes a determination on an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
filed under this part. The OFLC Administrator is the national CO. Other COs may be designated by the OFLC Administrator to also make the determinations required under this part.
Chief Administrative Law Judge (Chief ALJ).
The chief official of the Department's Office of Administrative Law Judges or the Chief ALJ's designee.
Closely held corporation.
A corporation that typically has relatively few shareholders and whose shares are not generally traded in the securities market.
Department of Homeland Security (DHS).
The Department of Homeland Security, as established by
6 U.S.C. 111
.
Employee.
A person who is engaged to perform work for an employer, as defined under the general common law of agency. Some of the factors relevant to the determination of employee status include: the hiring party's right to control the manner and means by which the work is accomplished; the skill required to perform the work; the source of the instrumentalities and tools for accomplishing the work; the location of the work; the hiring party's discretion over when and how long to work; and whether the work is part of the regular business of the hiring party. Other applicable factors may be considered and no one factor is dispositive.
Employer.
An individual or entity (
e.g.,
partnership, association, corporation, cooperative, firm, joint stock company, trust, public institution, or other organization with legal rights and duties) that seeks to permanently employ a full-time alien at a place within the United States and:
(1)(i) Has or will have an employment relationship (such as the ability to hire, pay, fire, supervise, or otherwise control the work performed by the employee) with respect to a worker;
(ii) Possesses a valid Federal Employer Identification Number (FEIN);
(iii) Has a place of business (physical location) in the U.S. and a means by which it may be contacted for employment The employer must employ at least one individual full-time at the place of business;
(iv) Files an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
other than as an agent or attorney; and
(v) Is an individual or entity on whose behalf an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
is filed.
(2) Persons who are temporarily in the United States, including but not limited to, individuals with temporary employment visas, adjustment applicants whose underlying work authorization was based on a temporary employment visa, foreign diplomats, intra-company transferees, students, and exchange visitors, visitors for business or pleasure, and representatives of foreign information media cannot be employers for the purpose of obtaining a labor certification for permanent employment in the United States.
(3) A foreign mission, determined applicable by the Secretary of State,
e.g.
22 U.S.C. 4302(a)(3)
inter alia, cannot be an employer for purposes of obtaining a permanent labor certification.
Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC).
The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, an independent Federal agency established by Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
Familial relationship.
A familial relationship includes any relationship established by blood, marriage, or adoption, even if distant. For example, cousins of all degrees, aunts, uncles, grandparents and grandchildren are included. It also includes any relationship established through marriage (including domestic partnerships, common-law marriages or civil unions), such as in-laws and step families.
Federal holiday.
Legal public holiday as defined at
5 U.S.C. 6103
.
Fraud.
A false representation of a material fact, or the concealment of a material fact, made with knowledge of its falsity and with the intent to deceive the Department, DHS, the Department of State, or another Government entity, or to obtain a benefit under this part or the Act to which the person is not entitled. Reliance by the Department on the false representation or concealment is not required.
Immigrant Petition.
The U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) Form I-140,
Immigrant Petition
(
printed page 74005)
for Alien Workers,
or successor form, and accompanying documentation required by DHS for employers seeking to employ foreign persons under an employment-based immigrant visa.
Job opportunity.
Full-time employment at a place in the United States to which U.S. workers can be referred. In the event of an audit, the employer must be prepared to document the permanent and full-time nature of the position by furnishing position descriptions and payroll records for the job opportunity involved in the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
Job offer.
The offer made by an employer or potential employer of an alien(s) to both U.S. and aliens describing all the material terms and conditions of employment, including those relating to wages, working conditions, and other benefits for the job opportunity.
Job order.
The document containing the material terms and conditions of employment that is posted by the State Workforce Agency (SWA) on its interstate and intrastate job clearance systems to recruit prospective U.S. applicants for the employer's job offer.
Layoff.
An involuntary separation of one or more workers by the employer without cause or prejudice, such as a personnel action characterized by the employer as a reduction in force, restructuring, or downsizing.
Material.
A fact, statement, representation, or omission is material if it has a natural tendency to influence, or is capable of influencing, a decision of the Department under this part or a decision of DHS or the Department of State on an Immigrant Petition or visa application that relies on a permanent labor certification, regardless of whether it actually influenced the decision. A misrepresentation is not immaterial merely because the Department could have discovered the truth through its own inquiry.
Metropolitan Statistical Area (MSA).
A geographic entity defined by OMB for use by Federal statistical agencies in collecting, tabulating, and publishing Federal statistics. An MSA contains a core urban area of 50,000 or more population, and a Micropolitan Statistical Area contains an urban core of at least 10,000 (but fewer than 50,000) population. Each metropolitan or micropolitan area consists of one or more counties and includes the counties containing the core urban area, as well as any adjacent counties that have a high degree of social and economic integration (as measured by commuting to work) with the urban core.
National Processing Center (NPC).
The offices within OFLC in which the COs operate and which are charged with the adjudication of
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification.
Non-profit or tax-exempt organization.
An organization that:
(1) Is defined as a tax exempt organization under the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, section 501(c)(3), (c)(4), or (c)(6) (
26 U.S.C. 501(c)(3)
, (c)(4) or (c)(6)); and
(2) Has been approved as a tax-exempt organization for research or educational purposes by the Internal Revenue Service.
Offered wage.
The salary or wage, or salary or wage range offered by the employer for the job opportunity. The offered wage must be included in the employer's
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
and advertisements and must equal or exceed the highest of the prevailing wage or Federal, State, or local minimum wage.
Office of Foreign Labor Certification (OFLC).
The organizational component within DOL that provides national leadership and policy guidance and develops regulations and procedures to carry out the responsibilities of the Secretary under the INA, as amended, concerning aliens seeking admission to the United States in order to work under section 212(a)(5)(A) of the INA, as amended.
OFLC Administrator.
The primary official of OFLC, or the OFLC Administrator's designee.
Occupational Network (O*NET).
The system developed by DOL, Employment and Training Administration, to provide to the general public information on skills, abilities, knowledge, work activities, interests and SVP levels associated with occupations. O*NET is based on the SOC system. Further information about O*NET can be found at
http://www.onetcenter.org
.
Pattern or practice.
A course of conduct in which the act or omission in question is repeated, routine, or the regular rather than conduct in which the act or omission in question represents an isolated, sporadic, or accidental act. A pattern or practice may be established by conduct on two or more
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification,
whether filed by or on behalf of the same employer or different employers, and, in the case of an attorney or agent, by conduct across the applications of different clients.
Permanent employment.
Employment in a job opportunity of indefinite duration in which an employee will ordinarily have an expectation of continued employment. To establish that a job opportunity is “permanent,” an employer must establish, at a minimum, that it: (1) has a bona fide need for a worker to fill a job opportunity whose services or labor are needed year-round, except for job opportunities such as members of the teaching profession and professional athletes; and (2) the employer will not require breaks or periods of inactivity, except where such periods stem from an established employer policy for leave that applies to other employees similarly employed by the employer; and (3) will not enter into a temporary staffing agreement to place the alien with one or more third-party clients.
Permanent labor certification.
Certification made by the OFLC Administrator, based on the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
and all supporting documentation, with respect to an employer seeking to file an Immigrant Petition with DHS to employ an alien under an immigrant visa, pursuant to section 212(a)(5)(A) of the Act,
8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(5)(A)
, and this part.
Place of employment.
A worksite or physical location where work under the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
is actually performed.
Prevailing wage determination (PWD).
The prevailing wage for the job opportunity that is the subject of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
The PWD is issued by an NPC on the Form ETA-9141,
Application for Prevailing Wage Determination,
or successor form.
Professional athlete.
An individual who is employed as an athlete by (1) A team that is a member of an association of six or more professional sports teams whose total combined revenues exceed $10,000,000 per year, if the association governs the conduct of its members and regulates the contests and exhibitions in which its member teams regularly engage; or (2) Any minor league team that is affiliated with such an association, as defined by
8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(5)(A)(iii)(II)
.
Purchase.
The transfer of ownership of a permanent labor certification application or certification from one person to another by voluntary act and agreement, based on a valuable consideration.
Sale.
An agreement between two parties, called, respectively, the seller (or vendor) and the buyer (or purchaser) by which the seller, in consideration of the payment or promise of payment of a certain price in money terms, transfers ownership of a permanent labor certification application or certification to the buyer.
(
printed page 74006)
Secretary of Labor (Secretary).
The chief official of the Department or the Secretary's designee.
Secretary of Homeland Security.
The chief official of DHS or the Secretary of Homeland Security's designee.
Secretary of State.
The chief official of the U.S. Department of State or the Secretary of State's designee.
State Workforce Agency (SWA).
A State government agency that receives funds pursuant to the Wagner-Peyser Act,
29 U.S.C. 49
et seq.,
to administer the State's public labor exchange activities.
Strike.
A concerted stoppage of work by employees as a result of a labor dispute, or any concerted slowdown or other concerted interruption of operation (including stoppage by reason of the expiration of a collective bargaining agreement (CBA)).
Substantially comparable.
A job or position where more than a majority (
i.e.,
51 percent or more) of the duties performed are the same as those disclosed in the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
and justified based on organizational charts and position descriptions, the amount and percentage of time spent performing the duties, and payroll records.
United States.
The continental United States, Alaska, Hawaii, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, and the territories of Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands.
U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS).
An operational component of DHS.
U.S. worker.
A worker who is:
(i) A U.S. citizen or national of the United States;
(ii) An individual who is lawfully admitted for permanent residence in the United States, is admitted as a refugee under
8 U.S.C. 1157
or is granted asylum under
8 U.S.C. 1158
.
Wages.
All forms of cash remuneration to a worker by an employer in payment for labor or services.
Willful.
Done knowingly, deliberately, and voluntarily, or in reckless disregard of the requirements of this part or of the truth or falsity of a representation, as distinguished from an act or omission that is accidental, inadvertent, or merely negligent. A person acts willfully with respect to a requirement of this part when the person knows of the requirement or shows reckless disregard for whether the person's conduct complies with it.
Willful misrepresentation.
A false representation of a material fact, made willfully, in connection with an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
a prevailing wage determination, or any other document, form, or communication submitted under this part. Intent to deceive is not an element of willful misrepresentation; it is sufficient that the person knew the representation was false, or made it with reckless disregard for its truth or falsity, and made it voluntarily.
§ 656.4
Persons and entities authorized to file and sign.
(a)
Persons authorized to file.
In addition to the employer, an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
may be filed by an attorney or agent, as defined in § 656.3.
(b)
Employer's signature required.
Regardless of whether the employer is represented by an attorney or agent, the employer is required to sign the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
and all documentation submitted to DOL.
§ 656.5
Requirements for agents and attorneys.
(a)
Representation agreement required.
An agent or attorney filing an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
on behalf of an employer must retain an original executed agreement or other document demonstrating their authority to represent the employer and make this documentation available upon request by the CO. Documentation to prove compliance with this requirement must be retained by the agent or attorney for a period of 5 years from the date on which the certified
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
expires or from the date of determination if the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
or Immigrant Petition is denied or withdrawn.
(b)
Consideration of U.S. workers.
(1) The alien and/or the alien's agent and/or attorney may not interview or consider U.S. workers for the job offered to the alien, unless the agent and/or attorney is the employer's representative, as described in paragraph (b)(2) of this section.
(2) The employer's representative who interviews or considers U.S. workers for the job offered to the alien must be a U.S. worker and one who normally interviews or considers, on behalf of the employer, applicants for job opportunities such as that offered the alien which do not involve labor certifications.
§ 656.6
Successors in interest.
(a)
Liability of successors in interest.
Where an employer, agent, or attorney has violated the requirements of this part, a successor in interest to that employer, agent, or attorney may be held liable for the duties and obligations of the violating employer, agent, or attorney in certain circumstances, regardless of whether such successor in interest has succeeded to all the rights and liabilities of the predecessor employer, agent, or attorney.
(b)
Definition of successors in interest.
The following factors, including those as used under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act and the Vietnam Era Veterans' Readjustment Assistance Act, may be considered in determining whether an employer, agent, or attorney is a successor in interest; however, these factors are not exhaustive, and no one factor is dispositive, but all of the circumstances will be considered as a whole:
(1) Substantial continuity of the same business operations;
(2) Use of the same facilities;
(3) Continuity of the workforce;
(4) Similarity of jobs and working conditions;
(5) Similarity of supervisory personnel;
(6) Whether the former management or owner retains a direct or indirect interest in the new enterprise;
(7) Similarity in machinery, equipment, and production methods;
(8) Similarity of products and services;
(9) The ability of the predecessor to provide relief; and
(10) For purposes of debarment, the personal involvement of the firm's ownership, management, supervisors, and others associated with the firm in the violation(s) at issue.
(c)
Effect of debarment on successors in interest.
When an employer, agent, or attorney is debarred under § 656.31(f), any successor in interest to the debarred employer, agent, or attorney is also debarred. No
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
may be filed by or on behalf of or approved for a successor in interest to a debarred employer, agent, or attorney, subject to the term limits set forth in § 656.31(f). If the CO determines that an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
was filed by or on behalf of a successor in interest to a debarred employer, agent, or attorney during the period of debarment as set forth in § 656.31(f), the CO will deny the application pursuant to § 656.24(d) solely on the basis that the entity is a successor in interest to a debarred employer, agent, or attorney. If the OFLC Administrator determines that a permanent labor certification was issued to a successor in interest to a debarred employer, the OFLC
(
printed page 74007)
Administrator may revoke the certification pursuant to § 656.32. The employer, agent, or attorney may appeal its status as a successor in interest to the debarred entity, pursuant to the procedures for appeals of CO determinations at § 656.26.

§ 656.10
Application filing requirements.
Except as otherwise permitted by statute or this subpart, an employer who desires to hire an alien for permanent employment in the United States must apply and obtain a labor certification from the Secretary by filing an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
with the NPC designated by the OFLC Administrator. This section provides the procedures employers must follow when filing.
(a)
What to file.
(1) An employer that desires to apply for permanent labor certification of an immigrant worker must file a complete
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
including a valid PWD as required by § 656.40, the employer's legal name, trade name(s), and valid FEIN as well as a valid place of business (physical location) in the United States and a means by which it may be contacted by prospective U.S. applicants for employment;
(2) A copy of the NOF providing notice to employees located at the place(s) of employment, as set forth in § 656.14, must be submitted with the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification;
(3) A copy of all records and documentation demonstrating compliance with pre-filing recruitment requirements set forth in § 656.17 or § 656.18, must be submitted with the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
unless the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
is subject to supervised recruitment procedures as set forth in § 656.21; and
(4) A recruitment report meeting the requirements set forth in § 656.17(f), and copies of all resumes and/or applications for each U.S. worker who applied for the job opportunity, must be submitted with the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
unless the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
is subject to supervised recruitment procedures as set forth in § 656.21.
(b)
Timeliness.
A complete
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
including all supporting documentation and information required at the time of filing under this subpart, must be filed within 30 calendar days after the completion of the recruitment procedures set forth in § 656.17 or the optional pre-filing recruitment procedures set forth in § 656.18.
(c)
Location and method of filing.
(1)
Electronic filing.
The employer must file the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
and all required supporting documentation with the NPC using the electronic method(s) designated by the OFLC Administrator. The NPC will return without review any application submitted using a method other than the designated electronic method(s), unless the employer submits the application in accordance with paragraph (c)(2) or (3) of this section.
(2)
Filing by mail.
Employers that lack adequate access to electronic filing may file the application by mail. The employer must indicate that it is filing by mail due to lack of adequate access to electronic filing. The OFLC Administrator will identify the address to which such filing must be mailed by public notice(s) and by instructions on DOL's website.
(3)
Reasonable accommodation.
Employers who are unable or limited in their ability to use and/or access the electronic
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
or any other form or documentation required under this part, as a result of a disability may request a reasonable accommodation to enable them to participate in the permanent labor certification program. An employer in need of such an accommodation may contact the NPC in writing to the address designated in a notice published in the
Federal Register
, or for individuals with hearing or speech impairments, 1-877-889-5627 (this is the TTY toll-free Federal Information Relay Service number) for assistance in using, accessing, or filing any form or documentation required under this part, including the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
All requests for an accommodation must include the employer's name, a detailed description of the accommodation needed, and the preferred method of contact. The NPC will respond to the request for a reasonable accommodation within 10 business days of the date of receipt.
(d)
Original signature.
The
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
must contain an electronic (scanned) copy of the original signature of the employer (and that of the employer's authorized attorney or agent if the employer is represented by an attorney or agent) or a verifiable electronic signature method, as directed by the OFLC Administrator. If submitted by mail, the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
must bear the original signature of the employer and, if applicable, the employer's authorized attorney or agent.
(e)
Additional documentation for certain job opportunities.
An employer who desires to hire an alien for permanent employment in the United States in one of the following job opportunities must maintain, at the time of filing, the additional documentation required by this section and be prepared to submit such documentation in the
(
printed page 74008)
event of an audit or in response to a request from the CO:
(1) For a live-in household domestic service worker job opportunity, an employer must maintain the following documentation:
(i) A copy of the executed contract signed and dated by the employer and alien containing, at a minimum, the same material terms of employment specified on the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
and the following information and employment guarantees:
(A) A description of the household living accommodations, including the type of residence (
e.g.,
house or apartment), number of rooms inside the residence, and number of adults and children, with ages of the children, residing in the residence;
(B) The total hours of employment per week and the expected hours of employment per day;
(C) The total amount of any money that the employer will advance to the alien, including a detailed description of each specific item and amount of advance, and the terms of repayment by the alien of any such advance;
(D) A statement that a private room on the employer's premises and board will be provided, at no cost, to the alien;
(E) A statement that the alien is free to leave the employer's premises during all non-work hours, except the alien may work overtime if paid for the overtime at no less than the legally required hourly rate;
(F) A statement that the alien will not be required to give more than two weeks' notice of intent to leave the employment contracted for and the employer must give the alien at least two weeks' notice before terminating employment; and
(G) Any other agreement or material term or condition of employment not specified on the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
(ii) Documentation that the alien possesses at least one year of full-time paid work experience, exclusive of any training, in the form of written statements, signed and dated from past or present employers, providing a detailed statement of the duties performed and equipment used, identifying the dates (month and year) employment started and ended, hours of work per day, number of days worked per week, place(s) where the alien was employed and the amount of wages paid per week or month.
(2) For a job opportunity with an employer that is a closely held corporation or partnership in which the alien has an ownership interest, or if there is a familial relationship between the stockholders, corporate officers, incorporators, or partners, and the alien, or if the alien is one of a small number of employees, the employer must maintain the following documentation:
(i) A copy of the articles of incorporation, partnership agreement, business license or similar documents that establish the business entity;
(ii) A list of all corporate/company officers and shareholders/partners of the corporation/firm/business, their titles and positions in the business' structure, and a description of the relationships to each other and to the alien;
(iii) The financial history of the corporation/company/partnership, including the total investment in the business entity and the amount of investment of each officer, incorporator/partner and the alien; and
(iv) The name of the business' official with primary responsibility for interviewing and hiring applicants for positions within the organization and the name(s) of the business' official(s) having control or influence over hiring decisions involving the position for which permanent labor certification is sought.
(v) If the alien is one of 10 or fewer employees, the employer must document any familial relationship between the employees and the alien.
(3) For a professional athlete or professional sports team coach job opportunity that meets the definition set forth in § 656.3, the employer must maintain the following documentation:
(i) A copy of the executed written contract, signed and dated by the employer and alien, covering the entire year or period that indicates the specific payment(s) made to the alien;
(ii) An employment letter stating that the alien will work a minimum of ten (10) hours per week during the off-season period; and
(iii) For an alien being sponsored for permanent employment as a professional athlete, a copy of a letter or response, whether electronic or print, from the Players' Association or applicable trade union(s) stating that it was provided notice from the employer, as required by § 656.14(a)(1), and has no objection to the filing of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
(f)
Filing date.
(1) The filing date for any
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
received using the electronic method(s) designated by the OFLC Administrator will be the date on which the complete application, including all applicable appendices and supporting documentation, is submitted and accepted for processing with the NPC. The filing date will be based on the time of submission in the Eastern time zone of the United States.
(2) The filing date for any
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
received in accordance with paragraph (c)(2) or (3) of this section will be the postmark date affixed to the employer's
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
submission, provided that the NPC determines the application is complete.
(g)
Completeness.
The employer must file a complete
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
that meets all the requirements of this part. If an employer submits an incomplete
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
it will be returned without review and will not retain a filing date. If an incomplete
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
is returned unprocessed, the decision will be a final action and will not be subject to reconsideration or review under § 656.26.
(h)
Record retention requirements.
Copies of
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification
filed with DOL and all supporting documentation and records demonstrating compliance with this part must be retained by the employer for a period of 5 years from the latest of the following dates: the date on which the Immigrant Petition is approved by USCIS; the date the approved
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
expires, if the employer does not file an Immigrant Petition using the certification; or the date the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
or Immigrant Petition is denied or withdrawn.
§ 656.11
Substitutions and modifications to applications.
(a) Substitution or change to the identity of an alien on any
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
and on any resulting permanent labor certification is prohibited.
(b) Requests for modifications to any
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
filed with the NPC and on any resulting permanent labor certification are prohibited.
§ 656.12
Improper commerce and payment.
The following provision applies to any
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
and permanent labor certification issued under this part.
(a)
Applications for Permanent Employment Certification
and permanent labor certifications issued under this part are not articles of commerce. They may not be offered for
(
printed page 74009)
sale, barter or purchase by individuals or entities. Any evidence that an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
or a permanent labor certification has been sold, bartered, or purchased will be grounds for investigation under this part and is grounds for denial under § 656.24, revocation under § 656.32, debarment under § 656.31(f), or any combination thereof.
(b) An employer must not seek or receive payment of any kind for any activity related to obtaining permanent labor certification, including payment of the employer's attorneys' fees, whether as an incentive or inducement to filing, or as a reimbursement for costs incurred in preparing or filing an
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
except when work to be performed by the alien in connection with the job opportunity would benefit or accrue to the person or entity making the payment, based on that person's or entity's established business relationship with the employer. An alien may pay his or her own costs in connection with a permanent labor certification, including attorneys' fees for representation of the alien, except that where the same attorney represents both the alien and the employer, such costs must be borne by the employer. For purposes of this paragraph (b), payment includes, but is not limited to, monetary payments; wage concessions, including deductions from wages, salary, or benefits; kickbacks, bribes, or tributes; in kind payments; and free labor.
(c) Evidence that an employer has sought or received payment from any source in connection with an
Application for Permanent Employment Certificatio
n or a permanent labor certification, except for a third party to whose benefit work to be performed in connection with the job opportunity would accrue, based on that person's or entity's established business relationship with the employer, will be grounds for investigation under this part or any appropriate Government agency's procedures, and is grounds for denial under § 656.24, revocation under § 656.32, debarment under § 656.31(f), or any combination thereof.
§ 656.13
Assurances and obligations of employers.
As part of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
and job offer, the employer seeking to employ an alien must declare, under penalty of perjury, that it has knowledge of and will comply with all the requirements of this part and the conditions of employment set forth in this section. The official or employee declaring compliance for the employer under this part must be the official or employee who is most familiar with the content of and recruitment for the job opportunity and is authorized to provide all information and documentation supporting the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
and to communicate with the Department on behalf of the employer. Each assurance in this section is a material condition of certification, and the employer's declaration of compliance with each is a representation of fact on which the Department relies. A certification is not a substitute for the evidence required by this part, and the CO will not accept a declaration as establishing any fact that the employer is required by this part to document. Failure to attest to compliance with any of the conditions listed below will result in a denial of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
A false declaration, or a failure to comply with any assurance or obligation in this section, is grounds for denial under § 656.31(a), revocation under § 656.32, and debarment under § 656.31(f); will be referred as provided in § 656.31(b); and is punishable under
18 U.S.C. 1001
,
1546
, and

.
(a)
Bona fide job opportunity and non-discrimination.
(1) The job opportunity identified in the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
is a bona fide full-time permanent position and the terms and conditions of employment comply with applicable Federal, State, and local laws and regulations.
(2) The job opportunity has been and will continue to be open to any qualified U.S. worker, regardless of race, color, national origin, age, sex, pregnancy, religion, disability, genetic information, or citizenship status, through the date on which the Immigrant Petition is approved by USCIS or the date of determination if the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
or Immigrant Petition is denied or withdrawn, whichever is later.
(3) Rejection(s) of any U.S. worker(s) who applied or apply for the job were or will be only for lawful, job-related reasons, and those not rejected on this basis have been or will be hired. The employer has not and will not reject any qualified U.S. worker over the prospective alien based on any cost justifications, including those based on differences in any term, condition, or privileges of employment, including compensation and fringe benefits, between any qualified U.S. worker and the prospective alien. The employer has and will continue to retain records of any hire(s) and rejection(s) as required by this part.
(4)
Compliance with anti-discrimination laws.
The employer has complied, and will continue to comply, with:
(i) Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964,
42 U.S.C. 2000e
et seq.,
which prohibits discrimination in hiring, discharge, compensation, and the terms, conditions, or privileges of employment because of race, color, religion, sex, or national origin, including discrimination against U.S. workers because of their national origin and in favor of workers of a different national origin, and which is primarily enforced by the EEOC; and
(ii)
8 U.S.C. 1324b
, which prohibits discrimination in hiring, recruitment or referral for a fee, and discharge because of citizenship status against protected individuals as defined in
8 U.S.C. 1324b(a)(3)
(including U.S. citizens and nationals, lawful permanent residents, refugees, and asylees), prohibits discrimination because of national origin by employers with four or more employees that are not covered by Title VII, prohibits unfair documentary practices in the employment eligibility verification process, and prohibits retaliation, and which is enforced by DOJ.
(iii) Nothing in this part limits any obligation under the laws described in paragraphs (a)(4)(i) and (ii) of this section, and compliance with this part is not a defense to liability under those laws.
(iv) The employer has retained documentation demonstrating that the wage and the terms, conditions, and privileges of employment offered to the alien do not differ from those offered to similarly situated U.S. workers employed in the same or substantially comparable positions within the area of intended employment.
(5)
No less favorable terms, conditions, and compensation for U.S. workers.
As a condition of certification under
8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(5)(A)(i)(II)
, and consistent with the obligations described in paragraph (a)(4) of this section, the employer has offered, and will continue to offer, to every able and qualified U.S. worker who applies for, is referred to, or is employed in the job opportunity or in a similarly situated position, terms, conditions, and privileges of employment—including hiring, job assignments, compensation, hours of work, training, fringe benefits, promotion, and demotion—that are no less favorable than those offered to the alien who is the subject of the
Application for Permanent Employment

Certification

8 U.S.C. 1324b
, or any other law.
(b)
No strike, lockout, or work stoppage.
The employer assures that this job opportunity, including all places of employment for which the employer is requesting permanent labor certification, is not vacant because the former occupant(s) is (are) on strike or being locked out in the course of a labor dispute involving a work stoppage.
(c)
Offered wage and ability to pay guarantees.
The employer has offered, and will continue to offer a wage that:
(1) Equals or exceeds the highest of the applicable Federal, State, or local minimum wage, the PWD for the occupation that is issued by the Department to the employer, as reflected on the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
If, after the issuance of a PWD, the Department issues a new or revised PWD that is assigned to the employer's
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
the employer will offer a wage that equals or exceeds the highest of the new prevailing wage, the applicable Federal, State, or local minimum wage, unless notified otherwise by the Department.
(2) Does not and will not result in less favorable treatment in compensation, fringe benefits, or other terms, conditions, and privileges of employment for current or prospective U.S. workers employed in, or seeking to be employed in, similarly situated positions at the employer, as required by all applicable federal anti-discrimination laws and regulations under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Immigration and Nationality Act's Antidiscrimination Provision,
8 U.S.C. 1324b
.
(3) Is not based on commissions, bonuses, or other incentives, unless the employer guarantees an offered wage earned on a weekly, bi-weekly, or monthly basis that equals or exceeds the prevailing wage.
(4) The employer has the ability to pay with existing, internally-available, non-contingent financial resources owned and controlled by the employer at the time of filing the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
for work performed in the job opportunity identified in the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification.
The employer will be able to place the alien on the employer's payroll on or before the date of application for a visa and admission to the United States.
(d)
Good faith recruitment of U.S. workers.
The employer has conducted, and will continue to conduct, recruitment of U.S. workers, as required under this part, in good faith, in the same manner, through the same channels, and on terms no less favorable to U.S. workers as those on which it normally recruits and considers U.S. workers in the same job opportunities for which the employer does not seek labor certification to employ an alien(s). This applies to, but is not limited to, the following:
(1) The method, manner, and location of job postings (
e.g.,
online versus paper job postings; posting in an employer's centralized job web page versus specialized, PERM-specific job web pages) and the duration of any job posting;
(2) The method by which an applicant may apply (
e.g.,
online via a centralized employer website versus PERM-specific email addresses, fax, or paper applications);
(3) The description of the job opportunity, qualifications, and requirements needed to perform the work, which cannot be tailored to the prospective alien and the requirements for applying cannot be unduly restrictive so as to make it difficult for U.S. workers to be deemed qualified.
(4) Interview requirements and procedures. Employers that wish to require interviews must conduct those interviews by phone or provide an alternative method (
e.g.,
virtual meetings or conferencing, cloud calls) for the interviews to be conducted in the location where the U.S. worker(s) is/are being recruited so that the worker incurs little or no cost due to the interview. Employers cannot provide a prospective alien with more favorable treatment than U.S. workers with respect to the requirements for applying and conducting interviews for the job opportunity. The employer representative conducting the interview must be a U.S. worker and one who normally interviews or considers, on behalf of the employer, applicants for job opportunities such as that offered the alien which do not involve labor certifications.
(5) Each method by which a U.S. worker may apply for the job opportunity must be operational, monitored, and capable of receiving and retaining applications throughout the period of recruitment, and the employer must retain and submit evidence of its operation as required by § 656.17(g).
(6) Recruitment for the job opportunity through any method, channel, or procedure that is less accessible or less favorable to U.S. workers than the employer's ordinary recruitment for similar job opportunities, or through an application channel that does not meet paragraph (d)(5) of this section, is presumed not to have been conducted in good faith; is an independent ground for denial under § 656.24; and will be referred under § 656.31(b) to DOJ and, where the facts indicate possible discrimination because of national origin, to the EEOC.

Layoffs and consideration of laid-off U.S. workers.
With regard to layoffs of any U.S. worker(s) in the same or similar occupation (
i.e.,
the same SOC code or a substantially comparable position) that is the subject of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
in the area of intended employment of the place(s) of employment, including the placement of the alien with another employer subject to paragraph (f) of this section, the employer:
(1) Must not have laid off any such U.S. worker(s) within 2 years prior to the filing of the application;
(2) If a layoff of any such U.S. worker(s) occurs after filing the application and before the date on which the Immigrant Petition is approved by USCIS, or the date of determination if the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
or Immigrant Petition is denied or withdrawn, whichever is later, the employer:
(i) Must notify the NPC, and USCIS in the case of a pending Immigrant Petition, in writing or by any other method specified by the Department in a notice published in the
Federal Register
or specified by USCIS not later than 5 business days after such layoff(s) occurs; and
(ii) Must offer the job opportunity that is the subject of the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification
to those laid-off U.S. worker(s), at no less than the offered wage and on the terms and conditions stated in the
Application for Permanent Employment Certification,
and document whether the U.S. worker(s) refused the job opportunity, was rejected for the job opportunity for lawful, job-related reasons, or was hired.

Placing contract workers with other employers engaging in layoffs prohibited.
The employer has not placed, and will not place, the alien who is the subject of the

with another employer (including that employer's parent, subsidiary, or affiliate) where:
(1) There are indicia of an employment relationship between the alien and that other employer,

or Immigrant Petition is denied or withdrawn, whichever is later.

Compliance with prohibition on improper commerce and employees paying fees.
The employer and its agents, attorneys, and/or employees have not offered, and will not seek to offer, for sale, barter or purchase to any individual or entity

at any time, including applications certified by the Department, and have not sought or received, and will not seek to receive, payment of any kind from the worker(s) for any activity related to obtaining permanent labor certification, including payment of the employer's attorneys' fees, whether as an incentive or inducement to filing, or as a reimbursement for costs incurred in preparing or filing a permanent labor certification application, except when work to be performed by the alien in connection with the job opportunity would benefit or accrue to the person or entity making the payment, based on that person's or entity's established business relationship with the employer. An alien may pay his or her own costs in connection with a labor certification, including attorneys' fees for representation of the alien, except where the same attorney represents both the alien and the employer, such costs must be borne by the employer. Payment includes, but is not limited to, monetary payments; wage concessions, including deductions from wages, salary, or benefits; kickbacks, bribes, or tributes; in kind payments; and free labor.
(h)
Compliance with applicable laws.
The employer has complied and will continue to comply with applicable Federal, State and local employment-related laws and regulations, including, but not limited to, employment-related health and safety laws, Federal, State, and local anti-discrimination laws, including Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (
