AGENCY:
Railroad Retirement Board.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
As required by the Railroad Unemployment Insurance Act (Act), the Railroad Retirement Board (RRB) hereby publishes its notice for calendar year 2027 of account balances, factors used in calculating experience-based employer contribution rates, computation of amounts related to the monthly compensation base, and the maximum daily benefit rate for days of unemployment or sickness.
DATES:
The balance in notice (1) and the determinations made in notices (3) through (7) are based on data as of June 30, 2026. The balance in notice (2) is based on data as of September 30, 2026. The determinations made in notices (5) through (7) apply to the calculation, under section 8(a)(1)(C) of the Act, of employer contribution rates for 2027. The determinations made in notices (8) through (11) are effective January 1, 2027. The determination made in notice (12) is effective for registration periods beginning after June 30, 2027.
ADDRESSES:
Secretary to the Board, Railroad Retirement Board, 844 N Rush Street, Chicago, Illinois 60611-1275.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Terri Lischka, Bureau of the Actuary and Research, Railroad Retirement Board, 844 N Rush Street, Chicago, Illinois 60611-1275, telephone (312) 751-3305.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The RRB is required by section 8(c)(1) of the Railroad Unemployment Insurance Act (Act) (
45 U.S.C. 358(c)(1)
) as amended by Public Law 100-647, to proclaim by October 15 of each year certain system-wide factors used in calculating experience-based employer contribution rates for the following year. The RRB is further required by section 8(c)(2) of the Act (
45 U.S.C. 358(c)(2)
) to publish the amounts so determined and proclaimed. The RRB is required by section 12(r)(3) of the Act (
45 U.S.C. 362(r)(3)
) to publish by December 11, 2026, the computation of the calendar year 2027 monthly compensation base (section 1(i) of the Act) and amounts described in sections 1(k), 2(c), 3 and 4(a-2)(i)(A) of the Act which are related to changes in the monthly compensation base. Also, the RRB is required to publish, by June 11, 2027, the maximum daily benefit rate under section 2(a)(3) of the Act for days of unemployment and days of sickness in registration periods beginning after June 30, 2027.
Pursuant to section 8(c)(2) and section 12(r)(3) of the Railroad Unemployment Insurance Act (Act) (
45 U.S.C. 358(c)(2)
and
45 U.S.C. 362(r)(3)
, respectively), the Board gives notice of the following:
1. The accrual balance of the Railroad Unemployment Insurance (RUI) Account, as of June 30, 2026, is $331,783,262.40;
2. The September 30, 2026, balance of any new loans to the RUI Account, including accrued interest, is zero;
3. The system compensation base is $5,059,021,508.02 as of June 30, 2026;
4. The cumulative system unallocated charge balance is ($540,735,331.54) as of June 30, 2026;
5. The pooled credit ratio for calendar year 2027 is zero;
6. The pooled charged ratio for calendar year 2027 is zero;
7. The surcharge rate for calendar year 2027 is zero;
8. The monthly compensation base under section 1(i) of the Act is $2,235 for months in calendar year 2027;
9. The amount described in sections 1(k) and 3 of the Act as “2.5 times the monthly compensation base” is $5,587.50 for base year (calendar year) 2027;
10. The amount described in section 4(a-2)(i)(A) of the Act as “2.5 times the monthly compensation base” is $5,587.50 with respect to disqualifications ending in calendar year 2027;
11. The amount described in section 2(c) of the Act as “an amount that bears the same ratio to $775 as the monthly compensation base for that year as computed under section 1(i) of this Act bears to $600” is $2,887 for months in calendar year 2027;
12. The maximum daily benefit rate under section 2(a)(3) of the Act is $107 with respect to days of unemployment and days of sickness in registration periods beginning after June 30, 2027.
Surcharge Rate
A surcharge is added in the calculation of each employer's contribution rate, subject to the applicable maximum rate, for a calendar year whenever the balance to the credit of the RUI Account on the preceding June 30 is less than the greater of $100 million or the amount that bears the same ratio to $100 million as the system compensation base for that June 30 bears to the system compensation base as of June 30, 1991. If the RUI Account balance is less than $100 million (as indexed), but at least $50 million (as indexed), the surcharge will be 1.5 percent. If the RUI Account balance is less than $50 million (as indexed), but greater than zero, the surcharge will be 2.5 percent. The maximum surcharge of 3.5 percent applies if the RUI Account balance is less than zero.
The ratio of the June 30, 2026 system compensation base of $5,059,021,508.02 to the June 30, 1991 system compensation base of $2,763,287,237.04 is 1.83079828. Multiplying 1. 83079828 by $100 million yields $183,079,828.00. Multiplying $50 million by 1. 83079828 produces $91,539,914.00. The Account balance on June 30, 2026, was $331,783,262.40. Accordingly, the surcharge rate for calendar year 2027 is zero.
Pooled Credit
A pooled credit is applied in the calculation of each employer's contribution rate, subject to the applicable minimum rate, for a calendar year whenever the balance to the credit of the RUI Account on the preceding June 30 is more than the greater of $250 million or the amount that bears the same ratio to $250 million as the system compensation base for that June 30 bears to the system compensation base as of June 30, 1991. If the balance is more than the greater of $250 million or the indexed $250 million, the excess amount is divided by the system compensation base for the preceding calendar year, resulting in the pooled credit amount.
The ratio of the June 30, 2026 system compensation base of $5,059,021,508.02 to the June 30, 1991 system compensation base of $2,763,287,237.04 is 1.83079828. Multiplying 1.83079828 by $250 million yields $457,699,570.00. The Account balance on June 30, 2026, was $331,783,262.40. Accordingly, the
(
printed page 73827)
pooled credit rate for calendar year 2027 is zero.
Monthly Compensation Base
For years after 1988, section 1(i) of the Act contains a formula for determining the monthly compensation base. Under the prescribed formula, the monthly compensation base increases by approximately two-thirds of the cumulative growth in average national wages since 1984. The monthly compensation base for months in calendar year 2027 shall be equal to the greater of (a) $600 or (b) $600 [1 + {(A−37,800)/56,700}], where A equals the amount of the applicable base with respect to tier 1 taxes for 2027 under section 3231(e)(2) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986. Section 1(i) further provides that if the amount so determined is not a multiple of $5, it shall be rounded to the nearest multiple of $5.
Using the calendar year 2027 tier 1 tax base of $192,300 for A above produces the amount of $2,234.92, which must then be rounded to $2,235. Accordingly, the monthly compensation base is determined to be $2,235 for months in calendar year 2027.
Amounts Related to Changes in Monthly Compensation Base
For years after 1988, sections 1(k), 3, 4(a-2)(i)(A) and 2(c) of the Act contain formulas for determining amounts related to the monthly compensation base.
Under section 1(k), remuneration earned from employment covered under the Act cannot be considered subsidiary remuneration if the employee's base year compensation is less than 2.5 times the monthly compensation base for months in such base year. Under section 3, an employee shall be a “qualified employee” if his/her base year compensation is not less than 2.5 times the monthly compensation base for months in such base year. Under section 4(a-2)(i)(A), an employee who leaves work voluntarily without good cause is disqualified from receiving unemployment benefits until the employee has been paid compensation of not less than 2.5 times the monthly compensation base for months in the calendar year in which the disqualification ends.
Multiplying 2.5 by the calendar year 2027 monthly compensation base of $2,235 produces $5,587.50. Accordingly, the amount determined under sections 1(k), 3 and 4(a-2)(i)(A) is $5,587.50 for calendar year 2027.
Under section 2(c), the maximum amount of normal benefits paid for days of unemployment within a benefit year and the maximum amount of normal benefits paid for days of sickness within a benefit year shall not exceed an employee's compensation in the base year. In determining an employee's base year compensation, any money remuneration in a month not in excess of an amount that bears the same ratio to $775 as the monthly compensation base for that year bears to $600 shall be taken into account.
The calendar year 2027 monthly compensation base is $2,235. The ratio of $2,235 to $600 is 3.72500000. Multiplying 3.72500000 by $775 produces $2,887. Accordingly, the amount determined under section 2(c) is $2,887 for months in calendar year 2027.
Maximum Daily Benefit Rate
Section 2(a)(3) contains a formula for determining the maximum daily benefit rate for registration periods beginning after June 30, 1989, and after each June 30 thereafter. Legislation enacted on October 9, 1996, revised the formula for indexing maximum daily benefit rates. Under the prescribed formula, the maximum daily benefit rate increases by approximately two-thirds of the cumulative growth in average national wages since 1984. The maximum daily benefit rate for registration periods beginning after June 30, 2027, shall be equal to 5 percent of the monthly compensation base for the base year immediately preceding the beginning of the benefit year. Section 2(a)(3) further provides that if the amount so computed is not a multiple of $1, it shall be rounded down to the nearest multiple of $1.
The calendar year 2026 monthly compensation base is $2,150. Multiplying $2,150 by 0.05 yields $107.50. Accordingly, the maximum daily benefit rate for days of unemployment and days of sickness beginning in registration periods after June 30, 2027, is determined to be $107.

Secretary to the Board.

ACTION:

SUMMARY:
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA or we) is proposing to issue a regulation finding that N-acetyl-L-cysteine (NAC) is not excluded from the dietary supplement definition in the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act). This action, if finalized, would allow products containing NAC to be lawfully marketed as dietary supplements, provided that such products are not otherwise in violation of the FD&C Act. I. Executive Summary
A. Purpose of the Proposed Rule
This proposed rule, if finalized, would provide by regulation that NAC is not excluded from the dietary supplement definition in the FD&C Act. This action would allow NAC-containing products to be lawfully marketed as dietary supplements, provided that such products are not otherwise in violation of the FD&C Act. Accordingly, if a product that is or contains NAC is labeled as a dietary supplement and otherwise meets the definition of a dietary supplement under section 201(ff) of the FD&C Act (
21 U.S.C. 321(ff)
), FDA would regulate such product as a dietary supplement. The proposed rule also would provide that the addition of NAC to a dietary supplement is not a prohibited act under section 301(ll) of the FD&C Act (
21 U.S.C. 331(ll)
).
B. Summary of the Proposed Rule
We are proposing to establish a regulation entitled “Dietary Ingredients Not Excluded from the Dietary Supplement Definition” at
21 CFR 190.1
(§ 190.1) to provide for the lawful use in dietary supplements of certain ingredients that would otherwise be excluded from the dietary supplement definition. Specifically, this proposed rule would provide that ingredients listed under this regulation are not excluded for use in or as a dietary supplement under section 201(ff)(3)(B) of the FD&C Act and that the addition of such ingredients to a dietary supplement is not a prohibited act under section 301(ll) of the FD&C Act. NAC would be the first ingredient listed under this new regulation.
C. Legal Authority
We are issuing this proposed rule to establish a regulation to provide for the lawful use of certain ingredients in dietary supplements that would otherwise be excluded from the dietary supplement definition and to list NAC as the first ingredient under this new regulation, consistent with our authority in sections 201(ff)(3)(B), 301(ll)(2), and 701(a) of the FD&C Act (
21 U.S.C. 321(ff)(3)(B)
,
331(ll)(2)
, and
371(a)
).
D. Costs and Benefits
This proposed rule, if finalized, would provide that NAC is not excluded from the dietary supplement definition in the FD&C Act and that the addition of NAC to a dietary supplement is not a prohibited act under section 301(ll) of the FD&C Act. Accordingly, if a product that is or contains NAC is labeled as a dietary supplement and otherwise meets the definition of a dietary supplement under section 201(ff) of the FD&C Act, FDA would regulate such a product as a dietary supplement.
To estimate benefits, costs, and transfers associated with the proposed rule, we assume that the appropriate baseline is the state of the world in which NAC is excluded from the dietary supplement definition but FDA exercises enforcement discretion with respect to the sale and distribution of certain products that contain NAC and are labeled as dietary supplements. We then compare the likely impacts of the proposed rule against this baseline. We do not estimate benefits due to the proposed rule. It is possible that firms may react to the legal clarity of NAC dietary supplement products by introducing new products to market. To the extent that this occurs, consumers may benefit from expanding availability of products that may serve different purposes and uses than the FDA-approved NAC drug products. However, the likelihood and magnitude of such impacts are difficult to estimate.
The costs of the proposed rule are associated with costs to industry for
(
printed page 73719)
reading and understanding the rule. Because there are few firms operating in the NAC market, these impacts are small. When annualized over a period of 10 years, we estimate these costs range from approximately $89 to $112 at a 3 percent discount rate. At a 7 percent rate of discount, these estimates range from $109 to $136. Our primary annualized estimates are approximately $99 and $121 at 3 and 7 percent rates of discount, respectively. The primary estimate of the present value of total costs resulting from any final rule that may be issued based on the proposed rule is approximately $848.
II. Background
A. Dietary Supplement Definition
Section 201(ff) of the FD&C Act defines the term “dietary supplement” and establishes requirements for what dietary supplements must contain, what they must not contain, how they must be used, and how they must be labeled. A dietary supplement must be a product intended to supplement the diet that contains one or more dietary ingredients (section 201(ff)(1) of the FD&C Act). Under section 201(ff)(1) of the FD&C Act, a “dietary ingredient” is any one of the following: a vitamin; a mineral; an herb or other botanical; an amino acid; a dietary substance for use by man to supplement the diet by increasing the total dietary intake; or a concentrate, metabolite, constituent, extract, or combination of any dietary ingredient from the preceding categories. In addition, under section 201(ff)(2) of the FD&C Act, a dietary supplement: must be intended for ingestion in tablet, capsule, powder, softgel, gelcap, or liquid form or comply with section 411(c)(1)(B)(ii) of the FD&C Act (
21 U.S.C. 350(c)(1)(B)(ii)
); must not be represented for use as a conventional food or as a sole item of a meal or the diet; and must be labeled as a dietary supplement.
Section 201(ff)(3)(A) of the FD&C Act provides that a product that otherwise meets the definition of a dietary supplement
does not
lose its status as a dietary supplement if it includes an article that is approved as a new drug under section 505 of the FD&C Act (
21 U.S.C. 355
) or licensed as a biologic under section 351 of the Public Health Service Act (
42 U.S.C. 262
), provided that the article was marketed as either a dietary supplement or as a food before it was approved as a new drug or licensed as a biologic. Section 201(ff)(3)(A) of the FD&C Act provides an exception to this general rule, authorizing the Secretary of Health and Human Services (Secretary) to issue a regulation, after notice and comment, finding that the article, when used as or in a dietary supplement under the conditions of use and dosages set forth in the labeling for such dietary supplement, is unlawful under section 402(f) of the FD&C Act.
Section 201(ff)(3)(B) of the FD&C Act (the exclusion clause) provides that a product that would otherwise meet the definition of a dietary supplement
loses
its status as a dietary supplement if the product includes certain articles. Specifically, the general rule of section 201(ff)(3)(B)(i) of the FD&C Act is that a dietary supplement cannot include an article that was approved as a new drug under section 505 of the FD&C Act, certified as an antibiotic under section 507 of the FD&C Act, or licensed as a biologic under section 351 of the Public Health Service Act before the article was marketed as a dietary supplement or as a food. The general rule of section 201(ff)(3)(B)(ii) of the FD&C is that a dietary supplement cannot include an article authorized for investigation as a new drug, antibiotic, or biological for which substantial clinical investigations have been instituted and for which the existence of such investigations has been made public, unless the article was marketed as a dietary supplement or as a food before such authorization. Section 201(ff)(3)(B) of the FD&C Act provides an exception to the general rules of sections 201(ff)(3)(B)(i) and (ii) of the FD&C Act. Under this exception, the article is not excluded if the Secretary, in the Secretary's discretion, has issued a regulation, after notice and comment, finding that the article would be lawful under the FD&C Act.
This proposed rule is the first use of our rulemaking authority described in section 201(ff)(3)(B) of the FD&C Act.
B. Regulatory Status of NAC
The names for NAC include, but are not limited to, acetylcysteine; L-acetylcysteine; L-alpha-acetamido-beta-mercaptopropionic acid; N-acetyl cysteine; N-acetyl-3-mercaptoalanine; N-acetyl-L-cysteine; NAC; and mercapturic acid. These names all refer to the same article.
Because the elements of the dietary supplement definition in sections 201(ff)(1), (2), and (3) of the FD&C Act are phrased conjunctively (separated by “and”), a product qualifies as a dietary supplement only if it satisfies the criteria in all three paragraphs (see section II.A of this document for a detailed explanation). Thus, demonstrating that a product satisfies the requirement in section 201(ff)(1) of the FD&C Act to contain a dietary ingredient does not establish that the product meets the other criteria in sections 201(ff)(2) and (ff)(3) of the FD&C Act. NAC is a dietary ingredient under section 201(ff)(1)(E) of the FD&C Act, but it also is excluded from the dietary supplement definition under section 201(ff)(3)(B)(i) of the FD&C Act, as discussed below.
NAC is a dietary ingredient under section 201(ff)(1)(E) of the FD&C Act,
i.e.,
a dietary substance for use by man to supplement the diet by increasing the total dietary intake. For example, a February 1995 advertisement in Vegetarian Times describes NAC as an ingredient in the advertised shake, a conventional food (Ref. 1).
NAC is not a “new dietary ingredient” under section 413(d) of the FD&C Act (
21 U.S.C. 350b(d)
). The term “new dietary ingredient” (NDI) means a dietary ingredient that was not marketed in the United States before October 15, 1994, and does not include any dietary ingredient which was marketed in the United States before October 15, 1994. We are aware of an August/September 1991 advertisement for an NAC-containing supplement (Ref. 2). Thus, NAC is not an NDI.
Although NAC is a dietary ingredient, NAC is excluded from the dietary supplement definition under section 201(ff)(3)(B)(i) of the FD&C Act because NAC was approved as a new drug before it was marketed as a dietary supplement or as a food. NAC was approved as a new drug under section 505 of the FD&C Act on September 14, 1963, under New Drug Application (NDA) 013601, Mucomyst (acetylcysteine) (see
28 FR 13509
, December 13, 1963). (In accordance with then-
21 CFR 130.33
, we provided notice of the new drug approval in the
Federal Register
in December 1963 (
28 FR 13509
, December 13, 1963).) We are not aware of any evidence that NAC was marketed as a dietary supplement or as a food before September 14, 1963, but request evidence to the contrary.
FDA stated NAC's regulatory status several times over the past 25 years. For example, we stated this position in July 2001 in response to a health claim petition for a claim about an NAC-containing product, when we allowed the petition to be denied by operation of law (Ref. 3). The petition did not meet the requirements for a health claim petition as established in
21 CFR 101.70
, including the requirement that the petition contain a complete explanation of how the substance that is the subject of the proposed claim conforms to the requirements of
21 CFR 101.14(b)
. Our response explained that the petition did not meet these requirements because, among other
(
printed page 73720)
things, the petitioner did not demonstrate that use of NAC in a dietary supplement was lawful. In particular, after citing the exclusion clause, we noted that NAC was approved as a new drug under section 505 of the FD&C Act on September 14, 1963, under NDA No. 013601, Mucomyst (acetylcysteine), and the petition failed to document a history of NAC having been marketed as a dietary supplement before that date (Ref. 3). Because the health claim petition was denied by operation of law, our July 2001 response was not made available to the public when it was sent to the company that submitted the petition, per section 403(r)(4)(A)(i) of the FD&C Act (
21 U.S.C. 343(r)(4)(A)(i)
) (Ref. 3). Consequently, this historical response has remained non-public to protect proprietary commercial information; however, a redacted copy of our July 2001 response is being placed in the public docket for this rulemaking (id.) to allow for public review and comment on FDA's administrative precedent.
In 2010, in response to an NDI notification for NAC ethyl ester, we stated that, under the exclusion clause, NAC-containing products cannot be dietary supplements (Ref. 4). In July 2020, as part of warning letters sent to companies illegally selling unapproved products that claimed to cure, treat, mitigate, or prevent hangovers while also labeling their products as dietary supplements, we stated that NAC-containing products are excluded from the definition of dietary supplement under the exclusion clause (Refs. 5 through 8).
In 2021, we received two citizen petitions requesting that we conclude that NAC is not excluded from the definition of dietary supplement under section 201(ff)(3)(B) of the FD&C Act (
https://www.regulations.gov
;
Docket Nos. FDA-2021-P-0523 and FDA-2021-P-0938). One citizen petition also asked that, if FDA did not change our position that products containing NAC are excluded from the definition of a dietary supplement under section 201(ff)(3)(B) of the FD&C Act, we recommend that the Secretary issue a regulation, after notice-and-comment rulemaking, finding that NAC would be lawful under the FD&C Act (see Docket No. FDA-2021-P-0938). On March 31, 2022, we issued a joint final response to both petitions, denying one petition in its entirety and denying the other petition in part. We stated our conclusion that NAC is excluded from the dietary supplement definition under section 201(ff)(3)(B)(i) of the FD&C Act, as described above. In addition, we explained that we had not yet reached a final decision on the request to initiate rulemaking and that we were considering initiating rulemaking under section 201(ff)(3)(B) of the FD&C Act to permit the use of NAC in or as a dietary supplement. We acknowledged that, although NAC-containing products labeled as dietary supplements have been sold in the United States for over 30 years, and consumers continue to seek access to such products, we needed additional time to complete our review, including a full safety review of NAC, before responding to the remaining request.
In the
Federal Register

87 FR 47220
), we announced the availability of a final guidance for industry entitled “Policy Regarding N-acetyl-L-cysteine: Guidance for Industry” (enforcement discretion guidance), which announced our intent to exercise temporary enforcement discretion with respect to the sale and distribution of certain products that contain NAC and are labeled as dietary supplements until either of the following occurs: we complete notice-and-comment rulemaking to allow the use of NAC in or as a dietary supplement, or we deny the citizen petition's request for rulemaking. The enforcement discretion guidance explained our determination that NAC is excluded from the dietary supplement definition because NAC was approved as a new drug before it was marketed as a dietary supplement or as a food (Ref. 9). We stated that, while FDA's full safety review of NAC remained ongoing, our initial review did not reveal safety concerns with respect to the use of NAC in or as a dietary supplement (id.). The enforcement discretion policy applies to products that would be lawfully marketed dietary supplements if NAC were not excluded from the dietary supplement definition and that are not otherwise in violation of the FD&C Act (id.). If this proposed rule is finalized, FDA intends to withdraw this enforcement discretion guidance.
III. Legal Authority
As discussed in section II.A of this document, section 201(ff)(3)(B) of the FD&C Act excludes certain articles from the definition of dietary supplement. Our discussion focuses primarily on the mention of new drug approval in section 201(ff)(3)(B) of the FD&C Act, as that is at issue for NAC; however, the same logic would apply to other articles described in clauses (i) and (ii) of section 201(ff)(3)(B) of the FD&C Act.
The general rule of section 201(ff)(3)(B) of the FD&C Act is if an article is approved as a new drug under section 505 of the FD&C Act, then that article is outside the dietary supplement definition unless the article was marketed as a dietary supplement or a food before such approval. However, there is an exception if FDA (under authority delegated by the Secretary) issues a regulation, after notice-and-comment rulemaking, “finding that the article would be lawful under this Act” (
i.e.,
the FD&C Act). In this context (the dietary supplement definition), we interpret this phrase to mean a regulation providing that the article is not excluded from the dietary supplement definition. In other words, because the regulation provides that the article is not excluded from the dietary supplement definition, such article may be lawfully marketed in or as a dietary supplement under the FD&C Act, provided that such product is not otherwise in violation of the FD&C Act.
Congress included section 201(ff)(3)(B) of the FD&C Act in the dietary supplement definition for two main reasons. The first reason is to prevent manufacturers from escaping appropriate safety and efficacy review and FDA oversight for drugs by classifying these products as dietary supplements. See,
e.g.,
Statement of Sen. Kennedy (“There continue to be differences among us as to how to achieve these goals most effectively. For example, the Hatch legislation offers a definition of dietary supplements that many feel is too broad. It will allow certain products which are treated as prescription drugs in other countries, or as unapproved drugs in this country, to be treated as dietary supplements and therefore subjected to inadequate safeguards.”) (Ref. 10); Statement of Sen. Harkin (“[T]he [Hatch-Harkin] compromise assures that prescription drugs cannot escape appropriate review and oversight by being classified as dietary supplements. This concern was raised by a number of Senators and the legislation before us addresses it in a sensible manner.”) (Ref. 11); Ref. 12, at V § 3 (“During consideration of S. 784, concerns were expressed that manufacturers or importers of drugs could avoid the drug approval process by marketing drug products as dietary supplements. Although current authorities should be adequate to deal with such potential problems, the committee is sensitive to those concerns. Accordingly, Senators Harkin and Hatch agreed to formulate additional language prior to consideration of S. 784 in the Senate.”). The second reason is to protect the incentives for new drug development. Section 201(ff)(3)(B)(ii) of the FD&C Act provides that the term dietary
(
printed page 73721)
supplement does not include an article authorized for investigation as a new drug, antibiotic, or biological for which substantial clinical investigations have been instituted and for which the existence of such investigations has been made public, unless certain criteria are met. This clause extends the scope of the drug exclusion provision beyond approved new drugs, certified antibiotics, and licensed biologics, which are covered by sections 201(ff)(3)(A) and (B)(i) of the FD&C Act. Accordingly, Congress's inclusion of this provision in addition to sections 201(ff)(3)(A) and (B)(i) of the FD&C Act demonstrates that Congress sought to protect investigational new drugs, antibiotics, and biologics that are not yet approved, certified, or licensed. In other words, one of the overarching purposes of section 201(ff)(3)(B)(ii) of the FD&C Act is to protect the incentives for new drug development.
Congress chose to accomplish these goals by establishing a general framework under which a substance is excluded from the dietary supplement definition if its approval as a new drug (or its authorization for investigation as a new drug) preceded its marketing as a dietary supplement or a food. However, recognizing that applying this general framework would not always further these goals, Congress delegated authority to FDA to make exceptions in limited circumstances, through notice-and-comment rulemaking, so that a substance could be used in or as a dietary supplement even though it was approved as a new drug (or authorized for investigation as a new drug) before it was marketed as a dietary supplement or a food. Accordingly, through the statutory structure, purpose, and legislative history of section 201(ff)(3)(B) of the FD&C Act, Congress limited FDA's authority to provide an exception for a substance that otherwise would be excluded from dietary supplements to situations where both of the following conditions are satisfied:
1. There would be adequate safeguards if the substance were regulated as a dietary supplement—
i.e.,
regulation as a dietary supplement would provide appropriate review and oversight of the substance; and
2. Allowing use of the substance in or as a dietary supplement would be unlikely to impede new drug development.
Further, because Congress defined “dietary supplement” in section 201(ff) of the FD&C Act, this restricts FDA's rulemaking authority under section 201(ff)(3)(B) of the FD&C Act to articles that are capable of meeting the definition of dietary supplement. Thus, if an article is not a dietary ingredient as described in section 201(ff)(1) of the FD&C Act, that article itself is not capable of meeting the definition of dietary supplement, even if such article is not excluded from the dietary supplement definition under section 201(ff)(3)(B) of the FD&C Act. Accordingly, if an article is not a dietary ingredient, FDA cannot use its rulemaking authority under section 201(ff)(3)(B) of the FD&C Act to provide that such article may be a dietary supplement. Moreover, when FDA uses its rulemaking authority in section 201(ff)(3)(B) of the FD&C Act, the article that is the subject of the rule (
e.g.,
NAC) becomes eligible to be used in or as a dietary supplement. In turn, a dietary supplement that is or contains such article would be deemed a food under section 201(ff) of the FD&C Act and subject to all applicable requirements for food as well as those requirements specific to dietary supplements under the FD&C Act and FDA regulations.
One consequence of a dietary supplement being deemed a food is that section 301(ll) of the FD&C Act, which applies to food, would apply to the dietary supplement. Section 301(ll) of the FD&C Act makes it a prohibited act to introduce or deliver for introduction into interstate commerce any food to which has been added a drug approved under section 505 of the FD&C Act, a biological product licensed under section 351 of the Public Health Service Act, or a drug or a biological product for which substantial clinical investigations have been instituted and for which the existence of such investigations has been made public unless an exception applies. One exception is if we have issued a regulation, after notice-and-comment rulemaking, approving the use of the drug or biological product in the food (section 301(ll)(2) of the FD&C Act).
Given the statutory language and structure of sections 201(ff) and 301(ll) of the FD&C Act, with respect to dietary supplements, the rulemaking authority provided by section 301(ll)(2) of the FD&C Act is inextricably linked with the rulemaking authority provided by section 201(ff)(3)(B) of the FD&C Act. That is, if we use our rulemaking authority under section 201(ff)(3)(B) of the FD&C Act to provide that an article is not excluded from the dietary supplement definition, that article would be eligible for use in or as a dietary supplement, and a dietary supplement that is or contains such article would be deemed a food under section 201(ff) of the FD&C Act and, thus, would be subject to section 301(ll) of the FD&C Act. However, if we do not simultaneously use our rulemaking authority under section 301(ll)(2) of the FD&C Act to provide that the addition of such article to a dietary supplement is not a prohibited act under section 301(ll) of the FD&C Act, this would lead to an illogical result. Specifically, the rule would make the article eligible for use in or as a dietary supplement and also bring that product within the scope of section 301(ll) of the FD&C Act, thereby making it a prohibited act under section 301(ll) of the FD&C Act to add the article to a dietary supplement. Accordingly, if we exercise our rulemaking authority under section 201(ff)(3)(B) of the FD&C Act to provide that an article is not excluded from the definition of dietary supplement, we would necessarily exercise our rulemaking authority under section 301(ll)(2) of the FD&C Act to provide that the addition of such article to a dietary supplement is not a prohibited act under section 301(ll) of the FD&C Act. Thus, in addition to the authority specified in section 201(ff)(3)(B) of the FD&C Act, section 301(ll)(2) of the FD&C Act provides authority to issue this proposed regulation.
In addition to the authority specified in sections 201(ff)(3)(B) and 301(ll)(2) of the FD&C Act to issue this proposed regulation, section 701(a) of the FD&C Act gives us the authority to promulgate regulations for the efficient enforcement of the FD&C Act.
IV. Application of Rulemaking Authority to NAC
We are aware that, for more than 30 years, NAC has been available for sale in the United States both as FDA-approved drugs and as products improperly labeled as dietary supplements. As discussed above, FDA may use its rulemaking authority under section 201(ff)(3)(B) of the FD&C Act to remove an ingredient from the dietary supplement exclusion and regulate such ingredient as a dietary supplement when such ingredient can be appropriately regulated as a dietary supplement and such removal would be unlikely to negatively impact drug development. We are proposing to apply this rulemaking authority to NAC based on its safety profile and the minimal, if any, impact this rule is likely to have on NAC drug development.
A. Safety Assessment of NAC in or as a Dietary Supplement
To help inform the decision of whether to exercise FDA's rulemaking authority for NAC, FDA reviewed published information on the use and safety of NAC. Safety determinations related to the FDA drug approval for
(
printed page 73722)
NAC are not directly applicable to the safety assessment of NAC as a dietary supplement, because drug safety review relies on a risk/benefit paradigm, whereas a safety assessment for a dietary supplement generally considers only risk. Therefore, to support the safety assessment of NAC as a dietary supplement, we collected safety endpoints from published studies using NAC in a variety of clinical contexts, largely outside its approved drug use. Specifically, we conducted a systematic review of studies of orally administered (
i.e.,
ingested) NAC to assess the adverse events (AEs) associated with NAC use in order to demonstrate an expectation of safety for NAC in or as a dietary supplement (Ref. 13). The protocol, results analysis, and conclusions underwent external peer review, as indicated on FDA's Peer Review of Scientific Information and Assessments web page (id.).
The systematic review identified 41 studies of high confidence, which were used for conclusions on AEs and NAC exposure (id.). One study identified a significant increase in nausea among NAC-treated patients, but most other studies reported no AEs or AEs that were not significantly different from non-NAC-treated comparators (id.). Studies included high NAC doses (up to 9000 milligrams (mg) per day (d)) and long durations (up to 3 years), which did not demonstrate an increase in AE reporting (id.). Doses used in the NAC clinical studies were comparable to the recommended serving of available NAC-containing products labeled as dietary supplements, demonstrating similarity of NAC exposure and, therefore, a similar safety profile (id.).
This systematic review evaluated the NAC literature on studies of orally administered (
i.e.,
ingested) NAC in healthy and patient populations to estimate a qualitative Level of Concern (LoC) for the known AEs related to NAC, then translated that LoC conclusion to an expectation of safety for NAC in or as a dietary supplement (id.). A “minimal” LoC was concluded based on the consistent reporting of no AEs or statistical conclusion that reported AEs were not attributed to NAC. The concern level was selected from the 5-point scale developed by the National Toxicology Program to provide a standardized summary of risk concern levels (Ref. 14). The reported AEs were found across disparate populations (
e.g.,
from healthy individuals to patients with end-stage renal disease) and varied exposure conditions (
e.g.,
200 mg/d to 9000 mg/d, for durations 5 days to 3 years); the noted exception is a singular report of non-serious nausea, which would be expected with ingestion of a sulfurous compound (Ref. 13). The commonly reported AEs in the NAC clinical data set are gastrointestinal (GI) pain/discomfort, nausea, vomiting, and rash, and suggest that these non-serious GI-related symptoms may occur in relation to NAC exposure, although only statistically proven in one study reviewed (id.).
NAC exposure from commercially available products labeled as dietary supplements based on the labeled serving size was compared to the doses reported in the collective NAC clinical data. There was significant overlap of the recommended servings of NAC in products labeled as dietary supplements with the doses of the NAC clinical studies. NAC-containing products labeled as dietary supplements recommend a serving of 600 mg/d, 1000 mg/d, or 1200 mg/d more frequently than other serving sizes, similar to the multiple studies that investigated a 1200 mg/d NAC dose. Based on the overlapping exposure to NAC, the conclusions of the systematic review derived from the study groups are relevant to the demonstration of an expectation of safety for NAC in or as a dietary supplement (id.).
Accordingly, we concluded a minimal LoC for the reports of GI-related AEs associated with NAC administration (id.). The studied doses were inclusive of the recommended servings of commercially available NAC-containing products labeled as dietary supplements (id.). As such, the minimal concern can be directly translated to a reasonable expectation of safety for the use of NAC in or as a dietary supplement based on the systematic review of clinical NAC studies (id.).
B. Impact on Drug Development
As stated previously, we first approved NAC as a new drug under NDA 013601 for oral inhalation under the brand name “Mucomyst” in 1963 (see
28 FR 13509
, December 13, 1963). NDA 013601 was withdrawn in 2009 at the sponsor's request for reasons other than safety or effectiveness (see
78 FR 67365
, November 12, 2013). In addition, Cumberland Pharmaceuticals Inc. received approval for acetylcysteine (injectable) under brand name Acetadote on January 23, 2004, under NDA 021539. Acetadote is an antidote for acetaminophen overdose indicated to prevent or lessen hepatic injury after ingestion of a potentially hepatotoxic quantity of acetaminophen in adults and pediatric patients who weigh 5 kilograms or greater with acute ingestion or from repeated supratherapeutic ingestion. We are aware of at least 19 Abbreviated New Drug Applications (ANDAs) for the active ingredient acetylcysteine (as of April 2, 2026, a search of the term “acetylcysteine” in the Orange Book: Approved Drug Products with Therapeutic Equivalence Evaluations identified 19 current ANDAs (see
https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/​scripts/​cder/​ob/​index.cfm
). Most of these ANDAs received approval after 1991, the first-known marketing of NAC in or as a dietary supplement. For example, Hospira Inc. received approval for ANDA 073664 and ANDA 074037 on August 30, 1994. Luitpold Pharmaceuticals Inc. (now American Regent, Inc.) also received approval for ANDA 072489 and ANDA 072547 on July 28, 1995. As a drug product, acetylcysteine is approved for the indication described above (
i.e.,
prevent or lessen hepatic injury after ingestion of a potentially hepatotoxic quantity of acetaminophen) as well as an adjuvant therapy for patients with abnormal, viscid, or inspissated mucous secretions in certain conditions, such as chronic bronchopulmonary disease. Thus, NAC is currently approved as a new drug under section 505 of the FD&C Act and has been continuously approved as a new drug under section 505 of the FD&C Act since September 14, 1963. Since at least August/September 1991, NAC has been available for sale in the United States both as FDA-approved drugs and as products labeled as dietary supplements.
Similarly, a search to identify the number of clinical trials for NAC, some of which correspond to Investigational New Drug applications (INDs), revealed 832 different trials regarding the use of NAC as a drug (see Ref. 15). This illustrates the fact that researchers continue to study NAC, including for use as a drug, even though NAC-containing products labeled as dietary supplements have been sold in the United States for more than 30 years.
NAC-containing products improperly labeled as dietary supplements have been sold in the United States since at least August/September 1991 (Ref. 2). When Congress defined the term “dietary supplement” in 1994, NAC became ineligible to be lawfully sold as a dietary supplement in the United States, but firms illegally continued to sell NAC-containing products labeled as dietary supplements in the United States. During a period of more than 30 years, the sale of NAC-containing products improperly labeled as dietary supplements in the United States does not appear to have negatively impacted NAC drug development.
(
printed page 73723)
Given the existence, study, and development of NAC-containing drug products for over 30 years despite the continued sale of NAC-containing products improperly labeled as dietary supplements, we have no reason to believe that removing the dietary supplement exclusion for NAC-containing products and allowing for their sale and regulation as dietary supplements will have an impact on any current or future development of NAC-containing drug products. We invite comment on whether the sale of NAC-containing products labeled as dietary supplements in the United States has negatively impacted NAC drug development or is anticipated to in the future.
We also note that in the notice announcing the availability of the draft enforcement discretion guidance (see
87 FR 24170
, April 22, 2022), we stated that we were considering initiating rulemaking under section 201(ff)(3)(B) of the FD&C Act to allow the use of NAC in or as a dietary supplement and, if, among other considerations, we did not identify safety-related concerns as we continued to review the available data and information, we were likely to propose a rule providing that NAC is not excluded from the dietary supplement definition (id. at 24171). We provided a 30-day comment period for the guidance; although, as is the case for all FDA guidance documents, parties may ask that we revise or withdraw an existing guidance document at any time (
21 CFR 10.115(f)(4)
). To date, we have not received any comments expressing concern or providing data to demonstrate that allowing the sale of NAC in or as a dietary supplement would impact drug development or identifying any other concerns.
V. Description of the Proposed Rule
Section 201(ff)(3)(B) of the FD&C Act authorizes FDA to issue a regulation, after notice-and-comment rulemaking, finding that an article previously excluded from the dietary supplement definition would no longer be excluded and, therefore, would be lawful under the FD&C Act for sale as a dietary supplement, provided that such product is not otherwise in violation of the FD&C Act. This proposed rule, if finalized, would remove the exclusion of NAC from the dietary supplement definition.
We propose to provide that certain ingredients are not excluded for use in or as a dietary supplement under section 201(ff)(3)(B) of the FD&C Act and that the addition of such ingredients to a dietary supplement is not a prohibited act under section 301(ll) of the  FD&C Act (see proposed § 190.1). Specifically, proposed § 190.1 would list “N-acetyl-L-cysteine” as the sole ingredient under proposed § 190.1(a), and we would reserve a new paragraph (b) to allow for additional ingredients to be added in the future. Thus, under proposed § 190.1(a), NAC would be allowed in or as a dietary supplement, provided that the NAC-containing product otherwise meets the dietary supplement definition under section 201(ff) of the FD&C Act. Such NAC-containing products would, therefore, be subject to the requirements that apply to dietary supplements under the FD&C Act and FDA's implementing regulations. Any adulterated or misbranded dietary supplement product may be subject to compliance or enforcement action. For example, if a dietary supplement has been prepared, packed, or held under conditions that do not meet current good manufacturing practice regulations (section 402(g)(1) of the FD&C Act (
21 U.S.C. 342(g)(1)
);
21 CFR part 111
), it may be subject to compliance or enforcement action.

Project: GLS State/Tribal Evaluation of the Garrett Lee Smith (GLS) State/Tribal Youth Suicide Prevention and Early Intervention Program Renewal
The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) Center for Mental Health Services (CMHS) is requesting clearance for the renewal of data collection associated with the previously approved evaluation of the Garrett Lee Smith (GLS) Youth Suicide Prevention and Early Intervention Program (GLS Suicide Prevention Program). The GLS State/Tribal Evaluation is a continuation of the previous evaluation (OMB No. 0930-0286; Expiration, January 31, 2027) that builds on prior published GLS evaluation findings from program
(
printed page 73770)
activities (
e.g.,
Condron, Godoy-Garraza, Walrath, McKeon, & Heilbron, 2014; Walrath, Godoy-Garraza, Reid, Goldston, & McKeon, 2015; Godoy-Garraza, Walrath, Kuiper, Goldston, & McKeon, 2018; Condron, Godoy-Garraza, Kuiper, Sukumar, Walrath, & McKeon, 2018; Godoy-Garraza, Kuiper, Goldston, McKeon, & Walrath, 2019; Godoy-Garraza, Kuiper, Cross, Hicks, & Walrath, 2020; Goldston & Walrath, 2023). As a result of the vast body of information collected and analyzed through the previous cross-site evaluation, SAMHSA has identified areas for additional investigation and the types of inquiry needed to move the evaluation into its next phase.
The purpose of the GLS State/Tribal Suicide Prevention Program is to facilitate a comprehensive public health approach to prevent suicide. Passed by Congress in 2004, the Garrett Lee Smith Memorial Act (GLSMA) was the first legislation to provide funding for states, tribes, and institutions of higher education to develop, improve, and evaluate early intervention and suicide prevention programs. GLSMA mandates that the effectiveness of the GLS Suicide Prevention Program be evaluated through both cross-site and local evaluation and reported to Congress.
The GLS State/Tribal Evaluation is designed to gather detailed outcome and impact data to provide SAMHSA with the data and information needed to understand what works, why it works, and under what conditions, relative to program activities.
The purpose of the GLS State/Tribal Evaluation is to build the program's knowledge base by expanding on information gathered through the prior evaluation related to the process, products, context, and impacts of the GLS State/Tribal Program.
The GLS State/Tribal Evaluation includes three evaluation components: the Implementation Evaluation, Outcome Evaluation (comprised of three studies—the Training Study, Youth Study, and Continuity of Care Study), and Impact Evaluation.
Implementation Evaluation
The Implementation Evaluation inventories the array of youth suicide prevention and early intervention strategies implemented by GLS grantees and addresses questions about the types of strategies, services, or products developed and/or implemented, including required and allowable activities and evidence-based practices; implementation settings (
e.g.,
schools, educational institutions, juvenile justice systems, substance use programs, mental health programs, foster care systems, and other child and youth-serving organizations); populations reached; the extent of implementation progress; and whether grantee strategies and activities are delivered in accordance with their work plans. In addition, the evaluation seeks to understand which elements of the National Strategy for Suicide Prevention are being implemented by grantees.
The approach employs methods consistent with the prior GLS evaluations, to enable an assessment of implementation context and progress over time, while focusing on current priorities for evaluation. Primary data collection will provide a comprehensive assessment of current grantee implementation activity at the grantee and program level. Data sources include:
Prevention Strategies Inventory (PSI)
Training Activity Summary Page (TASP)
Outcomes Evaluation
Training Study
As described above, prior evaluation indicates that counties where GLS trainings were implemented had lower suicide rates in the year following training events as compared with similar counties that did not have GLS trainings (Walrath et al., 2015; Godoy Garraza et al., 2019). Historically, such trainings focused predominantly on training community gatekeepers (
e.g.,
professionals and community members like parents, teachers, and coaches) to identify and refer youth and young adults at increased risk for suicide to appropriate services. Implementation of gatekeeper training was reported by 93% of state grantees and 97% of tribal grantees in 1 or more years between 2019 and 2026 (SAMHSA, 2026). Given the emphasis on training by grantees, the GLS Evaluation will continue to assess training activities and the related impact.
The Training Study will examine the impact of gatekeeper trainings and aligns with SAMHSA's National Strategy for Suicide Prevention (NSSP) goals 5 and 6 (SAMHSA, 2024). The Training Study will focus on the trainings for clinicians and staff that directly work with youth in crisis (
e.g.,
mental health professionals, staff and volunteers of prevention hotlines and helplines, juvenile justice staff, law enforcement, foster care providers, etc.). The study will focus on two types of training: community gatekeeper trainings that provide essential skills to successfully identify at-risk youth (
e.g.,
QPR, ASIST, safeTALK) and trainings for mental health professionals and clinical staff to identify and manage individuals expressing suicidal thoughts or behaviors (
e.g.,
AMSR and RRSR). To understand the training process and the impact that training has on behaviors, the Training Study will examine training participants' post-training behaviors and utilization of skills. Furthermore, this study will investigate the long-term gains in trainees' skills to identify and manage youth at increased risk for suicide. The study includes core questions about trainings implemented and their proximal outcomes. Three primary data sources inform the Training Study:
Training Skills Assessment—Post (TSA-P)
Training Skills Assessment 6- and 12-month follow-up (TSA-F6 and TSA-F12)
Training Skills Assessment—Phone Simulation (TSA-PS)
All trainees will complete a baseline TSA-P, and a sample of trainees will be invited to complete a TSA-F at 6 and 12 months after the training. In addition, a subset of TSA-P participants will also be invited to participate in the TSA-PS, which will occur approximately 3-6 months after the training.
Youth Study
GLS State/Tribal grantees are expected to implement programs that will increase the number of youth-serving organizations, however, the field has often overlooked youth as partners in research and evaluation designed to improve their outcomes. In addition, youth are not always seen as assets in their communities or experts on topics pertaining to them (Sprague-Martinez et al., 2018; Finn & Checkoway, 1998). Yet, it is important to understand how individuals served by the grant experience the intervention, services, and supports received in addition to understanding the effectiveness of the services.
Positive youth development (PYD) is “an intentional, prosocial approach that engages youth within their communities, schools, organizations, peer groups, and families in a manner that is productive and constructive; recognizes, utilizes, and enhances young people's strengths; and promotes positive outcomes for young people” (
youth.gov
). PYD builds resilience by enhancing and utilizing young people's positive assets, leadership, and knowledge, and PYD has been found to be associated with psychosocial outcomes, including anxiety, depression, and suicide ideation (Onyeka et al., 2022). A key tenet to PYD is youth engagement in program
(
printed page 73771)
development and evaluation. Listening and learning from youth is critical; youth can provide organizations with key insights that help create innovative and effective programs.
The Youth Study seeks to understand, from the youth's perspective, which skills are most useful in the self-management of thoughts, plans, and attempts at suicide; whether self-management skills increase because of the grant activities; and whether positive skills including resilience and stress tolerance are improved through participation in grant activities. The Youth Study will include a Youth Advisory Board to provide oversight and feedback on the evaluation's study design, data collection, and interpretation of findings. For all youth under the age of 18 parental consent and youth assent will be obtained. Youth who are 18 or older will be asked to complete their own consent forms.
Specific data collection instruments include:
Youth Outcomes and Resiliency Survey (YORS)
Youth Experience Reflective Journal (YER Journal)
The YORS will be administered at 3-, 6-, and 12-months post enrollment. Youth participating in the YORS will be invited to join the YER Journal study via contact through the YORS data collection activities. The GLS State/Tribal Evaluation team may follow-up with YER Journal where youth will be sent seven daily prompts that can be replied to with text, images, or short videos.
Continuity of Care Study
Best practices recommendations state that gatekeeper trainings must include post-identification protocols, community-specific suicide prevention resources, and supports that are available where the trainee works and/or lives—all of which demand that adequate supports/services are available to at-risk youth. Recommendations for screening include developing response protocols for youth perceived at risk, including imminent risk, to ensure the receipt of immediate guidance and referral—also demanding the availability of adequate services if an at-risk youth is identified. Previous evaluation data tracked three aspects of how grantees respond to youth who are identified as being at risk for suicide: (1) how they are identified, (2) what referral they receive at time of identification, and (3) the first two services they receive. The Continuity of Care study will continue with this data collection to understand the referral patterns and identify potential gaps in the identification, referral, and services receipt process. Furthermore, this study will expand to follow identified youth for a longer period of tracking (6 months) to track their services, additional referrals, and outcomes of additional assessment. This longer period of tracking will facilitate a better understanding of the path at-risk youth follow while receiving care (additional referrals and services), how long care continues, and at what points a youth may drop out of care.
This Continuity of Care Study will assess the practices of GLS State/Tribal grantees related to early identification, referral, and follow-up practices of grantees to ensure youth are not falling through gaps during the follow-up and services receipt process. The goal of this study is to understand the extent to which youth who are identified through a GLS State/Tribal Suicide Prevention program are referred to and receive services in the 6-month period following their identification. In addition to those youth identified as part of the GLS State/Tribal Program, this study seeks to follow up with and understand the care pathway of those youth who were not necessarily identified via the GLS Program but were discharged from an emergency department or inpatient psychiatric unit in the grant service area.
All state and tribal grantees who are participating in the evaluation will participate in continuity of care data collection activities. To understand what grantees are doing to support continuity of care throughout the identification, referral, and treatment process, GLS State/Tribal Evaluation team will use 3 instruments to collect administrative, behavioral health, and grantee respondent data.
The Continuity of Care Study comprises primary and secondary data collection activities—surveys, inventories, and existing data abstractions—to document the GLS-sponsored prevention activities that support and contribute to the early identification, referral, and follow-up of students and youth at risk for suicide.
To understand what grantees are doing, the study will rely on data gathered via the PSI. The PSI gathers the prevention strategies for the early identification, referral, and follow-up of at-risk youth and students; how grantees track and monitor at-risk youth identified through screenings; and the follow-up protocols for each screening activity (
e.g.,
the protocols and tracking tools used to ensure that youth referred for services are followed up with and get to adequate mental health or other support referral sources). Data from the PSI will provide insight about what activities GLS grantees are implementing. Additional data collection instruments for the Continuity of Care Study include:
Early Identification, Referral, Follow-up, and Treatment—Screening Form (EIRFT-S)
Early Identification, Referral, Follow-up, and Treatment—Individual Form (EIRFT-I)
To assess if GLS prevention activities are effective in developing and supporting continuity of care, grantee staff will submit EIRFT-I data for each youth identified as at risk. The EIRFT-I collects individual (de-identified) data on initial follow-up, referrals, and details on all services in the 6 months post-identification. The EIRFT-S gathers aggregate information about all screening activities completed as a part of the GLS State/Tribal Program (
e.g.,
the number of youth screened for suicide risk, the number screening positive, and the number confirmed to be at risk after initial positive screening). EIRFT-S forms are completed once per implementation of a screening tool in a group setting, once per month for clinical screenings, and once per month for one-on-one screenings. No personal identifiers are requested on either the EIRFT-I or EIRFT-S forms.
Impact Evaluation
The Impact Evaluation combines data from the Implementation and Outcome Evaluations with relevant secondary data to assess the effects of the GLS State/Tribal Program on suicide morbidity and mortality. The evaluation examines three complementary areas: the overall magnitude, timing, and persistence of program effects; variation in effects across populations, communities, and contextual conditions; and the relationship between variation in program implementation, intermediate outcomes, and longer-term suicide outcomes. These analyses will help identify whether GLS activities are effective, the settings and circumstances in which greater or lesser impacts occur, and the implementation characteristics and pathways associated with improved outcomes.

GLS State/Tribal Evaluation Instruments
PSI:
the PSI is a web-based survey that captures all GLS State/Tribal program prevention strategies and products. Data include strategy types and products distributed, intended audiences or populations of focus, and expenditures across major categories (
e.g.,
outreach and awareness, gatekeeper training, screening programs). Each major strategy includes sub-strategies, enabling grantees to specify and provide details about the sub-strategy, including implementation setting/location, timeframe, and intended audiences or populations of focus. The PSI is completed by grantee staff each quarter. PSI data inform the Training Study and Continuity of Care Study. Compared to the prior version of the PSI, the revised PSI removes the Behavioral Health Equity module; includes updated response options to align with the 2024 NSSP goals; and expands response options to allow for more relevant reporting of strategies.
TASP:
the TASP is a web-based survey collecting aggregate-level training data from all State/Tribal grantees. Data include information about the type of training delivered; the number of online trainings completed, train-the-trainer events held, and booster trainings that follow the initial training; the number and roles of training participants; and the setting of the training, including ZIP code where the training is held (for use in analysis of GLS program impact). The TASP also assesses intended outcomes, such as making referrals, training staff or community members to intervene, or providing direct services to youth who may be at-risk for suicide. The TASP also collects information about the inclusion of behavioral rehearsal or role-play and resources provided to trainees to improve understanding of how skills can be maintained over time with materials provided at trainings. A TASP is completed by grantee program staff within 2 weeks of each in-person training activity and quarterly for virtual training activities. The revised TASP includes expanded primary setting options to better reflect trainings completed in Tribal settings and additional response options for training curricula delivered.
TSA-P:
the TSA-P is a web-based survey to assess trainee confidence in identifying and managing youth at risk for suicide after participation in a GLS-sponsored training event. All trainees are invited to complete the TSA-P at the conclusion of all training events. The instrument assesses baseline confidence following the training, knowledge of suicide prevention, confidence in identifying and managing suicidal youth, and pretraining behaviors related to identifying and managing youth at risk of suicide. As part of the TSA-P, trainees complete a consent-to-contact web form indicating their willingness to be contacted by the GLS State/Tribal Evaluation team to participate in the TSA-F and TSA-PS. If a trainer is unable to administer the survey or consent-to-contact form electronically, or a trainee does not have access to a mobile device or computer, they may also complete the survey and consent-to-contact form on paper. The grantee will submit completed paper surveys to the GLS State/Tribal Evaluation team through direct data entry into the Suicide Prevention Data Center (SPDC) within 2 weeks of the training event. Once the GLS National State/Tribal team receives consent to contact, they will create a random sample of participants for the phone simulation and the 6- and 12-month follow-up surveys. The TSA-P has been updated so the sectors align with changes to the TASP and role options are expanded (based on “other” reported role categories in previous rounds of data and feedback from grantees). The TSA-P has also updated demographic question answer options.
TSA-F:
The TSA-F is a follow-up web-based survey to assess trainees' sustained confidence and skills in identifying and managing youth at risk for suicide, as well as experience with managing at-risk youth since training (interventions with youth, additional training, etc.). The survey is administered to a sample of training participants at 6- and 12-months after the initial TSA-P is completed. The TSA-P has been updated so the sectors align with changes to the TASP and TSA-P.
TSA-PS:
The TSA-PS is a follow-up phone simulation using a standardized interaction to assess trainee skills in
(
printed page 73773)
identification and management of a youth in suicidal crisis. A random subsample of training participants who completed the initial TSA-P are contacted by the evaluation team to participate in a simulated conversation portrayed by a trained actor. These simulations occur between 3 and 6 months following their initial training. The simulated conversation between the training participant and actor last approximately 10 to 30 minutes. In total, sessions are scheduled for 45 minutes to allow for consent, instructions, and a debrief. These phone sessions are administered via a video call and recorded for additional post-simulation scoring and analysis. All sessions are attended by the training participant, an actor, and an evaluation team member (observer), who will be responsible for facilitating the interaction, administering the consent, scoring the interaction (both in real time and based on the recording), and providing a short debrief to the training participant. The revised TSA-PS includes an updated youth scenario.
EIRFT-I:
the web-based EIRFT-I gathers data for each at-risk youth identified as a result of the GLS program (via a GLS-trained gatekeeper, a GLS-sponsored screening identification, or an acute or crisis care setting, such as an emergency room or inpatient psychiatric treatment). Initial screening, referral, and follow-up information (whether a service was received after referral or not) is obtained along with details on all services received in the 3 months following identification. Data can be extracted from case or clinical records or other existing data sources, including any organizational staff, community members, or family members who make a mental health identification and referral. Respondents include grantee program staff and service providers representing all grantees in all funding years. Grantee program staff enter EIRFT-I data on an ongoing basis. No personal identifiers are requested on the EIRFT-I. The revised EIRFT-I includes updated response options to reflect grantee feedback as well as to improve consistency and clarity, streamlined skip logic, reduced follow-up data collection, updated instructions to reflect changes made, and minor changes to item numbering and grammar.
EIRFT-S:
the web-based EIRFT-S gathers aggregate information about all screening activities conducted as part of the GLS program. Data include aggregate information on the number of youth screened for suicide risk through the GLS program, and the number that screened positive. EIRFT-S forms are completed once per implementation of a screening tool in a group setting, once per month for clinical screenings, and once per month for one-on-one screenings. For each screening event in which multiple youth are screened at a given time, one EIRFT-S is completed for the event. For one-on-one screenings in a clinical or other setting, one aggregated EIRFT-S is completed per month to reflect screening outcomes of all youth screened during the month. Grantees develop systems locally to gather identification and referral data, including extracting data from existing electronic health records or forms. No personal identifiers are requested on the EIRFT-S. The revised EIRFT-S includes minor changes to response options.
YORS:
the YORS is a web-based survey assessing the experience and outcomes of those youth who are served by the GLS Program. The instrument is designed to assess suicidality, positive youth development, satisfaction with services received, youth engagement experience, and family and school dynamics. Youth between the ages of 14-24 will have the option to review a recruitment flyer, scan a QR code, and complete a short interest form. A sample of eligible youth will be enrolled in the Youth Study. The age of the youth respondent will dictate how consent is obtained for the YORS. All youth under the age of 18 who express interest will be asked to have their parent complete consent forms for their participation and the youth will complete an assent form. Youth over the age of 18 will be asked to complete their own consent form. The YORS will be administered at 3-, 6-, and 12-months post enrollment. Revisions to the YORS include updates to the demographic questions.
YER Journal:
the YER Journal is a web-based survey consisting of 7 daily journal prompts that youth can respond to with text, a photo or short video. For example, youth may be asked to reflect on a recent experience receiving services. The youth would be asked to submit a photo that represents that experience, followed by a prompt that asks: “What words come to mind? How did it make you feel?” The narrative description of what the photo represents will be analyzed using qualitative methodologies. Up to 25 youth will be recruited to participate in the YER Journal each year. Youth participating in the YORS will be invited to join the YER Journal via contact through the YORS data collection activities. For example, a youth may complete their third quarterly YORS follow-up, and be invited to join the YER Journal study simultaneously. Our team will leverage innovative data collection technology to engage youth. Daily prompts will be sent to youth for 7 days post enrollment to discover, for example, which components of what youth are receiving are meaningful and helpful, and how youth may be utilizing skills or services following the initial screening, both in the short and long term. The revised YER Journal includes minor changes to question prompts.

Section 452(a)(11) of the Social Security Act requires the HHS Secretary to promulgate forms for administrative subpoenas and imposition of liens used by state child support agencies in interstate cases. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), Science Advisory Board (SAB) Branch is announcing a public meeting of the Science Advisory Board. The purpose of the meeting is to receive a briefing from EPA on the Unregulated Contaminant Monitoring Rule; the Draft Guidance for Reducing Risk from Perfluorooctanoic Acid (PFOA) and Perfluorooctane Sulfonic Acid (PFOS) in Biosolids; and hear public comments.
DATES:
Public meeting:
The Science Advisory Board will meet on December 7, 2026, from 11:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. Eastern Time.
Comments:
See the section titled “Procedures for providing public input” under
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
for instructions and deadlines.

The December 7, 2026 meeting will be conducted virtually. Registration is required to participate in the meeting. Please refer to the Science Advisory Board website at
https://sab.epa.gov
for additional information including how to register.

Any member of the public who wants further information concerning this document may contact Dr. Shaunta Hill-Hammond, Designated Federal Officer (DFO), via telephone at (202) 564-3343, or email
at
hill-hammond.shaunta@epa.gov
.
General information about the SAB, as well as any updates concerning this meeting, can be found on the SAB website at

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background:
The SAB was established pursuant to the Environmental Research, Development, and Demonstration Authorization Act (ERDDAA), codified at
42 U.S.C. 4365
, to provide independent scientific and technical advice to the EPA Administrator on the scientific and technical basis for agency positions and regulations. The SAB is a Federal Advisory Committee chartered under the Federal Advisory Committee Act (FACA),
5 U.S. Code 10
. The SAB will comply with the provisions of FACA and all appropriate SAB Staff Office procedural policies. Pursuant to FACA and EPA policy, notice is hereby given that the Science Advisory Board will hold a public meeting to receive a briefing from EPA on the Unregulated Contaminant Monitoring Rule; the Draft Guidance for Reducing Risk from Perfluorooctanoic Acid (PFOA) and Perfluorooctane Sulfonic Acid (PFOS) in Biosolids; and hear public comments.
Availability of meeting materials:
All meeting materials, including the agenda, will be available on the SAB web page at
https://sab.epa.gov
.
Procedures for providing public input:
Public comment for consideration by EPA's federal advisory committees and panels has a different purpose from public comment provided to EPA program offices. Therefore, the process for submitting comments to a federal advisory committee is different from the process used to submit comments to an EPA program office. Federal advisory committees and panels, including scientific advisory committees, provide independent advice to the EPA. Members of the public can submit relevant comments pertaining to the committee's charge or meeting materials. Input from the public to the SAB will have the most impact if it provides specific scientific or technical information or analysis for the SAB to consider or if it relates to the clarity or accuracy of the technical information. Members of the public wishing to provide comments should follow the instructions below to submit comments.
Oral statements:
In general, individuals or groups requesting an oral presentation at a meeting conducted virtually will be limited to three minutes. Each person making an oral statement should consider providing written comments as well as their oral statement so that the points presented orally can be expanded upon in writing. Persons interested in providing oral statements should contact the DFO, in writing (preferably via email) at the contact information noted under
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
, by December 1, 2026, for the December 7, 2026 meeting, to be placed on the list of registered speakers.
Written statements:
Written statements will be accepted throughout the advisory process; however, for timely consideration by SAB members, statements should be submitted to the DFO by December 1, 2026, for consideration at the December 7, 2026 meeting. Written statements should be supplied to the DFO at the contact information above via email. Submitters are requested to provide an unsigned version of each document because the SAB Staff Office does not publish documents with signatures on its websites. Members of the public should be aware that their personal contact information, if included in any written comments, may be posted to the SAB website. Copyrighted material will not be posted without the explicit permission of the copyright holder.
Accessibility:
For information on access or services for individuals with disabilities, please contact the DFO, at the contact information noted above, preferably at least ten days before the meeting, to give the EPA as much time as possible to process your request.
