Notice.
SUMMARY:
The Assembly of the Administrative Conference of the United States (ACUS) will meet during a one-day hybrid plenary session to consider four proposed recommendations and to conduct other business. Written comments may be submitted in advance, and the meeting will be accessible to the public.
DATES:
The meeting will take place on Thursday, December 10, 2026, from 9:30 a.m.-4:30 p.m. (ET). The meeting may adjourn early if all business is finished.
ADDRESSES:
For those attending in person, the meeting will be held at The George Washington University State Room, 1957 E Street NW, Washington, DC 20052. There will be a virtual attendance option. Information on how the public can access the meeting will be available on the agency's website prior to the meeting at
https://www.acus.gov/​event/​86th-plenary-session
.
ACUS members will receive member-only access information separately.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Shawne McGibbon, General Counsel (Designated Federal Officer), Administrative Conference of the United States, Suite 706 South, 1120 20th Street NW, Washington, DC 20036; Telephone 202-480-2080; email
smcgibbon@acus.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Administrative Conference of the United States makes recommendations to federal agencies, the President, Congress, and the Judicial Conference of the United States regarding the improvement of administrative procedures (
5 U.S.C. 594
). The membership of the Conference, when meeting in plenary session, constitutes the Assembly of the Conference (
5 U.S.C. 595
).
Agenda:
Four proposed recommendations will be considered by the Assembly. In addition, there will be updates on past, current, and pending Conference initiatives, as well as other business. Summaries of the recommendations appear below:
Improving Transparency in the Review of Applications for Licenses and Permits.
This proposed recommendation addresses what information about pending license and permit applications agencies make publicly available and how they do so. It identifies best practices to help agencies collect, analyze, and disclose information about their license programs and pending applications. It also addresses best practices for documenting license processes and identifying core milestones; communicating with applicants more effectively, including through the use of automation; and providing useful information to applicants and the general public in a timely and useful format.
General Permits and Permits by Rule.
This proposed recommendation addresses agencies' use of general permits and other standardized approaches to permitting. It identifies best practices to help agencies improve fairness, accuracy, efficiency, and timeliness, and transparency in the granting of permission to undertake regulated activities.
Regulatory Warnings.
This proposed recommendation provides best practices for determining whether federal agencies should issue regulatory warnings and ensuring that agencies provide recipients with the opportunity to respond to such warnings. It also addresses how agencies should manage regulatory warnings, when and how agencies should make regulatory warnings publicly available, and how agencies can use regulatory warnings in support of rulemaking to clarify legal requirements.
Frontline Decision Making in the Adjudication of Applications.
This proposed recommendation identifies best practices for frontline decision making in the adjudication of benefits, loans, grants, licenses, patents, and other applications in which there is a later opportunity for an evidentiary hearing. It addresses how agencies can improve the management of frontline decision making and communication with applicants and representatives at the frontline level. It also encourages agencies to facilitate the ongoing mutual exchange of information between frontline components and other agency components.
Additional information about the proposals and the agenda, as well as any changes or updates to the same, can be found at the 86th Plenary Session page on ACUS's website prior to the start of the meeting:
https://www.acus.gov/​event/​86th-plenary-session
.
Public Participation:
The Conference welcomes the virtual attendance of the public at the meeting. Members of the public wishing to view the meeting are asked to RSVP online at the 86th Plenary Session web page shown above no later than two days before the meeting to ensure adequate bandwidth. A livestream of the meeting will be posted the morning of the meeting on the 86th Plenary Session web page. A video recording of the meeting will be available on the Conference's website shortly after the conclusion of the event at
https://youtube.com/​@AdministrativeConference
.
Written Comments:
Persons who wish to comment on any of the proposed recommendations may do so by submitting a written statement either by email to
info@acus.gov
with “December 2026 Plenary Session Comments” in the subject line of the email, or by U.S. Mail addressed to: December 2026 Plenary Session Comments, Administrative Conference of the United States, Suite 706 South, 1120 20th Street NW, Washington, DC 20036. Written submissions must be received no later than 10:00 a.m. (ET), Friday, December 4, 2026, to ensure consideration by the Assembly.

)

II.
Executive Order 14300
: Ordering the Reform of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission
On May 23, 2025, President Donald J. Trump signed Executive Order (E.O.) 14300, “Ordering the Reform of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.” Section 4(b) of
E.O. 14300
directs the NRC to reduce the personnel and functions of the ACRS to the minimum necessary to fulfill the ACRS's statutory obligations. It also directs the NRC to focus the ACRS's review of permitting and licensing issues on issues that are truly novel or noteworthy. This rulemaking implements Section 4(b) by revising the NRC's regulations to focus the ACRS's reviews on safety-significant issues, commensurate with risk, and novel or noteworthy technologies or analytical approaches.
III. Rulemaking Procedure
The NRC uses the “direct final rule procedure” for rulemaking when the NRC anticipates the rule is unlikely to attract significant adverse comments because the rule is non-controversial. As explained below, this rulemaking would limit the ACRS's functions to those obligations required by the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, as amended (AEA), and cease review of matters not identified as statutorily required. Moreover, the rescission of these regulations, which authorize the ACRS to conduct activities not expressly required by statute, does not prevent the Commission from requesting that the ACRS undertake a particular review or study in the future. Therefore, because the NRC does not anticipate significant adverse comments on this rulemaking and considers it to be non-controversial, the NRC is using the “direct final rule procedure” for this rule. The amendments are effective on February 1, 2027. However, if the NRC receives significant adverse comments on this direct final rule by December 17, 2026, then the NRC will publish a document that withdraws this action and will address the comments received in a subsequent final rule as otherwise appropriate. Absent significant modifications to the revisions requiring republication, the NRC will not initiate a second comment period on this action.
A significant adverse comment is a comment where the commenter explains why the rule would be inappropriate, including challenges to the rule's underlying premise or approach, or would be ineffective or unacceptable without a change. A comment is adverse and significant if:
(1) The comment opposes the rule and provides a reason sufficient to require a substantive response in a notice-and-comment process. For example, a substantive response is required when:
(a) The comment causes the NRC to reevaluate (or reconsider) its position or conduct additional analysis;
(b) The comment raises an issue serious enough to warrant a substantive response to clarify or complete the record; or
(c) The comment raises a relevant issue that was not previously addressed or considered by the NRC.
(2) The comment proposes a change or an addition to the rule, and it is apparent that the rule would be ineffective or unacceptable without incorporation of the change or addition.
(3) The comment causes the NRC to make a change (other than editorial) to the rule.

IV. Background
The ACRS was established by a 1957 amendment to the AEA as a statutory committee with an independent advisory role and focus to advise the Atomic Energy Commission. Following the enactment of the Energy Reorganization Act of 1974, the ACRS was assigned to the NRC with its statutory requirements intact. The ACRS assists the Commission's review and resolution of certain technical safety issues associated with the licensing of production and utilization facilities and the establishment of NRC reactor safety regulations.
The ACRS's minimum statutory obligations are specified in sections 29 and 182b. of the AEA.
42 U.S.C. 2039
,
2232
. Since its formation, the ACRS has provided independent reactor safety advice to the Commission in the review of safety issues associated with regulation of nuclear power plants. Since 1975, the Commission has codified minimum statutory obligations and referred additional duties to the ACRS, as authorized by the AEA, in the NRC's regulations in title 10 of the
Code of Federal Regulations
(10 CFR) parts 1, “Statement of Organization and General Information,” 2, “Agency Rules of Practice and Procedure,” 50, “Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities,” 52, “Licenses, Certifications, and Approvals for Nuclear Power Plants, 53, “Risk-Informed, Technology-Inclusive Regulatory Framework for Advanced Reactors,” and 54, “Requirements for Renewal of Operating Licenses for Nuclear Power Plants.” Over time, the depth of ACRS review increased beyond its minimum statutorily required functions, due to additional duties referred to it by the Commission and additional reviews assumed by the ACRS without Commission referral. While ACRS recently began making certain improvements to perform more focused and efficient reviews, this rulemaking codifies some of those improvements and redefines the scope of the ACRS reviews to ensure that the size and duties of the ACRS are consistent with the statutorily required functions, to support timely and efficient licensing and rulemaking while maintaining its ability to conduct independent safety analyses.
V. Discussion
The NRC is amending its regulations to ensure the personnel and functions of the ACRS are reduced to the minimum necessary to fulfill the ACRS's statutory functions and to focus the ACRS's review of permitting and licensing issues on issues that are novel or noteworthy. This direct final rule aligns with the purpose of
E.O. 14300
to efficiently promote the deployment of safe, abundant civilian nuclear energy and reform the structure, personnel, regulations, and basic operations of the NRC. Specifically, the NRC is amending its regulations governing the ACRS to focus on safety-significant reviews, promote balanced expertise, provide flexibility in the ACRS's structure, and clarify the scope and conduct of the ACRS's reviews and meetings. These amendments will reduce unnecessary regulatory burden on licensees and applicants and save the NRC resources without any compromise in the NRC's commitment to protect public health and safety and to promote the nation's common defense and security.
The ACRS's minimum statutory obligations are specified in AEA sections 29 and 182b. Section 29 states that the Committee shall “advise the Commission with regard to the hazards of proposed or existing reactor facilities and the adequacy of proposed reactor safety standards, and shall perform such other duties as the Commission may request.” In addition, Section 182b. states in part that the ACRS shall review certain license applications. The review of and reporting on the hazards of proposed and existing facilities and proposed reactor safety standards are the core statutory functions of the ACRS under the AEA. Section 29 also directs the ACRS to “perform such other duties as the Commission may request.” Over the past 50 years, the Commission has added additional duties for the ACRS via regulation. This direct final rule will modify the NRC's regulations to make licensing more efficient by limiting the
(

ACRS's work to its statutory obligations contained in the AEA without compromising safety.
Scope of ACRS Review and Reports
When discharging its duty under AEA section 29 to “advise the Commission with regard to the hazards of proposed or existing reactor facilities and the adequacy of proposed reactor safety standards,” and its duty under AEA section 182b to review certain license applications the scope of the ACRS's review and reports should be focused on novel or noteworthy attributes of a facility's design, siting, and operation associated with (1) safety-related structures, systems, and components as described by the definitions given in NRC rules and regulations or (2) structures, systems, and components that perform safety-significant functions. This includes safety analyses and methodologies used to evaluate and classify structures, systems, and components, as well as structures, systems and components used to prevent reactor accidents and mitigate the consequences of a spectrum of analyzed events, including those used to control reactivity, ensure heat removal, or retain radionuclides to appropriately manage the radiological risks to the public.
This scope of review includes, for instance, issues such as reviewing and developing reports on licensing documents for construction permits and operating licenses for production and utilization facilities, advising the Commission regarding the hazards of proposed or existing nuclear facilities and the adequacy of proposed reactor safety standards, and evaluating new safety bases and analytical methods. However, the scope of ACRS's review does not include issues that are unrelated or merely tangential to a facility's safety. Examples include offsite emergency preparedness and response, threat assessment, physical security, force-on-force assessments, or operational radiation protection and siting matters that do not present significant reactor safety questions. Under this direct final rule the ACRS will focus its review on novel or noteworthy aspects of license applications or reactor safety standards. Re-reviewing technology or methods that have already been reviewed by the ACRS during previous licensing reviews or reviewing matters of no safety significance does not assist the Commission in making the findings that it is required to make under the AEA. This rule does not prohibit the ACRS from recommending that the Commission request the ACRS's review of specific safety-significant matters in a license application consistent with the discretionary review authority in AEA sections 29 and 182b., which specify the Commission may request the ACRS to perform other duties.
Accordingly, the NRC is amending §§ 1.13, 2.809, 50.58, 52.23, 52.53, 52.87, 52.141, 52.165, 52.177, 53.1155, 53.1215, 53.1245, 53.1286, 53.1324, 53.1381, 53.1431, and 53.1470 to clarify that the ACRS must report on those portions of the application which directly relate to safety issues that are novel or noteworthy. These changes clarify the scope of the ACRS's review to align with the minimum statutory responsibilities of the ACRS and with
E.O. 14300
, and to support timely and efficient licensing and rulemaking without compromising safety.
Review of Manufacturing License Applications
This direct final rule revises § 52.165 and § 53.1286 to focus the ACRS's review of manufacturing license applications on those portions of the application that concern reactor safety issues that are novel or noteworthy. Although the AEA does not address manufacturing license applications, allowing the ACRS to review portions of the license application directly related to reactor safety will increase efficiency by providing regulatory stability and finality on the issues reviewed and streamline downstream licensing actions.
Under section 182b of the AEA, the ACRS is required to review an “application under section [103] or section [104](b) . . . for a construction permit or an operating license for a facility” and an “application under section [104](c) . . . for a construction permit or an operating license for a testing facility.”
42 U.S.C. 2232(b)
. For all other activities that require a license—like manufacturing—ACRS review of the license application is not statutorily required.
Notwithstanding that ACRS review is not required for the NRC to issue a manufacturing license, a manufacturing license does provide regulatory stability and finality under § 52.171 with respect to the design of the reactor described in the Final Safety Evaluation Report (FSAR) submitted as part of the manufacturing license application. That is, the NRC makes regulatory findings on the adequacy of the design proposed in the manufacturing license application that can then be applied in a proceeding on a construction permit, operating license, or combined license without the need for further review by the NRC. This process streamlines downstream licensing actions. Specifically, an applicant may reference the use of one or more manufactured nuclear power reactors in a construction permit, operating license, or combined license application. In the proceeding on the referencing application, the Commission must treat as resolved those matters resolved in the proceeding on the manufacturing license application, including the adequacy of the design of the manufactured reactor.
Accordingly, to increase efficiency by providing regulatory finality on reactor safety issues, the NRC staff and applicant would engage with the ACRS on aspects of the manufacturing license that would otherwise be reviewed and reported as part of a construction permit, operating license, or combined license review. Under this scenario, the ACRS would have completed its statutory function by reviewing at the manufacturing license stage reactor safety issues that the ACRS otherwise would have to review in each application for a construction permit, operating license, or combined license.

Qualifications for Appointment to the ACRS
This direct final rule revises § 1.13 to require that members of the ACRS possess demonstrated and recognized experience and backgrounds relevant to reactor safety, while not establishing a minimum number of years of education or professional experience. The AEA neither prescribes nor implies a minimum number of years of experience for appointment to the ACRS. Several past
Federal Register
notices issued by the Commission to solicit candidates for the ACRS have sought candidates with “approximately 20 years of education and experience.”

While such statements were non-binding recruiting

guidance rather than firm eligibility requirements, such language may be misconstrued as establishing a de facto minimum experience threshold. This direct final rule revises § 1.13 to standardize the solicitation notices and eliminate references to a specific number of years of experience to be considered for appointment to the ACRS. The Commission will continue to seek highly qualified candidates with demonstrated expertise, judgment, or specialized knowledge directly relevant to reactor safety issues and the ability to provide independent advice on reactor safety matters. Eliminating references to a specific number of years of experience while maintaining a high standard for membership qualification would provide the benefit of an expanded pool of potential qualified applicants. Further, modern reactor safety issues frequently span multiple technical and operational disciplines and therefore benefit from hiring members across a range of multidisciplinary backgrounds. Eliminating references to a specific number of years of experience and recruiting members to the ACRS across multidisciplinary backgrounds would also avoid limitations on viewpoints within the ACRS, particularly for novel or noteworthy technologies that may be developed in the future where multidisciplinary backgrounds may be more beneficial to reviews involving novel or noteworthy technologies. Therefore, this direct final rule clarifies that members of the ACRS, collectively, should have expertise across multiple disciplines, without prescribing rigid experience requirements.
Restructuring the ACRS Membership
This direct final rule revises the NRC's regulations to restructure the membership of the ACRS to implement
E.O. 14300
, Section 4(b). Specifically, this direct final rule revises § 1.13 to establish a minimum of seven members for the ACRS. While the AEA states that the ACRS consist of a maximum of 15 members appointed by the Commission, codified as
42 U.S.C. 2039
, the statute does not prescribe a minimum number of members on the ACRS. Based on past experience, the Commission has determined that 7 members is an adequate number of members for carrying out the ACRS statutory functions in ordinary circumstances. The determination of the minimum number of ACRS members necessary to effectively and efficiently fulfill its statutory obligations is predicated on ensuring the ACRS has the balanced technical expertise necessary to fulfill the Committee's statutory functions. However, the ACRS can scale up its membership, when needed, to respond effectively to increased demands associated with licensing activity, new reactor technologies, or other emerging safety issues. Although the Commission has set the minimum number of ACRS members at 7, it is understood that ACRS membership may temporarily drop below 7 members due to unexpected attrition.
Coordination Requirements Between the ACRS and the NRC Staff
This direct final rule also revises the NRC's regulations in § 1.13 to make a change to improve coordination between the ACRS and the NRC Staff. The NRC is revising its regulations to require that the ACRS work with leadership in the NRC's program offices to ensure that meetings between the ACRS and the NRC staff are limited to issues within the ACRS's scope of review. The purpose of this amendment is to promote disciplined meeting agendas and improve coordination between the ACRS and the NRC staff.
Self-Initiated Safety Reviews and Conducting Studies
This direct final rule revises § 1.13 so that the ACRS may not, on its own initiative, conduct reviews of specific generic matters or nuclear facility safety-related items. Nothing in this direct final rule prohibits the ACRS from requesting review of safety matters from the Commission nor does it limit the Commission's ability to request additional advice from the ACRS. In 1977, Congress amended AEA Section 29 to require a research study and annual report to Congress. Sec. 5, Public Law 95-209, 91 Stat. 1483. The relevant provision stated: “Section 29 of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 is amended by adding the following at the end thereof: `In addition to its other duties under this section, the committee, making use of all available resources, shall undertake a study of reactor safety research and prepare and submit annually to the Congress a report containing the results of such study.' ” Congress then removed this requirement in 1998. Sec. 1201(a),
Public Law 105-362
, 112 Stat. 3292. From 1998 to 2004 the ACRS provided an annual report to the Chairman, per Commission direction, evaluating the NRC's safety research program. From 2004-2021, this report was biennial, and the frequency changed to triennial with the last report issued in March 2025. Rescinding this review authority from NRC regulations will align the ACRS's function with the AEA, promote timely and efficient agency operations, and will not affect NRC reactor safety research.
Authority To Recommend Rulemaking
This direct final rule rescinds § 2.809(a) and removes the authorization for the ACRS to recommend that the Commission initiate rulemaking in a particular area and require a response from the Commission within 90 days. The rescission of this provision will align the ACRS's function with the AEA, while retaining the ACRS's ability to review and report to the Commission on reactor safety standards. In addition, § 2.809(b) is moved to § 1.13(e), “Review of Rulemakings,” to more appropriately relocate it to § 1.13, “Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards,” where additional regulations on ACRS functions are located.
Referral of Applications for License Amendments
This direct final rule revises paragraph § 50.58(a) to remove the language that an application for an amendment to a construction permit or operating license may be referred to the ACRS for review and report. However, the Commission retains discretion to refer such applications to the ACRS in appropriate circumstances.
Section 182b. of the AEA states that the ACRS shall review “any application for an amendment to a construction permit or an amendment to an operating license under section 103 or 104 a., b., or c. specifically referred to it by the Commission.” Absent Commission referral, the ACRS review of amendments to licenses is not statutorily mandated by the AEA.
Referral of Applications for License Renewals
The direct final rule also amends §§ 52.29(d), 52.57(c), 52.177(e), and 54.25, to remove the requirement that the Commission refer license renewal applications. Section 182b. does not explicitly refer to applications for renewal of a license as requiring ACRS review. Therefore, the rescission of the corresponding regulations related to review of license renewal applications will align the ACRS's function with the AEA statutory obligations in accordance with
E.O. 14300
and promote timely and efficient licensing decisions without compromising safety.

VII. Regulatory Analysis
A. Need for the Rule
The NRC was created by Congress in 1974 to ensure the safe use of radioactive materials for beneficial civilian purposes while protecting people and the environment. The NRC protects public health and safety and advances the nation's common defense and security by enabling the safe and secure use and deployment of civilian nuclear energy technologies and radioactive materials through efficient and reliable licensing, oversight, and regulation for the benefit of society and the environment. From an economic perspective, common defense and national security are public goods for which the markets cannot maximize net benefits, and markets alone can sometimes create unintended impacts to public health and safety. Consistent with its statutory authority, NRC's regulatory framework provides reasonable assurance of adequate protection of public health and safety.
One way to conceptualize nuclear reactor licensing is not as a departure from a well-functioning market, but as a response to market failures that could cause a purely private market to produce suboptimal outcomes. Under this framework, the licensing regime exists because the market, left to itself, could systematically underprice certain risks and overproduce others.
The principal market failure is that an unregulated market may not account for the presence of significant negative externalities. A nuclear accident can impose costs on people who are not parties to the transactions between the reactor owner, its investors, its insurers, and its customers. Those costs include offsite health effects, environmental contamination, emergency response expenditures, long-term land-use restrictions, and broader economic disruption. Because these harms fall on third parties, a reactor developer may not fully internalize them when making capital investment decisions.
A second market failure that exists is information asymmetry. Reactor safety depends upon technical engineering judgments. Members of the public generally lack both the expertise and the access to evaluate whether a reactor has been designed and will be operated safely. The developer therefore possesses substantially better information than those who bear the risk. Licensing functions as a certification mechanism that reduces this asymmetry by requiring the applicant to demonstrate compliance with objective safety standards before construction or operation.
A third market failure arises from the creation of public goods in an efficient market. Much of the knowledge necessary to evaluate nuclear safety is costly but broadly beneficial once available. Because private firms cannot capture all the benefits of generating this information, they could underinvest in its development. A centralized regulator can produce and maintain this body of knowledge as a public good.
Another market failure concerns coordination. The safety of one reactor affects perception of the entire nuclear industry. A catastrophic accident at a single facility may reduce public confidence in all reactors. Individual firms therefore may have incentive to free ride on the safety investments of others while externalizing reputational risks onto the industry as a whole. Uniform licensing standards mitigate this by imposing minimum safety requirements.
These benefits must be weighed against the costs of regulation. Licensing imposes direct compliance costs and the time required to deploy new reactors, raising financing costs and exposing projects to regulatory uncertainty. Excessively prescriptive regulation may discourage innovation, favor incumbent technologies over novel designs, and create barriers to entry that reduce competition. From an economic perspective, these costs represent the deadweight losses associated with correcting the underlying market failures.
The normative justification for reactor licensing therefore depends on whether the social benefits of correcting these market failures exceed the social costs of regulation. An efficient licensing regime is one that requires applicants to internalize the expected external costs of reactor operation, reduces information asymmetries sufficiently to permit informed public and private decision-making, creates credible long-term commitments to safety, and supplies public safety information, while minimizing unnecessary delays, compliance burdens, and impediments to technological innovation.

B. Discussion
The NRC is amending its regulations to ensure the personnel and functions of the ACRS are reduced to the minimum necessary to fulfill the ACRS's statutory obligations in the AEA. By amending, removing, and providing administrative changes to these provisions, the NRC anticipates a more streamlined approval process for license renewal applications. The direct final rule will also result in alleviating the economic burden associated with the ACRS's review of license renewal applications and reactor safety research. As part of this rulemaking, the ACRS will no longer perform self-initiated reviews and will not recommend rulemaking that requires a Commission response within 90 days. These two provisions have historically been used infrequently and there is no data to determine what cost savings would occur due to their removal.
The NRC is also codifying language in § 1.13 to promote balanced expertise, provide flexibility in the ACRS's structure, and clarify the scope and conduct of the ACRS's reviews and meetings. Since its formation, the ACRS membership size has increased and decreased due to its workload. Revising § 1.13 to establish a minimum of 7 members for the ACRS is within the statutory requirement of maintaining a maximum number of 15 members. The ACRS has been operating above the minimum of 7 members with 9 members the past year; therefore, the change in regulation to include a minimum number of members does not result in a quantifiable cost savings for the NRC. This direct final rule also amends and
(
printed page 73652)
clarifies ACRS membership solicitation, screening, and qualification requirements that have been utilized by the NRC in the past. These revisions to the NRC's regulations do not result in quantifiable cost savings for the NRC, since these are matters of routine agency management.
Finally, the direct final rule's revisions to § 1.13(e) codifies existing ACRS practices relating to conduct of meetings and coordination with NRC staff. Therefore, the subpart to § 1.13 does not present any quantifiable cost savings in this direct final rule.
In addition, this direct final rule adds new clarifying language in
10 CFR part 52
for early site permit, design certification, combined license, standard design approval and manufacturing licenses that would focus future ACRS reviews. The ACRS implemented these focused reviews in June 2025, prior to this direct final rule. The NRC staff is unable to determine what cost savings would occur due to the clarification of the scope of the ACRS's review to align with the minimum statutory responsibilities of the ACRS, since there is no available data.
The remaining regulatory analysis focuses the calculations on the changes resulting from the ACRS no longer reviewing referred applications for license amendments (license renewal) or conducting studies of reactor safety research (triennial reviews).
For calculation purposes, the NRC assumed five license renewal applications per year with 85 plants anticipated for both initial and subsequent license renewals in the coming years. The ACRS normally allocates 87.5 hours to review a license renewal application. Therefore, during a one-year period, the ACRS spends a total of 437.5 hours reviewing 5 license renewals. The NRC estimates the annualized savings from rescinding the regulatory requirements for the ACRS's review of license renewal applications at $69,125, given the NRC's labor rate of $158 per hour. Moreover, during the application process, the licensee, the NRC regional staff, and the ACRS members meet to discuss the license renewal applications. The NRC staff has estimated the cost of attending this meeting at about $1,000 per person per meeting with 5 meetings occurring annually. The staff also estimates the number of participants in these meetings to be 23 in total including licensee, NRC, and ACRS personnel, at a cost of $23,000 for travel per meeting. Total annual savings for rescinding requirements for ACRS review of renewal applications is $115,000 non-discounted ($23,000 per meeting * 5 meetings annually). The staff calculated the total savings over a 17-year
[

period from rescinding ACRS involvement in license renewal applications to be $3.1 million non-discounted with total net present values (NPV) of 7 and 3 percent at $1.74 million and $2.3 million respectively. The staff assesses the annualized savings to be $184,125 discounted at both 7 and 3 percent.
In addition, the NRC is also rescinding ACRS triennial reviews of reactor safety research. The NRC observed a 50-year period for calculating the savings attributed to rescinding triennial reviews. In our analysis, the NRC determined that 17 triennial reviews would take place over a 50-year period.

The NRC also estimated that a triennial review meeting results in 430 hours of ACRS and NRC staff time. There are approximately 10 meetings that occur every triennial review period, for a total of 170 meetings throughout the 50-year period of analysis. The NRC calculated the amount of time saved from rescinding triennial reviews at 73,100 hours (430 hours per meeting * 170 meetings) over 50 years. The NRC estimated travel costs associated with triennial reviews to be $10,000 per meeting for the 170 meetings, totaling $1.7 million non-discounted. To quantify the savings from rescinding triennial reviews, the staff multiplied total hours saved over 50 years by using an NRC wage rate of $158 resulting in $11.6 million saved, non-discounted. With the combined hours saved and travel costs, the staff estimates total savings of $13.25 million non-discounted with total NPVs of 7 and 3 percent at $3.6 million and $6.7 million respectively, and an annualized savings of $259,800 at both 7 and 3 percent discount.

VIII. Backfitting and Issue Finality
This direct final rule does not constitute backfitting as that term is defined in the backfit rule in § 50.109, “Backfitting,” or affect the issue finality of an approval issued under
10 CFR part 52
, “Licenses, Certifications, And Approvals for Nuclear Power Plants,” because it does not impose new or revised requirements on existing licensees or approval holders. As a general matter, eliminating a requirement does not meet the definition of “backfitting” because such an act by the NRC would be a nonmandatory relaxation of an existing requirement. For the same reason, the elimination of a requirement would not affect the issue finality of a
10 CFR part 52
approval.

The NRC may not conduct or sponsor, and a person is not required to respond to, a collection of information unless the document requesting or requiring the collection displays a currently valid OMB control number.
XII. Executive Orders
The following are Executive Orders that are related to this direct final rule:
A.
Executive Order 12866
: Regulatory Planning and Review (as Amended by
Executive Order 14215
, Ensuring Accountability for All Agencies)
E.O. 12866
provides that the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) within the OMB will review all significant rules. OIRA has determined that this direct final rule is a significant regulatory action under section 3(f) of
E.O. 12866
; though not economically significant under section 3(f)(1). Accordingly, the NRC submitted this direct final rule to OIRA for review. The NRC has prepared an economic analysis in accordance with section 6(a)(3)(B) of
E.O. 12866
. More information can be found in Section VII of this document, “Regulatory Analysis.”
B.
Executive Order 14154
: Unleashing American Energy
The NRC has examined this direct final rule and has determined that it is consistent with the policies and directives outlined in
E.O. 14154
.
C.
Executive Order 14192
: Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation
This action is a deregulatory action as defined by
E.O. 14192
. Details on the estimated costs of this direct final rule can be found in Section VII of this document, “Regulatory Analysis.”
D.
Executive Order 14270
: Zero-Based Regulatory Budgeting To Unleash American Energy
E.O. 14270
, “Zero-Based Regulatory Budgeting to Unleash American Energy,” requires the NRC to insert a conditional sunset date into all new or amended NRC regulations provided the regulations are (1) promulgated under the AEA, the Energy Reorganization Act of 1974, as amended (ERA), or the Nuclear Waste Policy Act of 1982, as amended (NWPA); (2) not statutorily required; and (3) not part of the NRC's permitting regime. The NRC determined that the regulatory changes amended in this direct final rule are part of the NRC's regulatory permitting scheme authorized by the AEA, ERA, or NWPA. Therefore, the NRC views this rulemaking to be outside the scope of
E.O. 14270
and did not insert conditional sunset dates for the regulatory changes in this direct final rule.
XIII. Congressional Review Act
This direct final rule is a rule as defined in the Congressional Review Act (
5 U.S.C. 801-808
). However, the Office of Management and Budget has not found it to be a major rule as defined in the Congressional Review Act.

§ 1.13
Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards.
(a)
Establishment and purpose.
The Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards (ACRS) was established by section 29 of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, as amended. The ACRS reviews and reports on safety studies and applications for construction permits and facility operating licenses; advises the Commission with regard to hazards of proposed or existing reactor facilities and the adequacy of proposed reactor safety standards; upon request of the Department of Energy (DOE), reviews and advises with regard to the hazards of DOE nuclear activities and facilities; and reviews any generic issues or other matters referred to it by the Commission for advice.
(b)
Membership and qualifications.
The ACRS must consist of no fewer than seven members and no more than 15 members, appointed by the Commission. No specific years' education and experience requirement is necessary to become a member of the ACRS. Individuals appointed to the ACRS should possess demonstrated technical competence, recognized expertise in disciplines relevant to reactor safety, sound judgement, intellectual independence, and the ability to contribute effectively in a multidisciplinary advisory environment. Collectively, the membership of the ACRS should provide balanced expertise across the relevant disciplines.
(c)
Conduct of meetings and coordination with the NRC staff.
The ACRS and the NRC staff are jointly responsible for ensuring that meetings between the ACRS and the NRC staff are conducted on matters limited to the statutory responsibilities of the ACRS and matters that are novel or noteworthy.
(d)
Scope of ACRS review.
(1) The ACRS will review novel or noteworthy attributes of a facility's design, siting, and operation associated with either:
(i) Safety-related structures, systems, and components as described by the definitions outlined in NRC rules and regulations; or
(ii) Structures, systems, and components that perform safety-significant functions.
(2) This includes safety analyses and methodologies used to evaluate and classify structures, systems, and components, as well as structures, systems and components used to prevent reactor accidents and mitigate the consequences of a spectrum of analyzed events, including those used to control reactivity, ensure heat removal, or retain radionuclides to appropriately manage the radiological risks to the public.
(e)
Review of rulemakings.
When a rule is within the purview of the ACRS, as defined in paragraph (d) of this section, and under development by the NRC staff, the NRC staff will ensure that the ACRS is given an opportunity to provide advice to the Commission on the adequacy of the rule focusing on novel or noteworthy issues.
(f)
Advice and recommendations.
Nothing in this section alters the Commission's ability to consider reports and recommendations by the ACRS that are timely received, nor does it limit the Commission's ability to request additional advice from the ACRS.

SUMMARY:
The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) is proposing to amend its regulations in response to Section 4.(b) of Executive Order (E.O.) 14300, “Ordering the Reform of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.” Specifically, this proposed rule revises the NRC's regulations to reduce the personnel and functions of the Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards (ACRS) to the minimum necessary to fulfill the ACRS's statutory obligations.

as well as enter the comment submissions into ADAMS. The NRC does not routinely edit comment submissions to remove identifying or contact information.
If you are requesting or aggregating comments from other persons for submission to the NRC, then you should inform those persons not to include identifying or contact information that they do not want to be publicly disclosed in their comment submission. Your request should state that the NRC does not routinely edit comment submissions to remove such information before making the comment submissions available to the public or entering the comment into ADAMS.
II. Rulemaking Procedure
Because the NRC considers this action to be non-controversial, the NRC is publishing this proposed rule concurrently with a direct final rule in the Rules and Regulations section of this issue of the
Federal Register
. The direct final rule will become effective on February 1, 2027. However, if the NRC receives significant adverse comments by December 17, 2026, then the NRC will publish a document that withdraws the direct final rule. If the direct final rule is withdrawn, the NRC will address the comments in a subsequent final rule. Absent significant modifications to the proposed revisions requiring republication, the NRC will not initiate a second comment period on this action in the event the direct final rule is withdrawn.
A significant adverse comment is a comment where the commenter explains why the rule would be inappropriate, including challenges to the rule's underlying premise or approach, or would be ineffective or
(
printed page 73704)
unacceptable without a change. A comment is adverse and significant if:
(1) The comment opposes the rule and provides a reason sufficient to require a substantive response in a notice-and-comment process. For example, a substantive response is required when:
(a) The comment causes the NRC to reevaluate (or reconsider) its position or conduct additional analysis;
(b) The comment raises an issue serious enough to warrant a substantive response to clarify or complete the record; or
(c) The comment raises a relevant issue that was not previously addressed or considered by the NRC.
(2) The comment proposes a change or an addition to the rule, and it is apparent that the rule would be ineffective or unacceptable without incorporation of the change or addition.
(3) The comment causes the NRC to make a change (other than editorial) to the rule.
For procedural information and the regulatory analysis, see the direct final rule published in the Rules and Regulations section of this issue of the
Federal Register
.
III. Background
The ACRS was established by a 1957 amendment to the AEA as a statutory committee with an independent advisory role and focus to advise the Atomic Energy Commission. Following the enactment of the Energy Reorganization Act of 1974, the ACRS was assigned to the NRC with its statutory requirements intact. The ACRS assists the Commission's review and resolution of certain technical safety issues associated with the licensing of nuclear power plants and the establishment of NRC reactor safety regulations.
The ACRS's minimum statutory obligations are specified in sections 29 and 182b. of the AEA.
42 U.S.C. 2039
,
2232
. Since its formation, the ACRS has provided independent reactor safety advice to the Commission in the review of safety issues associated with regulation of nuclear power plants. Since 1975, the Commission has codified minimum statutory obligations and referred additional duties to the ACRS, as authorized by the AEA, in the NRC's regulations in
title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations
(10 CFR) parts 1, “Statement of Organization and General Information,” 2, “Agency Rules of Practice and Procedure,” 50, “Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities,” 52, “Licenses, Certifications, and Approvals for Nuclear Power Plants, 53, “Risk-Informed, Technology-Inclusive Regulatory Framework for Advanced Reactors,” and 54, “Requirements for Renewal of Operating Licenses for Nuclear Power Plants.” Over time, the depth of ACRS review increased beyond its statutorily required functions, for the additional duties referred to it by the Commission, and for additional reviews assumed by the ACRS without any Commission referrals. While ACRS recently began making certain improvements to perform more focused and efficient reviews, this rulemaking codifies those improvements and further redefines the scope of the ACRS reviews to ensure that the size and duties of the ACRS are consistent with the statutorily required functions and support timely and efficient licensing and rulemaking while maintaining its ability to conduct independent safety analyses.
IV. Plain Writing
The Plain Writing Act of 2010 (
Pub. L. 111-274
) requires Federal agencies to write documents in a clear, concise, and well-organized manner. The NRC has written this document to be consistent with the Plain Writing Act as well as the Presidential Memorandum, “Plain Language in Government Writing,” published June 10, 1998 (
63 FR 31883
). The NRC requests comment on this proposed rule with respect to clarity and effectiveness of the language used.
V. Paperwork Reduction Act
This proposed rule does not contain any new or amended collections of information subject to the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3501
et seq.
). Existing collections of information were approved by the Office of Management and Budget, approval numbers 3150-0011, 3150-0151, 3150-0274, and 3150-0155.
Public Protection Notification
The NRC may not conduct or sponsor, and a person is not required to respond to, a collection of information unless the document requesting or requiring the collection displays a currently valid OMB control number.
VI. Executive Orders
The following are Executive Orders that are related to this proposed rule:
A.

: Regulatory Planning and Review (as Amended by
Executive Order 14215
, Ensuring Accountability for All Agencies)
The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) within the OMB has determined that this proposed rule is a significant regulatory action under section 3(f) of

E.O. 12866

B.

C.

E.O. 14192
.
D.
Executive Order 14270
: Zero-Based Regulatory Budgeting To Unleash American Energy
E.O. 14270
, “Zero-Based Regulatory Budgeting to Unleash American Energy,” requires the NRC to insert a conditional sunset date into all new or amended NRC regulations provided the regulations are (1) promulgated under the AEA, the Energy Reorganization Act of 1974, as amended (ERA), or the Nuclear Waste Policy Act of 1982, as amended (NWPA); (2) not statutorily required; and (3) not part of the NRC's permitting regime. The NRC determined that the regulatory changes proposed in this rule are part of the NRC's regulatory permitting scheme authorized by the AEA, ERA, or NWPA. Therefore, the NRC views this rulemaking to be outside the scope of

Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106881; File No. SR-NasdaqTX-2026-057]
November 12, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”),
[
1
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
notice is hereby given that on November 6, 2026, Nasdaq Texas, LLC (“Nasdaq Texas” or “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I, II, and III below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange proposes to amend Rule General 8, Section 1(b) to provide that the installation fee and ongoing monthly fee for interfirm cabinet connectivity will apply separately to each of the two customers connected through an interfirm cabinet connectivity order, as described further below.
The text of the proposed rule change is available on the Exchange's website at
https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/​rulebook/​nasdaqtx/​rulefilings
,
and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
(
printed page 73855)
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to amend Rule General 8, Section 1(b) to provide that the installation fee and ongoing monthly fee for interfirm cabinet connectivity will apply separately to each of the two customers connected through an interfirm cabinet connectivity connection, as described below. Currently, the Exchange assesses the applicable installation fee and ongoing monthly fee only to the customer that submits the order. The other customer that accepts and participates in the connection is not separately assessed those fees. Under the proposal, each customer participating in a new interfirm cabinet connectivity connection will be assessed the existing $550 installation fee and $385 ongoing monthly fee for its respective leg of the connectivity path. For interfirm cabinet connectivity connections already in place as of the implementation date, the accepting customer will be assessed the ongoing monthly fee, but not the installation fee, for its respective leg, and the fees assessed to the ordering customer will not change.
Background
The Exchange's data center campus consists of the original data center (“NY11”), an initial expansion area (“NY11-4”), and a second expansion area (“NY11-5”) (collectively, the “Data Center” or “Data Center Campus”). Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity is a fiber-based connectivity service that links cabinets used by two different colocation customers (“Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity”) throughout the Data Center Campus. The interfirm cabinet connection consists of two customer-side legs that meet at the Nasdaq-provided distribution point:
[
3
]
one leg extends from the first customer's cabinet to the Nasdaq-provided distribution point, and the other extends from the Nasdaq-provided distribution point to the second customer's cabinet.
Before the Exchange implemented equalized connectivity
[
4
]
throughout its Data Center, a customer would order Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity through the Nasdaq customer portal and identify the customer to which the ordering customer wanted to connect, with the ordering customer being solely responsible for both the installation and the ongoing monthly fiber connectivity fees. No separate installation or ongoing monthly fees were assessed, or are currently assessed, to the non-ordering customer for its side of the Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity.
With respect to provision and installation of the service, the fiber for the Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity was provided and installed by a third-party provider or by the customer. The Exchange did not provide or install such fiber or manage such services.
Equalization places greater emphasis on the way Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity is supervised and managed, with Nasdaq taking a more central role in those functions. While customers still request the interfirm cabinet connection through the Nasdaq Customer Portal, the pre-existing fiber in the Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity has been replaced with Exchange-provided, equalized fiber. Under this structure, the Exchange supervises and audits the interfirm cabinet connection on an ongoing basis.
[
5
]
As discussed above, the Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity consists of two customer-side legs that meet at the Nasdaq-provided distribution point: one leg extends from the first customer's cabinet to the Nasdaq-provided distribution point, and the other extends from the Nasdaq-provided distribution point to the second customer's cabinet. The Exchange provides and manages the cabling and standardized demarcation points and performs inventory management, implementation support, ongoing maintenance, monitoring, audit, and operational oversight for the connection.
Both customers must act before the connection is implemented: one customer initiates the Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity order through the Nasdaq Customer Portal, and the other customer accepts it. If the second customer does not accept the order, the connection is not implemented. Each participating customer consequently receives a distinct customer-side leg of a Nasdaq-provided, Nasdaq-managed, equalized connectivity path. Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity is optional and is not required for a customer to obtain colocation services or to connect to the Exchange's trading systems.
Proposal
The Exchange proposes to retain the existing installation and ongoing monthly fees for Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity and extend their application to the non-ordering, accepting customer side of the connection. Under the proposal, each customer participating in a new Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity connection will be assessed the existing $550 installation fee and $385 ongoing monthly fee for its respective leg of the connectivity path. For Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity connections already in place as of the implementation date, the accepting customer will be assessed the ongoing monthly fee, but not the installation fee, for its respective leg, and the fees assessed to the ordering customer will not change.
The Exchange anticipates implementing the proposed rule change during the first quarter of 2027 and will announce that implementation date through an Equity Trader Alert or other customer communication.
The Exchange believes that assessing the existing fees separately to each customer appropriately reflects the Exchange's increased role in managing Data Center connectivity following Equalization. The Exchange now provides the fiber and manages, supervises, monitors, and audits the connection after installation. The proposal also aligns the allocation of fees with the structure of the service: two separately provided and managed customer-side legs join at the Nasdaq-provided distribution point, and each customer must authorize and receive the benefit of its own leg. The proposal therefore assesses each customer for the Nasdaq-provided and Nasdaq-managed connectivity furnished to that customer.
[
6
]
(
printed page 73856)
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes that its proposal is consistent with Section 6(b) of the Act,
[
7
]
in general, and furthers the objectives of Sections 6(b)(4) and 6(b)(5) of the Act,
[
8
]
in particular, in that it provides for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees and other charges among members and issuers and other persons using any facility, and is not designed to permit unfair discrimination between customers, issuers, brokers, or dealers.
The Exchange believes that the proposed fees are reasonable because each customer receives a distinct leg of an equalized connectivity path that the Exchange actively provides and manages. Each customer-side leg is a defined, Exchange-managed component of that path. Following equalization, the Exchange provides the fiber connectivity and administers the cabling, standardized demarcation points, inventory, and ongoing operational support associated with each leg, and it supervises and audits the connection on an ongoing basis. Each customer's leg is a component the Exchange implements, administers, monitors, and supports. Applying the existing $550 installation fee and $385 monthly fee to each customer is reasonable because each customer receives, and the Exchange manages, a distinct leg of the equalized path.
[
9
]
The Exchange believes this approach equitably allocates the fees among the customers that receive and use each Exchange-managed leg of the connection. Each customer receives connectivity through its respective leg of the connectivity path, and each customer is accordingly responsible for the fees associated with the connectivity provided to it. The fact that the two connectivity paths collectively facilitate communication between the customers does not alter the fact that each customer receives a separately identifiable connectivity service. The Exchange further believes that assessing each customer for its respective connectivity leg avoids requiring one customer to pay for the leg that another customer receives. The Exchange therefore believes that its methodology represents an equitable allocation of fees among the customers using Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity.
The amount of each fee is also reasonable because it is unchanged from the Fiber connectivity fee amounts currently assessed to the ordering customer for Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity and is the same amount charged for certain other Fiber connectivity offerings.
[
10
]
The Exchange also believes that the proposal is reasonable because it supports a uniformly administered and auditable Interfirm Cabinet connectivity pathway within the Data Center. As the Exchange has explained, equalization is intended to enhance the integrity of the Data Center network by establishing standardized connectivity requirements for each component of the connectivity path and exercising greater management oversight over those components.
[
11
]
A standardized, Nasdaq-managed path in which the Exchange oversees the cabling, demarcation points, and supporting architecture enhances the Exchange's ability to monitor, maintain, and audit that connectivity.
[
12
]
Each customer-side leg of Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity is a component of that path. Assessing the existing fees to each customer for its own leg allocates those fees among the customers that receive and use each Exchange-managed leg of the path and does not alter the path's availability or operation.
The Exchange further believes the proposal is reasonable because Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity is an optional service. Customers are not required to purchase Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity to obtain colocation services or to connect to the Exchange's trading systems. Rather, a customer purchases the service only if it elects to establish a fiber connection between its cabinet and the cabinet of another colocation customer, and each customer may determine for itself whether the service, at the proposed fees, is appropriate for its business.
The Exchange believes that applying the fees separately to both customers is equitable and not unfairly discriminatory because both customers receive a substantially similar customer-side service and both benefit from the Exchange's provision and ongoing management of the equalized path. Under the current billing model, only the ordering customer pays even though the accepting customer also receives a Nasdaq-provided and Nasdaq-managed leg of the connection. The proposal allocates the fees to both beneficiaries and treats the ordering and accepting customers alike. Each customer would pay the same, existing fee for the Exchange-provided and Exchange-managed leg that it receives, and no customer would be asked to bear the fees attributable to another customer's leg of the connection.
The Exchange also believes that it is reasonable, equitable, and not unfairly discriminatory not to assess the installation fee to the accepting customer for Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity connections already in place as of the implementation date. The installation fee is a one-time charge assessed when a connection is ordered and established. For a connection already in place, the connection has been established and the installation fee has already been assessed to the ordering customer. The Exchange therefore believes that it would be
(
printed page 73857)
inappropriate to assess a one-time installation charge for a connection that is not being newly established. Those accepting customers will, however, be assessed the ongoing monthly fee beginning on the implementation date, which is consistent with the Exchange's rationale for assessing each customer for the Exchange-managed leg of the connection that it receives and uses. The distinction is drawn by whether a connection is in place as of the implementation date, and not by the identity, size, or trading activity of any customer, and it applies uniformly to every accepting customer with an existing connection.
The Exchange will apply the same fee amounts and billing methodology to all similarly situated customers. The proposal does not distinguish among customers based on their identity, trading activity, or anticipated use of the connection. Rather, each new customer will pay the same installation fee and monthly fee for its own leg of the standardized, equalized connectivity path.
[
13
]
Because both parties must affirmatively participate in the Nasdaq Customer Portal order process before implementation, as described above, each customer will have notice of the fee treatment before the Exchange provisions the connection.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act.
The Exchange does not believe that the proposal will impose an undue burden on intramarket competition because it will apply the same fees to each customer participating in an Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity order. The proposal will eliminate the current difference in the ongoing monthly fee treatment of the ordering and accepting customers, each of which receives a customer-side leg of the Exchange-provided and Exchange-managed connection, and, for new orders, the difference in their installation fee treatment.
The proposal therefore will treat similarly situated customers consistently. Each customer participating in an Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity arrangement through a new order will be assessed the same installation and recurring monthly fees for its respective connectivity leg. For connections already in place as of the implementation date, the Exchange will not assess a one-time installation fee to the accepting customer because the connection has already been established, but the accepting customer will be assessed the same ongoing monthly fee as the ordering customer. This distinction turns on whether a connection is in place as of the implementation date and applies uniformly to all such connections. It does not favor or disadvantage any customer relative to another. The fees do not distinguish among customers based on their identity, business model, trading activity, or the identity of the customer with which they establish connectivity.
The Exchange also does not believe that the proposal will impose an undue burden on intermarket competition. Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity is an optional service that customers are not required to purchase to obtain colocation services or connect to the Exchange's trading systems. The proposal does not alter the availability or technical operation of the service. Instead, it applies the existing fees separately to each customer that elects to participate in and receive a customer-side leg of the connection: for new orders, the existing installation fee and ongoing monthly fee, and for existing connections, the existing ongoing monthly fee.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
No written comments were either solicited or received.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The foregoing rule change has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)(ii) of the Act.
[
14
]
At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is: (i) necessary or appropriate in the public interest; (ii) for the protection of investors; or (iii) otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission shall institute proceedings to determine whether the proposed rule should be approved or disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file number SR-NasdaqTX-2026-057 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-NasdaqTX-2026-057. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-NasdaqTX-2026-057 and should be submitted on or before December 8, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
[
15
]
Sherry R. Haywood,
Assistant Secretary.
Footnotes

                         As used in this context, a “distribution point” is a designated passive cabling node within the Data Center's structured telecommunications architecture, where backbone or feeder cabling terminates, and from which downstream cabling is routed to customer cabinets or equipment locations. Distribution points serve as standardized, auditable locations used for organizing, patching, and managing connectivity.

                        customer's cabinet.
See

                        See

(Mar. 20, 2026) (SR-NasdaqTX-2026-005); 105766 (June 24, 2026),

NYSE offers a “Data Center Fiber Cross Connect” service, for which it charges the User that requests the service an initial charge of $500 plus a monthly charge of $600 for a single cross connect, or $7,700 over the first year. 
                        See 
                         NYSE Connectivity Fee Schedule (last updated Oct. 2, 2026), Section A (Co-Location Fees). By comparison, under the proposal each customer participating in a new Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity connection would pay $5,170 over the first year for its own leg (a $550 installation fee plus twelve monthly fees of $385), or approximately 33% less than NYSE's first-year charge for a single cross connect. This comparison is based solely on NYSE's published fee schedule, which does not identify a separate charge to any other party to the connection, and the Exchange makes no representation regarding NYSE's billing practices beyond what that schedule states. The Exchange offers this comparison as context. The proposal need not replicate NYSE's fee structure to be consistent with the Act. The Act does not require an exchange to adopt another exchange's approach to pricing a similar service. The question under Section 6(b)(4) is whether the proposed fees are reasonable and equitably allocated among the persons using the Exchange's facilities, and the proposal meets that standard. Each customer would pay the same, existing monthly fee for the Exchange-provided and Exchange-managed leg that it receives. For new connections, each customer would also pay the same, existing installation fee for its leg. No customer would be asked to bear the fees attributable to another customer's leg of the connection path. Under the Exchange's current model, the ordering customer alone pays the fees for a connection in which two customers each receive a leg. Under the proposal, neither customer subsidizes the other. Each pays the same fee for its own leg, and only for the leg it receives. For connections already established as of the implementation date, the accepting customer would pay the ongoing monthly fee for its leg but not the installation fee, because that one-time fee has already been assessed to the ordering customer when the connection was established.
