Department of Justice
Executive Office for Immigration Review
8 CFR Parts 1003, 1208, and 1240
[Docket No. EOIR-26-AB37; Dir. Order No. 12-2026]
RIN 1125-AB37
(
printed page 73876)
AGENCY:
Executive Office for Immigration Review (“EOIR”), Department of Justice (“DOJ” or “Department”).
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
In February 2026, the Department issued an interim final rule (“IFR”), effective March 9, 2026, to streamline Board of Immigration Appeals (“Board” or “BIA”) procedures. The IFR's comment period closed on April 8, 2026. In this final rule, the Department responds to comments received and finalizes the IFR with minor changes.
DATES:
This rule is effective on December 17, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Jamee E. Comans, Assistant Director, Office of Policy, Executive Office for Immigration Review, 5107 Leesburg Pike, Suite 2500, Falls Church, Virginia, 22041, telephone (703) 305-0289.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
On February 6, 2026, the Department published an IFR that: (1) streamlined the process for the Board to review Immigration Judge decisions by making such review discretionary regarding certain aspects of the review; (2) established briefing schedules for cases being reviewed; and (3) streamlined other aspects of the appellate process to ensure timely adjudications and avoid adding to the Board's backlog.
See
Appellate Procedures for the Board of Immigration Appeals,
91 FR 5267
(Feb. 6, 2026). The IFR also made technical and non-substantive changes to EOIR's regulations.
See id.
These changes are discussed in more detail in Section I.C of this preamble.
The comment period for the IFR opened on February 6, 2026, and, after an extension,
[
1
]
closed on April 8, 2026, with 1,615 comments received.
In this final rule, the Department adopts as final the amendments made by the IFR with some changes. These changes are described in Section II of this preamble. In Section III of this preamble, the Department summarizes and responds to public comments received on the IFR.
A. Purpose of This Rulemaking
As discussed in the IFR, the Department issued the IFR in an effort to address lengthy and unprecedented appeal backlogs at the Board.
See
91 FR 5270
. The Department has attempted to address the Board's backlog multiple times over the years,
see
91 FR 5268-70
, yet the Board's pending caseload has continued to increase. Specifically, the Board's pending caseload increased from 35,837 cases in Fiscal Year (“FY”) 2017 to 325,774 cases in FY 2026—a nearly ninefold increase.
[
2
]
Lengthy backlogs and their accompanying adjudication delays significantly undermine the Government's efforts to effectively administer the Nation's immigration system, where many aliens with non-meritorious claims know they can potentially remain in the United States for years upon the filing of an appeal with the Board.
See INS
v.
Doherty,
502 U.S. 314, 323 (1992) (“[A]s a general matter, every delay works to the advantage of the deportable alien who wishes merely to remain in the United States.”).
These unsustainable numbers required the Department to fundamentally “reconsider[ ] the Board's role as an appellate tribunal” and, in turn, implement significant reforms to the Board's adjudicatory role and processes to better allow it to simultaneously keep up with incoming filings and meaningfully reduce its backlog.
See
91 FR 5270
. In issuing this rule, the Department ultimately determined that anything less than a significant departure from past practice would not achieve the necessary outcomes. Indeed, when the Department proposed its streamlining reforms in 2002, it laid out similar objectives to those animating this rulemaking: “(1) Eliminating the current backlog of cases pending before the Board; (2) Eliminating unwarranted delays in the adjudication of administrative appeals; (3) Utilizing the resources of the Board more efficiently; and (4) Allowing more resources to be allocated to the resolution of those cases that present difficult or controversial legal questions—cases that are most appropriate for searching appellate review.”
See
Board of Immigration Appeals: Procedural Reforms to Improve Case Management,
67 FR 7309
,
7310
(Feb. 19, 2002) (notice of proposed rulemaking). Learning from that effort, the Department decided here that, rather than continuing a path of modest and likely ineffectual changes, fundamental reform was needed.
Importantly, although the changes made in this rule are a significant departure from past Board processes—in particular, the switch to summary dismissal as the default outcome—this rule does not alter an alien's statutory right to obtain Federal court review.
See generally
INA 242,
8 U.S.C. 1252
.
B. Legal Authority
The Department issues this final rule through authority granted by section 103(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (“INA” or “the Act”),
8 U.S.C. 1103(g)
, as amended by the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (“HSA”),
Public Law 107-296
, 116 Stat. 2135.
See
91 FR 5267-68
.
C. Summary of Regulatory Changes Made by IFR
The IFR revised
8 CFR 1003.1-1003.3
,
1003.5-1003.6
,
1003.18
,
1003.38
,
1003.42
,
1003.55
,
1208.31
,
1208.35
,
1240.15
,
1240.26
, and
1240.53
in
Chapter V of title 8 of the Code of Federal Regulations
(“CFR”).
The IFR amended EOIR's regulations to:
(1) Require appeals to be summarily dismissed by a single Board Member within 15 days of the appeal being filed, except where the appeal has been referred for consideration by the Board
en banc
and a majority of permanent Board members vote to accept the appeal for further consideration within 10 days of the appeal being filed,
91 FR 5270-71
;
(2) Shorten the timeline for filing an appeal with the Board (except for appeals of asylum decisions on the merits) from 30 days to 10 days,
91 FR 5272
;
(3) Standardize briefing schedules by requiring simultaneous briefing in all appeals that are not summarily dismissed within 20 days of the Board setting the briefing schedule, with no reply briefs permitted and grants of extensions of time limited to “exceptional circumstances,”
91 FR 5272-73
;
(4) Eliminate the requirement that Immigration Judges review transcripts of their oral decisions before the Board adjudicates appeals of their decisions,
91 FR 5273-74
;
(5) Remove or revise regulatory provisions authorizing the Chief
(
printed page 73877)
Appellate Immigration Judge to either extend adjudication deadlines in particular cases or to hold cases based on pending action,
91 FR 5274
;
(6) Codify the requirement that all arguments must be raised in a Notice of Appeal to the Board, and that all other arguments will be deemed waived,
91 FR 5278
;
(7) Correct outdated regulatory cross-references,
91 FR 5274
; and
(8) Align the regulatory terminology with statutory terminology by updating the term “noncitizen” to “alien” and the term “unaccompanied child” or “unaccompanied children” to “unaccompanied alien child” or “unaccompanied alien children,” as appropriate,
91 FR 5274
.
D. Procedural Validity of the Final Rule
A few weeks after the IFR published, a group of advocacy organizations challenged it in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. On March 8, 2026, the court partially vacated the IFR, holding that certain portions violated the Administrative Procedure Act's (“APA”) notice-and-comment requirements.
See Amica Ctr. for Immigrant Rights
v.
EOIR,
822 F. Supp. 3d 119, 168 (D.D.C. 2026).
Specifically, the court vacated the following three of the IFR's amendments
[
3
]
because, in the court's view, the procedural rule and foreign affairs exemptions to the APA's notice-and-comment requirement did not apply: (1) shortening the timeline for filing an appeal with the Board (except for appeals of the merits of certain asylum decisions) from 30 days to 10 days; (2) requiring that issues not raised in the Notice of Appeal be deemed waived; and (3) requiring that appeals be summarily dismissed by a single Board Member within 15 days of the appeal being filed, unless referred for consideration by the Board
en banc
and a majority of permanent Board members vote to accept for further consideration within 10 days of the appeal being filed.
Amica,
822 F. Supp. 3d at 156-60 (procedural rule exemption analysis), 163-65 (foreign affairs exemption analysis).
However, in issuing this final rule, the Department has fully complied with the requirements of the APA, thereby obviating the basis for the
Amica
court's decision regarding these three provisions. As the Supreme Court has explained, an IFR containing all of the APA-required elements of a notice of proposed rulemaking (“NPRM”), as provided in
5 U.S.C. 553(b)-(d)
, satisfies the APA's procedural requirements.
See Little Sisters of the Poor Saints Peter & Paul Home
v.
Pennsylvania,
591 U.S. 657, 682-86 (2020). That notice of a final rule's provisions was provided via an IFR rather than an NPRM does not itself invalidate a final rule; rather, the focus is on whether fair notice was provided to the public.
Id.
at 684 (quoting
Long Island Care at Home, Ltd.
v.
Coke,
551 U.S. 158, 174 (2007)).
Here, the IFR contained all APA-required elements of an NPRM: a reference to legal authority, as required by
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(2)
(
91 FR 5267-68
); a description of the terms and substance of the rule, as required by
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(3)
(
91 FR 5270-74
); and a request for public comment, as required by
5 U.S.C. 553(c)
(
91 FR 5267
). Additionally, this final rule provides a statement of the rule's purpose and basis, as required by
5 U.S.C. 553(c)
. Further, this final rule is being published 30 days prior to its effective date, as required by
5 U.S.C. 553(d)
and reiterated in
Little Sisters
.
See
591 U.S. at 686.
In sum, this final rule is now being issued after the notice-and-comment procedures required by the APA, thus alleviating the procedural concerns raised by the
Amica
court. As such, all provisions of the rule are presumed operative on the effective date.
E. Severability
To the extent that any portion of this rule is stayed, enjoined, or held invalid by a court, the Department intends for all other parts of the rule to remain in effect. Each change may operate independently of the others and would be unaffected if any other part of the rule were stayed, enjoined, or held invalid.
II. Revisions to IFR in Final Rule
This final rule adopts the provisions of the IFR, with the following revisions:
A. Clarifying Effect of a Summary Dismissal Order
First, in response to some commenters' confusion, the Department is updating regulatory language at
8 CFR 1003.1(d)(2)(ii)
to clarify the contents and effect of a summary dismissal order for Federal court review purposes.
In the IFR, the Department included regulatory language stating that, when an appeal is summarily dismissed under the relevant paragraph, “the Immigration Judge's decision is adopted by the Board and articulates the rationale for removal that is subject to judicial review.”
8 CFR 1003.1(d)(2)(ii)
. The IFR explained that this language “would not change any existing understandings regarding when a removal order becomes final or when a petition for review must be filed.”
91 FR 5271
. Nevertheless, commenters expressed confusion over various issues relating to the processes for Board appeals and Federal circuit court petitions for review (“PFRs”), such as exhaustion or issue-preservation requirements.
Therefore, the Department is replacing this language with more specific procedures to ensure that parties and courts understand the effect of a summary dismissal order under this rule, including that such dismissal is done after consideration of the substance of the appeal. To do so, the new regulatory language mirrors the Board's pre-existing affirmance-without-opinion language in
8 CFR 1003.1(e)(4)
. For example, under this rule's summary dismissal procedures, when the Board summarily dismisses an appeal, the new regulatory language states that the Board will issue an order stating: “The Board dismisses, without opinion, the appeal from the Immigration Judge's decision. The decision below is, therefore, the final agency determination.
See
8 CFR 1003.1(d)(2)(ii)
.”
8 CFR 1003.1(d)(2)(ii)
. Moreover, the newly added regulatory language at
8 CFR 1003.1(d)(2)(ii)(C)
states that no further explanation or reasoning will be included and explains what this means for purposes of summary dismissals without opinion. Specifically, a summary dismissal without opinion shall, like affirmances without opinion, be deemed to reflect the following considerations: (1) that the result reached in the Immigration Judge's decision under review was correct; (2) that it does not necessarily imply approval of all of the reasoning of the Immigration Judge's decision; (3) that any errors in the decision under review were harmless or nonmaterial; and (4) that either the issues on appeal are squarely controlled by existing Board or Federal court precedent and do not involve the application of precedent to a novel factual situation, or the factual and legal issues raised on appeal are not so substantial that the case warrants the issuance of a written opinion in the case.
These changes will standardize the contents of summary dismissal orders issued pursuant to
8 CFR 1003.1(d)(2)(ii)
and specify the impacts of such orders, thereby reducing confusion over the scope of such orders and, relatedly, the attendant impacts they will have on issue exhaustion or
(
printed page 73878)
preservation requirements before the Federal circuit courts.
Finally, the Department is also inserting language in
8 CFR 1003.1(d)(2)(ii)
to make clear that the new summary dismissal procedure remains subject to the Board's existing prohibition on “issu[ing] a decision affirming or granting to an alien an immigration status, relief or protection from removal, or other immigration benefit, as provided in
8 CFR 1003.47(b)
, that requires completion of identity, law enforcement, or security investigations or examinations if” those checks have not been completed or need to be updated.
8 CFR 1003.1(d)(6)(i)
;
see also
8 U.S.C. 1158(d)(5)(A)(i)
(prohibiting the granting of asylum until appropriate checks have been completed regarding the applicant). Because such checks are required to be complete and current before an Immigration Judge grants status, relief, protection, or a benefit,
see
8 CFR 1003.47(g)
, under the new procedures, it is unlikely that those checks will have expired by the time the Board would summarily dismiss any appeal. Nevertheless, the inserted language makes clear that if the checks expire between the date of the Immigration Judge order and the Board's decision to summarily dismiss the appeal, then the Board must wait until the checks have been updated.
B. Clarifying Appeal Deadline for Practitioner Discipline Cases
In the IFR, the Department stated that it had reconsidered the appeal timeline before the Board and was “reducing the appeal period from 30 days to 10 days for all cases” except for certain cases involving asylum applications.
See
91 FR 5272
. Other than the narrow exception for certain cases involving asylum applications, the Department intended for the 10-day appeal deadline to apply to all appeals, including appeals from decisions of an adjudicating official in practitioner discipline cases.
See
8 CFR 1003.1(b)(13)
(providing the Board with jurisdiction over appeals filed from “[d]ecisions of adjudicating officials in disciplinary proceedings involving practitioners or recognized organizations as provided in [subpart G of
8 CFR 1003
]”).
To clarify this intent, the Department is now amending
8 CFR 1003.106(c)
to explicitly state that appeals from decisions in practitioner discipline cases must also be filed with the Board within 10 calendar days of the decision issued under
8 CFR 1003.106(b)
. The 10-day deadline applies regardless of which party files the appeal.
See
8 CFR 1003.106(c)
(noting either or both parties may file an appeal with the Board). This change will ensure that the intent of the IFR—to harmonize appellate deadlines across EOIR—is fully effectuated.
See, e.g.,
28 CFR 68.54(a)
(10-day deadline to appeal a decision of an Administrative Law Judge to the Chief Administrative Hearing Officer);
8 CFR 1003.6(c)(1)
(10-day deadline for the Department of Homeland Security (“DHS”) to file an appeal of an Immigration Judge's order to maintain an automatic stay of a custody redetermination order pursuant to
8 CFR 1003.19(i)
). Further, this change will ensure that EOIR can swiftly impose sanctions on practitioners subject to discipline as a result of criminal, unethical, or unprofessional conduct, or frivolous behavior.
8 CFR 1003.101(a)
. This change will apply only prospectively to appeals of decisions in practitioner discipline cases issued on or after the effective date of this final rule.
C. Clarifying Temporary Appellate Immigration Judge Authority To Summarily Dismiss Cases
The IFR introduced, and this rule finalizes, streamlining provisions involving the Board's expanded use of summary dismissal.
8 CFR 1003.1(d)(2)(ii)
;
see also
91 FR 5270-71
. The Department is now amending
8 CFR 1003.1(a)(4)
to clarify that Temporary Appellate Immigration Judges (“TAIJs”) have the authority to issue written orders summarily dismissing cases pursuant to
8 CFR 1003.1(d)(2)
. This was the intent of the IFR, and this change merely makes that intent explicit in the regulations to avoid confusion.
TAIJs possess all of the authority of permanent Appellate Immigration Judges, except they do not vote in the Board's
en banc
process.
See
8 CFR 1003.1(a)(4)
. They also have the experience necessary to make appropriate decisions on whether to issue orders summarily dismissing cases.
See
8 CFR 1003.1(a)(4)
(listing individuals qualified to serve as TAIJs, including “immigration judges, retired Board members, retired immigration judges, and administrative law judges” and “senior EOIR attorneys with at least ten years of experience in the field of immigration law”). Further, TAIJs are often appointed to help address fluctuations in the Board's caseload or changes in Board priorities.
See
Reducing the Size of the Board of Immigration Appeals,
90 FR 15525
,
15527
(Apr. 4, 2025) (explaining role and purpose of TAIJs). Allowing TAIJs to summarily dismiss cases will thus further advance this rule's goal of streamlining Board procedures and increasing the efficient processing of appeals. Although TAIJs do “not have the authority to vote on any matter decided by the Board
en banc,”
including whether a case should be decided pursuant to the procedures finalized in this rule or if a decision should be designated as precedent,
see
8 CFR 1003.1(a)(4)-(5)
,
(d)(2)(ii)
,
(g)(3)
, under this rule, TAIJs will summarily dismiss cases or refer them to the permanent Appellate Immigration Judges for an
en banc
vote.
The Department is not making any changes to existing regulations limiting
en banc
voting to permanent Appellate Immigration Judges. However, TAIJs “may serve as the author or panel member for a precedent decision” or may adjudicate a case assigned to them if a majority of the Board votes to decide an appeal with full briefing.
See
90 FR 15527
n.3.
D. Other Technical Changes
The Department is also making technical changes in this final rule to ensure consistency, clarity, and accuracy in the regulatory text.
First, the Department is making formatting changes to
8 CFR 1003.1(d)(2)(ii)
to add subparagraphs for readability.
Second, the Department is making a minor correction to
8 CFR 1003.1(e)(8)(ii)
to remove a reference to an “extension period.” The IFR amended
8 CFR 1003.1(e)(8)(ii)
to remove language that previously authorized the Chief Appellate Immigration Judge to extend adjudication deadlines or hold cases based on a pending precedential decision or new regulatory actions, explaining that the previous language allowed the Chief Appellate Immigration Judge to “delay cases at whim, either to avoid applying established regulatory adjudicatory timeframes or to effectuate policy goals of delaying cases.”
See
91 FR 5274
. Consistent with the removal of language authorizing the extension of adjudication deadlines, this final rule removes a reference to an “extension period” in
8 CFR 1003.1(e)(8)(ii)
and clarifies that if a dissenting or concurring panel member fails to complete his or her opinion by the end of the established time limits for adjudicating cases, the majority decision will be issued without the separate opinion.
Third, the Department is amending
8 CFR 1003.1(d)(2)(ii)
to remove the date previously listed in that provision (March 9, 2026) and clarify that all appeals of any decision issued on or
(
printed page 73879)
after the effective date of this final rule—and not the IFR—are subject to this rule's summary dismissal procedures.
Fourth, the Department is making minor terminology amendments updating the terms “Chairman” and “Vice Chairman” to “Chief Appellate Immigration Judge” and “Deputy Chief Appellate Immigration Judge,” respectively, in a relevant section of this rule.
See
8 CFR 1003.1(e)(8)(ii)
. These changes will conform the regulatory text to current EOIR terminology and thereby promote clarity and consistency.
Fifth, the Department is making a minor technical edit to
8 CFR 1003.1(e)(3)
to avoid confusion regarding the production of transcripts. After issuance of the IFR,
8 CFR 1003.1(e)(3)
stated that “[i]n any case that has not been summarily dismissed, the case management system shall arrange for the prompt completion of the record of proceeding and transcript, and the issuance of a briefing schedule, as appropriate.” The phrase “as appropriate” may not clearly convey that transcripts need not be produced in every Board case that has not been summarily dismissed. For example, the Board routinely considers several types of appeals that do not have transcripts, such as where there was no hearing to transcribe in the underlying proceeding (
e.g.,
appeals of motions to reopen or reconsider decisions and appeals of certain visa decisions by DHS), the hearing in the underlying proceeding was not recorded (
e.g.,
appeals of custody redetermination decisions), or a new transcript is not necessary or germane to the procedural posture of the case (
e.g.,
interlocutory appeals; consideration of appeals remanded from Federal court). Thus, the Department is making a minor edit to
8 CFR 1003.1(e)(3)
to make clear that, in any case not summarily dismissed, the Board will produce a transcript only if a transcript is otherwise warranted, which excludes the examples given above where the Board has historically not created a transcript.
III. Public Comments and Responses
A. General
The Department received 1,615 public comments on the IFR. Many commenters opposed the IFR based on policy disagreements, while several commenters wrote in support. In general, comments in opposition raised policy concerns about the IFR's narrowing of appellate review before the Board, and the burdens that the IFR would place on aliens and their counsel. Commenters also noted legal concerns based on purported violations of due process and the APA. In contrast, supportive commenters reiterated and reinforced the Department's concerns regarding the need to efficiently process appeals and reduce the Board's significant backlog, which they argued encourages illegal immigration into the United States due to lengthy adjudication delays. The Department has thoroughly reviewed and considered all comments received and responds to specific concerns raised by commenters below.
[
4
]
While the Department appreciates the policy-based opposition comments, ultimately, they are not persuasive for the reasons outlined below. Similarly, the Department disagrees with the results-oriented view of due process raised by many commenters, and the issues raised relating to the Department foregoing notice and comment are obviated by the issuance of this final rule, as discussed in Section I.D of this preamble.
B. Ineffectiveness of/Improper Motivation for IFR
1. Rule Based on Inappropriate Data and Reasoning
Comment:
Commenters argued that the IFR relies on erroneous data to support its determination that it is appropriate to increase the use of summary dismissal on the basis that the appealing party rarely succeeds before the Board. Commenters stated that the cited statistics were misleading because the Department's data related to successful appeals did not accurately capture cases that were remanded to an Immigration Judge. Commenters posited that the Department counted appeals given the specific decision code of “SUS,” which stands for “sustained,” but did not count the many cases that were both sustained and remanded, coded “REM,” that also reflect disagreement with the decision below. In support of their assertion, commenters provided separate data purporting to show at least 450 appeals in an approximately 14-month period that had been sustained but not marked “SUS.” Commenters also asserted that the Department should have considered other decision codes as representative of the Board's disagreement with the Immigration Judge, referencing “TER” (termination) and “ACR” (administrative closure).
Commenters also objected to the IFR's statement that the data related to the number of sustained appeals established that “the Board generally agrees with the outcome of the decision below,” because cases where the Board remands a case to the Immigration Judge or terminates removal proceedings altogether do not reflect agreement with the Immigration Judge's decision. Commenters asserted that these remanded cases, which they estimated—without citing any data or evidence to support—to number in the thousands or tens of thousands, suggest that the Board identified an error that required correction before the Immigration Court. Commenters stated that such remands should be calculated as a “substantive win” for the appealing party because the Board is required to defer to Immigration Judges on factual issues.
More broadly, commenters stated that the Department did not sufficiently explain why the Board should relinquish its appellate review function, even if there were only a small portion of sustained appeals. Commenters claimed that the fact that the Board sustained any appeals or remanded any cases to the Immigration Judge is sufficient proof that careful appellate review is warranted. Commenters also stated that the IFR's justification based on backlog statistics is flawed and said the Department has admitted that EOIR historically has not tracked case processing times accurately and has ignored Inspector General recommendations related to data integrity.
Response:
The Department disagrees with commenter assertions on this topic. As an initial point, the Department's decision to expand the use of summary dismissal rests on many grounds, not solely on the basis of the statistics with which commenters take issue.
See, e.g.,
91 FR 5270
. Even so, it is undisputed—even by opposition commenters—that the vast majority of appeals to the Board are not sustained or remanded; instead, they result in decisions upholding the underlying decisions of Immigration Judges. Thus, whether one counts Board decisions sustaining an appeal or all Board decisions resulting in a remand,
[
5
]
the
(
printed page 73880)
overall picture remains the same: the overwhelming majority of appeals to the Board—just like the overwhelming majority of appeals in court systems in the United States generally
[
6
]
—do not result in a different outcome for the appellant.
[
7
]
Similarly, counting actions that typically do not reflect a judgment regarding the merits of an Immigration Judge's decision, such as terminations or administrative closures, does not change the overall picture. Both actions, particularly in recent years, reflect policy choices, generally tied to exercises of prosecutorial discretion, that provide no commentary on the specific issues on appeal.
[
8
]
Thus, in most cases, they reflect no judgment about the merit of the appeal, only a decision that the case should not be resolved on the merits. Contrary to commenter suggestions that an “ACR” decision should be considered reflective of the Board's disagreement with an underlying Immigration Judge decision, administrative closure has been used primarily as a policy tool to avoid reaching the merits in cases where a straightforward conclusion of the case would have likely resulted in an order of removal.
See generally
EOIR, Cancellation of Director's Memorandum 22-03 (Apr. 18, 2025),
https://www.justice.gov/​eoir/​media/​1397161/​dl?​inline
[
https://perma.cc/​SH9J-CKXL
]. Before the Board, this could have involved cases where the Appellate Immigration Judge agreed with an Immigration Judge that, on the merits, an alien was properly ordered removed, but, for policy reasons, allowed the indefinite delay of proceedings through administrative closure.
Even where not used for policy purposes, termination or administrative closure generally has no bearing on whether the Appellate Immigration Judge believes the Immigration Judge erred. Thus, codes for both administrative closure and termination were properly excluded.
Additionally, the Department disagrees with commenters' claims that remands reflect disagreement with the decision below. A remand for new background checks often means that DHS was the appellant for a grant of relief to an alien and the Board dismissed DHS's appeal, but that the length of time the Board took to decide the appeal meant that the background checks had expired and new ones were required.
[
9
]
And a remand to correct a defective transcript says nothing about the merits of a case and therefore is not a “win” for either party.
Remands for further factfinding are similarly not a “win” for either party. As commenters stated, the Board is, with limited exception, precluded from engaging in factfinding and may remand a decision to the Immigration Court where it has determined that further factfinding is needed.
8 CFR 1003.1(d)(3)(iv)
. A remand for further factfinding does not, by itself, signal that the Board agrees or disagrees with the Immigration Judge's ultimate conclusions pertaining to removability or relief and protection, or whether the alien or DHS will ultimately prevail before EOIR. Rather, a remand for such purpose represents only that the Board has determined that additional factfinding is required in a particular case. The Department reiterates that including these types of remands as “wins” for the appellant—regardless of whether the appellant is an alien or DHS—is inappropriate and misleading.
Thus, although the Department appreciates commenters' views, it does not find them persuasive. Moreover, even according to some commenters' own assessments, on average over the past 25 years, fewer than 20 percent of the Board's cases were remanded to the Immigration Courts and, of that small subset, only a little more than half resulted in an “outcome that was favorable” to the alien. Extrapolating commenters' assessment to the current pending caseload, approximately 289,000 of the 325,774 currently pending cases will not be remanded or result in an outcome that the commenter would deem “favorable” to the alien.

10
]
Thus, at bottom, commenters did not present any data or analyses that undermine the Department's position that the Board affirms the Immigration Judge's underlying decision in the vast majority of cases.
91 FR 5270
. Therefore, the Department continues to believe that it is prudent to develop a framework for
(

administrative review that focuses Board resources on adjudicating cases that will be most impactful to EOIR due to the novel or complex issues involved.

en banc

8 CFR 1003.1(d)(2)(ii)

The Department also declines to add additional Board procedures, which
(

2. Rule Will Not Effectively Address Backlog
Comment:
Commenters stated that the IFR does not meaningfully address the root causes of the Board backlog. Commenters believe that the backlog is not created by the existence of full appellate review but by multiple other factors, including understaffing, expanding DHS enforcement priorities, insufficient EOIR resources, inconsistent Immigration Judge decision-making, politicized adjudications, and agency mismanagement. Commenters also disagreed with the Department's characterization that the backlog of pending appeals is a result of inefficiency. Further, commenters asserted that the IFR will not reduce the existing backlog of pending cases because it only applies prospectively. Commenters stated that a backlog is not a legal justification for shrinking individual rights and expressed that efficiency cannot come at the expense of due process. Additionally, commenters proposed several policy alternatives to the IFR that, they asserted, would reduce the backlog of pending appeals and improve efficiency.
Response:
The Department shares commenters' concerns about the Board's sizeable backlog of pending appeals. The Board's backlog impairs the timely adjudication of appeals, delays aliens' ability to access judicial review in Federal courts and hinders the efficient administration of the Nation's immigration laws. However, the Department disagrees with commenters that this rule will not effectively address the backlog.
As explained in the IFR, since 2021, the only regulatory change implemented to increase case completions was a rule to increase the number of Board members to 28, despite a rapidly growing backlog of pending appeals.
91 FR 5270
(discussing Expanding the Size of the Board of Immigration Appeals,
89 FR 22630
(Apr. 2, 2024)). That measure failed to result in a meaningful reduction of the backlog of pending appeals, and the Board's current backlog exceeds 320,000 pending appeals.
15
See id.
Even if the Board were to have additional resources and better case management, it would be unable to resolve the significant backlog of pending appeals while keeping pace with new incoming filings using the current procedures and tools available.
Id.
Accordingly, given the size of the current backlog of pending appeals and the demonstrated insufficiency of currently available procedures, the Department assessed—and continues to believe—that the streamlining changes implemented in this rule are the best way to efficiently and expeditiously resolve new appeal filings and free up adjudicatory resources to address the backlog. Commenters are correct that this rule does not apply to appeals already pending before the Board. But they are incorrect in asserting that this rule will not impact the existing backlog. The rule's streamlining measures—to wit, the implementation of default summary dismissals, condensed adjudicatory timelines, standardized filing and briefing, and more efficient transcription procedures—give the Board additional adjudicatory resources to resolve its backlog of pending appeals in a more timely and efficient manner and will prevent the backlog from continuing to grow at an unsustainable rate.
The Department acknowledges that EOIR's backlog of pending cases at the Immigration Court level is impacted by the number of initial receipts of cases from DHS, which in turn impacts the number of appeals filed with the Board. However, comments about DHS enforcement operations and its determinations about how to exercise prosecutorial authority are outside of the scope of this rulemaking and are more appropriately directed to DHS. Instead, measures such as those outlined in this rule are intended to improve EOIR's ability to efficiently complete removal proceedings and appeals even as DHS continues to enforce the immigration laws.
The Department also disagrees with comments suggesting that the Department restore the Board to a larger size to reduce the backlog. As the Department has explained, “increasing the size of the Board has not necessarily equated to a corresponding increase in the number of cases adjudicated or a reduction in the pending caseload.”
90 FR 15526
. In reality, an increased number of Board members created difficulties in administrative oversight and coherent management and strained the Board's limited legal staff.
Id.
The Department believes that this rule's procedural changes will be a far more effective way to reduce the backlog of pending cases.
[
16
]
Additionally, the Department continues to prioritize hiring Immigration Judges who are committed to following the law and to remaining neutral and free of bias, as well as other attorney and non-attorney support staff to aid EOIR's ongoing efforts to reduce the backlog at both the Immigration Court and Board levels. The Department is also utilizing Temporary Immigration Judges and TAIJs to provide additional support in reducing EOIR's backlog of cases and appeals. Still, the Department has determined that increased staffing alone is insufficient to fully address the Board's backlog absent the broader reshaping of the Board's procedures as implemented by this rule.
Separately, the Department appreciates commenters who provided streamlining and case management suggestions to improve the efficient processing of appeals, and the Department will continue to evaluate additional measures to maximize efficiency in the Board's internal operations. Overall, the Department believes that this rule is the best option for responding to the current, untenable situation at the Board.
The Department has fully considered all of commenters' proposed policy alternatives. Many of them—
e.g.,
changes to DHS immigration enforcement priorities—are well beyond the scope of this rule. Others—
e.g.,
hiring politically neutral Board members—are based on inaccurate factual premises, as all Board members are career positions chosen based on merit. Others—
e.g.,
expanding Immigration Judges' training or hiring more Immigration Judges who would hear more cases leading to more appeals—are poorly tailored to improving efficiency at the Board. Moreover, EOIR has been hiring more Immigration Judges and the likely resulting increase in appeals only underscores the importance of implementing this rule. Others—
e.g.,
allowing aliens to waive production of a hearing transcript—raise both due process concerns and would do little to address efficiency because DHS may still need a transcript for an appeal. Still others—
e.g.,
consulting with stakeholders outside of the notice-and-comment process—would accomplish little due to the binary polarization of
(
printed page 73883)
opinions on immigration by stakeholders. Most, if not all, stakeholders in the immigration field want EOIR to adopt measures that will lead to more of their preferred case outcomes—either more or fewer aliens being allowed to remain in the United States—rather than measures that improve the efficiency and performance of EOIR itself. Further, the comment period for this rule has provided stakeholders ample ability to make their thoughts known. In sum, none of the proposals is persuasive enough to warrant changing the final rule in the ways such commenters would prefer.
Comment:
Commenters stated that the Department did not consider a 2017 Booz Allen Hamilton (“BAH”) report referenced in litigation over a previous rulemaking, which commenters claimed recommended other backlog-reduction ideas, including a requirement that Immigration Judges issue written, rather than oral decisions.
Response:
The Department is aware of the 2017 BAH report, commonly called a Legal Case Study (“LCS”). However, the Department has repeatedly debunked the LCS as unscientific and unsound, first in 2018,
see
EOIR,
LOP Cohort Analysis
7 n.13 (Sept. 5, 2018),
https://www.justice.gov/​eoir/​file/​1091801/​dl?​inline=​
[
https://perma.cc/​E96E-556M
], and, more recently, in 2025,
see
EOIR, PM 25-15,
Office of Legal Access Programs
2 n.3 (Jan. 31, 2025),
https://www.justice.gov/​eoir/​media/​1387916/​dl?​inline
[
https://perma.cc/​DM54-B8DU
] (“The 2017 [LCS] was methodologically flawed due to a selection bias issue regarding its interviews with EOIR personnel and a failure to control for the biases or valences of its non-EOIR subjects. In light of these flaws, EOIR cannot necessarily validate any of the conclusions of the 2017 [LCS].”). Due to the methodological flaws in creating it, the Department does not consider any of the 2017 LCS's recommendations to be scientifically or analytically sound. Moreover, requiring written decisions—which necessarily take longer than oral decisions, slow the completion of cases, and would potentially force detained aliens to remain in custody longer—in all Immigration Court cases would delay the overall adjudication of cases at the Board, not make it more efficient.
3. Impacts to Board's Role and Functions
Comment:
Commenters stated that the Board serves an important error-correction and accountability function and asserted that the IFR functionally removes the ability of most aliens to remedy errors in decisions in their cases via an appeal to the Board. Commenters stated that the purpose of administrative appeals is to have a more careful review of a particular case, and that the IFR undermines that purpose. Commenters also asserted that Immigration Judges are more likely to engage in rushed or less detailed decision-making if they believe their decisions are unlikely to be reviewed substantively by the Board.
Commenters expressed concern that the Board would issue fewer precedential decisions if considering fewer cases with full procedures. Commenters stated that precedential decisions are important to provide clarity and uniformity across immigration adjudications. However, other commenters disagreed and asserted that fewer precedential decisions would be preferable—because commenters perceived that precedential decisions tend to disfavor aliens—and expressed policy-driven concerns regarding the IFR's stated goal of focusing Board resources to permit the Board to issue more precedential decisions.
Response:
The Department disagrees with commenters that this rule prevents aliens from raising alleged factual or legal errors for correction. First, nothing in this rule prevents the Board from accepting an appeal for further review and full briefing where an alien identifies errors of law or fact in the underlying Immigration Judge decision. Second, this rule does not change the availability of existing procedures for seeking error correction through a motion to reconsider. Indeed, aliens have a statutory right to file a motion to reconsider a decision determining that an alien is removable from the United States. INA 240(c)(6),
8 U.S.C. 1229a(c)(6)
. Such motions allow aliens to “specify the errors of law or fact in the previous order.” INA 240(c)(6)(C),
8 U.S.C. 1229a(c)(6)(C)
. To the extent that an alien feels unable to raise an error of law or fact through a Notice of Appeal, he or she may do so through a motion to reconsider. Third, this rule does not change existing Federal court review of issues over which the Federal courts have jurisdiction.
See
INA 242,
8 U.S.C. 1252
. Accordingly, several avenues remain available for an alien to raise an alleged error in an Immigration Judge's decision.
Further, commenters' suggestion that Board review is necessary to correct errors that may arise as a result of concerns related to EOIR's personnel practices and training are misplaced.
[
17
]
Immigration Judges must be qualified, are evaluated through a competitive process before being selected for their role, and receive significant training before being appointed to the bench.
See
8 CFR 1003.0(b)(1)(vii)
(stating that the Director has authority to “[p]rovide for comprehensive, continuing training and support for Board members, immigration judges, and EOIR staff in order to promote the quality and consistency of adjudications”), 1003.9(b)(2) (providing the Chief Immigration Judge with authority to “[p]rovide for appropriate training of the immigration judges and other [Office of the Chief Immigration Judge] staff on the conduct of their powers and duties”), 1003.10(a) (requirement that Immigration Judges be attorneys);
see also
EOIR, Fact Sheet: Immigration Judge Training Fact Sheet (Aug. 2026),
https://www.justice.gov/​eoir/​page/​file/​1513996/​dl?​inline
[
https://perma.cc/​Q3AK-N7ZF
]. EOIR monitors the performance of Immigration Judges and Appellate Immigration Judges and has an established process if an adjudicator's conduct falls short of EOIR's professional expectations.
[
18
]
Finally, commenters' concerns related to the Board issuing fewer precedential decisions are unwarranted. As explained in the IFR, one goal of the streamlining measures adopted in this final rule is to allow the Board to focus on resolving cases presenting novel or complex legal issues, and the Department expects that the Board will have greater bandwidth to issue precedential decisions clarifying the law for Immigration Judges to ensure consistent adjudications.
See
91 FR 5271
(“This change will allow the Board to focus on appeals with particularly novel or complex legal questions without becoming bogged down in mine-run or straightforward cases that may already be subject to being affirmed without an opinion or summarily affirmed.”). The Department also disagrees with the assertion that precedential cases will favor one party; the Board adjudicates cases based on the relevant facts and applicable law using the appropriate standard of review.
(

C. Opposition to Specific Rule Provisions
1. Summary Dismissal
a. Due Process Concerns
Comment:
Commenters expressed concern that the IFR's summary dismissal procedures undermine an alien's due-process rights by prioritizing efficiency at the expense of constitutional protections. According to these commenters, the IFR's summary dismissal procedures effectively deprive aliens of due process by eliminating individualized, meaningful review of most Board appeals. Commenters claimed this procedure diminishes the Board's function from an appellate tribunal into a discretionary screening body that will essentially “rubber stamp” Immigration Judge decisions through summary dismissal. Commenters similarly asserted that by making meaningful review of appeals by the Board discretionary rather than a guaranteed right, the IFR sacrifices fundamental fairness for the sake of efficiency.
Commenters further stated that the IFR's summary dismissal procedures restricting meaningful review by the Board will force aliens to seek judicial review in Federal court as the only recourse to meaningful review of their cases. However, commenters also pointed out that, due to jurisdiction stripping provisions in the INA, Federal courts do not have jurisdiction to review Immigration Judge decisions on discretionary applications for relief, such as adjustment of status. Commenters explained that if cases involving discretionary applications for relief are subjected to default summary dismissal, then the decisions in those cases are final and aliens will not have an opportunity to seek meaningful review of the discretionary decisions made in their cases.
Another commenter raised due-process concerns in cases involving a bilateral or multilateral agreement as described in section 208(a)(2)(A) of the Act,
8 U.S.C. 1158(a)(2)(A)
(“Asylum Cooperative Agreement” or “ACA”), asserting that Immigration Judge review is limited in those cases and that the Board is unlikely to accept such cases for review under the IFR's provisions, leaving only Federal court review, at which point aliens may be subject to prolonged detention.
Separately, commenters stated that the IFR undermines the purpose of the DOJ Recognition and Accreditation program and the work of nonprofit legal service providers. Additionally, commenters also stated that the Department did not adequately consider or address the fact that aliens will have more limited access to representation before the Federal courts because EOIR authorizes Accredited Representatives to provide immigration legal services before administrative bodies, but they cannot provide representation in Federal court.
Further, as several commenters noted, when an alien files an appeal before the Board, he or she is generally subject to an automatic stay of removal pending adjudication of the appeal. However, in the Federal courts, aliens are not subject to automatic stays of removal while their PFRs are pending. INA 242(b)(3)(B),
8 U.S.C. 1252(b)(3)(B)
. Therefore, if an alien's case is summarily dismissed under the IFR, and he or she seeks judicial review of his or her case before the Federal courts, the alien must file a motion requesting a discretionary stay of removal. If the alien's request for a discretionary stay of removal is denied, the alien could be removed before the Federal court issues a decision.
Response:
The Department disagrees that the IFR's summary dismissal procedures violate due process. As a general matter, comments on this issue either proceeded from a flawed or inaccurate understanding of due process in immigration proceedings or highlighted issues that exist under the current regulations, which are unaffected by the rule.
As an initial point, the well-established definition of “due process” is notice and a meaningful opportunity to be heard.
See, e.g., Goldberg
v.
Kelly,
397 U.S. 254, 267-68 (1970). Neither of those principles is violated by the rule. Nothing in this rule alters the substantial procedural protections available to aliens when presenting their claims before an Immigration Judge.
See generally
INA 240(b)(4),
8 U.S.C. 1229a(b)(4)
. And, as discussed further below in this section, there is no constitutional due process right entitling an alien to an administrative appeal before the Board.
Dia
v.
Ashcroft,
353 F.3d 228, 242 (3d Cir. 2003) (
en banc
);
see also Alexander-Mendoza
v.
Att'y Gen.,
55 F.4th 197, 204 (3d Cir. 2022) (“An alien's right to administratively appeal a removal order is not grounded in the Constitution.”). Nevertheless, beyond the underlying proceedings before an Immigration Judge, which themselves guarantee due process before EOIR, aliens still have notice of the right to appeal to the Board, and they still have a meaningful opportunity to do so. That the rule no longer guarantees that the Board will take more than a certain amount of time to decide an appeal does not change those fundamental facts.
However, many commenters used the term “due process” in a different, outcome-determinative sense—
e.g.,
an alien who is not granted relief or protection necessarily did not receive due process.
[
19
]
Further, many commenters considered “due process” on a continuum related to outcomes, such that their criticisms were couched in terms of “due process” because, according to commenters, “due process” means more favorable outcomes for aliens. Yet, due process is not measured by outcome, and viewing due process through a results-oriented lens is incorrect.
See, e.g.,
Walters
v.
Nat'l Ass'n of Radiation Survivors,
473 U.S. 305, 321 (1985) (noting that “we must keep in mind . . . that the very nature of the due process inquiry indicates that the fundamental fairness of a particular procedure does not turn on the result obtained in any individual case”). Because this is not the appropriate view of due process implicated by the rule, the Department strongly disagrees with commenters' assertions that the rule violates due process.
The Department emphasizes that the summary dismissal procedures employed by this rule are simply common-sense measures to help address the backlog of immigration cases pending before the Board and ensure efficient processing of cases moving forward. These procedures increase efficiency by streamlining appellate review of Immigration Judge decisions and promote fairness through expeditious review of meritorious claims. Prior to this rule, review of such cases would have been delayed behind a backlog of meritless claims. Importantly, the rule's summary dismissal procedures affect only the Board's review process, which exists only as an exercise of the Attorney General's discretion, not as a result of any constitutional requirement. Put more directly, there is no constitutional due process right entitling an alien to an administrative appeal before the Board.
Dia,
353 F.3d at 242 (quoting
Albathani
v.
INS,
318 F.3d 365, 376 (1st Cir. 2003));
Guentchev
v.
INS,
77 F.3d 1036, 1037-38 (7th Cir. 1996);
see also Alexander-Mendoza,
55 F.4th at 204.
Congress has afforded aliens subject to removal the right to a trial-type
(
printed page 73885)
hearing (removal proceedings) before an Immigration Judge.
See
INA 240,
8 U.S.C. 1229a
. Congress has also provided aliens with substantial procedural protections during removal proceedings to ensure that due process is not undermined, including notice of the charges against them, the right to be represented by counsel, and the right to examine and present evidence, among others.
See generally
INA 239, 240,
8 U.S.C. 1229
,
1229a
.
Thus, the provisions in the INA ensure removal proceedings are conducted at a meaningful time and in a meaningful manner to afford aliens full and fair hearings in accordance with standards of due process. The Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment requires nothing more.
See Antia-Perea
v.
Holder,
768 F.3d 647, 656 (7th Cir. 2014) (“Any proceeding that meets the requirements of the [INA] also satisfies the requirements of constitutional due process.”). And, as already noted, due process does not require substantive review of every determination made by an Immigration Judge in removal proceedings.
See, e.g., Dia,
353 F.3d at 242;
Guentchev,
77 F.3d at 1037.
Furthermore, the Department finds commenters' assertion that aliens will be deprived of due process because they will be unable to seek meaningful review of decisions on discretionary applications for relief before the Federal courts after summary dismissal is meritless. Fundamentally, there is no constitutionally protected due process interest in purely discretionary forms of relief.
Alkotof
v.
U.S. Att'y Gen.,
106 F.4th 1289, 1298 (11th Cir. 2024). Moreover, Federal courts retain jurisdiction to consider constitutional claims and questions of law raised in a PFR of a discretionary decision.
See
INA 242(a)(2)(D),
8 U.S.C. 1252(a)(2)(D)
. And to the extent a discretionary decision turns on a factual determination, aliens retain their statutory right to file a motion to reconsider with the Immigration Judge.
See
INA 240(c)(6),
8 U.S.C. 1229a(c)(6)
.
The Department similarly disagrees with commenters' generalized due process concerns about detention and the availability of counsel before the Federal courts. Nothing in this rule affects detention decisions made by DHS, EOIR, or the Federal courts, nor prevents aliens from obtaining counsel for the PFR process. Moreover, the rule does not affect the Department's Recognition and Accreditation Program at all, nor does it prohibit Accredited Representatives from providing representation to aliens on appeal. To the extent commenters have concerns about the lack of representation in Federal court, those concerns (1) reflect the status quo, which is unchanged by the rule and (2) are beyond the authority of EOIR to address.
Lastly, although commenters may prefer an automatic stay at the Board to a discretionary stay before the Federal courts, they have not alleged any colorable argument as to why a Federal court's denial of a motion for stay amounts to a due process violation. Congress explicitly made such stays discretionary,
see
INA 242(b)(3)(B),
8 U.S.C. 1252(b)(3)(B)
, and this rule in no way affects Federal court adjudication of any such stay motions.
See generally Nken
v.
Holder,
556 U.S. 418, 433-34 (2009) (explaining stay factors in the PFR context). Moreover, the scenario raised by commenters already existed prior to the promulgation of the IFR—
i.e.,
once the Board dismisses or denies an appeal of a removal order, then the removal order is subject to execution, absent a stay from a Federal court—and nothing in this rule would alter that situation. Further, the Department is unaware of any creditable argument that the status quo constitutes a due process violation. To be sure, aliens may not receive as lengthy a stay of removal from the Board as they currently enjoy, but a reduction in the length of a stay does not change the conclusion. If the Board's decision results in an administratively final removal order, then affected aliens will need to seek a further stay from Federal courts, just as they are required to do now in such circumstances.
Moreover, longstanding Board precedent recognizes that the stay of removal that accompanies an appeal to the Board encourages frivolous appeals.
See Matter of Holguin,
13 I&N Dec. 423, 424 (BIA 1969). The Board has been combatting appellate delays for over 55 years, and commenters' desires for continued delays are simply unpersuasive, particularly in light of the Board's increasing backlog of cases.
See id.
at 424-25 (“Frivolous and dilatory appeals are extremely wasteful of . . . this Board's limited resources. They require needless transcription of the records of deportation hearings. They impinge upon the time and professional attention needed for truly meritorious cases, of which there are many. Effective administration of the immigration laws requires that we discourage frivolous appeals. We try to do this by expediting our consideration and decision in appeals of that sort.”).
b. Statutory Concerns
Comment:
Numerous commenters expressed concern that the IFR's summary dismissal procedures violate the INA. Commenters stated that the INA creates a statutory right to “meaningful” administrative review before the Board, citing for example, to sections 101(a)(47)(B), 240(c)(4)(C) and (c)(5), and 292 of the Act,
8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(47)(B)
,
1229a(c)(4)(C)
and
(c)(5)
, and
1362
, as well as Supreme Court precedent such as
DHS
v.
Thuraissigiam,
591 U.S. 103 (2020), and
Garland
v.
Ming Dai,
593 U.S. 357 (2021). Commenters claimed that the IFR's summary dismissal procedures violate this statutory right to appeal by treating such appeals as discretionary, with many appeals likely to be summarily dismissed without any review.
Further, some commenters claimed that certain INA provisions also provide for baseline procedural requirements. For example, commenters pointed to language in section 101(a)(47)(B) of the Act,
8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(47)(B)
, referencing a “determination” by the Board “affirming” an order as requiring a substantive review and decision on each appeal. Similarly, commenters argued that the statutory right to counsel “in any appeal proceedings before the Attorney General” in section 292 of the Act,
8 U.S.C. 1362
, and the rebuttable presumption of credibility “on appeal” in section 240(c)(4)(C) of the Act,
8 U.S.C. 1229a(c)(4)(C)
, would be rendered superfluous if the Board did not conduct a substantive review in each case. Also, commenters asserted, Congress would not have set such a significant Board appeal filing fee in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act
[
20
]
if appeals were going to be summarily dismissed as the default.
Commenters further stated that the IFR's summary dismissal procedures are contrary to the INA's exhaustion requirements in section 242(d)(1) of the Act,
8 U.S.C. 1252(d)(1)
, because the summary dismissal procedures make the Board's administrative appeal process discretionary, which conflicts with the exhaustion statute's references to exhausting all administrative “remedies” that are available to the alien “as of right.” Citing
Santos-Zacaria
v.
Garland,
598 U.S. 411 (2023), commenters explained that this statutory language provides an administrative remedy through the Board appeal process as a matter of right, and they argued that the IFR's summary dismissal procedures violate this right by treating appeals as discretionary by default, thereby preventing aliens from receiving meaningful review of their claims.
(
printed page 73886)
Commenters further argued that to hold otherwise would render section 242(d)(1) of the Act,
8 U.S.C. 1252(d)(1)
, superfluous, as there are no other administrative remedies available under the INA for aliens in removal proceedings to exhaust other than a Board appeal.
Response:
The Department disagrees with commenters that the IFR's summary dismissal procedures violate the INA. As an initial matter, commenters mischaracterize the appellate process contained in the rule as discretionary; it is not. The rule still allows an alien to file an appeal and requires the Board to review the appeal. It does not authorize the Board to reject an appeal out of hand without review, as a matter of discretion or otherwise. This mischaracterization compounds commenters' confusion of an alien's ability to file an appeal—which the rule does not alter—with an alien's alleged entitlement to a non-summary decision by the Board, which is not located in any text of the INA. Assuming there is a statutory right to an appeal to the Board located in the INA,
[
21
]
this rule does not alter that right. In other words, this rule's summary dismissal procedures do not address an alien's ability to file an appeal; rather, the rule modifies the Board's procedures after such an appeal has been filed.
Further, as some commenters acknowledged, the INA does not contain any explicit references to—let alone mandates for—specific Board procedures. Rather, the statute contains one explicit reference to the Board,
see
INA 101(a)(47)(B),
8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(47)(B)
, and a handful of cursory references to “appeals” or “administrative appeals,”
see, e.g.,
INA 208(d)(5)(A)(iii)-(iv),
8 U.S.C. 1158(d)(5)(A)(iii)-(iv)
; INA 238(a)(3)(A),
8 U.S.C. 1228(a)(3)(A)
; INA 240(c)(5),
8 U.S.C. 1229a(c)(5)
; INA 292,
8 U.S.C. 1362
.
Most importantly, far from creating a detailed statutory framework for administrative appeals, these provisions are silent as to the form or structure of such appeals. Indeed, Congress could have—and can at any time—provide for specific procedures for administrative appeals, just as Congress provided extensive procedures for removal proceedings before Immigration Judges.
See
INA 240,
8 U.S.C. 1229a
et seq.
But Congress has not done so. Rather, to the extent the statute creates any right to an administrative appeal, Congress has remained silent as to the procedures for adjudicating any such appeals; those procedures are thus left to the Attorney General to prescribe by regulation.
See
HSA 1102, 116 Stat. at 2273-74; INA 103(g)(2),
8 U.S.C. 1103(g)(2)
;
see also Dia,
353 F.3d at 237;
Blanco de Belbruno
v.
Ashcroft,
362 F.3d 272, 280 (4th Cir. 2004) (“One section of the INA refers to the existence of the BIA . . . and other sections refer to an administrative appeal for asylum seekers . . . . But the INA is simply silent as to what procedures should apply to that appeal . . . . This fact suggests that the INA vests broad discretion in the Attorney General to fashion the procedures of the BIA.”).
So long as such procedures are constitutionally permissible and such regulations comply with the APA—as the Department believes the IFR and this final rule are and do—the Attorney General has the full authority to modify such procedures by regulation to address problems as they arise.
See Zhang
v.
Dep't of Justice,
362 F.3d 155, 157 (2d Cir. 2004);
Blanco,
362 F.3d at 280;
see also Vt. Yankee Nuclear Power Corp.
v.
Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc.,
435 U.S. 519, 524 (1978) (“Even apart from the Administrative Procedure Act this Court has for more than four decades emphasized that the formulation of procedures was basically to be left within the discretion of the agencies to which Congress had confided the responsibility for substantive judgments.”).
Under the Attorney General's authority, the Department has carefully reviewed Board processes in an attempt to address critical backlogs at the Board, just as it did over 25 years ago in its past streamlining efforts,
see, e.g.,
Executive Office for Immigration Review; Board of Immigration Appeals; Streamlining,
64 FR 56135
,
56137-38
(Oct. 18, 1999), and attempted to further address in 2020,
see
Appellate Procedures and Decisional Finality in Immigration Proceedings; Administrative Closure,
85 FR 81588
(Dec. 16, 2020). Recognizing that past streamlining efforts, while beneficial, have not kept pace with unprecedented appeal numbers, the Department understood that dramatic changes were necessary.
See
91 FR 5268-70
. Those changes include, as relevant here, shifting the administrative appellate process to expand the use of summary dismissal to allow the Board to focus its resources on issuing written opinions in cases presenting novel or complex legal issues. The Department believes that this summary dismissal change will create significant efficiencies and make a meaningful difference in addressing the Board's lengthy backlog.
Additionally, the Department disagrees that any of the statutory references or cases cited by commenters create any specific procedural requirements before the Board. Some commenters pointed to references in section 101(a)(47)(B) of the Act,
8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(47)(B)
, to a “determination” by the Board “affirming” an order as creating requirements for the Board to review each appeal and issue a substantive opinion. However, commenters read too much into this language, and that argument has been rejected by Federal courts previously during litigation over prior regulations streamlining Board procedures.
See, e.g., Dia,
353 F.3d at 237 (explaining that section 101(a)(47)(B) “says absolutely nothing about procedures to be employed by the BIA, or the right to, or manner of, review generally”). This definitional language simply explains when an order of deportation is final, which is when a Board's order is issued or, if no appeal is taken, when the appeal period ends. In no way does this language convey any substantive requirements for what such a Board order must contain, much less the procedures by which the Board must issue an order.
Atemnkeng
v.
Barr,
948 F.3d 231, 239 (4th Cir. 2020);
Blanco,
362 F.3d at 280;
Dia,
353 F.3d at 237.
Furthermore, this rule is consistent with the INA's language. Under this rule's summary dismissal procedures, if the Board does not vote
en banc
to accept an appeal for full briefing and further review, the Board will dismiss the appeal without opinion by issuing an order summarily dismissing the alien's appeal. However, in no way does that suggest that the Board did not review the appeal; instead, it simply means the Board did not find it worthy of further consideration.
See
8 CFR 1003.1(d)(2)(ii)
.
Commenters' references to other sections of the INA are similarly misplaced. The ability to retain counsel during the Board appeals process, INA 292,
8 U.S.C. 1362
, or to maintain a rebuttable presumption of credibility on appeal, INA 208(b)(1)(B)(iii),
8 U.S.C. 1158(b)(1)(B)(iii)
, are discrete provisions that provide exactly what they state—no more, no less. Neither provision is affected by the IFR's summary dismissal procedures; aliens continue to have the statutory right to counsel during the Board appeals process, as well as a rebuttable presumption of credibility during the appeals process, when applicable.
(
printed page 73887)
Similarly, commenters argued that the INA's exhaustion statute for Federal court review in section 242(d)(1) of the Act,
8 U.S.C. 1252(d)(1)
, requires aliens to exhaust administrative remedies available “as of right,” which in turn requires Board appeals to be treated as a legal entitlement with no discretion to deny review under
Santos-Zacaria,
598 U.S. at 424-26. However, as explained in the IFR, the Department drafted the IFR with the intention that the rule “would not change any existing understandings regarding when a removal order becomes final or when a petition for review must be filed.”
See
91 FR 5271
. Put differently, nothing about the rule affects section 242(d)(1) of the Act,
8 U.S.C. 1252(d)(1)
, because the rule does not affect an alien's ability to seek review by the Board.
In sum, “[a]bsent constitutional constraints or extremely compelling circumstances, the administrative agencies should be free to fashion their own rules of procedure and to pursue methods of inquiry capable of permitting them to discharge their multitudinous duties.”
Vt. Yankee Nuclear Power Corp.,
435 U.S. at 543 (internal quotations omitted). That is all the Department has done here.
c. Additional Concerns With Summary Dismissal
Commenters raised a number of additional miscellaneous concerns regarding the IFR's summary dismissal procedures. The Department acknowledges the comments and has thoroughly considered them; however, none is persuasive, and the criticisms in them are vastly outweighed by the efficiency benefits that the rule would provide.
Comment:
Commenters stated that summarily dismissing most appeals will allow erroneous legal decisions by Immigration Judges to stand, thereby undermining EOIR's mission to adjudicate immigration cases by fairly and uniformly interpreting immigration laws, as well as likely leading to erroneous removals.
Response:
If an alien's appeal to the Board is summarily dismissed, the alien may raise any alleged legal errors made by the agency before the Federal circuit courts for further review, except where Congress has expressly stated that Federal court review is not available. Additionally, the alien may file a motion to reconsider before the Immigration Court or the Board, as applicable. Under the current procedures, there is also a risk of erroneous decisions by Immigration Judges being affirmed by the Board.
[
22
]
Because the Board will still review each appeal, however, the rule does not alter the possibility of the Board making an erroneous decision. Moreover, as is the case now, erroneous decisions by the Board will still be subject to correction by Federal courts.
Comment:
Commenters similarly noted that summary dismissal will functionally exhaust all appeal options for most types of claims for discretionary immigration relief.
Response:
This point describes the situation currently, which is unchanged by the rule. Once the Board rules on an appeal regarding a discretionary form of relief other than asylum, there is limited recourse to Federal court. The rule does not alter that dynamic.
Comment:
Commenters argued that Federal court review is not sufficient, as Federal courts have narrower jurisdiction and use more deferential standards of review than the Board, and that PFRs serve a fundamentally different purpose: to review the appellate determinations made by the Board.
Response:
The scope of Federal court review, including comments related to jurisdiction and applicable standards of review, is outside the scope of the rule, and the Department declines to predict how Federal courts will interpret the provisions of the rule. The Department emphasizes, however, that this rule does not change any procedures related to seeking Federal court review or existing substantive standards that constrain Federal court jurisdiction.
Nothing in this rule affects the baseline process of filing a PFR to allege errors in the underlying proceedings. Immigration Judges will continue to issue decisions in removal proceedings, which may then be addressed by the Board through a summary dismissal order or an adjudication with briefing. Regardless of how the Board chooses to handle a specific appeal, the alien will then maintain the existing ability to further file a PFR of that decision with the relevant Federal court, which will accept briefing and provide further review of the alleged issues according to existing procedures.
See, e.g.,
INA 242(b),
8 U.S.C. 1252(b)
(providing requirements and standards for PFRs).
With regard to the alleged limitations of Federal court review, the Department notes that Congress explicitly exempted from review denials of certain discretionary forms of relief and factual issues when the alien is removable on certain criminal grounds.
See
INA 242(a)(2)(B)-(D);
8 U.S.C. 1252(a)(2)(B)-(D)
. If Congress wished to provide specific procedures for administrative review of such claims in lieu of or in addition to Federal court review, or to provide certain standards of review for any administrative appeals, it could certainly do so; but it has not. Instead, Congress chose to explicitly limit Federal court review while leaving any administrative appellate processes and standards to the Attorney General.
See, e.g., Dia,
353 F.3d at 237 (“[I]t seems clear that Congress has left all procedural aspects of the BIA, especially how it hears cases, entirely to the Attorney General's discretion.”). As a result, in implementing this rule's summary dismissal procedures, the Department balanced any limitations on the availability of Federal court review, among other concerns, with the strong need to address the Board's growing backlog of overwhelmingly straightforward cases.
See
91 FR 5271
.
In doing so, the Department also notes that, in addition to PFRs in the Federal courts, Congress explicitly provided aliens with a statutory right to file a motion to reconsider an Immigration Judge's removability decision.
See
INA 240(c)(6),
8 U.S.C. 1229a(c)(6)
. As the statute clearly states, such motions are intended to address “errors of law or fact in the previous order . . . .” INA 240(c)(6)(C),
8 U.S.C. 1229a(c)(6)(C)
. Thus, to address the kinds of potential Immigration Judge errors raised by commenters, Congress provided aliens with an additional statutory process for correcting such errors.
Comment:
Commenters stated that the IFR did not include a timeline for single Board members to refer a case for consideration by the Board
en banc.
Commenters asserted that this could result in a scenario where a case is automatically dismissed because the timeline to vote to consider an appeal has passed. Commenters also noted that if the Board does not have a quorum, it will be unable to vote to consider an appeal, and all cases would be summarily dismissed until a quorum is available. Commenters worried that meritorious appeals could be summarily dismissed if the Board lacks sufficient members. Alternatively, commenters claimed that without a quorum, DHS would instead refer all potential Board appeals to the Attorney General in lieu of Board review.
Response:
The Department is confident that the Board will have no
(
printed page 73888)
issues establishing a quorum to vote on whether to accept appeals for full briefing and further consideration and thus does not share commenters' concerns that DHS will make large numbers of referrals directly to the Attorney General to bypass the Board. Further, it is unnecessary to provide specific timelines for single member referrals in this rule, as the Department expects that the Board will implement internal case-processing procedures to ensure compliance with the timelines in this rule.
Comment:
Commenters noted that the rule does not contain any standards for determining whether an issue is sufficiently novel or complex to warrant further Board adjudication.
Response:
There is no universal standard for determining novelty or complexity, and the Department believes that it is an issue best reserved for the Board to determine on a case-by-case basis.
The Department also clarifies that the rule itself does not explicitly limit the Board to only adjudicating “novel or complex” issues and, as such, has no need to set any such regulatory standards interpreting these terms.
See
8 CFR 1003.1(d)(2)(ii)(A)
(only requiring a Board vote on whether to accept an appeal for full briefing and further consideration). Rather, the Department expects that the Board will, in its discretion, focus its resources on requesting further briefing and issuing written opinions in appeals presenting novel or complex legal or factual issues, rather than mine-run appeals involving issues sufficiently addressed by the Immigration Judge or controlled by existing Board or Federal court precedent.
Comment:
Commenters raised concerns that summary dismissal will occur before briefing, which is where novel or complex legal issues often surface. Commenters also stated that Board members will have to vote whether to accept a case for adjudication without the benefit of a full record or briefing, which will prevent Board members from fully determining the legal and factual issues in the proceedings before the Immigration Judge.
Response:
These comments proceeded from erroneous factual premises. First, even under current rules, issues must be raised in the Notice of Appeal—before briefing—or else they will be waived. Thus, if an issue does not surface until briefing, it will be waived anyway, and the Board will not consider it. Consequently, the commenters' concerns are misplaced.
Second, the Board will have the full record of proceedings from the Immigration Court when it considers the appeal, including the Immigration Judge's written decision, if applicable, as well as access to the hearing recordings and the Notice of Appeal, which, for purposes of notifying the Board of the legal and factual issues for review, serves a similar function to the appellant's brief, as it must identify the alleged errors made by the Immigration Judge. Should the Board decide it needs further information and orders briefing, the appellant would expand upon those issues in his or her brief.
See Matter of Valencia,
19 I&N Dec. 354, 355 (BIA 1986) (“Depending on the complexity of the issues raised, a brief may be essential to an adequate presentation of the appeal. In all cases, however, the reasons for an appeal must be meaningfully identified on the Notice of Appeal.”).
Novel or complex issues or obvious errors in an Immigration Judge decision can be easily signaled in a Notice of Appeal. For example, underlying criminal convictions often create complex issues in immigration law, but those issues can be succinctly summarized in the Notice of Appeal sufficient to flag for the Board a specific legal issue on which the Board could determine whether to accept the appeal for full briefing and further review. If the Board then voted affirmatively, a briefing schedule would subsequently be issued to fully develop the arguments.
Comment:
Commenters stated that summary dismissal would affect cases where administrative review is most necessary, such as appeals filed pro se or under emergency conditions.
Response:
The Board will determine whether fulsome review is necessary, and there is no statutory, regulatory, or other legal basis to mandate that all appeals of a particular category automatically receive full review. Moreover, the Department does not believe that there is a policy justification weighing in favor of requiring full briefing of appeals filed by certain classes of aliens. The most efficient use of the Board's limited resources is to decide appeals involving novel or complex legal or factual situations. Commenters offered no data indicating that the personal characteristics of a specific alien (for example, pro se or detained) make the substantive legal basis of the alien's appeal any more likely to involve such issues. Thus, rather than treating certain categories of aliens as automatically entitled to further consideration after additional briefing, it is better policy for the Board to consider all appeals equally and determine whether the legal claims themselves merit further consideration.
Comment:
Commenters also stated that the rule would favor DHS. For example, because a single Board member would decide whether to refer a case to
en banc
