Petitioner:
Coeur Alaska Inc., 3031 Clinton Drive, Suite 202, Juneau, AK 99801.
Mine:
Kensington Mine, MSHA ID No. 50-01544, located in Juneau, Alaska.
Regulation Affected:
30 CFR 57.6603
, Air gap.
Modification Request:
The petitioner requests modification of the application of
30 CFR 57.6603
to permit an alternative method of complying with the requirement to maintain a minimum 15-foot air gap between electric power lines and blasting lines.
The petitioner states that:
(a) The petitioner requests a clarification of
30 CFR 57.6603
to permit the use of non-electric (NONEL) shock tube and electronic detonator initiation systems. The section currently calls for maintaining a minimum 15-foot air gap between electric power lines and blasting lines in underground drifts but does not specify if it pertains to electronic or electric initiation means. The current practice at Kensington is to maintain a minimum of 2 feet between blast and electrical lines, as per
30 CFR 57.6308
manufacturer (Dyno Nobel) recommendations for the electronic initiation system. The petitioner would like to continue this workflow—using a central blast system to initiate electronic detonators and subsequently NONEL detonators in the hole.
(b) The petitioner operates an underground metal/nonmetal mine with numerous existing drifts ranging from approximately 10 to 16 feet in width.
(c) Due to these dimensional constraints, maintaining a 15-foot air gap between installed electric power lines and blasting lines, as required by § 57.6603, is not feasible in certain areas without significantly altering mine infrastructure.
(d) The petitioner currently utilizes blasting initiation products along with central blasting hardware and software from Dyno Nobel.
(e) The petitioner utilizes NONEL (non-electric) shock tube and Driftshot Starter electronic initiation systems for development blasting activities. For the latter, the system is initiated via a central blast computer that requires both a coded signal and a blast specific voltage to trigger an initiation response in the Driftshot Starters.
(f) Production blasts adopt the same principal but are fully electronic and do not rely on NONEL delays.
(g) Unlike traditional electric blasting caps, Dyno Nobel electronic systems are not susceptible to stray electrical currents, or induced voltages from nearby energized power lines. They require a secondary coded signal and specific voltage to be initiated. The continuous communication between the central blast system and the blast control units would throw a fault and prevent initiation should this state be upset and left unresolved. The petitioner also submitted an official certification from electrical testing taken by Detnet—who partnered with Dyno Nobel when developing the electronic initiation systems.
(h) After a successful handshake between the Driftshot starters and central blasting computer, a blasting voltage is initiated from the blast control units down the blast lines. The blast lines are attached to the Driftshot starters via a segment of harness wire. The Driftshot starters are attached to a segment of Detcord, which in turn sets off the NONEL caps with appropriate delays.
(i) High voltage testing up to 30 kV and lightning simulations were performed on the electronic detonators. No degradation in performance was reported and there was no unplanned initiation.
(j) Kensington is compliant with
30 CFR 57.6308
, wherein initiation systems have been installed, and used, in accordance with the manufacturer's recommendations. Dyno Nobel has recommended a minimum of 2 feet separation between live electrical wires and trunk/harness wires. Should there be a need to cross over the two lines, these can be done on a 90 degree angle, with a slight drop on the blast line.
(k) The existing standard was developed primarily to address hazards associated with electric detonators and the risk of premature initiation due to electrical energy.
(l) The application of the 15-foot air-gap requirement to Kensington's current electronic initiation systems does not directly address the same hazard profile and presents operational challenges in narrow underground headings.
(
printed page 73807)
(m) Detnet has been used reliably throughout the industry and Kensington since its implementation. It has also undergone rigorous testing that renders
30 CFR 57.6603
not applicable for this scenario.
(n) Electronic initiation systems differ from the susceptibility of stray currents as with electric initiation—and require several more steps for positive initiation.
(o) Kensington has implemented the electronic initiation system as per
30 CFR 57.6308
, and separated blast cables double the distance away from high voltage lines.
(p) Should faults occur, problem areas cannot be blasted until the problem is resolved.
(q) Electric detonators have been removed from Kensington underground, as per manufacturer recommendation.
(r) The petitioner states that the proposed alternative method provides no less than the same measure of protection while allowing safe and practical blasting operations within existing underground constraints.
The petitioner proposes the following alternative method:
(a) All development blasting initiation shall be conducted using NONEL shock tube and Driftshot electronic starter systems. No electric detonators shall be used in the mine without leadership approval.
(b) Shock tubes shall be visually inspected prior to use to ensure integrity and proper condition.
(c) Blasting circuits shall continue to be physically organized and secured to prevent entanglement, abrasion, or damage from mobile equipment. Audits shall also be conducted on new and existing headings to ensure compliance with manufacturer install guidelines.
(d) Detnet user manuals have suggested that a 1 foot minimum is sufficient for separation between live cable and blast line infrastructure. However, Dyno Nobel guidelines prefer a 2 foot separation to further reduce noise interference in electronics.
(e) Electric power lines shall be properly installed, insulated, and maintained in accordance with applicable MSHA standards.
(f) Blasting activities shall be conducted in accordance with established safe blasting procedures, including clearing, guarding the blast area, and only connecting the blast lines at end of shift.
(g) All personnel involved in blasting operations shall be trained in the safe handling and use of NONEL and electronic systems, including recognition of potential hazards and proper setup techniques.
(h) Misfire procedures specific to NONEL and electronic systems are in place and shall be strictly followed.
(i) The miners at Kensington Mine are represented by a miners representative and the petition for modification has been served to the miners representative on May 10, 2026.
In support of the petition, the petitioner provided additional information including manufacturer safety and testing documentation, Detnet and Dyno Nobel cable installation recommendations, and a manufacturer note on electronic vs. electric detonators.
The petitioner asserts that the alternative method will guarantee no less than the same measure of protection afforded the miners under the mandatory standard.

AGENCY:
Mine Safety and Health Administration, Labor.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
This notice is a summary of a petition for modification submitted to the Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) by Crimson Oak Grove Resources, LLC.
DATES:
All comments on the petition must be received by MSHA's Office of Standards, Regulations, and Variances on or before December 17, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments and informational materials, identified by Docket No. MSHA-2026-1026, electronically at the Federal eRulemaking Portal,
https://www.regulations.gov
.
Follow the online instructions for making electronic submissions. You should not include personal or proprietary information that you do not wish to disclose publicly. If you mark parts of a comment as “business confidential” information, MSHA will not post those parts of the comment. Otherwise, MSHA will post all comments without change, including any personal information provided. MSHA cautions against submitting personal information.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Corliss A. Josephs-Conway, Acting Director, Office of Standards, Regulations, and Variances at 202-693-9440 (voice);
Petitionsformodification@dol.gov
(email); or 202-693-9441 (fax). These are not toll-free numbers.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Section 101(c) of the Federal Mine Safety and Health Act of 1977 and
Title 30 of the Code of Federal Regulations
(CFR) part 44 govern the application, processing, and disposition of petitions for modification.
I. Background
Section 101(c) of the Federal Mine Safety and Health Act of 1977 (Mine Act) allows the mine operator or representative of miners to file a petition to modify the application of any mandatory safety standard to a coal or other mine if the Secretary of Labor determines that:
1. An alternative method of achieving the result of such standard exists which will at all times guarantee no less than the same measure of protection afforded the miners of such mine by such standard; or
2. The application of such standard to such mine will result in a diminution of safety to the miners in such mine.
In addition,
30 CFR 44.10
and
30 CFR 44.11
establish the requirements for filing petitions for modification.
II. Petition for Modification
Docket Number:
M-2026-026-C.
Petitioner:
Crimson Oak Grove Resources, LLC, 8800 Oak Grove Mine Road, Adger, AL 35006.
Mine:
Oak Grove Mine, MSHA ID No. 01-00851, located in Jefferson County, AL.
Regulation Affected:
30 CFR 75.507-1(a)
, Electric equipment other than power-connection points; outby the last open crosscut; return air; permissibility requirements.
Modification Request:
The petitioner requests modification of the application of
30 CFR 75.507-1(a)
to permit the use of non-permissible electronic testing or diagnostic equipment located in return air outby the last open crosscut (subject area).
The petitioner states that:
(a) The equipment allowed under the Proposed Decision and Order (PDO)
(
printed page 73801)
granted by MSHA (low voltage or battery-powered non-permissible electronic testing and diagnostic equipment) shall be limited to: AMS 2140 Machinery Health Analyzer; laptop computers; oscilloscopes; insulation testers (meggers); signal analyzer devices; ultrasonic measuring devices; electronic component testers; and electronic tachometers for testing or troubleshooting mining equipment. Fault detectors are not allowed in the subject area.
(b) Where commercially available, the operator must use equipment that meets IEC 60079-11 or the ANSI/UL 60079-11 for two-fault IS (marked ia), one-fault IS (marked ib), or no-fault IS (marked ic) in that order of preference. The equipment must have an IP 66 rating or higher when available. When an IP 66 rating is not available, the highest IP rating available must be used. When equipment contains lithium batteries, the equipment must meet lithium battery safety standard UL1642 or IEC 62133. All other equipment in the subject area must be permissible.
(c) A record for this equipment shall be maintained on mine property either in a secure book or electronically in a secure computer system not susceptible to alteration. The record will contain the date of manufacture and/or purchase of each particular piece of electronic testing and diagnostic equipment and include proof of compliance with any lithium battery safety standard. The original equipment manufacturers' user and maintenance manuals shall be followed and maintained on mine property. The record and manuals shall be made available to Authorized Representatives of the Secretary and miners at the mine.
(d) This equipment shall be used only:
(1) until MSHA-approved permissible electronic testing and diagnostic equipment is available;
(2) if mechanical equipment is not commercially available that can perform the work; or
(3) when the mining equipment being tested cannot be towed or moved under its own power to intake air, out of the subject area.
The petitioner proposes the following alternative method:
(a) The equipment to be used in the subject area shall be examined by a qualified person, as set forth in
30 CFR 75.153
, prior to taking the equipment underground to ensure the equipment is being maintained in a safe operating condition. At a minimum, the qualified person conducting the exam shall:
(1) Check the instrument for any physical damage and the integrity of the case;
(2) Remove the battery and inspect for corrosion;
(3) Inspect the contact points to ensure a secure connection to the battery;
(4) Reinsert the battery and power up and shut down to ensure proper connections;
(5) Check the battery compartment cover or battery attachment to ensure that it is securely fastened; and
(6) For equipment utilizing lithium type cells, ensure the lithium cells and/or pack are not damaged or swelled in size.
(b) The equipment shall be examined at least weekly by a qualified person as required by
30 CFR 75.512-2
and the exam results shall be recorded weekly in the equipment's record. Examination entries in the record may be expunged after one year.
(c) The equipment shall be serviced according to the manufacturers' recommendations. Dates of service shall be recorded and include a description of the work performed.
(d) The equipment shall not be put into service until MSHA has initially inspected the equipment and determined it is in compliance with all the terms and conditions of the PDO granted by MSHA. The equipment shall be tested for potential adverse effects of Radio Frequency Interference (RFI) and Electromagnetic Interference (EMI) for any disturbances with performance of remote control transmitters, atmospheric monitoring systems, fire sensors, machine-mounted methane monitors, hand-held detectors, miner's cap lamps, tracking and communication systems, proximity detection systems, etc. A record of the test performed, similar to those conducted by NIOSH, shall be maintained on mine property for the service life of the equipment and made available to MSHA upon request. MSHA should be notified at least 5 working days before such testing will be performed.
(e) The equipment shall not be used if methane is detected in concentrations at or above 1.0 percent methane. When 1.0 percent or more of methane is detected while the equipment is being used, the equipment shall be de-energized immediately and withdrawn out of the subject area to fresh air. Batteries shall not be removed to de-energize equipment because removing the battery exposes battery contacts to accidental short-circuiting. All requirements of
30 CFR 75.323
must be met before returning the equipment to the subject area.
(f) For additional safety, prior to taking the equipment to the subject area or energizing the equipment in the subject area, a certified person (as set forth by
30 CFR 75.100
) shall conduct a visual examination of the location where the equipment will be used for:
(1) Evidence that the subject area appears to be sufficiently rock-dusted; and
(2) The presence of accumulated combustible material including float coal dust in suspension.
If the rock-dusting appears insufficient, or the presence of float coal dust is observed in suspension, the equipment may not be energized until sufficient rock dust has been applied and/or the accumulations of combustible materials including float coal dust in suspension have been cleaned-up or removed.
(g) All hand-held methane detectors shall be MSHA-approved and maintained in permissible and proper operating condition as set forth by
30 CFR 75.320
. Measurement devices shall be calibrated or bump tested before each shift to verify proper operation. In addition, all methane detectors must provide visual and audible warnings when methane is detected at and above 1.0 percent.
(h) Prior to energizing the equipment in the subject area, methane tests must be made at least 12 inches from the roof, face, ribs and floor, as set forth in
30 CFR 75.323(a)
.
(i) The subject area must be examined, as set forth by
30 CFR 75.360
, prior to using the equipment. If the area has not been examined, a supplemental examination, as set forth by
30 CFR 75.361
, must be performed before any non-certified person enters the area.
(j) Before using the equipment in the subject area, the air quantity on the section, for that shift, is at least the minimum quantity required by the mine's approved ventilation plan. A qualified person shall continuously monitor for methane immediately before and during the use of the equipment in the subject area. The qualified person shall have a hand-held methane detector and be strategically positioned in locations with the greatest potential to detect hazardous gas in the area where the equipment is being used. A qualified person shall also remain with the equipment while the equipment is used in the subject area.
(k) Batteries contained in the equipment must be “changed out” in intake air, out of the subject area. No work shall be performed on any testing and diagnostic equipment listed in the PDO granted by MSHA while such equipment is in the subject area.
(
printed page 73802)
Replacement batteries for the equipment shall not be brought in the subject area. On each entry into the mine, all batteries for the equipment must be fully charged and protected (
i.e.,
carried only in the compartment provided for a spare battery in the equipment or the equipment carrying case). Batteries for the equipment listed within the PDO granted by MSHA shall not be charged underground. The following maintenance and use conditions shall apply to equipment containing lithium-type batteries:
(1) The battery pack must not be disassembled or modified by anyone other than permitted by the manufacturer of the equipment;
(2) The battery pack must only be charged using the original equipment manufacturer's recommended charger on the surface of the mine;
(3) The battery must not be exposed to water or allowed to get wet. This does not preclude incidental exposure of sealed battery packs;
(4) The battery must not be placed in direct sunlight or used or stored near a source of heat; and
(5) The battery must not be used at the end of its life cycle (
e.g.,
when there is a performance decrease of greater than 20% in battery operated equipment). The battery must be disposed of properly.
(l) Personnel engaged in the use of the equipment shall be properly qualified, as specified in
30 CFR 75.153
, and trained in accordance with the manufacturers' recommended safe use procedures and trained to recognize hazards associated with the use of the equipment where methane could be present.
(m) All qualified persons and miners affected shall receive specific training on the terms and conditions of the PDO granted by MSHA before using the equipment in subject areas. A record of any training on the PDO granted by MSHA shall be maintained and provided upon request by an Authorized Representative of the Secretary.
(n) The equipment used shall be no older than 10 years from date of manufacture or removed at the end of its service life as recommended by the manufacturer, whichever is shorter.
(o) The operator is responsible for ensuring that all persons, including contractors, are using the equipment in accordance with the PDO granted by MSHA. The conditions of use in this PDO granted by MSHA shall apply to all non-permissible electronic equipment used in the subject area, regardless of whether the equipment is used by an employee or by an independent contractor.
(p) The operator shall post the PDO granted by MSHA in unobstructed locations on mine bulletin boards and/or in other conspicuous places where notices to miners are ordinarily posted for a period of not less than 60 consecutive days.
(q) The subject equipment shall not be used when coal production is occurring on the section. All mining on the section shall cease prior to use of the equipment in the subject area. A positive means of preventing mobile equipment from tramming in the same entry or crosscut of the affected area shall be provided and addressed in the mine ventilation plan.
(r) Unless specifically mentioned herein, nothing in the PDO granted by MSHA changes or supersedes the requirements otherwise imposed by the Mine Act, other mandatory standards or regulations, or approved ventilation or other plans.
The miners at Oak Grove Mine are represented by the United Mine Workers of America (UMWA). The petition for modification was provided to UMWA representative, Blake Layton, on August 31, 2026.
In support of the petition, the petitioner submitted a product data sheet for the AMS 2140 Machinery Health Analyzer.
The petitioner asserts that the alternative method will at all times guarantee no less than the same measure of protection afforded the miners under
30 CFR 75.507-1(a)
.

Acting Director, Office of Standards, Regulations, and Variances.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Section 101(c) of the Federal Mine Safety and Health Act of 1977 and
Title 30 of the Code of Federal Regulations
(CFR) part 44 govern the application, processing, and disposition of petitions for modification.
I. Background
Section 101(c) of the Federal Mine Safety and Health Act of 1977 (Mine Act) allows the mine operator or representative of miners to file a petition to modify the application of any mandatory safety standard to a coal or other mine if the Secretary of Labor determines that:
1. An alternative method of achieving the result of such standard exists which will at all times guarantee no less than the same measure of protection afforded the miners of such mine by such standard; or
2. The application of such standard to such mine will result in a diminution of safety to the miners in such mine.
In addition, sections 44.10 and 44.11 of 30 CFR establish the requirements for filing petitions for modification.
II. Petition for Modification
Docket Number:
M-2026-022-C.
Petitioner:
Ramaco Resources Land Holdings, LLC, 499 Fork Ridge Road, Raven, Virginia, 24639.
Mine:
Tiller No. 1, MSHA ID No. 44-06804, located in Tazewell County, Virginia.
Regulation Affected:
30 CFR 75.301
, Air Course.
Modification Request:
The petitioner requests a modification of the existing standard,
30 CFR 75.301
to permit the
(
printed page 73803)
return air course to enter a ventilation tube at the bottom of the existing slope and be coursed to the surface.
The petitioner states that:
(a) The petitioner seeks modification of
30 CFR 75
. 301 as it pertains to the definition of an air course.
(b) That standard
30 CFR 75.301
provides in relevant part:
Air Course.
An entry or a set of entries separated from other entries by stoppings, overcasts, other ventilation control devices, or by solid blocks of coal or rock so that any mixing of air currents between each is limited to leakage.
(c) Tiller No. 1 Mine is a Slope/Shaft Underground Coal Mine with existing developments in the Tiller Coal Seam.
(d) The underground mine is currently idle with no underground ventilation. The petitioner intends to restart the mine in the future to conduct additional mining in the Tiller Seam as well as to use the existing developed works to access the underlying Castle Seam.
(e) In July 2026, the petitioner conducted a re-entry and exploration of the mine to determine the feasibility and actions needed to rehabilitate the mine to resume operation. During the exploration it was determined the set of entries previously used to direct return air to the surface (Mud Lick Mains) are no longer accessible due to mine roof deterioration and collapses. The loss of these entries has resulted in the Tiller No 1 Mine having only two usable openings to the surface; the Belt Neutral Slope and the Intake Shaft (Blowing Mine Fan).
(f) Currently, to comply with
30 CFR 75.301
, the petitioner must have at least three usable openings to the surface to facilitate
(1) an Intake Air Course/Primary Escapeway,
(2) Neutral Air Course Belt/Alternate Escapeway, and
(3) Return Air course.
(g) The petitioner seeks an alternative method to the mandatory safety standard, asserting it will at all times guarantee no less than the same measure of protection afforded the miners under the mandatory standard.
The petitioner proposes the following alternative method:
(a) An isolated return air course using a separate entry or set of entries, separated from other air courses using traditionally accepted ventilation controls, will be maintained in the underground areas of the mine from the bottom of the Slope to all areas within the mine where a return air course is needed.
(b) At the bottom of the existing slope the return air course will enter a ventilation tube and be coursed to the surface. The ventilation tube will be continuous from the bottom of the slope to the surface where it will be connected to an exhausting mine fan installation.
(c) The ventilation tube will have a minimum outside diameter of 42″ and will be constructed of MSHA Approved materials.
(d) The ventilation tube will be attached to the mine roof using non-combustible chains, cables or straps as deemed appropriate, or the tubing will be placed on the mine floor and secured and protected from damage.
(e) The entry where the tubing will be placed will be the belt/neutral slope entry (Alternate Escapeway). This entry will be ventilated from the main blowing mine fan with air traveling outby to the surface. This entry will be examined each shift as required by
30 CFR 75.360
. Examinations will include ensuring the tubing is properly maintained.
(f) The slope where the Tubing Return Air Course will share the same entry as the Belt Neutral Air Course is 1,030′ in length.
(g) The tubing will be connected to a mine fan installation on the surface installed in compliance with all applicable requirements of
30 CFR 75.310-312
. The fan to be used will be a 929 RBB Centrifugal exhauster capable of operating at 900 RPM producing up to 30 IN/WG of vacuum.
(h) The current Main Mine Fan (Blowing) is a Joy Axivene, 9 foot Direct Drive Centrifugal Fan.
(i) The current Main Mine Fan (Blowing) and the Return Mine Fan (Exhausting) will operate at all times. The Main Mine Fan will be adjusted to introduce enough air into the mine to supply the working areas of the mine ventilated by the Exhaust Mine Fan (Ventilation Tube Split) as well as to ventilate areas to be coursed to the Belt/Neutral Air Course. This will ensure constant air flow in all areas without any unplanned reversals.
(j) The air entering the mine from the Main Mine Fan (Blowing) will always be 40% or more greater than the air exiting the mine through the exhausting ventilation tube. The anticipated air flow through the Exhausting Mine Fan and tubing will be 60,000 CFM. The Main Mine Fan (Blowing) will be adjusted to deliver 84,000 CFM or more into the mine.
(k) Examinations of the return air courses, per compliance with
30 CFR 75.364
, will be accomplished by a certified examiner traveling at least one entry of the return air course in its entirety. These examinations will end when the return air enters the exhaust ventilation tubing near the bottom of the slope.
(l) The examination of the portion of the return air being course through the tubing will consist of examining the outside perimeter of the tube along the 1,030′ entirety. This examination will include all connectors and means used to secure the tubing into place. Ports will be provided for inserting a Pitot Tube for measuring the air flow inside the ventilation tubing. A minimum of three ports will be installed as follows:
(1) within 50′ of the beginning of the tube near the slope bottom,
(2) at the approximate mid-point (500′ from the bottom of the slope), and
(3) within 50′ of the fan installation on the surface. Obtaining these three readings will allow the examiner to quantify the air flow to determine the amount of leakage if any. Due to the pressure differential of the exhaust system, any leakage would travel from the neutral air course into the tubing and would therefore pose no hazard of return air short circuiting into the neutral. These examinations of the tube conducted weekly will be in addition to the examinations which will be conducted each shift in accordance with
30 CFR 75.360
as detailed in item (f).
(m) The petitioner intends to develop new air shafts once the mine reaches the Castle Seam, at which time this alternative Return Air Course will no longer be needed. The petitioner anticipates completion of the new air shafts within 9 to 12 months after the slope construction begins.
The miners at Ramaco Resources Land Holdings, LLC are not represented by a labor organization and this petition is posted on the mine bulletin board as September 8, 2026. The petitioner asserts that the alternative method will guarantee no less than the same measure of protection afforded the miners under the mandatory standard. In support of the proposed alternative method, the petitioner has also submitted a mine map depicting the location of the mine fans, ventilation tubing, ventilation controls and the air courses.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Notice of Final Decision
OSHA hereby gives notice of the expansion of the scope of recognition for TUV SUD America Inc. (TUVAM). TUVAM's expansion covers the addition of five test standards to the NRTL scope of recognition.
OSHA recognition of a NRTL signifies that the organization meets the requirements specified in
29 CFR 1910.7
. Recognition is an acknowledgment that the organization can perform independent safety testing and certification of the specific products covered within its scope of recognition. Each NRTL's scope of recognition includes (1) the type of products the NRTL may test, with each type specified by its applicable test standard; and (2) the recognized site(s) that has/have the technical capability to perform the product-testing and product-certification activities for test standards within the NRTL's scope. Recognition is not a delegation or grant of government authority; however, recognition enables employers to use products approved by the NRTL to meet OSHA standards that require product testing and certification.
The agency processes an application by a NRTL for initial recognition and for an expansion or renewal of this recognition, following requirements in Appendix A,
29 CFR 1910.7
. This appendix requires that the agency publish two notices in the
Federal Register
in processing an application. In the first notice, OSHA announces the application and provides its preliminary finding. In the second notice, the agency provides the final decision on the application. These notices set forth the NRTL's scope of recognition or modifications of that scope. OSHA maintains an informational web page for each NRTL, including TUVAM, which details the NRTL's scope of recognition. These pages are available from the OSHA website at:
https://www.osha.gov/​nationally-recognized-testing-laboratory-program
.
TUVAM submitted an application to OSHA for expansion of the NRTL scope of recognition on December 17, 2024 (OSHA-2007-0043-0073), requesting the expansion of the NRTL scope of recognition to include seven additional test standards. This application was revised on February 6, 2026 (OSHA-2007-0043-0072) to remove two standards from the original request. This expansion covers the remaining five standards. OSHA did not perform any on-site reviews with respect to this application.
OSHA published the preliminary notice announcing TUVAM's expansion application in the
Federal Register
on August 21, 2026 (
91 FR 54392
). The agency requested comments by September 8, 2026; however, no comments were received in response to this notice.
To review copies of all public documents pertaining to TUVAM's application, go to
http://www.regulations.gov
or contact the Docket Office, Occupational Safety and Health Administration, U.S. Department of Labor at (202) 693-2350. Docket No. OSHA-2007-0043 contains all materials in the record concerning TUVAM's recognition. All submissions, including copyrighted material, are available for inspection through the OSHA Docket Office. Contact the OSHA Docket Office at (202) 693-2350 for assistance in locating docket submissions.
II. Final Decision and Order
OSHA staff examined TUVAM's expansion application and examined other pertinent information. Based on its review of this evidence, OSHA finds that TUVAM meets the requirements of
29 CFR 1910.7
for expansion of its recognition, subject to the limitations and conditions listed in this notice. OSHA, therefore, is proceeding with this final notice to grant TUVAM's expanded scope of recognition. OSHA limits the expansion of TUVAM's recognition to include the testing and certification of products for demonstration of conformance to the test standards shown below in Table 1.
Table 1—List of Appropriate Test Standards for Inclusion in TUVAM's NRTL Scope of Recognition
Test standard

UL 1004-6 *

UL 1004-8 *
Inverter Duty Motors.
UL 61010-2-011 *

UL 61010-2-012 *
Electrical Equipment for Measurement, Control and Laboratory Use—Part 2-012: Particular Requirements for Climatic and Environmental Testing and Other Temperature Conditioning Equipment.
* Represents standard that OSHA is adding to the NRTL Program's List of Appropriate Test Standards.
OSHA's recognition of any NRTL for a particular test standard is limited to equipment or materials for which OSHA standards require third-party testing and certification before using them in the workplace. Consequently, if a test standard also covers any products for which OSHA does not require such testing and certification, a NRTL's scope of recognition does not include these products.
In this notice, OSHA also announces the final decision to add four new test standards to the NRTL Program's List of Appropriate Test Standards. Table 2 below lists the test standards that are new to the NRTL Program. OSHA has determined that these test standards are appropriate test standards and will add them to the NRTL Program's List of Appropriate Test Standards.

The American National Standards Institute (ANSI) may approve the test standards listed above as American National Standards. However, for convenience, OSHA may use the designation of the standards-developing organization for the standard as opposed to the ANSI designation. Under the NRTL Program's policy (see OSHA Instruction CPL 01-00-004, Chapter 2, Section VIII), any NRTL recognized for a particular test standard may use either the proprietary version of the test standard or the ANSI version of that standard. Contact ANSI to determine whether a test standard is currently ANSI-approved.
A. Conditions
Recognition is contingent on continued compliance with
29 CFR 1910.7
, including but not limited to, abiding by the following conditions of recognition:
1. TUVAM must inform OSHA as soon as possible, in writing, of any change of ownership, facilities, or key personnel, and of any major change in its operations as a NRTL, and provide details of the change(s);
2. TUVAM must meet all the terms of its recognition and comply with all OSHA policies pertaining to this recognition; and
3. TUVAM must continue to meet the requirements for recognition, including all previously published conditions on TUVAM's scope of recognition, in all areas for which it has recognition.
Pursuant to the authority in
29 CFR 1910.7
, OSHA hereby expands the scope of recognition of TUVAM as a NRTL, subject to the limitations and conditions specified above. Additionally, OSHA will add four standards to the NRTL Program's List of Appropriate Test Standards.

AGENCY:
Mine Safety and Health Administration, Labor.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
This notice is a summary of a petition for modification submitted to the Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) by Crimson Oak Grove Resources, LLC.
DATES:
All comments on the petition must be received by MSHA's Office of Standards, Regulations, and Variances on or before December 17, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments and informational materials, identified by Docket No. MSHA-2026-1025, electronically at the Federal eRulemaking Portal,
https://www.regulations.gov
.
Follow the online instructions for making electronic submissions. You should not include personal or proprietary information that you do not wish to disclose publicly. If you mark parts of a comment as “business confidential” information, MSHA will not post those parts of the comment. Otherwise, MSHA will post all comments without change, including any personal information provided. MSHA cautions against submitting personal information.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Corliss A. Josephs-Conway, Acting Director, Office of Standards, Regulations, and Variances at 202-693-9440 (voice);
Petitionsformodification@dol.gov
(email); or 202-693-9441 (fax). These are not toll-free numbers.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Section 101(c) of the Federal Mine Safety and Health Act of 1977 and
Title 30 of the Code of Federal Regulations
(CFR) part 44 govern the application, processing, and disposition of petitions for modification.
I. Background
Section 101(c) of the Federal Mine Safety and Health Act of 1977 (Mine Act) allows the mine operator or representative of miners to file a petition to modify the application of any mandatory safety standard to a coal or other mine if the Secretary of Labor determines that:
1. An alternative method of achieving the result of such standard exists which will at all times guarantee no less than the same measure of protection afforded the miners of such mine by such standard; or
2. The application of such standard to such mine will result in a diminution of safety to the miners in such mine.
In addition,
30 CFR 44.10
and
30 CFR 44.11
establish the requirements for filing petitions for modification.
II. Petition for Modification
Docket Number:
M-2026-025-C.
Petitioner:
Crimson Oak Grove Resources, LLC, 8800 Oak Grove Mine Road, Adger, AL 35006.
Mine:
Oak Grove Mine, MSHA ID No. 01-00851, located in Jefferson County, AL.
Regulation Affected:
30 CFR 75.500(d)
, Permissible electric equipment.
Modification Request:
The petitioner requests modification of the application of
30 CFR 75.500(d)
to permit the use of non-permissible electronic testing or diagnostic equipment located inby the last crosscut (subject area).
The petitioner states that:
(a) The equipment allowed under the Proposed Decision and Order (PDO) granted by MSHA (low voltage or battery-powered non-permissible electronic testing and diagnostic equipment) shall be limited to: AMS 2140 Machinery Health Analyzer; laptop computers; oscilloscopes; insulation testers (meggers); signal analyzer devices; ultrasonic measuring devices; electronic component testers; and electronic tachometers for testing or troubleshooting mining equipment. Fault detectors are not allowed in the subject area.
(b) Where commercially available, the operator must use equipment that meets IEC 60079-11 or the ANSI/UL 60079-11 for two-fault IS (marked ia), one-fault IS (marked ib), or no-fault IS (marked ic) in that order of preference. The equipment must have an IP 66 rating or higher when available. When an IP 66 rating is not available, the highest IP rating available must be used. When equipment contains lithium batteries, the equipment must meet lithium battery safety standard UL1642 or IEC 62133. All other equipment in the subject area must be permissible.
(c) A record for this equipment shall be maintained on mine property either in a secure book or electronically in a secure computer system not susceptible to alteration. The record will contain the date of manufacture and/or purchase of each particular piece of electronic testing and diagnostic equipment and include proof of compliance with any lithium battery safety standard. The original equipment manufacturers' user and maintenance manuals shall be followed and maintained on mine property. The record and manuals shall be made available to Authorized Representatives of the Secretary and miners at the mine.
(d) This equipment shall be used only:
(1) until MSHA-approved permissible electronic testing and diagnostic equipment is available;
(2) if mechanical equipment is not commercially available that can perform the work; or
(3) when the mining equipment being tested cannot be towed or moved under its own power to intake air, out of the subject area.
The petitioner proposes the following alternative method:
(a) The equipment to be used in the subject area shall be examined by a qualified person, as set forth in
30 CFR 75.153
, prior to taking the equipment underground to ensure the equipment is being maintained in a safe operating condition. At a minimum, the qualified person conducting the exam shall:
(1) Check the instrument for any physical damage and the integrity of the case;
(2) Remove the battery and inspect for corrosion;
(3) Inspect the contact points to ensure a secure connection to the battery;
(4) Reinsert the battery and power up and shut down to ensure proper connections;
(5) Check the battery compartment cover or battery attachment to ensure that it is securely fastened; and
(6) For equipment utilizing lithium type cells, ensure the lithium cells and/or pack are not damaged or swelled in size.
(b) The equipment shall be examined at least weekly by a qualified person as required by
30 CFR 75.512-2
and the exam results shall be recorded weekly in the equipment's record. Examination entries in the record may be expunged after one year.
(c) The equipment shall be serviced according to the manufacturers' recommendations. Dates of service shall be recorded and include a description of the work performed.
(d) The equipment shall not be put into service until MSHA has initially inspected the equipment and determined it is in compliance with all the terms and conditions of the PDO granted by MSHA. The equipment shall be tested for potential adverse effects of Radio Frequency Interference (RFI) and Electromagnetic Interference (EMI) for any disturbances with performance of remote control transmitters, atmospheric monitoring systems, fire sensors, machine-mounted methane monitors, hand-held detectors, miner's
(
printed page 73805)
cap lamps, tracking and communication systems, proximity detection systems, etc. A record of the test performed, similar to those conducted by NIOSH, shall be maintained on mine property for the service life of the equipment and made available to MSHA upon request. MSHA should be notified at least 5 working days before such testing will be performed.
(e) The equipment shall not be used if methane is detected in concentrations at or above 1.0 percent methane. When 1.0 percent or more of methane is detected while the equipment is being used, the equipment shall be de-energized immediately and withdrawn out of the subject area to fresh air. Batteries shall not be removed to de-energize equipment because removing the battery exposes battery contacts to accidental short-circuiting. All requirements of
30 CFR 75.323
must be met before returning the equipment to the subject area.
(f) For additional safety, prior to taking the equipment to the subject area or energizing the equipment in the subject area, a certified person (as set forth by
30 CFR 75.100
) shall conduct a visual examination of the location where the equipment will be used for:
(1) Evidence that the subject area appears to be sufficiently rock-dusted; and
(2) The presence of accumulated combustible material including float coal dust in suspension.
If the rock-dusting appears insufficient, or the presence of float coal dust is observed in suspension, the equipment may not be energized until sufficient rock dust has been applied and/or the accumulations of combustible materials including float coal dust in suspension have been cleaned-up or removed.
(g) All hand-held methane detectors shall be MSHA-approved and maintained in permissible and proper operating condition as set forth by
30 CFR 75.320
. Measurement devices shall be calibrated or bump tested before each shift to verify proper operation. In addition, all methane detectors must provide visual and audible warnings when methane is detected at and above 1.0 percent.
(h) Prior to energizing the equipment in the subject area, methane tests must be made at least 12 inches from the roof, face, ribs and floor, as set forth in
30 CFR 75.323(a)
.
(i) The subject area must be examined, as set forth by
30 CFR 75.360
, prior to using the equipment. If the area has not been examined, a supplemental examination, as set forth by
30 CFR 75.361
, must be performed before any non-certified person enters the area.
(j) Before using the equipment in the subject area, the air quantity on the section, for that shift, is at least the minimum quantity required by the mine's approved ventilation plan. A qualified person shall continuously monitor for methane immediately before and during the use of the equipment in the subject area. The qualified person shall have a hand-held methane detector and be strategically positioned in locations with the greatest potential to detect hazardous gas in the area where the equipment is being used. A qualified person shall also remain with the equipment while the equipment is used in the subject area.
(k) Batteries contained in the equipment must be “changed out” in intake air, out of the subject area. No work shall be performed on any testing and diagnostic equipment listed in the PDO granted by MSHA while such equipment is in the subject area. Replacement batteries for the equipment shall not be brought in the subject area. On each entry into the mine, all batteries for the equipment must be fully charged and protected (
i.e.,
carried only in the compartment provided for a spare battery in the equipment or the equipment carrying case). Batteries for the equipment listed within the PDO granted by MSHA shall not be charged underground. The following maintenance and use conditions shall apply to equipment containing lithium-type batteries:
(1) The battery pack must not be disassembled or modified by anyone other than permitted by the manufacturer of the equipment;
(2) The battery pack must only be charged using the original equipment manufacturer's recommended charger on the surface of the mine;
(3) The battery must not be exposed to water or allowed to get wet. This does not preclude incidental exposure of sealed battery packs;
(4) The battery must not be placed in direct sunlight or used or stored near a source of heat; and
(5) The battery must not be used at the end of its life cycle (
e.g.,
when there is a performance decrease of greater than 20% in battery operated equipment). The battery must be disposed of properly.
(l) Personnel engaged in the use of the equipment shall be properly qualified, as specified in
30 CFR 75.153
, and trained in accordance with the manufacturers' recommended safe use procedures and trained to recognize hazards associated with the use of the equipment where methane could be present.
(m) All qualified persons and miners affected shall receive specific training on the terms and conditions of the PDO granted by MSHA before using the equipment in subject areas. A record of any training on the PDO granted by MSHA shall be maintained and provided upon request by an Authorized Representative of the Secretary.
(n) The equipment used shall be no older than 10 years from date of manufacture or removed at the end of its service life as recommended by the manufacturer, whichever is shorter.
(o) The operator is responsible for ensuring that all persons, including contractors, are using the equipment in accordance with the PDO granted by MSHA. The conditions of use in this PDO granted by MSHA shall apply to all non-permissible electronic equipment used in the subject area, regardless of whether the equipment is used by an employee or by an independent contractor.
(p) The operator shall post the PDO granted by MSHA in unobstructed locations on mine bulletin boards and/or in other conspicuous places where notices to miners are ordinarily posted for a period of not less than 60 consecutive days.
(q) The subject equipment shall not be used when coal production is occurring on the section. All mining on the section shall cease prior to use of the equipment in the subject area. A positive means of preventing mobile equipment from tramming in the same entry or crosscut of the affected area shall be provided and addressed in the mine ventilation plan.
(r) Unless specifically mentioned herein, nothing in the PDO granted by MSHA changes or supersedes the requirements otherwise imposed by the Mine Act, other mandatory standards or regulations, or approved ventilation or other plans.
The miners at Oak Grove Mine are represented by the United Mine Workers of America (UMWA). The petition for modification was provided to UMWA representative, Blake Layton, on August 31, 2026.
In support of the petition, the petitioner submitted a product data sheet for the AMS 2140 Machinery Health Analyzer.
The petitioner asserts that the alternative method will at all times guarantee no less than the same measure
(
printed page 73806)
of protection afforded the miners under
30 CFR 75.500(d)
.

Acting Director, Office of Standards, Regulations, and Variances.

In accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has submitted the information collection request titled “Survey to Promote Resources and Opportunities for aUtistic Teens and young adults (SPROUT)” to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review and approval. CDC previously published a “Proposed Data Collection Submitted for Public Comment and Recommendations” notice on January 27, 2026, to obtain comments from the public and affected agencies. CDC received two related to the previous notice. This notice serves to allow an additional 30 days for public and affected agency comments.
CDC will accept all comments for this proposed information collection project. The Office of Management and Budget is particularly interested in comments that:
(a) Evaluate whether the proposed collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the agency, including whether the information will have practical utility;
(b) Evaluate the accuracy of the agencies estimate of the burden of the proposed collection of information, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used;
(c) Enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected;
(d) Minimize the burden of the collection of information on those who are to respond, including, through the use of appropriate automated, electronic, mechanical, or other technological collection techniques or other forms of information technology,
e.g.,
permitting electronic submission of responses; and
(e) Assess information collection costs.
To request additional information on the proposed project or to obtain a copy of the information collection plan and instruments, call (404) 639-7570. Comments and recommendations for the proposed information collection should be sent within 30 days of publication of this notice to
www.reginfo.gov/​public/​do/​PRAMain
.
Find this particular information collection by selecting “Currently under 30-day Review—Open for Public Comments” or by using the search function. Direct written comments and/or suggestions regarding the items contained in this notice to the Attention: CDC Desk Officer, Office of Management and Budget, 725 17th Street NW, Washington, DC 20503 or by fax to (202) 395-5806. Provide written comments within 30 days of notice publication.
Proposed Project
Survey to Promote Resources and Opportunities for aUtistic Teens and Young Adults (SPROUT)—New—National Center on Birth Defects and Developmental Disabilities (NCBDDD), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
Background and Brief Description
In 2022, an estimated one in 31 children eight years of age living in 16 communities across the United States had autism, a developmental disability that can cause significant social, communication, and behavior challenges. The Study to Explore Early Development (SEED) was implemented in 2006 to learn more about autism and other developmental disabilities in children 2-5-years of age. Extensive data, from interviews, in-person evaluations, and other sources were collected across three phases (SEED 1, 2, and 3) in eight geographic areas (California, Colorado, Georgia, Maryland, Missouri, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin). SEED 1-3 collected data on 9,808 preschool-aged children with autism, another developmental delay or disability, or from the general population. To date, almost 100 analyses of SEED 1-3 data have been published in peer-reviewed journals.
To better understand transition and lifespan issues affecting people with autism as they age, caregivers of children enrolled in SEED 1 (2006-2011) were eligible to participate in a pilot follow-up survey when their child was between 12-16 years of age (2018-2021; SEED Teen). An important outcome of SEED Teen was to demonstrate that longitudinal data collection from SEED participants is feasible (
i.e.,
contact was established with approximately 97% of eligible participants and, of those, 64% enrolled in SEED Teen). SEED Follow-Up was thus initiated in 2021 to survey the broader cohort of SEED 1-3 participants on adolescent and young adult health and well-being. SEED Follow-Up is currently ongoing until June 2026.
The federal government identified a need to improve efforts to better understand lifespan issues among people with autism in the Autism CARES Act of 2024 and a report to Congress in 2017. Despite this, a recent portfolio analysis from the Interagency Autism Coordinating Committee (IACC), indicated that lifespan issues continue to receive the least amount of autism funding from federal agencies. Both the SEED Teen and SEED Follow-Up surveys helped identify healthcare needs and experiences among adolescents with autism. However, gaps in understanding remain in how we can best support adolescents and young adults with autism and their families.
Draft chapters of the 2024 IACC Strategic Plan Update emphasize the
(
printed page 73756)
need for data on service and support needs and conditions that commonly co-occur with autism. On behalf of the IACC, the Office of National Autism Coordination (ONAC) released a Request for Public Comment on these topics from members of the autistic community. Some identified service and support needs were provider training, more benefits and insurance coverage, and help with system navigation. Some commonly reported co-occurring conditions were sensory and motor issues, anxiety disorder, sleep problems, attention deficits, hyperactivity, gastrointestinal issues, learning and memory issues, and suicidal ideation. Other topics identified as important to the autistic community are social, education, and vocational experiences and outcomes.
The current information collection request (ICR) is designed to conduct longitudinal follow-up surveys that offer unique information about autistic adolescents and young adults, thereby addressing the priorities established in the Autism CARES Act of 2024 and draft 2024 IACC Strategic Plan. Given the size of the original SEED birth cohorts and the wealth of baseline and follow-up information collected, additional surveys of participants can help address critical information gaps. Specifically, the information collected from the Survey to Promote Resources and Opportunities for aUtistic Teens and young adults (SPROUT) will allow us to better understand: (1) the healthcare utilization of, service and support needs of, and impact of co-occurring conditions on autistic people and their families; and (2) the educational, social, and/or vocational needs and experiences of autistic adolescents and young adults.
One survey will be administered to caregivers and another is a self-report survey administered to children, adolescents and young adults age 9-27. The survey version will be based on the child participant's age and ability to self-report on healthcare utilization, service and support needs, co-occurring conditions, and healthcare transition. CDC requests OMB approval for an estimated 1,867 annual burden hours. There are no costs to respondents other than their time to participate.
